China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.
Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”
China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.
Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.
Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.
“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”
It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.
After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.
Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.
India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.
No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has introduced a new scheme to expand UPI acceptance among small merchants. Under the new initiative, the payments body will offer incentives to banks for deploying QR codes and soundboxes to further drive transaction growth. The scheme will be funded through a portion of the merchant discount rate (MDR) earned by banks and other UPI ecosystem participants. In a circular dated November 11, NPCI announced the launch of the ‘UPI Vyapaar Saksham Scheme’, which aims to address the limited availability of digital payment acceptance infrastructure among small merchants, particularly in smaller cities and towns. The scheme will run for a period of three years from the implementation of UPI MDR, which is yet to be notified. The initiative will focus on merchants in Tier III to Tier VI cities, northeastern states, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. Small merchants covered under notified central government schemes, including PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma, will also be eligible. NPCI defines small merchants as businesses with an annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh in the preceding financial year. The fund will be created from MDR collections rather than a separate government allocation. Each issuing bank, acquiring bank, payer payment service provider (PSP) and UPI application provider participating in UPI will contribute 5% of its MDR share to the fund. The contribution will exclude MDR earned from categories that are not eligible for the scheme. The fund will be divided into three components, with the largest allocation going towards increasing transaction volumes among existing merchants. Under the first component, which accounts for 30% of the fund, acquiring banks will receive ₹300 for every physical QR code and ₹750 for every soundbox deployed at an eligible new small merchant. To qualify, a merchant will have to record at least 25 eligible transactions in any two months of a quarter, with a minimum transaction value of ₹5,000 per month. For context, the scheme defines eligible transactions as successfully settled UPI payments of up to ₹2,000 at small merchants. It excludes transactions that are subsequently reversed, refunded or cancelled, as well as artificial transactions created by splitting payments to remain below the ₹2,000 threshold. The second component will receive 50% of the fund and reward acquiring banks for growing UPI transaction volumes among existing and newly onboarded small merchants. Banks will need to demonstrate at least 5% QoQ growth in eligible transaction volumes to qualify for incentives. They will receive 0.03% of the aggregate value of eligible transactions, with merchants in the targeted geographies receiving an additional 50% incentive. The remaining 20% will be allocated towards incremental growth in targeted geographies. Under this component, acquiring banks will receive an incentive of 0.2% of the incremental value of eligible transactions compared with the previous quarter, over and above the incentive under the second component. NPCI has also set out ambitious deployment targets. The scheme is expected to facilitate 6 Lakh to 1 Cr new physical QR code deployments and 5 Lakh to 10 Lakh new soundbox installations annually. It also aims to drive 30% to 50% annual growth in transaction volumes among existing small merchants. UPI's MDR Transition This comes as the Centre is all set to re-introduce MDR on select “high-value” UPI transactions after nearly six years of a zero-MDR regime. In September 2026, the government notified amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, paving the way for MDR on select merchant transactions. Subsequently, NPCI introduced a framework under which person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract an MDR of 0.4%, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. Transactions of up to ₹2,000 and peer-to-peer (P2P) payments have been kept outside the MDR framework. Small merchants receiving up to ₹1 Lakh per month through UPI QR codes under the P2M-to-P2P merchant (P2PM) category were also exempted from MDR. The government said the move was intended to create a sustainable revenue stream for banks and payment companies while supporting the infrastructure required to operate UPI at scale. The MDR collected is distributed among ecosystem participants rather than retained by the government. The proposed MDR framework faced pushback from retailers, with a possible deferment of its rollout to January next year. Later, the imposition was pushed beyond Diwali. Four days after Diwali, NPCI is yet to come out with a date for the implementation for this. Whenever MDR comes into place, the new NPCI scheme would effectively channel a portion of the MDR revenue back into expanding UPI acceptance among this merchant segment. That said, NPCI will administer the fund, validate incentive claims and oversee settlements. Acquiring banks will submit claims quarterly, with NPCI required to process incentive payments within 30 days of claim submission, subject to validation. The scheme also mandates that acquiring banks report merchant locations, unique merchant identifiers and details of deployed QR codes and soundboxes to enable transaction-level monitoring. The underlying policy shift is significant: while the MDR framework creates a revenue stream for UPI ecosystem participants, the new scheme attempts to use a portion of that revenue to address the infrastructure gap that has kept digital payment acceptance concentrated among larger merchants and in urban markets.

A tiny, $900 wearable device being developed by an Indian billionaire entrepreneur and showcased by some of the country’s top sportspersons has sparked criticism from doctors who say its claims of tracking blood flow to the brain are exaggerated.
The Temple device is less than 1 inch (2.54 cm) wide and weighs under 2 grams (0.07 oz). It sticks to the side of the head between the forehead and the ear, or the temple area.
Promotional materials for the device, developed by Deepinder Goyal, say that its BrainFlow feature shows how well the brain is being supplied with blood in real time and its Entropy feature can detect how hard the body works to shed heat.
It can also measure thermal, immune, digestive, cognitive and emotional readings that help to transform how a person regulates their health, they say.
Priced at 85,000 rupees ($907), the device comes in six colours. India’s cricket captain Shubman Gill and Olympic medal-winning badminton player P.V. Sindhu have worn it.
Some well-known doctors in the country, however, are sceptical of the claims, saying the device’s capabilities are not backed by peer-reviewed research. In prime-time shows and on social media, they are calling for the device to come under the purview of medical regulators.
Prominent Indian hepatologist Cyriac Philips, known as “TheLiverDoc”, has been criticising the device on his X account with 328,000 followers, calling Temple “the biggest health scam”.
“People must be aware of wellness hacks such as wearables also, even though they are not marketed as health devices,” he told Reuters.
On one prime-time TV discussion, paediatrician and nephrologist Sanjeev Bagai called Temple a “gimmick”, saying it had “no formal approval or clearance”.
Goyal has hit back at the criticism from doctors, saying Temple is a “fitness tracker, and wellness device”, not a medical one.
Indian doctor Jason Philip wrote on X that assessing blood flow to the brain was not easy, and optical signals placed over the temple skin would only give data on the “superficial temporal artery” that supplies blood to the face and skin.
In a statement to Reuters, Temple said BrainFlow and Entropy were new metrics “with emerging science”, and that more research would follow, adding that some metrics would eventually need regulatory approval.
India’s health ministry did not respond to Reuters queries, and the government has so far not reacted to the public debate.
The debate on Temple comes as wearable makers overseas also face questions on when a fitness feature becomes a medical one.
Some Apple Watch features, such as hypertension notifications, have received US Food and Drug Administration clearance as software-based medical features. Last year, the US FDA warned Whoop, saying its wrist-worn fitness tracker’s blood-pressure feature looked like a medical one — a view the company disputes.
Goyal is best known for co-founding Eternal, which houses India’s biggest listed food-delivery company Zomato and has a market value of about $35 billion. The 43-year-old stepped down as chief executive of Eternal this year to focus on Temple.
Temple, which has professors from the University of Ottawa and Harvard on its advisory board, raised $54 million in February at a valuation of about $190 million.
Goyal said Temple has received orders from more than 62 countries since November 1.
On its website, Temple says it is also working on detecting conditions including snoring and jaw clenching.

Quick Answer
You can run AI models locally on Android and iPhone using Google AI Edge Gallery or PocketPal AI, and on Mac and Windows using LM Studio or Ollama. Simply install the app, download a compatible AI model, and start using it offline. Your data stays on your device, with no cloud access required after setup.
While many think AI is a bubble that is going to burst one day, it might be true, or it might not be at all. Only time will tell. But we should all accept that AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with our devices and do work.
For me, my life revolves around AI: I hand off some of my work to it and do things that once weren’t possible.
AI models are rapidly evolving. If you don’t know what an AI model is, it powers the apps and interfaces you interact with. For instance, the ChatGPT app uses GPT models, and the Claude app is powered by Claude models, which run behind the scenes.
While AI is fundamentally changing how we interact with devices and making work easier, handing your sensitive data to it has remained a major privacy concern.But thanks to rapid AI model development, many capable, powerful AI models enough to run locally on your device, without your data leaving your device
Companies like Google and Meta offer free AI models that can run locally on most consumer devices, including your mobile phone. Apps like Google’s AI Edge Gallery and PocketPal AI also make it easy to discover and run AI models locally without technical expertise.
If you have a capable computer with decent RAM, you can also run AI models locally to use them for writing your email, summarising PDFs, data analysis, coding, using their vision capabilities, and much more.
However, setting up an AI model locally involves downloading the app, choosing the model yourself, and understanding its capabilities first.
To help you out, I have created this detailed, comprehensive guide to set up and run local AI models on your device on Android, iPhone, Mac, or even on Windows.
I wrote this guide with beginners in mind, so every step is comprehensive and easy to follow. If you have questions, comment below. I am happy to help you. Most of these models can run locally on many consumer applications, but before that, don’t forget to check our prerequisites because that’s where your journey starts.
Table of Contents
Pre-Requirements To Run AI Models Locally on Device
Your device’s RAM determines whether it can run AI models.
Technically, a model loads into your RAM to run. As a general rule of thumb, a model needs about as much free RAM as its download size.
So, more RAM leaves room to run large AI models. A minimum of 6 GB of RAM is required to run decent, capable AI models locally on your device
Similarly, you need enough storage to download and store models locally. A model can generally range from 2 GB to 20 GB or even more, depending on its size and capabilities.
Finally, you need an internet connection and enough data to download the model so you can run it offline.
As I said before, these models can range from 2 GB to 20 GB. So it requires an internet connection to download the model and store it locally on your device.
Of course, Other minimum specifications, such as a capable Processor, Operating system, and platform, also matter but not as much as RAM does.
How to check how much RAM your device has
On Android:
Go to About Device to see how much RAM your smartphone has. To do that: Open Settings on your device, tap on the search bar at the top, and search for “About Device”. On some phones, scroll down and tap “About Device”. Look at the RAM specifications.
On some phones, you will see extra visible RAM after the plus sign, for example, 16GB + 12GB. However, only the first number is the real memory.
iPhone:
Apple generally doesn’t disclose the RAM used in iPhones. However, iPhone 15 Pro and newer devices generally have at least 8GB, while older iPhones have less than 6GB, which can run 1 billion to 2 billion models. You can check how much RAM your iPhone has from here.
Mac:
To check how much RAM on your MacBook: From the home screen, click on the Apple icon in the top left corner screen and tap on About This Mac. From here, you can check chip and memory options. Apple MacBooks running on Apple Silicon are especially good for running local AI models since the graphics chip shares all the memory.
Windows:
On Windows, you can go to Settings > System > About. From there, check the installed RAM, graphics card, and system type (x86 or ARM-based), which determines which applications you can download to run AI models locally.
Once your device meets the minimum RAM requirement, follow these steps to set it up to run AI models locally. Use the table of contents above to go to the device you want to set up. This guide covers Android, iPhone, Mac, and Windows.
How to Run AI Models Locally on Any Device
Android:
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on Android with Google AI Edge Gallery
You can run Google’s family of Open-weight AI models locally for free on your Android device using Google’s own AI Edge Gallery app (Free).
Gemma 4 is Google’s latest open-weight model. It comes in five model sizes. Gemma 4 E2B and Gemma 4 E4B are suitable for running on Android devices. 2B requires at least 8GB of RAM, and 4B requires at least 12GB of RAM.
Gemma 4 also supports vision capabilities, so it is not just text; you can also use it to understand images.
How to install and run the latest Google Gemma 4 models locally on your Android phone
Step 1: Download Google AI Edge Gallery from the Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI Chat.
Step 3: Under the recommended models, tap Download below. To download the model you want. Gemma 4 E2B is 2.6 GB and best for starters, while Gemma 4 E4B is 3.7 GB and smarter, but your phone needs at least 8 GB of RAM to run it locally.
Step 3: Once the model is downloaded, tap Try it.
Step 4: Type your prompt in the Type prompt box and tap the send button.
Step 5: Like the other AI apps, the model replies to your prompt. You can also see how fast the model runs, measured in tokens per second, and how much RAM it uses. On my Android phone, the Gemma 4 E2B model ran at about 30 tokens per second, and my model comes with 16 GB of RAM.
Method 2: Run any open model on Android with PocketPal AI
PocketPal is a popular free and open-source app for running AI models locally on Android.
Unlike Google’s AI Edge Gallery, it supports a wide variety of third-party models, including Google’s Gemma, Meta’s Llama, Microsoft’s Phi, Qwen, and more. It also supports GGUF models, including compressed versions.
How do I use the PocketPal app to run AI models locally on my device?
Step 1: Download and install the PocketPal app from the Google Play Store. Here is the direct download link.
Step 2: Open the app and, during onboarding, tap Download Model.
Step 3: Pick any available model to download and tap Download,
or tap the plus option to find more. To get a new model, tap the plus icon, select Hugging Face, then tap Choose and add from Hugging Face.
Step 4: From here, you can search for any model. In this case, I searched for the Qwen3 1.7B parameter model and tapped the download icon to download it locally.
Step 5: Once done, open the Models tab and select the model to load it. Now go to the chat interface and enter the prompt, and the model uses the model that you have loaded, in this case, the Qwen3 1.7 billion parameter model, to answer your queries. You can also see how much time it takes to run this model on your device.
iPhone
Method 1: Run Gemma 4 on iPhone with Google AI Edge Gallery
Google’s AI Edge Gallery is also available on iPhone and supports the latest Gemma 4 family of open-weight models, similar to Android. You can download and use E2B (around 2.6 GB) and the E4B model (around 3.7 GB).
Apple doesn’t disclose the RAM used on iPhones. However, the latest iPhone models, including the iPhone 15 Pro and later, support up to 8 GB of RAM, which can run these models faster and more reliably. However, older iPhones may struggle with slow responses, battery drain, and overheating, so keep that in mind.
Step 1: Download the Google AI Edge Gallery app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app and tap on AI chat
Step 3: Now download the compatible AI model. In this case, I’m downloading Gemma 4 E2B, which is about 2.59 GB. Click on the download icon under the model.
Step 4: Wait for the model to download, then tap Try It, enter the prompt, and wait for a reply. If you want to use the vision capabilities, tap on the plus icon and upload an image
Method 2: Run open models on iPhone with PocketPal AI
Similar to Google’s AI Edge Gallery app, the PocketPal app is also available on iPhone. It also gives access to some of the popular Hugging Face model library and other third-party models, including models from Meta, Cohere, and more. It also supports Google Gemma 4 models.
Step 1: Install the PocketPal AI app on your iPhone. Here is the link.
Step 2: Open the app, tap Download Model, select a model, and tap Download. In this case, I am downloading the Qwen3 1.7B model.
Step 3: Once downloaded, tap the Load option at the top, enter the prompt, and wait for the reply
Mac
Method 1: Run AI models on a Mac with LM Studio
You can use LM Studio on Mac to run AI models locally.
It supports a wide range of models, including models from Google Gemma, Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, and more. Like the mobile app, you can install LM Studio on your Mac, download a model, and start chatting. It also supports GGUF and Apple-optimized MLX models.
Depending on the model, you can have text conversations, image analysis, and more. You can also use it as a local API for other apps.
However, LM Studio is only available on Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or later). Intel Macs are not supported.
How to install and run AI models locally using LM Studio on Mac
Step 1: First, go to lmstudio.ai/download and download the LM Studio app for Mac. Select the compatible version and drag and drop LM Studio into Applications to install it.
Step 2: Open LM Studio on the Mac, click on the model search in the sidebar, and search for the model; for example, in this case, I searched for the Gemma 4 E4B model
Step 3: You can also pick a different model, select it, and click Download. A likely fit badge here means that it is suitable to run locally on your Mac using your Mac’s available memory. Once the model is downloaded, tap on Use in the new chat instead.
Step 4: On the home screen, click Load Model in the dialog and select the model. You can also raise the context length here if you are planning for long conversations.
Step 5: Now enter the prompt and press Enter. The model returns with an option. You can also click the model server in the sidebar and turn on the status to use the model for other apps via an OpenAI-compatible API at http://localhost:1234.
Method 2: Run AI models on a Mac with Ollama
You can also run AI models on your Mac using Ollama. It is a free, lightweight tool by Meta that lets you run local AI models in the terminal with one command. It also works with many local apps that support local AI.
Step 1: To run Ollama locally on your device, go to ollama.com/download and click on the Download manually option. You can also directly paste the command into the terminal if you are a developer.
Step 2: Next, open the Ollama.dmg, drag it into Applications, and open it
Step 3: On the onboarding screen, while setting up an account, Ollama asks you to sign up for an account; however, you can tap on No thanks, I will use Ollama locally’
Step 4: Next, to run ollama run llama3, copy the ollama run llama3 command, open Terminal, and paste it. Wait for the model to download completely. Ollama can run Qwen3 4B parameters and other models. In this case, I am going to run the Ollama run Qwen3 4B model. So, wait for the model to download completely.
Step 5: Finally, you can start using the Ollama model right there. You can enter the prompt directly, and it will reply in the same terminal.
Windows
Method 1: Run AI models on Windows with LM Studio
You can use the same LM Studio on Windows as well to run AI models locally on your device
Step 1: Download and install LM Studio for Windows. Here is the download page link.
Step 2: Open the LM Studio app and, in the left sidebar, tap Model Search and search for the model you want to run locally. In this case, Iam using Qwen3 1.7 billion parameters; on the model details page, click the download option.
Step 3: Wait for it to download, and once it has downloaded, tap on Use in new chat
Step 4: Now, on the home screen, in the model box, select the downloaded model. You can tap on the model to select and enable it, then enter the prompt and press enter.
Method 2: Run AI models on Windows with Ollama
Ollama is also available on Mac. It supports NVIDIA and AMD graphics cards, as well as the latest ARM-based Snapdragon PCs. You can download models and use them directly from the terminal. Here is how.
Step 1: First, download Ollama on Windows. Go to ollama.com/download/windows and click Manual download. If you are a developer, you can install it directly in PowerShell using the PowerShell command.
Step 2: Now install the Ollama app on Windows. While setting up, click Continue, and then tap on No thanks, I will use Ollama locally, so you can skip creating an account.
Step 3: Next, copy the command shown in the app, open Terminal, and run this command: ollama run qwen3:1.7b, and press Enter. It downloads the model. Wait for the download to complete.
Step 4: Now enter your question and press Enter.
This is how you can set up and run AI models locally on Android, iPhone, Windows, and Mac. Choosing the right model is important to get high-quality output. Bigger models don’t always mean better outputs, as their capabilities can vary. Our guide to the best AI models to run locally should help you choose the right model for your needs. If you have any issues setting them up, feel free to comment below, and I’ll be happy to help.

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

దీపావళి సందర్భంగా పంజాబ్ నేషనల్ బ్యాంకు, ఎయిర్టెల్ వంటి సంస్థలు వినియోగదారులకు ₹2000 నగదును కానుకగా ఇస్తున్నాయని సోషల్ మీడియాలో కొన్ని పోస్టులు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. ఈ నగదును పొందేందుకు, పోస్టులో ఉన్న లింకును క్లిక్ చేయాలంటూ అందులో పేర్కొనబడింది. దీనిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: దీపావళి కానుకగా పంజాబ్ నేషనల్ బ్యాంకు, ఎయిర్టెల్ సంస్థలు ₹2000 నగదును ప్రజలకు ఇస్తున్నాయి.
ఫాక్ట్: పంజాబ్ నేషనల్ బ్యాంకు, ఎయిర్టెల్ సంస్థలు అధికారికంగా ఇలాంటి ఆఫర్లు ఏవీ ప్రకటించలేదు.ఇవి కేవలం ప్రజల వ్యక్తిగత వివరాలను, డబ్బులను దొంగిలించడానికి సైబర్ నేరగాళ్లు సృష్టించిన నకిలీ (ఫిషింగ్) వెబ్సైట్లు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, పంజాబ్ నేషనల్ బ్యాంకు, ఎయిర్టెల్ సంస్థలు ఇటువంటి ఆఫర్ ఏమైనా ప్రకటించారా అని వెతకగా, వారి అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్లు, సోషల్ మీడియా ఖాతాల్లో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఎక్కడా కూడా వినియోగదారులకు దీపావళి కానుకగా డబ్బులు ఇస్తున్నట్లు వెల్లడించలేదు. పైగా, తమ సంస్థల పేరును వాడుకొని లింకులు, యాప్లను పంపి సైబర్ నేరగాళ్లు ప్రజలను మోసం చేస్తున్నారని, అందువలన అనుమానాస్పద లింక్లను క్లిక్ చేయవద్దని గతంలోనే వారు పలుమార్లు(ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) హెచ్చరించారు.
ఇక, వైరల్ అవుతున్న లింకులను పరిశీలించగా, అవి ఈ రెండు సంస్థలకు చెందినవి కావని, అనుమానాస్పద డొమైన్ పేర్లతో ఉన్న ఫిషింగ్ వెబ్సైట్లుగా చూడవచ్చు. ఇందులో ఇవ్వబడిన కామెంట్లు కూడా నిజమైనవి కావు, వినియోగదారులను నమ్మించడానికి ఇటువంటి కామెంట్లను సైబర్ నేరగాళ్లు సృష్టిస్తారు. ఈ వెబ్సైట్లు ఫోన్ నంబర్ వంటి వ్యక్తిగత వివరాలను సేకరిస్తాయి. తద్వారా, భవిష్యత్తులో మరిన్ని సైబర్ నేరాలకు ఈ వ్యక్తిగత సమాచారాన్ని వాడుకుంటారు.
అలాగే, భారత ప్రభుత్వం కూడా ప్రజలకు దీపావళి కానుకగా డబ్బు ఇస్తుందని కొన్ని లింకులు (ఆర్కైవ్) ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. ఇవి కూడా పూర్తిగా మోసపూరితమైనవని గతంలో మేము ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ ఆర్టికల్ ప్రచురించాం. సైబర్ క్రైమ్ విభాగాలు కూడా వీటి పైన ఎప్పటికప్పుడు ప్రజలకు అవగాహన కల్పిస్తూ, ఇటువంటి మోసపూరిత సమాచారాన్ని నమ్మవద్దని, అధికారిక సమాచారాన్ని మాత్రమే అనుసరించాలని పేర్కొంటున్నారు.
చివరిగా, పంజాబ్ నేషనల్ బ్యాంకు, ఎయిర్టెల్ సంస్థల పేరుతో ప్రచారంలో ఉన్న ఈ దీపావళి ఆఫర్లు ఫేక్.

Google and Samsung's next face computers have arrived. Nearly two years after the companies first announced the Android XR platform that powers the hardware, the smart glasses are finally on sale.
The “Intelligent Eyewear” is a collaboration between the two tech companies, with Samsung providing its hardware expertise and Google handling much of the software platform. Smart glasses are just one part of Android XR—there are also mixed-reality headsets and glasses for more immersive experiences, like last year's Samsung Galaxy XR and the upcoming Xreal Aura.
Eyewear brands Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are heavily involved in the new smart glasses, responsible for the design and fit, similar to how Meta tapped Ray-Ban for its competing—and market-leading—wearables. Google and Samsung are leveraging Warby Parker and Gentle Monster's brick-and-mortar presence and retail expertise, which lets people demo the glasses before buying them. (Kering Eyewear, which owns brands like Lindberg and Maui Jim, has also signed up to make glasses for Android XR in the future.)
The first models are available for preorder now, with official sales starting on December 10. Warby Parker's frames start at $395 and come in three styles—Alden, Reid, and Wren—as optical or sunglasses, with various prescription, lens, and width options. Gentle Monster's glasses start at $449 and come in six designs, various colors, and tints, with prescription options for most frames.
The hardware is identical across both brands. The glasses weigh around 41 grams (10 grams less than Meta's new Gen 3 glasses), have a nine-hour battery life, and include a charging case that can recharge the glasses up to seven times. They have a 12-megapixel camera with an LED indicator that shows everyone in eyeshot that you’re recording. There’s a button to capture photos and 90-second videos at up to 3K resolution with a press. A touch-sensitive temple piece lets you tap to activate the onboard Gemini assistant, or slide two fingers back and forth to control the volume of the audio coming out of the glasses' speaker.
They are the first devices to support the “Hey Gemini” hotword, though you can use the well-known “Hey Google” hotword if you'd like. Still, the new spoken wake phrase distinguishes the glasses as Gemini's “optimal form,” according to Juston Payne, Google's senior director of product management for XR.
“We felt that these are a Gemini-forward device,” Payne tells WIRED. “It's really you and Gemini going through your day together, so it was feeling a little dissonant for us. You're not talking to Google, you're talking to Gemini.”
Oddly, these glasses are only compatible with certain devices—Google Pixel phones, Samsung Galaxy phones, and iPhones—and only select models. You'll need a Pixel 7 or newer, Galaxy S or Z Fold running Samsung's One UI 9.0 or higher, and the iPhone 13 Pro or newer. A Google spokesperson tells WIRED the company will share more about how it plans to expand support to other phones in 2027 after launch.
Since you'll be buying the glasses from an eyewear brand, they will be the customer-facing party to handle any problems you may have with the device or prescriptions. On the backend, Payne says there are elaborate business integrations and handoffs, so the customer service workload is split between all the companies.
Google has already previewed Intelligent Eyewear glasses with displays built into the lenses—useful for showing navigation instructions or real-time captions for folks with hearing issues. However, they are not ready yet; Payne says they're currently being tested by “non-Googlers” and are still on the road map, though he didn't share a specific release window. As for plans to launch audio-only smart glasses, like Meta's recent Ray-Ban Audio, Warby Parker co-CEO Dave Gilboa tells WIRED, “There's a pretty robust pipeline of additional products.”
What Can They Do?
Smart glasses have been around for a few years, but they come in many forms. Unlike display smart glasses designed to plug into a laptop to mirror or extend your screen, or more immersive glasses like Meta's VR Glasses, which layer virtual experiences over the real world, Intelligent Eyewear is more akin to what Google pitched years ago with the original Google Glass.
You can hear notifications pipe through from your connected smartphone and respond to messages by speaking to Gemini. You can listen to music, take phone calls, and get audio navigation through Google Maps. Yes, you can snap photos and videos too, though Payne quickly notes that these glasses are designed more to have Gemini assist you throughout the day than to capture content.
That's likely because Meta has faced public scrutiny over how people use its smart glasses, so much so that it has spawned a new term for people wearing them: the Meta Creep (harkening back to when anyone wearing Google Glasses was called a “Glasshole”).
“We learned through Glass that you can make people uncomfortable if you're not clearly communicating,” Payne says.
To that end, Google is announcing a series of policies and features alongside the glasses to assuage concerns. They include tamper detection, so the camera will know if you tried to disable the indicator light. If you try to block the indicator light while recording, the camera will stop. When you ask Gemini to look at something, those visuals are not saved in your Gemini History, and Google says it will not use them to train AI models or target ads. The glasses will automatically redact the faces of people around you before Gemini processes the visual data. We've highlighted all of Google's privacy-focused announcements around its glasses in a separate story.
Most of the features that Google is positioning around Intelligent Eyewear rely on Gemini. See a poster for a comedy show? Just ask Gemini for more information, or add it to your calendar. You can ask Gemini to add items to your shopping list or whip up a travel itinerary with hotel recommendations and save them to a note. Some of these are saved in the Gemini app, but it can leverage other apps on your smartphone. For example, Gemini can play music on Apple Music if you're on an iPhone. And if you use Samsung Notes on a Samsung phone, it'll know that's where you likely want your notes saved.
When you activate Gemini, it's technically a “Gemini Live” experience, meaning the assistant activates and you can have a free-flowing conversation. A swipe back on the glasses' arm will end the interaction. When you want it to “look” at something in front of you, be specific in your query; otherwise, it won't use the camera. You can ask it to look at a page in a book and summarize the content, or if you have a bunch of cocktail ingredients in front of you but don't know what to make, you can ask Gemini for suggestions and step-by-step instructions to craft a drink—at your pace.
Some Gemini controls are on-device and don't need to travel to the cloud, like asking the assistant to play the next track. Speaking of, early next year, Google says users can use gestures on devices like the Fitbit Air or Google Pixel Watch to control music playback or activate Gemini on the glasses right from their wrist.
Another big capability is translation. Gemini will automatically detect languages and translate them to your preferred tongue. You do need to stare at the individual to hear their words translated, and there's a limited range; the quality depends heavily on the environment and noise level, but it worked remarkably well in my controlled demos, with only a few errors. The translation tries to mimic the speaker's tone and voice so it feels like their own words.
There's an accessibility feature called Guided Vision, which provides audio descriptions for people with impaired vision, like when reading fine print or locating everyday items. Google is also collaborating with Aira so you can stream the glasses' feed straight to a human interpreter for real-time visual support.
To help demystify these features—and convince consumers that smart glasses aren't just a fad for tech bros—Warby Parker and Gentle Monster are both launching pop-up experiences in New York City this week. These pop-ups will run for about a month, and they’ll give people the chance to walk through the experience with a pair of nonprescription glasses to demo the Gemini capabilities.
“These are the original wearables that have been around for hundreds of years,” Warby Parker's Gilboa says. “A lot of people start by getting an eye exam in one of our stores, and then come in, do a demo, buy these—we just want to make it as easy and seamless as possible.”

Is this the end of the Electoral College?
The Democratic takeover in states like Michigan and Pennsylvania means a controversial reform could be back on the table.
I don’t know how much time you spend in the more feverish right-wing corners of the internet, but some conservative commentators are growing very alarmed about a specific Democratic policy proposal that could be nearing fruition.
It’s not abolishing ICE. It’s not nationalizing grocery stores. It’s not even investigating President Donald Trump over his reported failure to act on intelligence about his newly jobless/disgraced pal, Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang.
Instead, they’re concerned about a wonky electoral workaround called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would essentially sidestep the Electoral College. (And in the words of one right-wing commentator, “effectively [rig] the system so Democrats could never lose again.”)
NPV isn’t quite as nefarious as that (Trump won the popular vote just two years ago!), though it would revolutionize how the United States conducts presidential elections. The compact is basically an agreement between states to award their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how their own state voted. Once enough states sign on, their combined electoral votes would guarantee the presidency to whoever wins the national popular vote.
The compact has laid dormant for two decades, however, while its backers lobby to sign on more states and their electoral votes. Eighteen states and Washington, DC, have signed on thus far, representing 222 votes.
But with Democrats soon controlling state governments in Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, NPV could finally gain the critical mass to become reality. Politico reported on Tuesday that lawmakers in several states, including Pennsylvania, are already discussing the possibility.
There’s just one problem: Conservative influencers aren’t the only ones worried about the plan. In fact, even one of its architects has come to regard NPV as a “doomsday machine” that could trigger gigantic constitutional problems.
Go a little deeper
My colleague Andrew Prokop called up this conflicted architect, the Yale University professor Akhil Amar, earlier this week. Andrew has been writing and thinking about NPV for years. But Amar has been thinking about it even longer — since the aftermath of the 2000 election that made George W. Bush president.
Famously, Bush was elected even though he lost the popular vote, which Al Gore won by roughly half a percentage point. Amar thought the Electoral College was historically and inherently flawed, but only a constitutional amendment could abolish it.
Recognizing the long odds there, Amar and his brother instead sketched out a quick thought experiment — the broad strokes of what is now the NPV compact. The concept was later picked up and championed by the computer scientist John Koza and his group National Popular Vote Inc.
Koza has had quite a lot of success getting states to sign on to this workaround. But all the signees so far have leaned Democratic, which concerns Amar. The institution of the Electoral College doesn’t inherently favor one party over the other (in fact, both parties nearly got rid of it after the 1968 election), and the NPV wasn’t designed to tilt the scales, either. But as the discourse on right-wing social media suggests, Trump’s 2016 victory with a popular vote minority has only further hardened views on each side, and all the Democratic signatories have made it look like a partisan proposition.
There’s another problem too, Amar says. The compact leaves each participating state to calculate the national total, without a centralized body to oversee a nationwide count or recount. A very close election could leave states disagreeing over who won. But in the current environment, it’s actually hard to imagine a centralized body that both parties would find credible: People just don’t trust institutions the way they did in, say, 2000.
That puts NPV advocates in a tricky spot: The political process may finally favor the compact, but it faces significant cultural problems that could undermine its legitimacy.
Amar, for his part, thinks that even the small risk of electoral disruption outweighs the benefits of NPV. Especially since the Electoral College does actually work, whatever its shortcomings.
“The one thing we really do need to avoid as the stabilizing superpower in the world is constitutional chaos,” he told Vox. “And because this is sort of a new plan, even if it’s in principle likely to be better in all sorts of scenarios, if in a certain small percentage of cases it would lead to chaos, that’s something we need [to] seriously consider.”
One link for later
➨ Stop subway scrolling. If social media feels exhausting and overwhelming to you — which it does to me, often — try to stop logging on from public places. “People feel more lonely when they use social media while in transit, around people they have close relationships with, and when they are in nature,” says Vox contributor Shayla Love. “In contrast, when people use social media for shorter periods when they are alone at home or in study locations, it doesn’t have as much of a negative effect.”

Industry minister 'fed up' after meeting with Stellantis, says automaker breached contract
Minister Joly met with representatives from company, union and Ontario government on Thursday
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she is "fed up" with automaker Stellantis after meeting with company representatives about its plan to sell its Brampton, Ont., plant to an armoured vehicle manufacturer.
"I was extremely clear. Stellantis is on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars," she told reporters in Toronto following the Thursday afternoon meeting.
"Patience has its limits. To be frank, I'm fed up. I'm fed up and Canadians are fed up and workers are fed up."
Joly also wrote to the CEO of Stellantis Canada on Thursday, saying the government is terminating a resolution process and notifying the automaker that it is in default of a 2022 government funding agreement.
The minister's letter to Stellantis suggests that the company has 30 days to take corrective action or the government could seek to terminate the 2022 agreement and recoup its subsidies.
Joly didn't specify how much the government would be seeking if it comes to a legal battle, but Stellantis issued a statement Tuesday saying it would voluntarily pay the government subsidies back, suggesting it amounts to at least $220 million.
"Stellantis knows how much it owes," Joly said. The minister said the government plans to meet with the Stellantis global CEO in the coming weeks.
Stellantis had been engaged with the government to find a possible alternative for the Brampton facility after the company announced last year that it wouldn't be going ahead with plans to build the Jeep Compass at that plant.
The government had signed an agreement to provide subsidies to the automaker to retool the plant to produce the Jeep model. Joly's letter says the company is in violation of that 2022 agreement and that the planned sale to Roshel Inc. indicates Stellantis is not interested in finding a satisfactory solution.
"I must conclude that Stellantis is no longer diligently working in good faith to prepare a satisfactory plan under the Resolution Process. Accordingly, the Resolution Process is terminated," the letter reads.
Union says government should've acted sooner
Joly had promised nearly a year ago that the government would serve a default notice to Stellantis.
Lana Payne — the national president of Unifor, the union representing the workers at the plant — said the federal government should've acted sooner.
"We have the sale of a plant and everybody in the country says they didn't want to have the sale of a plant. Yet here we are, the plant has been sold," Payne told reporters following Thursday's meeting.
"Why could not something have been done last week? Or the week before? Or the week before that?"
Stellantis and Roshel signed a memorandum of understanding regarding the potential sale in September. The automaker announced on Monday that it intends to go ahead with the sale.
When pressed during Thursday's news conference, Joly indicated that the government will be unable to block the sale.
More than 2,000 workers at Stellantis's Brampton plant have been out of work since the company halted operations in 2023 to retool the facility for the Jeep Compass.
In the deal announced by the Trudeau government in 2022, Ottawa said it would inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them retool to increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.
Stellantis paused the retooling plan at the Brampton plant in early 2025, announcing in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.
Part of the deal with Roshel that was announced on Monday could see Stellantis lease some of the property back.
Stellantis says there are still about 1,800 workers from the Brampton plant on layoff. Since 2023, those workers have continued to receive 70 per cent of their pay, as well as benefits.
Last week, Unifor demanded a meeting of all stakeholders, including the Ontario government, Stellantis and the federal government.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that his government had been informed of "some aspects" of Stellantis's plan to sell the auto plant to Roshel before the deal was announced earlier this week.
The prime minister made the comments a day after reports that his office and Industry Minister Mélanie Joly's office had been aware for months of the details of what was going to be made public.
Joly's office has insisted that the minister "had no part in negotiating the deal with Stellantis or Roshel" and didn't meet with the armoured vehicle manufacturer.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has called on Carney to remove Joly as minister over the plant sale. He reiterated that call on Thursday and said all the details of the 2022 agreement should be made public.
"Why not release the deal, Mr. Carney? Your government handed over our money. Canadians deserve to know how much they paid and what they got in return," he said during a news conference in Calgary.

The Justice Department says it’s joined with the two biggest stablecoin issuers in efforts to secure almost half the money stolen when hackers absconded with more than $6 billion from the Binance crypto exchange.
The department got court authorization to seize or restrain $1.2 billion of the $2.7 billion of funds frozen by Tether and Circle Internet Group Inc. in the immediate aftermath of the Oct. 29 break-in. Investigators are continuing to pursue the rest as the hackers, whom the FBI calls TraderTraitor, try to launder the cryptocurrency through bridges, mixers and exchanges.
“The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea’s ill-gotten gains,” M. Scott Proctor, principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, said in a statement. He said North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft to finance its government and weapons program.
The attack on the world’s largest crypto exchange was the biggest cryptocurrency theft on record, siphoning $6.3 billion in digital assets from customers. Binance has since replaced all of the stolen assets using profits and emergency funds.
The exchange has said the hackers initially compromised an engineer through a fake job interview before infiltrating other employees who worked on its digital wallets, part of what Binance described as a months-long operation involving malicious software, compromised devices and artificial intelligence.
The hackers then began moving the stolen assets through thousands of digital wallets and multiple blockchains to obscure their origins. Within a week, the laundering operation had used more than 20,000 wallets and executed at least 65,000 transactions, according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, while stablecoin issuers and other companies moved to freeze billions of dollars before they could be transferred.
Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said the Criminal Division and law enforcement partners froze Binance assets “before they got beyond law enforcement reach,” halting about half of what he called a “historic breach.”
The FBI, Secret Service and Internal Revenue Service issued an alert shortly afterward attributing the theft to North Korea and urging the digital-asset companies to block transactions involving addresses used by the hackers. North Korea has denied responsibility for cryptocurrency thefts attributed to it.
The Justice Department also said Thursday that it seized cloud infrastructure supporting a separate North Korean hacking operation that has stolen more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the past 18 months. The FBI calls the scheme FaceStealer.
FaceStealer uses victims themselves to make the next attack more convincing. Hackers hijack messaging and social-media accounts and use them to invite the victim’s contacts to fake Zoom or Microsoft Teams meetings. Once a target joins, they play prerecorded webcam footage of someone the target knows, manufacture an apparent technical problem and offer a “fix” that instead installs malware.
“If you can’t imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough,” Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the FBI’s Los Angeles field office, said in a statement.
The FBI seized more than 900 webcam videos secretly recorded from victims and later used to impersonate them. The hackers have also begun using deepfakes of prominent figures in the cryptocurrency industry to make fraudulent meetings more convincing.
The campaign is increasingly targeting open-source software developers, raising the prospect that compromising a single person could expose far larger numbers of users. Earlier this year, hackers infected the computer of a maintainer of a JavaScript library downloaded tens of millions of times a week and attempted to create malicious dependencies that would have been distributed with legitimate downloads. The effort was detected before the malicious software could spread, according to the FBI.

A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.
Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer.

Listed mattress brand Wakefit reported a net profit of ₹15.9 Cr in second quarter (Q1) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), almost flat from nearly ₹16 Cr in the year-ago quarter. However, on a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, the bottom line tanked 32% from ₹23.4 Cr in Q1 FY27. The company attributed the sequential decline in profitability to rising commodity prices, geopolitical disruptions and the “challenging” operating environment. “The operating environment remained challenging during the quarter, with crude-linked raw materials, particularly Polyol and TDI, continuing to remain elevated, with further price increases witnessed in recent months. Geopolitical disruptions in West Asia also impacted raw material availability and logistics across the industry…,” said Wakefit cofounder and executive director Chaitanya Ramalingegowda. Despite this, operating revenue rose nearly 20% to a record ₹452 Cr in the quarter under review as against ₹376.9 Cr in Q2 FY26. Sequentially, the top line also rose 11.6% from ₹404.9 Cr in the preceding quarter. While mattresses brought in 66% of revenue, furniture, furnishings and decor contributed the remaining 38%. Including other income of ₹16 Cr, Wakefit’s total income stood at ₹468 Cr in Q2 FY27. Meanwhile, total expenses for the quarter under review also shot up 19% to ₹441.4 Cr compared to ₹370.5 Cr in Q2 FY26. The listed company also incurred additional tax expenses of ₹10.7 Cr during the quarter. “The company recorded a deferred tax charge of ₹6.4 Cr in Q2 FY27, compared with nil in Q2 FY26 and ₹7.3 Cr in Q1 FY27. This is attributable to two factors: (i) normal-course reversal of timing differences relating to depreciation and provisions as they unwind through the P&L, and (ii) the unwinding of the deferred tax asset on carried-forward losses,” said the company in a statement. In its investor presentation, the company said that its operating EBITDA rose 25.8% to ₹30.5 Cr in the quarter under review compared to ₹24.2 Cr in Q2 FY26. Operating EBITDA margin also improved to 6.7% from 6.4% in the year-ago quarter. On the operational front, Wakefit opened 41 new offline stores in Q2 FY27, taking its total company-owned store count to 205 across 137 cities. It also had a presence across 2,589 multi-brand outlets spanning 787 towns and cities. Wakefit said that its own channels contributed 70% of its sales in Q2 FY27, while external channels accounted for the remaining 30%. The company also noted it operated a 1.6 Lakh sq. ft. mother warehouse in Hosur, 10 inventory holding points and 26 points of delivery at the end of September 2026. “Our planned FY27 capex of around ₹100 Cr to ₹120 Cr remains on track, with nearly 80% allocated towards retail expansion, particularly our jumbo store format. Construction of our first jumbo store in Bengaluru is progressing, and we are targeting its launch in Q2 FY28,” added Ramalingegowda. Shares of Wakefit closed Thursday's trading session 1.1% lower at ₹138.75 on the BSE.

India has had decades of unchanged high anaemia prevalence in women and children that has historically been thought to be due to iron deficiency. This has led firstly to an iron and folic acid (IFA) tablet supplementation targeted at women and children, and secondly to fitful implementation of mandatory fortification of staple foods. IFA is a ‘precision’ strategy, applying as it does to the vulnerable population it is intended for, while fortification is a broad strategy that applies to the entire population. The latter works in controlled settings such as clinical trials, but has not worked in real-world settings, and might have adverse effects when given to those it is unintended for.
The reason for pivoting: anaemia is mistakenly conflated with iron deficiency In India. The evidence is otherwise: in national Indian surveys, it has been shown that iron deficiency is not the major cause of anaemia. Indeed, fully one-third of anaemia cases demonstrate no micronutrient deficiency or obvious cause. Even so, giving iron should have sorted out those who did have iron deficiency anaemia, and reduced the general anaemia prevalence. While this could be a problem with inefficient programme implementation, two important questions arise: is there is really a deficiency in dietary iron intake in India? And is the administered iron being adequately absorbed and utilised for haemoglobin formation?

Srinagar, Nov 12: The Awami Itihaad Party (AIP) Thursday convened an Executive Committee meeting in Srinagar under the chairmanship of Party Vice Chairman Advocate G N Shaheen.
The meeting, as per a statement, was attended by General Secretary (Org) Prince Parveez General Secretary  Nazir Ahmad Khan, Chief Spokesperson Inam Un Nabi, State Secretary Sheikh Ashiq, senior party leaders including MLA Langate Sheikh Khursheed, Peerzada Firdous Ahmad Baba, Mir Nazir Ahmad, Parvez Ahmad Bhat and Advocate Dawood Ahmad.
The Executive Committee expressed concern over the continued incarceration of Party President and Member of Parliament Engineer Rashid. Taking note of the fact that the Delhi High Court has reserved its judgment on his regular bail application, the committee expressed hope that the verdict would be delivered at the earliest, paving the way for his release and enabling an elected Member of Parliament to resume his public responsibilities.
The meeting also reviewed the ongoing membership drive across Jammu and Kashmir. Members expressed satisfaction over the encouraging public response and described the growing interest in joining the party as a positive indication of its expanding organisational reach.
Detailed discussions were also held on strengthening the party organisation, reviewing existing party structures and improving coordination at different levels. Special emphasis was laid on expanding AIP’s organisational presence and building a stronger base across the Jammu Province.
The Executive Committee reiterated its commitment to organisational consolidation, grassroots outreach and strengthening the party’s presence across all regions of Jammu and Kashmir.

Question: Which two men's club sides have won three successive competition finals at the new Wembley?
You probably knew Pep Guardiola's Manchester City won three League Cups on the bounce between 2018 and 2020 before adding a fourth in 2021 – but another side did the silverware hat-trick first.
Whitley Bay, who play in the ninth-tier Northern Football League, won three successive FA Vase finals between 2009 and 2011 – an unprecedented achievement in non-league football.
The FA Vase, a national competition for amateur teams, was established in 1974; and in more than half a century The Seahorses are the only ones to win it four times – including those three on the trot.
And they did so under the eye of an unassuming IT manager from Sunderland, who used "quiet moments in the day" to plan historic cup success.
Ian Chandler, who had three spells at Whitley Bay as a player, became manager in 2004 and spent 10 years in charge.
It was no mean feat, as any non-league manager will tell you. Instead of focusing on work meetings, Chandler says he spent more time sorting hotel bookings or discussing scouting reports.
His team were inspired by missing out on Wembley in 2007-08, when Whitley Bay reached the FA Vase semi-finals. They lost 4-0 to Lowestoft Town in the first leg, and despite going 3-0 up inside 20 minutes of the return fixture at Bay's Hillheads Park stadium they were unable to overturn the deficit.
After that elimination, Chandler developed a superstition of never again giving pre-match interviews - as the last time he did so was before the 4-0 defeat.
Whether because of his renewed focus, or because of a desire among players to make amends, it steeled the group to make history.
"It's the hardest thing to keep a team together - as soon as players get noticed, they get picked up at higher level," Chandler tells BBC Sport.
"But after we got to the Vase semis, players wanted to stay and prove what they could do.
"Then the lads wanted to do it again."
And again.
Despite being a lifelong Sunderland fan, Chandler admits basing his team on Kevin Keegan's Newcastle - with entertainment even placed above winning.
"There was a standing joke in the team, two or three at the back? One time we chased a game with two at the back," he says.
"The Premier League can be so boring; fans want to be entertained, that's what we promised."
Chandler was already a Whitley Bay hero when he was appointed manager by chairman Paul McIlduff, having scored the winner in the 2002 FA Vase final against Tiptree United at Villa Park.
After a slow start as the then-35-year-old with no prior managerial experience found his bearings, Chandler built a talented team which became the envy of non-league football nationwide.
"We played good football. We had pace on the wing, fantastic midfielders, and strikers who were deadly," says McIlduff, who has been Whitley Bay chairman since 2001.
"When we brought them in, it was about fitting the psychology of the dressing room. No-one thought they were better than anyone else, they played for each other."
A growing influence in the side was the 'Whitley Bay Maradona'.
Paul Robinson came through Newcastle United's academy before a career spent across various non-league clubs in the north-east – including Whitley Bay from 2007 to 2013.
Like several other players and staff, he worked with Chandler both in his day job at software company Sage and at Hillheads Park.
"He was my manager at work and football, I was sick of him," he tells BBC Sport. "But it helped get time off for matches."
And it meant he also had an understanding boss if his mind drifted at work.
"Zoning out happened regularly, picturing scoring and winning, what the opposition would be like - hoping they were rubbish so we could have an easy stroll," he says.
Perhaps Robinson's greatest Whitley Bay moment came in the 2010 FA Vase semi-final second leg, when his last-minute diving header in the driving rain secured a 6-5 aggregate victory over Barwell, sparking a pitch invasion.
"Everyone goes to the finals, you were there, you could enjoy it," says Robinson, who is now academy head at South Shields.
"But the rounds before were the bigger games. At home, we would get 2,000 or 3,000 at every game. You felt like a real player. You associate those memories with 90s FA Cup you never think it will happen in non-league."
Chandler played in a 2-0 win over Preston in round two as they reached the FA Cup third round for the first and only time in the 1989-90 season, and they also progressed to round two the following campaign.
Those seasons of success - made The Bay a feared side for non-league clubs across England, and meant they were ready for the big games in a way most amateur sides are not.
"One quarter-final against Biggleswade [in 2009], they turned up in suits and ties," says Robinson. "We thought, this is their day out, their cup final. We won 5-2.
"By the end, teams were turning up afraid of us. We had it won beforehand."
Off the pitch, the team's success had an influence on the whole of Whitley Bay. A working-class town near Newcastle, which had its heyday as a Victorian-era holiday destination, sporting success brought local pride to the north-east coast.
And like any lower league club, that success could only be supported by dedicated volunteers, who went into overdrive before the Vase finals.
They would go door to door across shops in Tynemouth, North Shields and Whitley Bay to raise support. A van selling tickets was parked outside Woolworths on the high street.
"There was such excitement around the whole of Whitley Bay - every shop had things in the windows, the blue and white stripes," says one of the volunteers, Jenn Robinson.
She got involved because her late husband Mike was a club board member and if she wanted to see him she "had to go around there".
"Everyone wanted to come and watch, we got so many local sponsors," adds Jenn.
"I still do buffets and things for players and long-standing fans. We have a game tonight, and I'm making the sandwiches now."
Newcastle United helped out with selling tickets for the finals, while North Tyneside Council provided security services as thousands flocked to Hillheads Park for big cup games.
But even the best laid plans can go awry.
"We organised a train down to London, the guarantee was that it would go straight to Wembley," says McIlduff. "The first time it worked, second time they were taken to Kings Cross - we had to organise taxis up to Wembley."
By hook or by crook, The Seahorses army made it three times to the national stadium. Some even got royal treatment.
"It was absolutely surreal, and a delight," Jenn says. "The first Wembley final we played at, it had just opened. My husband being on the board, we sat in the royal box, which was fabulous.
"One of the security guys showing me to our seats said, 'Miss Robinson, this is Prince William's seat'. He hadn't even sat in it at that point."
Chandler, whose son Benjamin was a mascot at all three finals, said it was an overwhelming experience at times for the players too.
"The first year was crazy, everything was brand new," he says. "The first year the bus driver scraped the side up of the bus driving into the ground.
"The second year we tried to take everything in, all the lads had their mobiles. Then the third year, it was just a case of can we do it, win three in a row."
And three times, Whitley Bay rose to the occasion.
After beating Glossop North End 2-0 in 2009 in front of 12,200 supporters, Whitley Bay returned a year later to thrash Wroxham 6-1.
The opening goal was scored by prolific striker Paul Chow after only 21 seconds. At the time this was the quickest goal in a Wembley final and was only surpassed 13 years later when Ilkay Gundogan scored for Manchester City inside 13 seconds in the FA Cup final.
The hat-trick was completed in 2011 with a frantic 3-2 win over Coalville Town, who equalised twice before Chow was again the hero with an 86th-minute winner.
In total, nearly 30,000 fans were in the stands across the three finals.
After each final, Whitley Bay celebrated in The Green Man pub just 15 minutes' walk from the famous Wembley arch.
"In the first year we just went back to the bar and it was an anti-climax," Robinson says. "The second and third years the club got their act together and we rented a room; families, friends and fans were invited, they were brilliant nights.
"In 2010, we actually spent 10 days together - the week of the final we spent as a squad preparing, then we went to Marbella for five nights. Best 10 days of my life!"
The 2010 trophy lift was perhaps the most emotional though, as the players were joined by former team-mate Mark Taylor. He had played in the previous year's final, before being diagnosed with motor neurone disease, forcing an early retirement.
"Mark used to come on the away trips after he got diagnosed, he just wanted to be Mark - we had a good laugh everywhere we went," says Chandler. "He's still knocking about, abusing me on Facebook. He was the core of our second and third year."
Success ensured the lives of Chandler and his team were never quite the same again. Reporters turned up to Sage to speak with the manager and his players; even Chandler's mum was interviewed by BBC Radio Newcastle legend Paul Dixon.
Chandler - and his wife - even got up close and personal with managerial icons.
"I was invited to the annual sports awards in Manchester. There were people there like Sven Goran Eriksson and Sir Alex Ferguson [and] numerous others," he says.
"I had my wife with me and Sven came over gave her a peck on the cheek - she wasn't aware of who it was until I told her later that evening."
Robinson admitted that going back to work at an IT company after Wembley glory was a "massive comedown".
"One year I got a standing ovation when I walked into the office, but after that it was just back to normal," he says.
"People wind you up about it - 'are you talking about Wembley again? Give it a rest Robbo!"
Like all good things, Whitley Bay's golden era came to an end. Chandler departed in 2014 after a dip in form; the club have not won a major honour since the 2011 FA Vase and remain in the ninth tier.
But the memories in the football-mad north-east remain.
"Me and my wife went out on a Sunday at a pub in Durham just a few weeks back, and this guy came up out the blue and asked, 'Are you Ian Chandler?'" he laughs.
"Then he started talking about that team; in the north-east, everyone follows football. It was so lovely."
