Owono undecided over future following De Miguel death
- Published
FC Andorra manager Carles Manso says goalkeeper Jesus Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during a Spanish second division match on 2 November, with the Tenerife forward passing away the following day in hospital.
Manso said the goalkeeper, 25, is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return.
"What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to him," Manso said.
"We will give him space so that he feels completely free to make any decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.
"When he feels it is appropriate and when he feels genuinely ready to take a decision like that [he will do so]."
Andorra released a statement on behalf of Owono on 4 November, with the Equatorial Guinea keeper saying he was experiencing "the most difficult days of my life".
He added: "I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."
On Thursday, De Miguel's family released a statement via the Spanish Footballers' Association thanking those who had contributed to a crowdfunding page which has surpassed £170,000.
Fran Sol, a forward for Spanish third-tier side Hercules, set up the campaign with all proceeds going to relatives of De Miguel.
"We would like to express our heartfelt thanks for all the expressions of affection and support we have received," De Miguel's family said.
"We have been deeply moved to see so many of you rally behind this initiative."
Andorra will return to action for the first time since the forward's death on Saturday when they face Almeria in the Spanish second division.

Indian women’s hockey team head coach Sjoerd Marijne says he is working on “creating more depth” in the squad with the focus being on shaping versatile players, who can adapt to different positions and situations during the Women’s Asian Champions Trophy in Bhopal next week.
Besides India, the high-profile continental tournament, scheduled from November 19 to 28, will feature Paris Olympics silver medallists China, along with Japan, South Korea, Malaysia and Thailand.
India offered a glimpse of its growing versatility at the recent Asian Games in Japan, where it defeated China to clinch gold and secure automatic qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Three-time Asian Champions Trophy winner India will now have another opportunity to underline that its Asian Games triumph was no flash in the pan when it faces China again on home turf in Bhopal.
“We are busy creating more depth, which also makes training sessions more competitive. The players are also aware of that,” said Marijne, who is in his second stint with the Indian women’s team after previously coaching the side from 2017 to 2021.
“We want the players to be able to play in different positions. It’s to create more depth in the squad. It becomes helpful if a player gets injured, especially in a tournament like the Olympics, and it’s very helpful for the development of the players,” added Marijne.
Citing the examples of Ishika and Rutuja Dadaso Pisal, Marijne said the idea was to make players comfortable in roles beyond their primary positions. Ishika, for instance, is primarily a forward but is now also being groomed to operate in midfield.
“Ishika normally plays as a striker and now sometimes plays as a midfielder as well; it’s the same with Rutuja (Dadaso Pisal). So, they have to learn to adapt to playing in other positions and we want to see if this adds something to the game we want to play, to the improvements we want to see in the team,” he added.
Marijne said India would concentrate on its own game rather than get caught up in analysing opponents, their combinations or individual players.
“The main thing is what I’ve said the whole year, and it will be the same for this tournament: we have to focus on ourselves, what we want to improve after the Asian Games, what we want to do better. That is where the main focus is for us. And then it doesn’t matter who is the opponent.
“We have worked on those topics in the camp in Bengaluru, and now it’s time to see how they perform under pressure in a tournament,” he added.
The coach also sees the tournament as an opportunity for young players Pooja Sahu and Jyoti Singh to make their mark, while forward Mumtaz Khan’s return adds another option to the attacking line.
“There are youngsters like Pooja who will get a chance, Jyoti Singh for the first time and Mumtaz is back after a long time. I think this is a good platform for all of them to show what they are capable of.”
After ACT, India’s focus will shift to the Pro League, which begins early next year.
The team qualified for the competition after winning the FIH Nations Cup in June. Marijne expects it to be a challenging road ahead.
“Playing against Argentina and Germany in February immediately after the small break following a tournament like Hockey India League is not easy. It’s always a tough period to come back into the international rhythm because the competition level on the international stage is very, very different.”
“But that’s not only with India, that’s the same with every country. You need time to adapt. So, that will be a big challenge for us: how fast we can get the girls back in that zone,” said Marijne.

A Japanese team said that it has become the first in the world to create hybrid plant-animal cells, dubbed “planimal” cells, by fusing a unicellular alga called Cyanidioschyzon merolae into cultured animal cells.
According to the team from the University of Tokyo, the Institute of Science Tokyo, Kindai University and others, all of C. merolae’s DNA was integrated into the animal cells’ chromosomes.
But the hybrid cells were, in terms of function, animal cells because C. merolae’s DNA was suppressed and chloroplasts, which conduct photosynthesis, were degraded during fusion.
“We hope to introduce chloroplasts and activate C. merolae genes to generate oxygen through photosynthesis,” said Sachihiro Matsunaga, professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Frontier Sciences.
The team’s findings were published in the international journal Nature Communications.
Matsunaga had been working on the production of planimal cells since he proposed the creation of such a hybrid in 2018.
If cells that produce useful animal and plant proteins can be cultured in large quantities using photosynthesis, it could provide a new means of producing drugs and cultured meat. In this experiment, the cultured animal cells were derived from Chinese hamster ovaries, which are used to produce drugs and other products.
While plant cells have walls outside the cell membrane, C. merolae has no cell walls because it is primitive. In addition, its genome is very small.
Matsunaga and other members of the team fused C. merolae into cultured animal cells using a conventional method involving polyethylene glycol, in order to put the alga’s DNA into the animal cell nucleus.
Although the success rate was low, they produced planimal cells in which all of the alga’s DNA was integrated into the animal cells’ chromosomes.
The integrated DNA was frozen by a mechanism called methylation, acting as an “off” switch for gene expression. Like ordinary cultured animal cells, the planimal cells continued to divide and multiply for more than 150 generations.

BYD admits wheel assembly error on its flagship electric SUV
Some Great Tang SUVs had their wheels installed the wrong way.
BYD has apologized for an assembly mistake affecting some units of its newly released Great Tang — or Datang, as it's called in China — electric SUV. According to Bloomberg, several owners complained that the wider wheel rims that were supposed to be installed on the rear of the vehicle were installed on the front. Meanwhile, the narrower wheel rims for the front of the car were installed on the back instead.
The Chinese electric automaker has posted its apology on social network Weibo, explaining that it launched an investigation after getting complaints from owners. Apparently, it traced the problem to its Hubei-based wheel mesh assembly supplier. BYD said it has already fixed the issue, and the supplier has also added a visual inspection mechanism on the production line, so that future vehicles will no longer be affected.
BYD didn't say how many vehicles were affected by the assembly error, but it said that there was no safety risk associated with the wheels being installed the wrong way. Even so, it will replace the wheel rims of the those vehicles for free and will also offer their owners a replacement vehicle or compensation for what they will spend on transportation while their Great Tang SUVs are being repaired. In addition, the company will restart their vehicle's warranty period.
The company unveiled the Great Tang SUV in March, with prices starting at around $40,000. It received 150,000 orders in its home country. BYD is planning to release the electric vehicle in European and Asian markets outside China by the end of this year or in early 2027.

- Contrary to a claim circulating via social media posts, there's no evidence that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries explicitly threatened to withhold committee assignments from House members and members-elect who don't support his bid for speaker when Democrats take control of the legislative body in January.
- This rumor stemmed from Ohio Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard's comments about a dinner with senior Democratic representatives who allegedly warned Leonard that his life could become a "living hell" if he didn't support Jeffries. Leonard later told TMZ that potential consequences could include withheld committee assignments, but he framed it as a possibility as to what that "living hell" may entail.
- Snopes will update this report if we receive replies to our queries from either Leonard or Jeffries.
After Democrats won control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, a claim spread online that U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries was threatening to withhold committee assignments for any of his caucus members who didn't support him for speaker of the House.
The rumor circulated on X and Threads, and Snopes readers wrote in to ask us to verify it.
This claim originated from Ohio Democratic Rep.-elect Don Leonard's comments about "friendly advice with very stark consequences" he allegedly received from senior House Democrats in regard to supporting Jeffries' bid for speaker. Social media posts appear to have taken Leonard's comments somewhat out of context. There's no evidence that Jeffries has literally threatened to withhold committee assignments from anyone who does not support him as speaker.
Jeffries and Leonard's offices did not immediately return requests for more information. Here's what we know:
Leonard's allegations
Leonard, an Ohio Democrat who flipped a Republican-held seat, posted a video on Nov. 9 claiming that top House Democrats said his life will become a "living hell" if he doesn't support Jeffries. 
Leonard says in the video that he will not support Jeffries as speaker without the New York Democrat's commitments to two issues: ending U.S. support for Israeli military actions, including the war in Iran, and a constitutional amendment that would reverse Citizens United, a Supreme Court decision that gives free-speech protections to corporate money in politics.
Here's the transcript from that video (emphasis ours):
Tonight, I met with — we'll call 'em senior members of the Democratic House — who told me in no uncertain terms that the decision as to whether or not I support Jeffries, regardless of his willingness to speak with me and meet the interests of my constituents on a couple of key issues: No. 1, getting a constitutional amendment to end Citizens United, and No. 2, ending U.S. support for the war in Iran, and the country, Israel, that led us into it — that that would basically mean both making my life a living hell for the next two years in Washington as well as being sure to lose my election in two years.
You know, we kinda knew this stuff was coming. It's part of the stuff you see in the movies. It's a whole 'nother thing when, you know, it's in person by people who actually care about you and are cheering for you, but expect you to wear the team jersey and, you know, be a good team player. You know, we're searching our hearts tonight as to how we can reach Leader Jeffries and help him be a better speaker. At the end of the day, the big "D" Democratic Party needs some little "d" democracy and I'm just a stubborn SOB, so we'll continue meeting with our fellow members of Congress and members-elect and try and see if we can build support for what we're trying to do here. Please wish me luck. It's getting real, y'all.
On Nov. 11, TMZ posted a video in which a reporter with the tabloid asks Leonard about his comments. In that video, Leonard expands on what "living hell" could mean and says committee assignments could be withheld. However, he also makes it clear that the conversation he was referencing did not directly involve Jeffries, nor was it meant to be threatening.
As such, it's unclear whether anyone actually told Leonard that Jeffries would withhold committee assignments from him or any other Democrat who does not support Jeffries as speaker.
Here's a transcript of the TMZ interview (emphasis ours):
TMZ: You're in a room with top-level Dem officials. They say to you, "Listen, if you don't fall in line, we're going to make your life hell." Walk me through what that experience was like, just on your first couple of days here.
LEONARD: It was so much less cinematic. It was actually a dinner with senior elected officials, and I let them know where my position was on the speaker, and they were offering very friendly advice with very stark consequences. It wasn't in leadership, it wasn't their position to do it. It was just, you know, friendly advice from future colleagues.
TMZ: It doesn't sound that friendly. You literally said — your words — you said it was out of a movie. It sounds like something out of like "The Godfather."
LEONARD: What's out of a movie is the consequences of it, right? And the consequences are very real. Committee assignments will be withheld. You know, The ability to get, you know, legislation on the floor for votes will be difficult. And, you know, the ability to get support for the re-election will be a difficult case to make.
TMZ: Is this not what people criticize Trump for? It sounds very similar.
LEONARD: Yeah, I know, I think, you know, well, welcome to Washington, D.C., right? I mean, it's — I'm not shocked, but I'm —
TMZ: Sounds a little shocking. I think you're a little —
LEONARD: — I'm disappointed.
TMZ: Yeah, well listen. We can say — you already said what you had to say. And it's gone viral. But I think we gotta go the next step further, here, just for Americans. Who were these people who said it to you?
LEONARD: Yeah, no, that's how we build relationships and sustain them going forward. But I appreciate it.
TMZ: You don't want to get in trouble, hey man, I appreciate it.
Axios reportedly asked Leonard about the conversation, per a Nov. 11 story, and he emphasized that it was a "friendly" and "well-intentioned" conversation with senior House Democrats. Here's how he described it to Axios:
"They let me know that while we all agree on a lot of this stuff … the leader is going to pursue his message and agenda as he sees fit, and [said], 'Don't be insane. How could you possibly stand in the way?'"
Leonard also said he met Jeffries for the first time, per Axios, and there's no indication it was a threatening meeting:
The Ohio Democrat said he got a chance to meet Jeffries for the first time on Tuesday and arrange for their staffers to work out a time to sit down and talk.
- "I shook his hand and I asked him for six minutes," he said, telling Axios he wants to "look him in the eye, let him know that [I] respect his capacity as a leader ... but I need something to take back to my district that shows that my party understands the magnitude of the crisis we face."
Politico reported that California Democrat Rep. Pete Aguilar, who is running unopposed for House majority whip, said he didn't know which Democrats Leonard was referring to.
"It's my belief that he will be overwhelmingly selected to lead this caucus. I don't lose any sleep over that," Aguilar reportedly said of Jeffries. "Members could have ideas and interests, and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in question."
It's also worth noting that Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken progressive, told TMZ that no one has threatened her over Jeffries' bid for speaker. Omar suggested that Leonard simply received "advice that seems intimidating" and said Congress was "like high school: If people see any weakness, they'll roll with it, they'll take advantage of you."

Norwegian journalist Helle Lyng posted a video message to Home Minister Amit Shah on November 12. She said the Indian Embassy in Norway had called shortly before she was due to leave for India. According to Lyng, the call came 10 minutes before her planned departure for the airport. She had packed her bags for what would have been her first visit to India. Lyng said she had a visa in her passport and had received political clearance. Still, she said, the embassy told her she would be denied entry into India. She said the decision had apparently come from the Ministry of Home Affairs. Lyng asked HM Shah why she could not enter the country despite having a visa. She was due to speak at a conference in Hyderabad, Telangana. Her talk was to cover the links between the media, press freedom and democracy. Lyng said she still had 48 hours before she was scheduled to speak. She believed another flight could get her to Hyderabad in time. Lyng said the decision felt politically motivated. She wondered whether it was linked to her attempt to question Narendra Modi in Oslo. She also pointed to her criticism of PM Modi and his government. She said she had expressed those views in her Norwegian newspaper and online. The journalist also asked whether her criticism of Gautam Adani and Mukesh Ambani had played a role. “I'm also questioning whether my criticism of Adani and Ambani, two of Narendra Modi's alleged close friends, both very rich, the powerful billionaires of India and Asia, and I'm questioning whether that my criticism of them also might have something to do with this,” she said. She raised two other possibilities in her message. One was her favourable coverage of the Cockroach Janta Party movement. The other was her interview with Abhijit Dipke about a month earlier. She gave no confirmed reason for the decision. In May 2026, PM Modi and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store delivered joint statements. They took no questions after their statements. As Prime Minister Modi walked away, Lyng called out and asked why he would not take questions. Later that day, Lyng questioned senior Indian diplomat Sibi George at an embassy briefing. She asked about alleged human rights violations in India. George rejected the allegations and defended India’s constitutional democracy. The Oslo exchange drew sharply-different reactions. Critics called her approach disrespectful while press freedom advocates and opposition leaders praised her questioning. In her video message, Lyng reminded Shah that people in India were expecting her in Hyderabad. She also said people from the international community were waiting for her. She said the trip was still possible if she could leave soon. With time left to travel, she asked whether she would be allowed to enter. She called India the world’s largest democracy and urged Shah to make the visit possible. “Can we make it work? I think we should make it work,” she concluded. Social media reacted to the Norwegian journalist’s video message. “Helle, you didn't do anything wrong. Be proud of yourself,” wrote one user. “You aren't getting that visa for sure...they aren't listening! Please do a video conference...sorry you had to go through this trouble…” commented another user. One user posted, “If you’re guessing, the reason for your barring is “all of the above”; and some more…” “Don’t stop, dear!! Don’t step back. Try to report from there. Try to highlight the truth. Where does Kane rank among all-time England greats?

Harry Kane is now England's most-capped men's player as well as his country's record goalscorer, but harder to quantify is where these achievements place him among the Three Lions' greatest ever players.
This is a tricky debate with so many variables and a timescale as old as the game itself and, to my mind, not merely a determination of a player's individual ability but also a measure of their impact upon the nation's psyche.
Ballon d'Or winners Stanley Matthews, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen would surely have a shout if the criteria was such, not to mention genius technicians such as Glenn Hoddle, Chris Waddle and John Barnes.
Likewise, if any England boss managed to extract the best from Paul Scholes, Steven Gerrard and Frank Lampard they would be surely making a classic late dart from midfield.
But to qualify as one of the greatest England players of all time, you need the above ability combined with an impactful overall contribution - those memorable moments and an element of longevity - in a Three Lions shirt.
It might be controversial then to leave out Geoff Hurst, who produced the most recognisable performance in England history, while the man he replaced, Jimmy Greaves, would be a shoo-in were it not for injury earlier in the tournament.
It is also hard to rank the contribution of those whose best football came outside of major tournaments and before the dawn of continental competitions - see Eddie Hapgood, Tom Finney, Nat Lofthouse, Dixie Dean et al.
There are only 10 spots, after all, so here we go.
10. David Beckham
Spice Boy. Celebrity. Galactico. There is no argument David Beckham is one of the most iconic England players of all time, but he backed it up on the pitch, too.
Beckham was the face of the Three Lions for a generation, and to his credit managed to overcome the vicious fallout of his red card against Argentina in 1998.
At times he seemed to single-handedly carry England, most notably scoring a 93rd-minute free-kick against Greece to qualify for the 2002 World Cup.
Beckham's former team-mate Gary Neville called him the "most influential player out of England in transforming football".
It's true. On top of 115 caps, Beckham was part of Manchester United's 1999 Treble-winning outfit - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up - before joining Real Madrid.
His profile was truly global with spells at LA Galaxy, AC Milan and Paris St-Germain.
9. Paul Gascoigne
There's arguably no England star fans forged an emotional attachment with more than Gazza - crying with him in 1990, rejoicing in his spectacular effort against Scotland and desperately willing him to connect during that Euro 96 semi-final defeat by Germany.
Gascoigne won 57 caps and scored 10 goals. At his peak, he was captivating - transcending football as a cultural phenomenon during the summers of '90 and '96, having joined a star-studded Serie A between those tournaments.
Creative, unpredictable, vulnerable. He was a loveable but flawed genius.
He suffered long-term injuries as England missed out on Euro 92 and the World Cup in the USA, but helped the Three Lions qualify for France 98 before being dropped from the final squad, famously wrecking boss Glenn Hoddle's office.
8. Billy Wright
Goalscorers often grab the headlines but I've tried to credit players across positions and eras. From a defensive point of view Ashley Cole, arguably England's best-ever full-back, was close to making it.
But instead it's the great Billy Wright, the first men's player to surpass a century of international caps, including a remarkable 70 successive appearances over eight years.
Wright captained his country on 90 occasions, a joint-record recently broken by Kane, taking in three World Cups with impressive longevity for his era.
He was a true one-club man, winning three league titles, the FA Cup and becoming unofficial "world champions" with Wolves in 1954 - helping inspire the birth of the European Cup - while finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up to Alfredo di Stefano in 1957.
7. Jude Bellingham
It feels a little premature to include a 23-year-old with the bulk of his England career ahead of him, but that shows the impact Jude Bellingham has already made for England and Real Madrid.
A Champions League winner, the midfielder has also appeared at four major tournaments for the Three Lions, becoming the youngest player to do so at the delayed Euro 2020, aged 17.
But his role in helping carry England to the final two years ago and a third-place finish at last summer's World Cup really make him stand out.
Bellingham has delivered those moments a nation collectively remembers. The last-gasp overhead kick against Slovakia in 2024, a quickfire double at the Azteca against Mexico this summer and 93rd-minute quarter-final winner against Norway.
His seven goals at this World Cup were more than any previous Three Lions player in a single edition, the solo effort against France a thing of beauty.
The former Birmingham and Dortmund man doesn't turn 24 until June but has already collected 61 England caps and netted 14 times. As Roy Keane put it, Bellingham has the potential to be one of the "greatest of all time".
6. Wayne Rooney
In terms of natural ability, Wayne Rooney is among England's greatest ever talents.
Bursting on to the scene at Euro 2004 as an electric 18-year-old, having become England's youngest player and scorer the previous year, convinced fans and media the teen sensation could carry the Three Lions to glory in Portugal.
He bounced World Cup winner Lilian Thuram around in England's opener against France in a glimpse of his precocious strength, before scoring twice against both Switzerland and Croatia.
Who knows how far England would have gone had Rooney not been injured against Portugal in the quarter-final?
He was unable to replicate the impact of his first Euros - a red card at World Cup 2006, suspension for the Euro 2012 group stage, seven goals across six major tournaments - but was an all-rounder who brought more than just goals.
Rooney also won it all with Manchester United, becoming the club's all-time top scorer, and finished his 15-year England career with 53 goals from 120 caps.
5. Gordon Banks
There has to be a place for a goalkeeper, and Gordon Banks is the safest pair of hands.
A World Cup winner in 1966, his save from Pele four years later against Brazil is one of the most iconic of all time. Pele called him a "goalkeeper with magic".
Banks spent the majority of his career at Leicester and Stoke, winning a League Cup with each, and earned 73 England caps overall between 1963 and 1972.
His incredible athleticism and reflexes saw the shot-stopper named Fifa's best goalkeeper for five successive years between 1966 and 1971.
4. Gary Lineker
Gary Lineker's early club career did not deliver the silverware as his goals deserved, netting 40 times but finishing league and FA Cup runner-up in his one season at Everton before joining Barcelona.
He scored a Clasico hat-trick and won the Copa del Rey and Cup Winner's Cup, however, before adding an FA Cup with Tottenham in 1991.
Lineker netted 283 club goals (and famously no cards) in total across spells with Leicester, Everton, Barcelona, Spurs and Nagoya Grampus Eight.
But as a player Lineker is most renowned for his contribution in an England shirt, winning the Golden Boot as they reached the World Cup quarter-finals in 1986 - finishing Ballon d'Or runner-up that year - before netting another four as the Three Lions reached the semi-finals in 1990.
Lineker equalised against West Germany before England crashed out on penalties.
However, having missed a spot-kick against Brazil, he finished one short of Bobby Charlton's elusive goal record when his international career ended after Euro 92.
3. Harry Kane
Harry Kane is undoubtedly England's most important and influential player of a generation - it is hard to imagine how this Three Lions side functions once the skipper hangs up his boots.
The Bayern Munich striker, complete with Ballon d'Or, has been scoring goals for his country for almost 12 years, the first just 79 seconds into his debut after coming off the bench against Lithuania in March 2015.
Rooney's goalscoring benchmark is long in his rear view mirror - you wouldn't bank against Kane doubling his nearest rival's figure once his England days are over.
They have come on the biggest stage, too - 21 in 36 appearances from three World Cups and European Championships apiece, winning the World Cup Golden Boot in 2018.
Kane has come closer to winning a major tournament than any England men's captain since Bobby Moore - losing two World Cup semi-finals and back-to-back Euros finals. Team-mate Bellingham called him the "greatest player that has ever played for England".
"I think we'll appreciate him even more in another 10, 15, 20 years when you look back and see what he has achieved," said ex-England goalkeeper Paul Robinson.
2. Bobby Moore
In many ways, Bobby Moore would be the complete modern-day defender. Cool as you like under pressure, elegant in possession, a great passing range off both feet and, as his West Ham and England team-mate Geoff Hurst said: "Nobody out-ran him and nobody out-jumped him."
Moore's positioning and timing was perfect, that iconic tackle on Jairzinho at the 1970 World Cup the finest example of his poise and precision when defending.
He was also a composed and influential leader. A player built for the big occasions. England boss Sir Alf Ramsey called him: "My lieutenant on the field, a cool, calculated footballer I could trust with my life."
The Barking-born centre-back won the FA Cup and European Cup Winners' Cup with West Ham but his finest moment was leading England to glory in 1966. He was only 25 at the time, having become his country's youngest captain three years earlier.
In 1970, after the Bogota bracelet incident, Moore was imperious as England reached the quarter-finals before bowing out to West Germany.
It was, however, the final group game against Brazil, the most exciting side on the planet, that produced some of the most recognisable and renowned images in sporting history - not only Moore's tackle and Banks' save but the defender swapping shirts with Pele after the final whistle.
"The greatest defender I ever played against," was the Brazilian's verdict.
1. Sir Bobby Charlton
For more than a generation, Sir Bobby's England goalscoring record remained unmatched. It took 55 years from his 49th and final strike against Colombia in 1970 until Rooney surpassed him with his half century in 2015.
Charlton was, as Alan Shearer put it, "not only a great goalscorer but a scorer of great goals" and played a pivotal part of the Three Lions' World Cup success in 1966, netting three times on the way to the final.
A scampering run from the halfway line followed by a trademark long-range strike into the corner at Wembley gave England's campaign lift-off against Mexico, before he scored twice against Eusebio's Portugal in the semi-finals.
Manager Ramsey called the buccaneering midfielder his "lynchpin" as England triumphed over West Germany in the showpiece and those performances helped Charlton win the Ballon d'Or later that year.
He'd be runner-up in successive years after that, too.
Charlton won 106 England caps and was a star for Manchester United, with Rooney also the one to pip his club-record 249 goals for the Old Trafford outfit.
A survivor of the Munich air disaster on 6 February 1958, which killed 23 people including eight players and three members of the club's staff, Charlton won three league titles, an FA Cup and most poignantly the European Cup in 1968.
"England's greatest ever player," Lineker previously told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"He was unique. Wherever you go in the world, even if they didn't speak the language, they knew two words - Bobby Charlton."

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.
Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.
The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.
For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, December 13 as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.
Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-September 2026.
Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.
Temwa Chawinga
Age: 28 Country: Malawi
Club: Kansas City Position: Forward
Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.
Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.
Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.
Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.
Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.
Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.
Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.
Ewa Pajor
Age: 29 Country: Poland
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.
Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.
The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.
Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.
On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland as is the team's leading goalscorer.
Alexia Putellas
Age: 32 Country: Spain
Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder
Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.
After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.
Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.
Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.
Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3–0.
Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.
Alessia Russo
Age: 27 Country: England
Club: Arsenal Position: Forward
Russo has proven to once again be a trusted and integral attacking force for Arsenal, while remaining a key player for England.
She scored 13 WSL goals last season to finish second in the league's scoring charts, and also added six assists in her 22 appearances. In total, she registered 24 goals and eight assists across all competitions.
Among the highlights of her season was winning the inaugural Women's Champions Cup with Arsenal, beating Corinthians 3- 2 after extra time.
It was the first competitive trophy Arsenal's women's team had lifted at the Emirates, though they finished runners-up to Manchester City in the WSL.
Russo remains a first-choice striker for England and in April scored her 30th senior international goal to move into the top 10 of Lionesses goalscorers.
She was also nominated for the PFA Player of the Year award.
Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw
Age: 29 Country: Jamaica
Club: Manchester City Position: Forward
After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.
The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.
Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.
They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.
She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.
Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

A rumor that U.S. President Donald Trump wrote a social media post chastising Vice President JD Vance, including an order to change the vice president's name, circulated in November.
People on social media shared a purported screenshot of a social media post attributed to Trump that claimed, "I'm hereby signing an EXCLUSIVE ORDER legally changing JD Vance's name to JUDAS DISLOYAL VANCE!"
(X user @miribobs)
The alleged post was dated Nov. 5 and inspired readers to reach out about its authenticity. It circulated after Democrats enjoyed major victories in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
It read in full:
I'm hereby signing an EXCLUSIVE ORDER legally changing JD Vance's name to JUDAS DISLOYAL VANCE!
Nobody gave JD more than President Trump. I took him from the sidelines and gave him the biggest job of his life—and now he thinks he can DOUBLE CROSS THE BOSS and run for President in 2028 without my blessing?
EHHH!
WRONG!
You don't walk into the Trump Family, eat at the table, kiss the ring, and then decide you're the new Boss!
There is only ONE person who can make America Great Again the RIGHT WAY, and everybody knows who that is.
JD, you may have forgotten who made you—but I NEVER forget!
THE PRESIDENT HAS SPOKEN.
The post was fake, however.
A search of the president's Truth Social account and an online archive of his social media posts revealed no such post.
The fake Trump post circulated as an apparent response, likely satirical, to a Nov. 4 X post by Vance addressing the Republican turnout at the polls for the midterm elections. Vance wrote: "The main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026." His post sparked rumors that he's angling for a 2028 bid for the White House.
The engagement metrics displayed on the fake post — 14.3K reposts, 56.7K likes — exactly match those of other debunked Trump posts, suggesting it may have been generated using a template or a fake post generator. Note that the timestamp is written out as "11/5/26," while authentic Truth Social posts show dates written as "Nov 5, 2026."
The president made multiple posts on Truth Social on that date, but nothing about Vance or a rumored bid for the White House.
For further reading, check out Snopes' collection of alleged Trump social media posts we've debunked.

It wasn't too long ago — a week maybe? — that Jensen Huang's plethora of leather jackets were considered cool. But after his resignation as Nvidia CEO in the wake of an affair scandal, now his signature look is the butt of jokes.
Ok, so maybe not everyone considered him cool. He is, after all, a billionaire AI founder in his 60s, which isn't exactly a Keith Richards type of cool. But it was a look — a sort of zesty, zippy fun cool-dad look. Someone even paid nearly a million dollars for one of his used Tom Ford jackets in a charity auction recently.
The leather jacket look was a good mix of stylish and practical. It wasn't the severe utilitarian uniform of Steve Jobs' turtleneck, although it meant he didn't have to think hard about what to wear (he's said in interviews that his wife and daughter bought him the jackets and that he doesn't like to shop for himself).
It's more edgy and fashionable than the standard tech bro Arcteryx vest, but it's not as thirsty as Mark Zuckerberg with his gold chain and mullet or as gaudy as Jeff Bezos' mob chic.
How the leather jacket was looking at Jensen pic.twitter.com/GfiAIeYqtU
— Morning Brew ☕️ (@MorningBrew) November 11, 2026
But circumstances changed.
Huang reportedly had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a business client alleged to be Chinese spy — which China denies — as well as two Nvidia employees. (He resigned the day after news of the first employee affair broke on Wednesday, but before the second on Thursday afternoon.)
BREAKING: SpaceX lowers jackets to half-staff pic.twitter.com/fE7qnVSyLB
— Sound Dobad (@SoundDobad) November 12, 2026
Now, the leather jacket went from a cool quirky affectation to a desperate, horny, divorced-guy-energy look.
jensen leather jacket discourse reminds me of the time two years ago when i wore my beloved moto jacket to a party and my good friend said "great jacket, sorry you got divorced"
— Alex Yablon (@AlexYablon) November 12, 2026
The Cut wrote that "Jensen Huang's leather jacket confessed before he did":
A $9,000 leather moto is not the outerwear of a man faithfully going home to his wife and kids after a long day of architecting the AI revolution. That's a man in a midlife crisis with an active Raya profile and a Harley in the garage. If someone had consulted me years ago, I'd have said Huang is clearly someone who drinks wine with his mistress in the middle of the day. (The Times uncovered a 2023 photo of Jensen appearing to do exactly that at a luncheon in Shanghai with Alice.) 
The New York Times wrote that "Jensen Huang betrayed the leather jacket community":
We ask ourselves: Was Mr. Huang an easy mark because of his love of high-fashion, motorcycle-adjacent jackets that say both "I don't care what people think!" and "Do you like how I look?" Did our — I mean, his — armor make him a target? Is an expensive leather jacket on a middle-aged man the new symbol of a honeypot victim? 
Lol indeed.
And on social media, the jokes about the jacket being a glaring sign of an older guy ready to do some infidelity have been flowing.
Jensen Huang should've never leather jacket. Nor her. Nor her.
— Sridhar Ramesh (@RadishHarmers) November 12, 2026
Is there a lesson to be learned? I suppose it's that having a signature style is great until your career crashes around you and that's all everyone is joking about online.
At least the $960,000 someone paid for the used Jensen jacket went to charity.

The Chinese internet is lamenting the loss of Nvidia's "soul," aka its scandal-ridden former CEO Jensen Huang.
Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Thursday, after three of his extramarital affairs came to light.
Huang, who is both a Taiwanese and American citizen, has long since had clout in the East. With his Taiwan food crawls, annual Computex visits, and fluency in Mandarin, he's a fan favorite in the region.
Users on Weibo, the Chinese equivalent of X, shared disappointment about Huang's resignation on Thursday. Huang's resignation was the top tech topic on the platform all through Thursday, with hundreds of thousands of comments on his ouster flooding Weibo.
"I feel that Jensen Huang has become the spiritual symbol of Nvidia," said a user posting from Chongqing. "With his departure, Nvidia may still be incredibly successful, but it will lack its soul."
A lengthy post from a user in Guangdong Province said Nvidia's track record proves that Huang is an "irreplaceable leader."
Another user from Guangdong Province went so far as to say that the AI era had lost its "spiritual leader" and questioned whether the narrative of AI could continue without Huang.
Others sounded out concern for Chinese Americans, saying there was a risk that they could be targeted in a crackdown on Chinese espionage. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with the Singapore-based Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who was believed to be passing sensitive Nvidia information to Beijing.
Hu Xijin, the former editor in chief of the state-owned news outlet Global Times, wrote on Weibo that the move to oust Huang amounts to a "national security coup," saying it will have "a profound impact on the situation of Chinese Americans."
China stands to win from the Nvidia fallout
While Huang's fans on Chinese social media lament his departure from Nvidia, China has a lot to gain from the fallout.
As Business Insider's Alistair Barr wrote on Thursday, the scandal could pose a setback to the US in the AI race with China.
China, which has struggled to close the AI gap with the US because of a shortage of advanced AI chips, could benefit from Nvidia losing its edge. The company's stock price has fallen more than 8% in the past week.
"This would be a setback for the US, particularly as China continues aggressively investing in its own AI capabilities," Brad Gastwirth, global head of research at Circular Technology, told Barr.
While China's semiconductor industry remains constrained, other parts of its AI industry have made significant strides, including AI labs that develop advanced AI models. Just this year, models like Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, Z.ai's GLM-5.3-Flash, and Alibaba's Qwen have made a splash in the global tech scene, for their frontier-level capabilities at a fraction of the cost of US frontier models.

Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt
A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt.

On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang resigned from the company that had become, in many ways, synonymous with its chief executive.
Less than an hour later, when the markets opened, Nvidia’s stock had lost roughly $546 billion in market value. Though it has rebounded somewhat, the last weeks of scandal—including a reported second affair with an Nvidia employee—have tanked the chip maker’s valuation by more than $1 trillion.
Huang’s very public downfall began in late October, when the The New York Times reported that the CEO had a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based chip buyer Megaspeed and alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. (The two are not known to be related.) At that time, Nvidia’s market cap was around $5.2 trillion.
On November 8, Nvidia announced it was investigating its CEO, after Jensen publicly acknowledged the affair. By the following morning, roughly $1 trillion had been erased since the scandal started.
If you hang out with a certain type of person who thinks of themselves as a day trader, they might have talked about “buying the dip” over drinks last weekend. If you believe Nvidia can thrive without Huang, there’s still time! The dip has dipped even further. But the early consensus seems to be that this could be more of a prolonged plunge.
“Huang is irreplaceable,” Ryan Fedasiuk, a senior fellow at the think tank Foundation for American Innovation, told WIRED last week. “He built Nvidia into the juggernaut it is today, and he was the visionary behind the GPU, which has sustained the intelligence revolution.”
There are very real questions about what the end of Huang means for the global economy. Not only are Nvidia’s chips used to train most major AI models, the company has invested billions in a number of other tech companies. As of an August regulatory filing, Nvidia owned nearly $30 billion worth of Intel stock and roughly $21 billion of SpaceX stock.
For now, Nvidia’s loss is other chipmakers’ gain. AMD shares are up 28 percent over the last five days, and Broadcom is up nearly 16 percent. Nothing to see here.
More Numbers That Illuminate Huang’s Value:
- Nvidia’s market share of chips used in training frontier AI models: Roughly 90 percent
- AI companies in which Nvidia has invested at least $100 million: 8, as of its August filing.
- Huang’s pay last year: $36 million
- Portion of Nvidia owned by Huang: 3.5 percent, as of March—which means the scandal has devalued Huang’s own share of the company by more than $50 billion.
- Reported affairs: 2 (so far)
- PR firms hired with expertise in sex scandals: At least one
- Huang relatives employed by Nvidia: One son, one daughter, and one son-in-law
- Leather jackets owned: Several, including a $960,000 Tom Ford number. (But not that vintage Saint Laurent jacket everyone was talking about on X.)

Mumbai, Nov 13: The rupee traded in a narrow range and gained marginally by 7 paise to 94.05 against the US dollar in early trade on Friday, as the support from foreign fund inflows was negated by broad-based strength in the dollar.
Forex traders said the rupee is showing positive momentum, driven by consistent foreign investments, lower crude oil prices, and a favourable external environment.
However, strengthening of the American currency in the overseas market weighed on investors' sentiment.
In the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened at around 94.07, then touched 94.05, up 7 paise from its previous closing level.
On Thursday, the rupee depreciated 41 paise to close at 94.12 against the US dollar.
"The external environment remains supportive of the rupee, backed by softer crude oil prices and renewed FII inflows. However, after appreciating sharply from 97.00 to around 94.00, a near-term pullback could push USD/INR towards 94.50–95.00.
"Such a move should be viewed as a dollar-selling opportunity, with the broader trend still favouring rupee appreciation towards 93," CR Forex Advisors MD Amit Pabari said.
Meanwhile, the dollar index, which gauges the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was trading at 103.15, lower by 0.02 per cent.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, was trading 0.37 per cent lower at USD 95.47 per barrel in futures trade.
India's retail inflation surged to 6.09 per cent in October, breaching the Reserve Bank of India's upper tolerance limit for the first time in two years and prompting economists to anticipate a policy rate hike by the RBI next month.
With inflation now above the upper tolerance band, markets are pricing in a cumulative 75-bps rate hike, comprising a 25-bps hike delivered in October 2026, followed by expectations of further 25-bps hikes each in December 2026 and February 2027, Pabari said.
"Expectations of consecutive rate hikes in December and February could provide additional support to the rupee by improving the attractiveness of domestic assets, encouraging foreign inflows and strengthening confidence in the RBI's commitment to currency stability," he added.
On the domestic equity market front, Sensex tumbled 460 points to 81,441.17 in early trade, while the Nifty fell 179.05 points to 25,119.50.
Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) purchased equities worth Rs 7,830.60 crore on Thursday, according to exchange data.

EXCLUSIVE: Rick Cosnett, Richard Kind and Tammy Blanchard are the latest confirmed cast for grief-themed indie The Long Run. They join previously announced Alice Eve in the film, directed by Harold Cronk (Unbroken: Path to Redemption).
The character-driven film revolves around a woman named Claire (Eve) who made a promise to her husband, Ben, that they would one day run the Marine Corps Marathon together. After Ben is killed in an overseas explosion, Claire is left numbed by grief and becomes a single mother. To honor his memory, she decides to run the 26.2-mile marathon alone, guided by the weight of her grief and love. Eve’s Claire rediscovers life thanks to the unruly rescue dog her husband left behind — an unlikely companion who pulls her, mile by mile, toward the marathon they once promised to run together and a deeper connection with her young son.
Cosnett plays Ben, Kind portrays Walter and Blanchard is Vanessa.
Watch on Deadline
Production is currently underway in Louisville, KY.

Global TB Report 2026: Nearly 10.6 million fell ill with TB worldwide; India accounts for 25% of cases
The WHO’s Global Tuberculosis Report 2026 estimates 10.6 million people fell ill with TB worldwide in 2025, with India accounting for nearly a quarter of cases.
An estimated 10.6 million people fell ill with tuberculosis (TB) worldwide in 2025, a decline of 75,000 from the previous year, while India continued to account for about a quarter of the global disease burden, according to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report 2026, released on Thursday.
The report also noted a 38% reduction in TB deaths in India since 2015, compared with a 35% decline globally.
The global TB, the report added, incidence rate declined by 1.6% between 2024 and 2025, from 131 to 129 cases per one lakh people. However, the reduction remains far below the World Health Organization’s End TB Strategy milestones, which called for a 50% decline in TB incidence by 2025 and an 80% reduction by 2030, compared with 2015 levels. Between 2015 and 2025, the global incidence rate fell by 14%.
Tuberculosis remained the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide and ranked 13th among all causes of death, the report said. The 30 countries with a high TB burden accounted for 88% of the estimated global cases in 2025. Eight countries accounted for about two-thirds of the total, with India alone contributing nearly a quarter, followed by Indonesia (10%), the Philippines (6.8%), China (6.5%), Pakistan (6.4%), Nigeria (4.9%), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (3.9%) and Bangladesh (3.7%).
The top five countries accounted for more than 50% of the global total, data showed.
India’s progress in TB prevention and treatment
India carries roughly a quarter of the global TB burden. The report, however, noted the country’s overall progress.
“In recent years, the National TB Elimination Programme in India has made substantial efforts to improve TB prevention and care, with the goal of accelerating reductions in TB mortality and TB incidence… India has established a system for district-level sentinel surveillance of population-level trends in the prevalence of TB disease and TB infection,” it said.
Last year’s report also highlighted progress in India. Despite carrying the world’s largest TB burden, India outpaced global progress on key indicators. Between 2015 and 2024, India’s TB incidence fell by 21%, nearly twice the global rate, while deaths fell by 25% and treatment coverage rose from 53% to 92%.
The Indian Council of Medical Research’s (ICMR) National TB Prevalence Survey found that nearly half of people with TB have no symptoms. In response, India shifted its focus from waiting for patients to visit clinics to actively identifying cases in communities. Under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, the National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP) has deployed AI-compatible handheld X-ray machines for community screening, expanded molecular testing to nearly 11,000 facilities, and provided nutritional support through the Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana and Ni-kshay Mitras.
Under the TB Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, India is finding more people with TB than ever before. Between December 2024 and March 2026, the campaign screened more than 28 crore vulnerable people and notified over 39 lakh TB patients, including nearly 13 lakh who had no symptoms.
India has built one of the world’s largest molecular testing networks, with nearly 11,000 facilities, most of them using Truenat, a homegrown platform, alongside GeneXpert. According to the WHO’s 2025 report, around 60% of people with presumptive TB underwent a molecular test in 2024. Community screening is now identifying lakhs of people with TB, many of them without symptoms. The next phase is to make molecular testing universal. This will require tests that work without sputum, handle much higher volumes, cost less at scale and reach the places where people are being identified.
New diagnostic tools to expand testing
This year, the WHO issued its first-ever recommendations on three tools --- Near point-of-care (nPoC) molecular tests,Tongue swabs, and Sputum pooling --- aimed at addressing these needs.
The nPoC are portable tests for primary health centres and community settings, at less than half the cost of many current molecular tests, while the tongue swabs involves a needle-free sample collection method for adults and adolescents who cannot produce sputum. Sputum pooling is testing several people’s samples together on existing platforms such as Truenat and GeneXpert, reducing costs and machine time.
At ICMR’s India Innovation Summit, 86 TB diagnostic innovations were showcased. An ICMR panel found that 10 were already approved and available for NTEP use, 15 more were recommended for fast-tracking, and 33 were at an earlier stage of development.
Two kinds of tools are considered crucial.
First, nPoC tests using tongue swabs can take testing closer to communities. ICMR-validated tools such as Huwel Lifesciences’ UniAMP MTB use a tongue swab and give results in under 30 minutes on a portable device. Molbio’s Truelyse extends Truenat testing to oral swabs. Tools such as these can bring a confirmatory test to the same primary health centre (PHC) or screening camp where an AI-compatible X-ray identifies a person with presumptive TB.
Second, open-system reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests can handle larger volumes. Quantiplus MTB FAST is the first ICMR-validated open-system TB assay. It runs on RT-PCR machines already in public laboratories, many of them from India’s COVID-19-era testing network, and processes up to 96 samples in a single run at less than ₹200 per test. That is a fraction of the cost of current nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs), and the assay requires no new machines.
According to the report, India recorded a 38% reduction in TB mortality since 2015, compared with a global decline of 35%, alongside a 94% treatment success rate among patients with drug-susceptible TB.
The TB death rate also declined from 28 per lakh people in 2015 to 18 per lakh in 2025.
“These achievements, highlighted in the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Tuberculosis Report reflect India’s sustained progress towards eliminating TB through early detection, timely treatment, technological innovation and comprehensive patient care,” the Union health ministry said in a statement.

Such interventions are a daily occurrence at Arlington Cemetery, where swarms of tourists brush up against strict military protocol.

The rare unscripted moment and its aftermath pointed to a larger truth about the military and its relationship to the country it serves.

May, who stopped travelling to the United States last year amid Trump's repeated threats against Canada, said he and his wife Patti aren't ready to go south of the border again just yet though.

Drop in travel
Many Canadians, including those with relatives or business interests south of the border, have continued to travel to the U.S. amid Trump's threats and the trade war with Canada.

According to Statistics Canada, return border crossings from the U.S. fell by about 25 per cent in 2025 compared with the previous year.
There has been a slight increase in 2026: A total of 1.9 million return trips by car and air from the U.S. were reported in October, marking the seventh consecutive month of year-over-year growth and a three per cent increase from October 2025, Statistics Canada reported.

The IPL 2027 trade window has been marked by big names changing teams, but the more interesting story is what franchises are trying to fix. Mumbai Indians and Sunrisers Hyderabad have addressed specific squad weaknesses, while Punjab Kings has made the biggest statement by acquiring Hardik Pandya.
Punjab’s gamble, Mumbai’s gain
Punjab Kings has made the boldest move by acquiring Hardik from Mumbai Indians in exchange for Arshdeep Singh. Hardik offers an Indian seam-bowling all-rounder who can strengthen the middle order and give Punjab greater flexibility with its overseas combination.
But his value depends on how much he contributes with the ball. If his workload needs managing, Punjab could end up paying Rs. 18 crore for a middle-order batter and an occasional bowling option. His arrival also raises questions about the team’s leadership structure. Though for now, co-owner Ness Wadia has clarified that Shreyas Iyer will continue to lead.
Mumbai, meanwhile, has acquired a frontline Indian left-arm fast bowler. Arshdeep’s 111 IPL wickets in 96 matches underline his value, particularly his ability to operate with the new ball and at the death. His partnership with Jasprit Bumrah could give Mumbai a formidable Indian pace attack.
CSK and SRH: Power versus bowling depth
The four-player exchange between Chennai Super Kings and Sunrisers Hyderabad is arguably the most interesting deal of the window.
CSK has acquired Liam Livingstone for Rs. 6 crore, down from the Rs. 13 crore SRH paid for him, and Jack Edwards for Rs. 3 crore. Livingstone offers explosive middle-order batting and two types of spin, but his IPL returns have not always matched his reputation. Chennai must identify a settled batting position rather than expect him to solve its power-hitting problems immediately.
Edwards, meanwhile, is an investment in potential. He missed the 2026 season through injury and is yet to make his IPL debut. Accommodating both overseas all-rounders in the XI could also prove difficult.
SRH’s business looks more coherent. It has acquired Khaleel Ahmed and Nathan Ellis, addressing a bowling department that needed reinforcement. Khaleel returns to a franchise he represented between 2018 and 2021, while Ellis brings variations and death-bowling experience.
Considered alongside its earlier acquisition of T. Natarajan from Delhi Capitals, SRH has been proactive in addressing the weaknesses exposed last season, parting with two peripheral members of its 2026 squad to do so.
All three acquisitions come with injury concerns, but SRH has at least targeted a specific weakness. CSK, by contrast, has added players whose roles in the side remain unclear.
Delhi’s complicated reconstruction
Delhi Capitals’ two trades have produced a mixed outcome. Rishabh Pant has returned from Lucknow Super Giants for Rs. 15 crore, considerably less than the Rs. 27 crore LSG paid for him at the 2025 auction.
Pant strengthens Delhi’s batting and wicketkeeping options, besides bringing leadership experience. But the price of his return is Kuldeep Yadav, one of Delhi’s most prolific, albeit mercurial, wicket-takers. LSG has acquired an Indian wrist-spinner capable of attacking through the middle overs.
Delhi subsequently traded Natarajan to SRH and acquired Zeeshan Ansari for Rs. 40 lakh. Ansari is a promising leg-spinner, but his six wickets in 10 IPL appearances hardly make him a like-for-like replacement for an established international fast bowler.
Delhi has improved its batting identity but surrendered two proven bowling options. Its auction strategy will now be crucial. LSG, meanwhile, looks like one of the quieter beneficiaries of the window.
Who has won so far?
Mumbai and SRH have the clearest arguments behind their acquisitions. Mumbai has addressed its Indian pace requirements, while SRH has added bowling depth. LSG has secured Kuldeep, a proven middle-overs wicket-taker.
Punjab’s acquisition of Hardik has a high ceiling but carries questions about availability, workload and leadership. CSK has made an interesting investment in Livingstone, but must find the right role for him. Delhi has the most substantial rebuilding job ahead.
The financial adjustments are equally revealing. Pant’s contract has fallen from Rs. 27 crore to Rs. 15 crore, Natarajan’s from Rs. 10.75 crore to Rs. 5 crore, and Livingstone’s from Rs. 13 crore to Rs. 6 crore.
Franchises are increasingly willing to correct expensive auction decisions rather than persist with them. That matters particularly ahead of a mini-auction, where purse management and limited squad vacancies make targeted trades valuable.
The November 17 retention deadline will further shape the market before the December 16 auction in Goa.

After the India-UK Free Trade Agreement (FTA) encountered its first hurdle following its implementation in July 2026, the Commerce and Finance ministries reportedly held a meeting on Wednesday to resolve the issue of a proposed 150% customs duty on bulk Scotch whisky imports by Pernod Ricard and Diageo.
ANI, citing sources, reported that the meeting was held to address liquor companies' concerns over the classification of imported Scotch whisky. Officials from both ministries discussed the matter at length and expressed hope that it would be resolved soon.
The development comes after representatives of the International Spirits and Wine Association of India (ISWAI) and the Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies (CIABC) met Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agarwal on November 2 and raised concerns over the difference in tariff rates. Subsequently, customs officials held shipments belonging to several companies, including Pernod Ricard India, Diageo, Radico Khaitan and Allied Blenders and Distillers.
The industry has objected to a memorandum issued by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), which classified imported Scotch whisky as alcoholic beverage concentrate rather than finished whisky. This triggered a dispute over the applicable HS code and customs duty. The issue has also been described as a technical complication in the implementation of the India-UK FTA.
ANI reported, citing sources, that the Commerce Secretary assured industry representatives that the government would take a decision on the matter soon.
The HS code determines the applicable customs duty and rules. The DRI's position is that the imported products should be classified as alcoholic beverage concentrate rather than finished Scotch whisky because they enter India at a higher alcohol strength and are diluted later at a domestic facility. This classification could alter the duty calculation and raise questions about the accuracy of the original declarations.
The DRI says the imported concentrate has an alcohol content of 62–66%, compared with 42–46% for finished Scotch whisky. Since the two products fall under different HSN codes, the companies maintain that their imports qualify under the code eligible for concessions under the FTA.
DRI officials are examining whether some bulk Scotch whisky imports by the companies were classified in a manner that allowed them to claim lower customs duties under the India-UK trade agreement.
The sources clarified that the probe does not amount to a fresh increase in customs duty or establish any wrongdoing by the companies. Instead, authorities are examining which categories of Scotch imports qualify for the lower rate introduced under the India-UK trade agreement on July 15, 2026. Under the pact, the duty on eligible imports was reduced from 150% to 75%, effectively halving the rate.
However, the DRI has argued that the reduced duty applies only to finished products, including bottled, ready-to-drink Scotch, and not to bulk Scotch concentrates used in the manufacture of whisky brands.
Reuters recently reported that it had reviewed a confidential DRI memorandum dated November 4, which instructed customs officials across the country to continue applying the 150% duty on bulk Scotch imports. The memo described importers' claims for benefits under the trade agreement as "incorrect", stating that the products were concentrates or compound preparations requiring further manufacturing. It also flagged the potential for large-scale and recurring revenue implications arising from misclassification.
The classification dispute has also resulted in Scotch whisky shipments being held up at Indian ports. Reuters reported that Pernod Ricard and Diageo each have more than 40 containers awaiting clearance, while Bacardi has five containers on hold. The companies are reportedly reluctant to pay the 150% duty, and prolonged delays could disrupt supplies.
Bulk shipments account for nearly 80% of Scotch whisky imports from Britain by volume. These imports are subsequently used to produce Indian-Made Foreign Liquor (IMFL), in which Scotch is blended with other spirits and ingredients.
India's Scotch whisky imports were valued at $335 million in 2024. The Scotch Whisky Association has projected that the India-UK trade agreement could increase the value of bilateral trade by $1.34 billion over five years.

On November 12 (Thursday), Dubai Airports, which owns and operates Dubai International Airport and Al Maktoum International Airport, stopped cash-strapped SpiceJet’s check-in services over non-payment of around 14 million UAE dirhams (approximately ₹35.85 crore), even as the airline said it was working to resolve the issue without specifying how.
The action forced the airline to cancel four flights to Amritsar, Jaipur, Mumbai and Delhi on November 12. Other departures from Dubai were cancelled until the issue was resolved.
A SpiceJet spokesperson said the airline is resolving the matter with the concerned authorities. “We have adequate bank guarantee cover in place and are working to ensure that the issue is sorted out at the earliest.”
In a November 13 (Friday) communication, the airline informed BSE Limited about a meeting of the Board of Directors of the company on Wednesday (November 18) to consider and approve the proposal to raise fresh capital, including by issuing equity shares, preference shares, debt securities and/or other permissible instruments.
Operational difficulties, shrunk fleet
SpiceJet has been facing mounting financial and operational difficulties. Its fleet has shrunk to around 12 aircraft, with only nine operational, Mint reported on November 12. The airline’s domestic market share fell to 0.6% in September, down from 3.9% in January. It flew around 73,000 domestic passengers in September, compared with nearly 592,000 in January.
Data from the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) showed that SpiceJet cancelled 20.29% of its scheduled flights in September. Its on-time performance at major airports fell to 16.6%. The carrier has struggled to clear supplier dues. ₹63.03 crore owed to small businesses remained unpaid beyond the stipulated 45-day period during April-September 2026, according to regulatory filings.
In the fiscal year that ended March 2026, the Ajay Singh-promoted SpiceJet flew 6.24 million passengers (17,352 passengers daily on average), including international, through 46,063 departures (an average of 126.2 daily). It had a market share of 4.7%, as per provisional DGCA data.
From April to September 2026, departures dipped to 13,422, including international (74 daily on average). The number of passengers declined to 1.8 million, including international (2,043.87 passengers daily on average), according to DGCA data.
Neither the Civil Aviation Ministry nor the aviation regulator DGCA has announced the weekly flights each domestic carrier will operate in the ongoing winter schedule (October 25-March 2027).
A back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that SpiceJet filed around 550 arrivals and departures weekly (around 80 flights per day) under its winter schedule. But the aircraft fleet tracking website planespotter.net said the airline had only 11 aircraft (including two regional jets) in its fleet as of November 12, and 38 of them were on the ground.
Considering that one aircraft can operate an average of seven domestic flights daily, an airline roughly requires a fleet of 11-12 aircraft with some in buffer in case of a glitch.
Outstanding dues
People aware of the matter said the airline has failed to clear outstanding dues to vendors, including aircraft and engine lessors, jet fuel suppliers, and airport operators, amid a cash crunch. They added that the airline has failed to pay salaries to a majority of its employees for months.
Oil companies and air operators have put the struggling carrier on a pay-as-you-fly mode. As long as payments are not made, flights are not allowed to depart, resulting in delays and sometimes in last-minute cancellations.
The airline is struggling with an inadequate operational fleet, financial constraints, and mounting payment obligations. These factors appear to have affected its ability to operate flights as scheduled, resulting in cancelled flights, prolonged delays, uncertainty, and, in some cases, difficulties in securing refunds.
Rights and protections
The 2019 Ministry of Civil Aviation Passenger Charter, which outlines key rights and protections for air travellers and is enforced through DGCA Civil Aviation Requirements, mandates that airlines must inform passengers about a flight cancellation at least two weeks before the scheduled departure time. Airlines must arrange an alternate flight or refund, based on what the customer accepts.
The compensation includes free meals and a monetary component ranging from ₹5,000-10,000 depending on scenarios, including the nature of delay, the flight’s block time, or the booked one-way basic fare plus airline fuel charge, whichever is lower.
If a flight is delayed, passengers who have checked in on time are entitled to free meals and refreshments, depending on the waiting time.
For domestic flights expected to be delayed by over six hours, the airline must offer an alternative flight within six hours or a full refund. If the total delay exceeds 24 hours, or six hours for flights scheduled to depart between 8 pm and 3 am, the airline must provide hotel accommodation, including transfers, where applicable.
If an airline fails to provide the prescribed compensation or facilities, passengers can first approach the airline. They can also lodge a complaint through the government’s AirSewa portal or app. If they are dissatisfied with the resolution, they can approach the appropriate statutory body or court.
Airlines are exempt from paying compensation when cancellations or delays result from extraordinary circumstances beyond their control, such as adverse weather, security risks, certain Air Traffic Control restrictions, or other qualifying force majeure events.

Islamabad- At least 11 people were killed and two others injured when a passenger van plunged into a river in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir’s Gilgit-Baltistan region, police said on Friday.
The accident occurred on Thursday evening when the van was travelling from Gilgit to Yasin Valley in Ghizer district.
Police said the driver lost control of the vehicle near Morkah Bridge, causing it to plunge into the Yasin River, Dawn newspaper reported.
Rescue teams retrieved the bodies of 10 passengers, including two women, and rescued three injured passengers, including a child. They were taken to Gupis Civil Hospital for treatment.
The child later succumbed to injuries, taking the death toll to 11, police said.
The deceased and injured were residents of Yasin Valley in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK).
Police said an investigation was underway to ascertain the cause of the accident.
Road accidents are frequent in the region. Last week, eight people were killed and 30 others injured when a passenger bus travelling from Gilgit to Islamabad collided with a dumper truck near the Havelian Interchange on the Hazara Motorway, according to Dawn.

A Mexican Singer Gives Old Ballads New Heroines
Grammy-nominated songwriter Vivir Quintana is known throughout Latin America for giving voice to women who fought back against domestic violence.
Against the backdrop of a centuries-old stone church in the Mexican city of Oaxaca, the singer Vivir Quintana raised her deep, husky voice above the blare of trumpets, trombones and the booming pulse of a tuba.
Behind her stood a brass band of young Indigenous girls in embroidered white blouses and brightly colored skirts. Hat in hand and fist raised, Ms. Quintana sang a corrido, a traditional Mexican folk ballad usually used to recount tales of revolutionaries, outlaws, folk heroes, and more recently, drug traffickers.
Corridos are typically sung by men, about men. Ms. Quintana sang a corrido she wrote based on the true story of a woman who fought back when her abusive partner tried to gouge out her eyes with a knife.
“I used to think that what united us women was our pain. Now I have realized it is love and resistance,” Ms. Quintana told the crowd in October during a women’s conference in Oaxaca called Decididas, drawing a roar of applause. “We must keep defending ourselves!”
On Thursday, Ms. Quintana will take the stage at the Latin Grammy Awards in Las Vegas alongside the Colombian pop superstar Juanes, with whom she is nominated for song of the year for “Humano.” It is her second Latin Grammy nomination.
