To optimize WhatsApp privacy, hide your Last Seen, Online status, profile info, and status sharing under Settings > Privacy. Turn off read receipts, silence unknown callers, restrict group invites, disable link previews, and enable disappearing messages, passkeys, two-step verification, biometric locks, and end-to-end encrypted backups.
I don’t need to specifically tell you about WhatsApp’s popularity. It has billions of users worldwide, and it is the go-to messaging app for many people. Thanks to the network effect, most popular messaging apps haven’t replaced WhatsApp, even with better features and privacy.
One of the biggest reasons most people use WhatsApp, besides the fact that their friends or family are already on it, is that it is free to use. And since Meta owns it, free usually comes with a caveat. And that’s your data and how Meta tracks your WhatsApp chats. Although your chats are encrypted and Meta openly says it won’t use your data for advertising, you can talk to a friend on WhatsApp and still see relevant ads on other Meta platforms like Instagram instantly. Don’t you believe me? Just try it once.
Fortunately, WhatsApp also offers various privacy settings to keep your conversations private, prevent scams, and more. In this ultimate guide, we’ll cover all the privacy settings you need to enable on WhatsApp for maximum privacy. This guide includes all the methods, and I update it frequently and make changes if the features or flow change. Bookmark this page and revisit it anytime to keep your WhatsApp privacy settings up to date.
Table of Contents
WhatsApp Privacy Settings You Should Enable
Hide your Last Seen and Online status
If you care about your privacy and don’t want your people to know when you were online and when you last used the app, WhatsApp allows you to hide the last seen and online status completely
By default, WhatsApp shows the exact time when you last used the app and shows users when you are actually using the app
While these two features let others know when you use WhatsApp, they can also be a downside, especially if others are expecting an immediate reply when they see you online
Fortunately, WhatsApp lets you disable your last seen and completely hide your status. It also gives you more flexibility by letting you hide these from specific contacts, from your contacts, or disable them entirely for everyone.
Here is how to hide your last seen and online status on WhatsApp:
Open WhatsApp on your Android or iPhone and tap the You tab in the bottom-right corner, then tap Privacy.
Now scroll down and, under Who can see your personal info, tap Last seen and online. To hide it from everyone, select Nobody. To show it only to my contacts, select My contacts; to show it only to specific contacts, tap My contacts except.
Hide your profile photo, About, and Links from strangers
Like Last Seen and online status, WhatsApp also shows your profile picture and About to contacts. This also applies to contacts you have outside your network.
Fortunately, like Last Seen and Online Status, WhatsApp also lets you hide your profile photo and About info from strangers, specific contacts, or no one.
How to hide your profile and About from strangers
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture in the bottom right corner of the screen, then tap on Privacy, and then tap on the Profile Picture option
Now you can hide your profile picture, About, and links. To hide it from everyone, set it to Nobody.
If you want to share with all your contacts, select My contacts. To share your profile picture only with specific contacts, tap My contacts except and select the contacts you want to hide your profile picture, About, and links from.
Control who can see and reshare your Status
WhatsApp’s status feature is slowly turning into Instagram Stories. You can now also reshare statuses on WhatsApp. However, unlike Last Seen, this feature is disabled by default.
If you accidentally enabled it and don’t want others to share your status, you can turn off sharing in the status privacy settings. From there, you can also turn off Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your WhatsApp status from being shared on other platforms.
How to turn off status sharing on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, and from here tap on the privacy option
Scroll down, tap Status, then turn off Allow sharing and set your status to be visible only to my contacts. You can also remove specific people by setting up exceptions for contacts, or you can share only with specific contacts. From the bottom, also disable Facebook Stories and Instagram Stories to prevent your status from automatically sharing to Facebook and Instagram Stories.
Turn off read receipts
Even if you hide your online status and last seen on WhatsApp, read receipts can still show blue checkmarks when you read their messages. However, if you don’t want them to know you have read their messages and feel pressured to reply instantly, or if you want better privacy and to balance work and personal WhatsApp chats, you can disable read receipts.
Remember, if you disable it, you also cannot see whether they have read your messages. WhatsApp only shows grey ticks even if you read their messages.
Here is how to turn off read receipts on WhatsApp
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture. Scroll down and tap Privacy. Scroll down again and turn off Read Receipts.
Stop strangers from adding you to groups
Another feature that WhatsApp turns on by default is the ability to let your contacts add you to any groups. This includes the number you have temporarily shared with users you don’t know, and once you add it to the group, your number will be shared with everyone in that group, which is a total privacy nightmare.
Fortunately, WhatsApp allows you to stop random people from adding you to groups.
How to stop people from adding you to random groups
Open WhatsApp and tap on your profile picture, then tap on the privacy option
Scroll down and tap on Groups, then select who can add you to groups. However, WhatsApp doesn’t let you set nobody as an option, but you can still do it by selecting My contacts except and selecting all contacts.
Silence calls from unknown numbers
Since WhatsApp primarily requires your phone number to create an account, once your number is exposed, anyone can contact you on WhatsApp. This is why many of us often receive spam business calls.
However, you can silence unknown calls so that you won’t get notified of random spam calls.
How to silence unknown callers on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp, tap on your profile picture, and tap on the privacy option
Now scroll down, tap on Calls, and enable the Silence unknown callers option
Make new chats disappear automatically
WhatsApp now supports disappearing messages, which deletes chats from both the sender and receiver after a set time. WhatsApp allows you to enable disappearing messages for individual chats or for the entire WhatsApp for up to 90 days
This is especially useful if you don’t want the other person to save your chats.
Since WhatsApp keeps your messages forever even if you delete your own copy, the other person’s phone still has everything.
When you turn on disappearing messages, WhatsApp also prevents the other person from taking a screenshot and reminds you when they try to save a specific chat.
How to enable disappearing messages on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, then tap Privacy. From here, tap on Default message timer and select how many days you want to set for WhatsApp. You can select up to 90 days or even 24 hours.

How to stop WhatsApp from showing media in your device gallery
Open WhatsApp, tap your profile picture, scroll down, tap Chats, then under Chat settings, disable Media visibility.
Turn on two-step verification with a password
WhatsApp also supports two-step verification to prevent your account from getting hacked. While WhatsApp sends a six-digit SMS code for verification, someone with access to that code can log in to your WhatsApp account. However, you can set a second verification method, such as a password, to prevent anyone from accessing your WhatsApp.
Here is how having two-factor authentication adds better security for your WhatsApp account.

Now create a new password. Tap Create password and create a new password.
Once you add two-factor authentication, remember to add a recovery email. This is especially useful if you lose your network; your email acts as a secondary verification method, where WhatsApp sends a code to your email instead of sending a verification SMS.
Create a passkey for phishing-proof login
WhatsApp also added support for passkeys; if you’re not sure what a passkey is, we have explained it in a detailed guide.
Passkeys use your fingerprint or Face ID for authentication instead of depending on SMS or passwords. Setting up passkeys lets you log in to your WhatsApp account using your device ID, which is unique to you.
But it also comes with downsides: if someone else has registered a Face ID or fingerprint, they can also log in to your WhatsApp account, so keep note of it.
How to enable passkeys for your WhatsApp account
To enable passkeys, open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner, then tap Account. From here, under the Login and Security section, tap on Passkeys. Then follow the on-screen instructions to create a passkey.
Turn on security notifications
Next, enable security notifications on your WhatsApp account so WhatsApp notifies you if someone switches phones, reinstalls WhatsApp, or changes linked devices. This could also mean someone else accessed their WhatsApp account and signed in on a new device. Turn on security notifications and confirm with the other person why the security key changed.
How to enable security notifications on WhatsApp
To do that, open WhatsApp on your phone. Tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen, then tap Account. Scroll down, tap Security notifications, and turn on the option that says Show security notifications on this device.
Check linked devices and log out unknown sessions
WhatsApp lets you link and use your account on multiple devices. However, this could also mean someone could link your account to their device without you knowing. So, if you are suspicious about your account activity, you can check linked devices and sign out of any you don’t recognize.
How to check linked devices and log out of unknown devices on your WhatsApp account
Lock WhatsApp with your Biometrics
WhatsApp includes a native app lock feature that lets you lock it with your fingerprint or a pattern. WhatsApp also lets you lock immediately or after a set time. Turn on Advanced chat privacy for sensitive chats
While disappearing messages remove your chat after a set period, you can turn on Advanced Chat Privacy for chats with sensitive content. Hide your IP address in calls
WhatsApp also supports voice calls. Direct calls can connect your phone to another person’s phone, which can reveal your IP address and, in turn, your location. However, WhatsApp allows you to hide your IP during calls. Here is how.
How to protect your IP address in calls

Disable link previews
WhatsApp also supports link previews, which show a preview of the website content. However, to do that, your phone connects to your website and sends a request from your IP address.

How to disable link previews on WhatsApp?
Open WhatsApp and tap your profile picture in the bottom-right corner of the screen. Scroll down and tap on Privacy. From here, scroll down again, tap Advanced, and enable Disable link previews.
Block floods of messages from unknown accounts
WhatsApp also introduced a new feature that blocks messages from unknown accounts. It blocks unknown accounts that send you high volumes of messages, which is especially useful if you receive frequent spam texts or your WhatsApp is being bombed with multiple messages.

Encrypt your chat backup

North Korean hackers used fake video calls in $400m crypto hack, says FBI
- Published
State-sponsored hackers from North Korea have taken more than $400 million in cryptocurrency by using fake video calls to steal people's identities, US authorities say.
More than 900 victims have fallen prey to the scheme, which the FBI refers to as FaceStealer, in the last 18 months, according to the bureau.
"The North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years," says FBI cyber director Brett Leatherman.
This comes a week after the world's largest crypto exchange Binance revealed that hackers had used fake job interviews to steal a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from the company.
US law enforcement agencies attributed the Binance hack, thought to be the largest crypto hack to date, to North Korea-linked actors. Pyongyang has denied this claim.
Authorities say FaceStealer, the latest scheme, "aggressively targets" those who work in the cryptocurrency and web3 sectors, particularly those who are involved in the development and maintenance of open-source software.
According to the FBI and US Justice Department, FaceStealer hackers use fake or hijacked social media accounts to invite potential victims into video calls hosted over "imposter versions" of Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet.
Next, the hackers play pre-recorded videos of previous victims the target is acquainted with to simulate a legitimate call – except that the audio would appear to malfunction.
A message then pops up on the target's screen, asking them to "fix" the audio by clicking on a link. This "fix" would eventually download malware onto the target's device, which allows hackers to access their contact lists and apps, widening their pool of potential victims.
Hackers would secretly record these calls and use the recordings as material to scam their new victims, according to the US authorities.
The FBI has described FaceStealer as "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user".
"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships," Patrick Grandy, assistant director in charge of the bureau's Los Angeles field office, said in a statement on Thursday.
"If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough."

U.S. envoys meet with Putin in the Kremlin after Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi
MOSCOW — U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys met Thursday with President Vladimir Putin as Washington sought new momentum in peace efforts after two days of U.S.-mediated negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations.
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, brokered the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Those were the first direct discussions between representatives of Moscow and Kyiv in nine months as the push for peace stalled.
The two days of talks that ended Wednesday produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced.
Kushner and Witkoff went straight to the Kremlin to brief Putin in a meeting that lasted about two hours and are scheduled to fly to Dublin, Ireland, for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.
U.S. envoys want Europe at the negotiating table, too
Kushner said that one of the goals of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader's blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent's broader security arrangements.
The U.S. and Zelenskyy want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.
But Moscow doesn't want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent.
Many in Europe see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO's eastward expansion as a main security threat to Russia. Putin has demanded the trans-Atlantic alliance's troops be pulled back from Russia's borders.
Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine — a possibility that alarms European leaders.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi "agreed on many of the principles, but are still apart on some of the way to accomplish" peace, Kushner said in Moscow.
Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire would be "absolutely unacceptable" and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate targets. "In other words, the war would resume immediately," he said.
He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.
Zelenskyy sees a political "window of opportunity"
Zelenskyy is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.
Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are "very much aligned" on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. "But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire," Rutte said.
Zelenskyy said political changes, including Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following midterm elections and balloting in France next year, could bring "a window of opportunity" for a peace deal.
"The political landscape in Europe could change in 2027. … We also see changes already taking place in the United States," Zelenskyy said in Dublin late Wednesday.
He called the proposed prisoner exchange a positive step but also insisted Ukraine won't surrender Russian-occupied territory in return for peace.
Russia and Ukraine have occasionally swapped prisoners, but both sides remain far apart in their terms for accepting a settlement.
Fighting continues as another bitter winter approaches
Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.
Russia's bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow's drone and missile strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a "weaponization of winter."
Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.
Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.
U.S. Starlink problems return, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelenskyy said Thursday on social media.
Military units have recorded "significant disruptions," including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelenskyy said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.
Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.
Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.
Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn't be used for offensive strikes against Russia.
Zelenskyy said in Dublin that the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on. "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going," he said.
Russian colonel reportedly killed by a car bomb
A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to Russia's Investigative Committee, the country's main criminal investigation agency. It didn't identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing.
The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.
Several senior Russian military officers have been killed by bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.

Sepahvand intended to physically carry out a ‘violent attack’ against at least one of the targets

Two Iranian men have been found guilty of spying on journalists and a lawyer in conduct that was likely to assist Iran’s intelligence service.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in a bid to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.
These “subjects” included journalists for London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.
The defendants were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online.
The prosecution said Sepahvand intended to physically carry out a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets, while Farhad Javadi Manesh, who was also convicted of engaging in conduct likely to assist Iran’s intelligence service, assisted in planning.
Sepahvand lent forward and held his head in his hands when they were found guilty on Thursday after a trial at Woolwich Crown Court.
Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was cleared of the same charge after jurors deliberated for 19 hours and nine minutes.
Manesh and Noori were acquitted of engaging in surveillance and reconnaissance, with the intention that serious violence against a person in the UK would be committed by others.
Frank Ferguson, chief Crown prosecutor of the CPS’s Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said: “This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime.
“Sepahvand and Manesh were promised rewards to send intelligence back to contacts in Iran, and Sepahvand himself was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit serious violence against their targets.
“Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place.
“Cases like this show Iranian intelligence’s willingness to use proxies to target the regime’s critics abroad.
“The CPS is alive to these ever-evolving threats and, through our work with Counter Terrorism Policing, stands ready to prosecute any hostile actors who might try and jeopardise our country’s security.”

Sydney Swans players will not be charged after hotel incident, police say
- Published
Four top Australian Football League (AFL) players who were investigated in relation to an alleged sexual assault at a hotel in Melbourne earlier this year will not be charged, police have said.
After a "thorough investigation and based on legal advice" police would not proceed with criminal charges due to "insufficient evidence", police said in a statement.
Four Sydney Swans players - Isaac Heeney, James Jordon, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey, who now plays for North Melbourne - had been suspended for the rest of the season over the incident in August.
The men previously denied wrongdoing but apologised for breaching club standards by inviting women back to the hotel after a game and drinking.
Australian media reported that three women, understood to be adult entertainers, had alleged inappropriate touching during the incident at the Pullman Hotel and are looking into civil action.
"Due to the ongoing civil matter, Victoria Police is unable to make further comment," police said in a statement on Friday.
A fifth player, Riley Bice, who was also suspended by the club, had already been cleared by police.
A lawyer for one of the women said she was "devastated" by the police decision.
Jackson Pannam, of Slater and Gordon law firm, added that the move "does not amount to a finding that the incident our client reported did not occur, nor does it diminish the seriousness of what she says happened or its profound impact on her".
John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, acting for the other two women, told the ABC his clients were "very disappointed and distressed".
They would "vigorously pursue" a civil action, he said.
"My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said.
Heeney welcomed the police announcement, saying the past three months had been "incredibly difficult for my family, [my fiancee] Steffie and those close to me".
"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice," he continued.
The Swans said in a statement that it had been "clear from the outset" that its decision to suspend the players was "separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision".
"The Club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," it said.
Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich told reporters it was "not a day for anyone to really celebrate" and "we're still looking very hard at the programme and understanding where we need to get better".
He said the club would be doing everything to "restore the standards that this club has held for a long period of time".
In a separate statement the AFL acknowledged the police decision and said it reserved the right to investigate should any further relevant information come to light.

Reliance Industries Ltd, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions Pvt. Ltd, Megha Engineering and Infrastructures Ltd, JSW Neo Energy Ltd, Exide Energy Solutions Ltd, ACME Solar Holdings Ltd and Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies Pvt. Ltd are among 22 bidders shortlisted for the Centre’s 10GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) tender under the ₹18,100 crore production-linked incentive scheme for advanced chemistry cells (PLI-ACC). The PLI-ACC scheme aims to create 50GWh of domestic cell-making capacity. The latest 10GWh tender follows the allocation of incentives for the remaining 40GWh to Ola Electric (20GWh), Reliance Industries and its subsidiary Reliance New Energy Ltd (15GWh), and Rajesh Exports Ltd (5GWh), which has faced controversy. In June, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) alleged that Rajesh Exports and its promoters were responsible for financial misrepresentation to the tune of ₹15 trillion. This 10GWh capacity, for which the government has shortlisted 22 bidders, was earmarked for grid-scale storage in light of the country's growing power requirements and renewable energy deployment, whereas earlier incentive allocations were end-use-agnostic, the ministry of heavy industries said on Thursday. The tender is significant because ₹3,620 crore in government incentives will be available to selected bidders once they make the required investments in cell manufacturing and begin selling domestically made advanced chemistry cells, according to the scheme guidelines and tender documents. The remaining shortlisted companies are: Avaada Electro Ltd, Fujiyama Power Systems Ltd, GK Energy Ltd, Godawari New Energy Pvt. Ltd, JPM Energy Solutions Pvt. Ltd, Lineage Power Pvt. Ltd, Mahendra Sponge and Power Ltd, Nsure Reliable Power Solutions Pvt. Ltd, Renew Photovoltaics Pvt. Ltd, Sai Bioenergy Pvt. Ltd, Shirdi Sai Electricals Ltd, Sun Drops Energia Ltd, Utex New Energy Pvt. Ltd, Vikram Solar Ltd, Zetsol Energy Pvt. Ltd. Mint's queries emailed to Reliance, Waree, Amara Raja and Exide late on Thursday evening did not receive an immediate response. Launched in 2021, the PLI ACC scheme has failed to gain traction, with disbursements under the flagship battery-manufacturing incentive scheme remaining at zero. The government has previously cited a lack of available technology and skilled manpower, delays in importing critical machinery, and the unavailability of upstream components as key reasons developers have been unable to meet their targets. As of February 2026, Ola Electric had developed 1GWh of cell-manufacturing capacity, while the other beneficiaries had developed none. Mint reported in August that the government had given Ola Electric and Reliance New Energy an extension to complete their respective projects by 2031, while the third beneficiary, Rajesh Exports, was not given one in light of the Sebi investigation. The extension applied only to companies that won contracts in the first round in 2022. Reliance secured another 10GWh in a subsequent round in September 2024, with a gestation period until July 2027 and incentives running until 2032. That allocation has not received any extension. The tender for grid-scale energy storage is significant because it is critical for storing surplus electricity and supplying it when demand rises. India routinely curtails solar generation during peak daylight hours because of inadequate storage capacity, forcing renewable power to be backed down when the grid cannot absorb the excess. BESS, seen as critical to the global shift away from fossil fuels, are also key to India’s energy transition. They store electricity and feed it into the grid during peak demand. India aims to achieve 500GW of non-fossil fuel capacity, including wind and solar, by 2030. Before Fireside, Mohanty had spent about seven years as a principal at IvyCap Ventures from 2013 to 2020, and was involved in deals for listed jewellery giant BlueStone, BiryaniByKilo and Vinculum. The key departures come less than a year after Fireside announced the final close of its Fund IV at ₹2,265 Cr (about $253 Mn) in December 2025. With Singh’s exit, the firm is being led by founder and managing partner Kanwaljit Singh and cofounders and partners Kannan Sitaram and Dipanjan Basu. The fund drew commitments from LPs including the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (ADIA), Investment Corporation of Dubai, HarbourVest, Waterfield and Fidelity International. With Fund IV, Fireside's assets under management across four funds stand at ₹5,300 Cr (about $650 Mn).

In the Israeli legislative elections held in late October 2026, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority required to govern. The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, alongside other opposition factions, won 48 seats. Notably, Arab-led parties made historic gains, winning 19 seats and becoming potential “kingmakers”. Following the vote, President Isaac Herzog formally accepted the results. He opened a two-day consultation window with party leaders to determine who is best positioned to assemble a stable coalition.
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament building.
Fact: The video does not show the Palestinian flag being hoisted in the Israeli Parliament. It shows a pro-Palestine activist replacing the German national flag with a Palestinian flag on a flagpole outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on 08 November 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring visuals similar to those seen in the viral video. According to these reports, the incident took place outside the Reichstag building, which houses the German Parliament (Bundestag), in Berlin on Sunday, 08 November 2026.
The reports (here, here) state that a 22-year-old pro-Palestine activist climbed a 30-metre-high flagpole in front of the Reichstag building at around 11:30 am, removed the German national flag, and replaced it with a Palestinian flag.
The group ‘Peacefully Against Genocide‘ claimed responsibility for the incident, stating that the action was a protest against the German government’s pro-Israel policy and its silence on alleged human rights violations in Gaza.
According to a press release issued by Berlin Police on 08 November 2026, two people who allegedly assisted the 22-year-old activist were detained and later released after their identities were established. The Palestinian flag was subsequently removed with the assistance of the Berlin Fire Brigade. Police also launched an investigation into suspected offences, including insulting state symbols, damaging government property, trespassing, and violating Berlin’s assembly law.
To sum up, the viral video shows the Palestinian flag hoisted outside the German Parliament, not the Israeli Parliament.

A widespread outage at Microsoft brought Outlook, Teams and several other Microsoft 365 applications to a standstill for thousands of users globally on Thursday. Users faced disruption accessing emails, work files and productivity tools for over 10 hours during the outage. The disruption also spilled over to third-party platforms, with OpenAI and Anthropic reporting issues with their Microsoft 365 connectors. As per outage reports on Downdetector, outages in India peaked at 2,162 around 11:44 PM on Thursday (November 12. Reports climbed again to 2,254 around 8:59 AM. Globally, Downdetector recorded more than 38,000 reports of Microsoft 365 problems and around 4,500 reports related to Microsoft Teams at around 2:07 PM ET on Thursday. Microsoft initially attributed the disruption to elevated load across its infrastructure in multiple regions. Later, it clarified that the issue was not driven by an increase in traffic but by several servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable, placing additional pressure on the remaining infrastructure. In an update on X, the company said it had paused all deployments, redirected additional traffic away from the affected infrastructure and begun restoring services. "We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure. We're working to safely return them to service," Microsoft said. Microsoft has been issuing regular updates on X about its efforts to restore services. The company initially said it was testing a configuration change to address a problem that was causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable. However, the recovery efforts did not provide the expected relief. Microsoft subsequently found that a core process on affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, resulting in capacity loss. It also found that some of the servers that returned to service became unresponsive again upon receiving traffic. To address the issue, Microsoft began redirecting traffic through alternative routes, temporarily restricting certain types of traffic and adjusting network protocols. It also introduced strategic traffic-blocking measures to improve server stability. In a subsequent update, the company said these measures had resulted in partial recovery across some regions but had not delivered sustained service restoration. Microsoft said it was exploring alternative approaches to address persistent traffic management imbalances and improve infrastructure stability. In its latest update on X, posted today, Microsoft said it was pursuing multiple workstreams to reduce the impact of the outage. “We're engaged in multiple workstreams to alleviate impact, address our current blocker, and returning portions of service infrastructure back to a healthy state. A more comprehensive update can be found at MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, as well as http://status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is not available to you,” the company posted. What Services Were Affected? The disruption primarily affected services dependent on Exchange Online, Microsoft's cloud-based email and messaging platform. Outlook users faced difficulties accessing their mailboxes through web, desktop and mobile applications. Email delivery was also delayed, while some users reported connectivity issues. The disruption extended to Microsoft 365 applications, with users experiencing difficulties accessing recently used files. Some pages in the Microsoft 365 admin centre also failed to load. Microsoft Copilot was among the affected services. Users reported problems loading Copilot Chat and receiving responses through web and desktop applications. Its ability to retrieve work-related information, including emails, calendars and files, was also disrupted. Microsoft Teams continued to support core messaging and online meetings largely normally. However, features dependent on Exchange Online, including calendars and meeting scheduling, were affected. Some users also reported difficulties creating chats in organisations using Information Barriers. Other affected services included Microsoft Planner, Microsoft To Do, Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Graph, Microsoft Fabric, Power BI, SharePoint Online, Universal Print and Windows 365. The outage extended beyond Microsoft's own applications, affecting third-party services that depend on its infrastructure. OpenAI said it was investigating an issue with its Microsoft connectors that could prevent new connections from being established and cause certain tools to malfunction. Anthropic also reported an issue with an upstream provider affecting its Microsoft 365 connector. The disruption highlighted how outages in widely used cloud infrastructure can have a cascading impact on businesses and services that rely on third-party integrations. The outage also affected businesses and government organisations that depend on Microsoft's tech suite. Microsoft earlier reported an outage affecting its Azure cloud platform in October 2026, which disrupted its productivity software suite and affected businesses across several industries. The latest update indicates that the recovery process is still ongoing, with the company yet to confirm a complete restoration of affected services.

Congo's Ebola cases have crossed 11,000 cases in another development that shows the severity of the outbreak.
Also Read: Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow spread in African countries
The latest Health Ministry data on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) showed 11,042 people have been infected by the deadly virus that has now killed 5,387, nearly half of those infected, in the country's deadliest outbreak.
Since the outbreak was declared mid-May, Congolese authorities have struggled to contain it due to a series of factors including conflicts and a health system crisis.
The Bundibugyo virus responsible for this outbreak has no known vaccine or treatment and has spread to the eight of the country's 26 Provinces.
Dozens of Ebola outbreaks have been reported since the disease was first discovered in 1976. The largest and deadliest occurred in West Africa from 2014 to 2016, with 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.
The current outbreak already ranks second, and has had at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared compared with the West Africa outbreak. Health officials declared the outbreak in May, but medical evidence suggests infections were occurring months earlier.

A promising new medicine against heart disease fails unexpectedly
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
An experimental drug doctors hoped would be the next big advance in preventing heart attacks and strokes failed a crucial test, researchers reported Saturday.
The medicine, which reduces levels of a particle in the blood associated with heart attacks and strokes, didn't protect volunteers in a closely watched study.
"I was shocked. I had high hopes for success," says Steven Nissen, a cardiologist at the Cleveland Clinic who led the study. "Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death in developed countries. And so we really were hoping to find additional therapies that would reduce risk."
The research aimed to help people who seem to do everything right. They keep their cholesterol and blood pressure low, eat well, maintain a healthy weight, and exercise regularly. But many still suffer heart attacks and strokes.
"That sort of patient we see very frequently, and we were really doing our best to try to find a way to help those patients," Nissen says.
Many of these patients have elevated blood levels of a cholesterol-carrying protein called lipoprotein(a) or Lp(a), which has long been thought to increase the risk for heart disease.
"About 20% of the global population have elevated levels. And that's about a billion people. So it's a common disorder," Nissen says.
Researchers have been searching for a drug to lower Lp(a)
Until recently, doctors didn't have any drugs that could lower Lp(a) levels. But several drug companies have developed experimental new medications in recent years that can slash elevated Lp(a).
So Nissen and his colleagues gave 8,350 adults who already had heart disease either a placebo or a drug called pelacarsen, which cuts Lp(a).
The drug did suppress Lp(a) levels by about 78%, the researchers showed. But after five years, that drop didn't translate into saving people from suffering cardiovascular complications.
"Very disappointing, terribly disappointing," says Nissen, who presented the first details about the study at an American Heart Association meeting in Chicago Saturday and published more specifics in the New England Journal of Medicine and the NEJM Evidence.
Drugmaker Novartis, which sponsored the study, announced last month that the study results hadn't met its goals but without releasing specifics.
In a statement, Novartis said the study "provides meaningful evidence" about the relationship between Lp(a) and heart disease and may "help inform future approaches to cardiovascular management." "Progress in science depends on pursuing challenging questions and studies [like the pelacarsen study] play a crucial role in moving the field forward, even if the results are not what we had hoped for," the company said.
What went wrong?
The failure of the drug to help patients is stunning because so many scientists, doctors and drug companies hoped Lp(a)-lowering drugs would provide the next major weapon in the fight against cardiovascular disease, which kills more than 900,000 Americans each year.
"I think it's a big deal because the expectation was so high that this would end up being positive," says Harlan Krumholz, a Yale University cardiologist. "And so it was really jarring to see this."
Researchers are scratching their heads about what went wrong.
It could turn out that high Lp(a) doesn't actually cause heart attacks and strokes, but instead is a marker for something else that increases the risk.
There could be other reasons for why the study failed.
"Maybe you need to treat longer. You may need to treat earlier, before people have advanced hardening of the arteries," says Roger Blumenthal, a cardiologist at Johns Hopkins University.
Another possibility is that Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only help people with higher Lp(a) levels.
"Maybe a higher Lp(a) should have been required for entry into the trial," says David Maron, a Stanford University cardiologist who serves as the president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology.
The pelacarsen study could also have failed because Lp(a)-lowering drugs may only benefit people whose blood pressure and bad cholesterol weren't as well controlled, several experts said.
Another explanation could be that there's something about pelacarsen, the experimental drug, that doesn't produce a benefit.
It's possible other Lp(a)-lowering drugs might.
Several other drugmakers, including Amgen and Eli Lilly, are testing other experimental Lp(a)-lowering drugs. The results of those trials are expected to become available over the next few years.
"The take-home message is the story's not over," says Karol Watson, a cardiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. "It's kind of just starting."

A Mumbai-based man's account of his cook's monthly earnings of ₹1.05 lakh has sparked a discussion about income, financial security and conventional measures of professional success. The cook reportedly earns through assignments across multiple households and by catering to film crews during night shoots. He is now planning his first international holiday with friends, with Thailand as the destination. In a LinkedIn post, Manuraaj Garg compared the cook's financial circumstances with those of some of his MBA-educated friends. He highlighted how multiple sources of income, a limited commute and relatively low expenses have shaped the cook's approach to money. Garg detailed the cook's earnings from different assignments. The cook charges ₹18,000 for preparing meals twice a day at Garg's home. He earns another ₹16,500 from a flat in the same building and ₹38,000 from a larger family nearby for cooking and managing kitchen-related work. The cook also works at a film set on Friday nights, preparing food for the crew during night shoots. “Friday nights he’s at a film set – feeding a unit through a night shoot, dal-chawal at 1 am while the hero does retakes: ₹7,500 a night,” Garg said. Garg added that the cook's wife earns ₹45,000 a month, taking their combined household income to approximately ₹1.5 lakh. Comparing these earnings with the financial realities of some of his MBA-educated friends, Garg said higher salaries do not necessarily translate into equivalent disposable income once taxes, equated monthly instalments (EMIs) and childcare expenses are accounted for. “What’s actually left for the month is often his number – without the paper.” Garg also drew attention to the difference between the cook's earnings and the formal employment structures followed by salaried professionals. “His money has never met the system. No Form 16, no TDS, no CTC breakup, no 'variable component'. Not because he’s hiding – the system was simply never built to see him,” he said, adding that what the cook earns is what he gets to keep. The cook's work is spread across four employers, all within a two-kilometre radius. According to Garg, this arrangement allows him to diversify his income rather than depend on a single employer. Losing one assignment would affect only a portion of his earnings. Garg also said the cook regularly receives enquiries from prospective employers willing to pay more for reliable service. He contrasted this with the experiences of some of his IIT-educated friends, who sometimes struggle to receive responses from employers even after completing multiple interview rounds. Another difference, Garg noted, is the cook's approach to spending. He does not face the same pressure to maintain an expensive lifestyle or meet social expectations around cars, schooling and appearances. “His financial advisor is one sentence: 'Arre pagal hai kya, bahut mehenga hai.' My friends’ financial advisor is also one sentence: 'Chalo yaar, let’s do it,'” Garg wrote. Despite his relatively cautious approach to spending, the cook does have an indulgence: the latest iPhone Pro, which he purchased on EMI. Garg said he otherwise avoids unnecessary expenses and is careful about his spending. The 34-year-old is now preparing for his first international holiday with friends. The planned Thailand trip will also mark his first flight and his first passport. Garg recalled sharing travel tips with the cook, including recommendations to visit Maya Bay, sample street food and rent a scooter. Their conversation, he said, briefly moved beyond the employer-employee relationship as they exchanged travel stories and holiday plans. “For ten minutes, nobody was anybody’s employer – just two boys talking Thailand,” he wrote, adding that his wife eventually asked them to return to their respective work. Concluding his post, Garg questioned conventional ways of measuring financial well-being. “He is not poor. He is not rich. He is something our spreadsheets don’t have a column for: a man whose maths still works,” he said. Through the account, Garg highlighted how multiple income sources, manageable expenses and personal spending choices can shape an individual's financial circumstances beyond the conventional measures of salary and job titles. Srinagar- Fresh snowfall continued in several higher reaches of Jammu and Kashmir on Friday, bringing down temperatures and disrupting road connectivity, while Sonamarg in central Kashmir received the season’s first snowfall, officials said.
Sadhna Top and Razdan Pass received over a foot of snow during the past 24 hours, while Sinthan Top recorded 8-10 inches of fresh snowfall, they said.
Z-Gali and Margan Top received 6-8 inches of snow each, while Zojila Pass recorded 5-6 inches. Peer Ki Gali received 5-8 inches, Baltal 4-6 inches and Gurez Valley 3-5 inches of fresh snowfall.
Sonamarg recorded 2-3 inches of snow, while Gulmarg received around one centimetre, officials said, as per news agency KNO.
Fresh snowfall was also reported from the higher reaches of Doda and Rajouri districts in the Jammu region, intensifying cold conditions across the Union Territory.
Meanwhile, the Mughal Road, which connects south Kashmir’s Shopian district with the twin districts of Poonch and Rajouri, remained closed for the second consecutive day following heavy snowfall at Pir Ki Gali.
The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) has launched snow-clearance operations along the road, but continued snowfall is likely to hamper restoration efforts. Officials said the road could be reopened for traffic on Friday, subject to favourable weather conditions.
Snow-clearance operations have also been initiated along the Chowkibal-Tangdhar road in north Kashmir’s Kupwara district.
The Meteorological Centre Srinagar has forecast generally cloudy weather, with light to moderate rain in the plains and snowfall in higher reaches at most places on Friday.
For November 14 and 15, the weather department has predicted brief spells of light rain and snowfall at a few places. Generally dry weather is expected across Jammu and Kashmir from November 16 to 20.
The MeT department has also forecast a drop of 6-8 degrees Celsius in daytime temperatures during November 12 and 13, with thunderstorms, hailstorms and gusty winds likely at isolated places.
Advising farmers to ensure safe storage of harvested crops, the department cautioned that moderate to heavy snowfall in higher reaches could disrupt traffic on important mountain passes and hilly roads.
Travellers, transporters and tourists have been advised to plan their journeys accordingly and follow traffic advisories issued by the authorities.

The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has imposed a penalty of ₹10 Lakh on ANI Technologies Pvt Ltd, parent of ride-hailing platform Ola, for misleading customers into paying extra to improve their chances of getting a ride. In an order dated November 10, the consumer watchdog said Ola's advance tipping feature is an unfair trade practice and an unfair contract under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The CCPA also directed Ola to stop the practice immediately, pay the penalty within 15 days of receiving the order and submit a compliance report within the same period. The proceedings followed a complaint received against this issue where the app prompted users to pay extra to get bookings faster. "Adding a tip might help increase the chances of getting a ride faster,” a message read. Customers were initially offered preset amounts ranging from ₹10 to ₹40. These later increased to as much as ₹140, while customers could also enter custom amounts of up to ₹499. Ola argued that the payment was voluntary and went directly to drivers. It said the feature encouraged drivers to accept rides that were less attractive to them, particularly those requiring longer distances to reach passengers. The company also said that tipping did not affect its ride allocation system or guarantee faster ride confirmation. However, the CCPA found that Ola's own data did not support its claims. Data for June 1-15, 2026, showed that in Delhi, drivers accepted 38% of ride requests with an add-on, compared with 62% of requests without one. In Bengaluru, the acceptance rates were 40% and 68%, respectively, while in Mumbai they stood at 39% and 68%. The authority also noted that Ola changed the feature's name from 'tip' to 'add-on' on May 22, 2025, but continued to show messages suggesting that additional payments could help customers get a ride faster. During a hearing in June 2026, Ola demonstrated that its app still displayed messages such as "Improve your chances of quicker ride confirmation!" alongside preset payment amounts. The CCPA said the change in wording did not alter how the feature worked. The authority also examined Ola's data for Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai for June 1-15, 2026. The platform received nearly 39.94 Lakh ride requests across the three cities, of which 3.93 Lakh, or around 9.8%, included an add-on. Drivers accepted 1.51 Lakh of these requests. Based on the average add-on amounts reported by Ola, the CCPA estimated that customers paid around ₹56 Lakh over and above the disclosed fares for these accepted rides. The share of customers opting for add-ons also increased between June 2025 and June 2026. In Delhi, it rose from 8.2% to 11.04%, while in Bengaluru it increased from 9.7% to 10.64%. In Mumbai, it went up from 7.9% to 8.37%. The CCPA rejected Ola's argument that only a small number of customers used the feature, noting that everyone booking a ride was shown the prompts while waiting for confirmation. It also said the feature could particularly affect people booking rides from hospitals, railway stations, bus terminals and airports, where they may be in a hurry and more dependent on getting a ride quickly. CCPA Flags Confirm Shaming Dark Pattern The CCPA's action comes after the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) directed ride-hailing aggregators, including Uber, Rapido and Ola, to remove tipping prompts displayed before or during a ride, citing violations of the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025. In a directive dated August 11, the ministry flagged prompts such as "Advance Tip", "Choose an Add-on" and "Improve your chances of quicker ride confirmation". It also objected to messages suggesting that tipping could increase the chances of a driver accepting a ride. Under Clause 14.15 of the guidelines, passengers can tip drivers only after completing a ride. Aggregators cannot offer tipping options during booking, before a ride starts or while it is in progress. The guidelines also stipulate that the entire tip must go to the driver, without any commission charged by the aggregator, and that tipping options must not be misleading or manipulative and must comply with the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The CCPA rejected Ola's argument that the additional payment was merely a voluntary tip, observing that tipping ordinarily represents appreciation for services already rendered, whereas Ola solicited payments before drivers accepted bookings. It also highlighted a contradiction in Ola's arguments. If the add-on did not influence ride acceptance, the representation that it improved booking chances was misleading. If it did, customers who did not pay were placed at a relative disadvantage. The authority classified the interface as confirm shaming, a dark pattern prohibited under the Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023. It noted that the prompts created apprehension among customers that declining to pay could result in delayed confirmation or no ride at all. The absence of an option to decline or close the prompt was also flagged. The CCPA further rejected Ola's contention that it did not derive any commercial benefit from the feature because the entire add-on amount went to drivers. It observed that the feature could improve the platform's attractiveness to drivers and its ride fulfilment rates, thereby serving Ola's commercial interests. In September 2026, the CCPA had imposed a similar ₹10 Lakh penalty on ride-hailing platform Rapido over its advance tipping feature, citing misleading advertisements, unfair trade practices and dark patterns. While determining Ola's penalty, the authority considered the scale and duration of the practice, its impact on consumers and the company's financial position. It noted that Ola operated across more than 200 cities in India and had over 40 Mn users. The CCPA also noted that Ola reported standalone revenue from operations of around ₹1,060 Cr in FY25. It said the ₹10 Lakh penalty was less than 0.01% of the company's revenue and was warranted to deter similar violations.

What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration
Congress to probe White House response to intelligence reports of Huang's affair with Chinese spy
Jensen Huang's 33-year tenure as CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia is now finished, but the political repercussions of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy are only just beginning.
For Nvidia, the turmoil over the sex-and-spy scandal and Huang's resignation have cost in excess of $1 trillion US in market value. For U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration, the political costs remain to be tallied.
The scandal matters because of its far-reaching implications that go well beyond tech and the stock market. Nvidia absolutely dominates global manufacture of the most advanced computer chips essential to the development of artificial intelligence.
U.S. policy had been to keep those chips out of the hands of China — over concerns about national security and commercial competition — by using strict export controls. Huang lobbied Trump to loosen those controls.
The president and his Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did just that last year, as part of a deal to end the U.S. trade war with China. Last December, the White House allowed Nvidia to export its advanced H200 AI chips to China in exchange for the U.S. government getting a cut of sales.
Additionally, multiple U.S. news outlets report that Lutnick and his department turned a blind eye to evidence that China was illegally obtaining Nvidia's top-of-the-line chips through intermediary companies in southeast Asia.
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after affair raises national security concerns
- Who is Alice Huang? Alleged Chinese spy, businesswoman involved with Nvidia CEO
One such company was Megaspeed, run by Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence reportedly believes was recruited to spy for Beijing after she'd begun her affair with the Nvidia CEO.
Trump was told twice in the past year about the intelligence, including in May, when the president invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One to attend his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, the New York Times reported.
'Did they follow the trail?'
It's all poised to become fodder for Congressional investigations, potentially starting as early as this month even while the Republicans still hold their House and Senate majorities.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Lousiana wants Lutnick to testify on Capitol Hill.
"Apparently, the Department of Commerce greenlit the sale of $4 billion in advanced chips to the spy's company," Kennedy said Thursday in an interview on CNN.
"I mean, why were they selling the chips? Did they follow the trail? How do they know the chips went to the company and not to the Communist Party of China?" Kennedy said.
Huang, left, joined Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, centre, for an event in the Oval Office with U.S. President Donald Trump on July 29. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)
Kennedy's comments are part of a strong and brewing bipartisan push for answers about the scandal.
The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Congressman Brian Mast, told reporters Thursday that Huang has agreed to go before the committee ahead of its Thanksgiving break.
'Concerning links'
Democrats poised to lead two powerful Congressional committees come January are investigating the Trump administration's move to allow Nvidia to sell advanced microchips to China despite national security concerns.
The investigation will probe why the administration greenlit sales to companies with "concerning links to the Chinese government, military, and sanctioned entities," said a letter to Lutnick on Thursday from U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, and Congressman Richard Neal, the ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee.
- Nvidia CEO's resignation after affair with suspected Chinese spy rattles markets, tech world
- Trump downplays FBI probe into Nvidia chief's affair with alleged spy
Mike Pompeo, a China hawk who served as CIA director and secretary of state in Trump's first term, says he, too, wants answers from the administration because of the national security implications.
"This will not be the last instance where the Chinese Communist Party is working hard against the United States," Pompeo told Fox News.
"They are diligently trying to smuggle our chips and build an AI ecosystem and defeat Western civilization."
Possible political consequences
Questions mounted Thursday about how Trump will respond to the growing controversy over his administration's links to Huang.
Trump was all but silent Thursday in response to Huang's resignation, making just one social media post saying the CEO did a "fantastic job" and floating the ex-CEO of Apple, Tim Cook, as a successor.
Trump called Huang earlier this week, urging him to fight to keep his job and supported him to the end despite the intelligence conclusion that he'd been having an affair with a Chinese spy, the New York Times reported Thursday.
Senior White House officials were discussing Thursday whether Lutnick should be pushed out, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the situation.
- FRONT BURNER Espionage, chips and the 'Nvidia state'
- How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips
Of particular concern are allegations, initially reported by Axios, that Lutnick repeatedly failed to follow White House directives to crack down on Megaspeed and dozens of other companies suspected of violating U.S. law by diverting advanced AI chips to China.
Democratic Congressman Greg Stanton, a member of the House select committee on China, says Trump should fire Lutnick.
"These are incredibly serious issues of national security," Stanton told CNN on Thursday. "The commerce secretary has failed America and he's got to go."
It all suggests there will be political consequences in Washington from the Huang scandal. The only question is how high it will go.

No clear link between recent data breaches; incidents appear to be result of 'opportunistic attacks': PDPC
The Personal Data Protection Commission advised organisations to regularly check and patch vulnerabilities, protect access and credentials, and encrypt or store sensitive data offline.
SINGAPORE: Recent data breaches involving several organisations appear to have been the result of opportunistic attacks, with no clear connection between them, the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) said on Friday (Nov 13).
Preliminary indications were that the “significant data breaches” reported in the past week resulted from opportunistic attacks exploiting common vulnerabilities in IT systems, the commission said.
It added that there was no clear connection between incidents, and some were related to global data breaches.
On Friday, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) also said that the recent cyber incidents did not appear to be part of coordinated campaigns targeting Singapore.
Instead, they reflected "a broader global trend of opportunistic attacks".
In recent weeks, cyberattacks have hit multiple organisations in the healthcare sector, including Minmed, Doctor Anywhere, Fullerton Health and the Agency for Integrated Care.
Data breaches have also been reported by M1, Singapore Airlines and SPH Media, involving the exposure or potential exposure of personal information.
Connected systems support business efficiency and innovation, but their interconnectedness also carries risks, PDPC said.
These include third-party supply chain risks and the exploitation of application programming interfaces (APIs).
“When threat actors find a vulnerability at any part of these connected systems, they find it easier to move laterally through the different systems,” PDPC said.
“They may also find it easier to gain remote access to the systems, as well as impact other third parties in the organisation’s supply chain.”
PDPC advised organisations to regularly check for vulnerabilities, have plans to patch them, protect access and credentials, and use industry-standard encryption for sensitive data or store it offline.
Organisations should also collect and retain only necessary data and put measures in place to prevent data loss or theft.
Under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), organisations must report data breaches to the PDPC and notify affected individuals if a breach is likely to result in significant harm and/or is of significant scale.
“Encouragingly, PDPC has seen more organisations affected by data breaches voluntarily notifying customers. This brings greater visibility to data breaches and allows consumers to take steps to protect themselves,” the commission said.
PDPC advised consumers to share only necessary personal information and use secondary email accounts for non-essential services.
They should also remain vigilant against phishing scams, particularly after being notified that their personal data has been affected by a data breach.

Misty Jones keeps her Grammy in the fridge, alongside a near-empty Tupperware of chicken broth and, well, not a whole lot else: A former country superstar turned burnt-out rural hermit, she more or less lives off what once was, but her memories don’t exactly nourish her. Peculiar details like these enliven “Heartland,” a missing-person mystery that returns writer-director Shana Feste to the Nashville milieu of her 2010 sophomore feature “Country Strong.” So does Jessica Chastain‘s surprisingly brash, beery performance as Misty, whose no-bullshit demeanor serves her well when she must turn amateur detective, investigating the disappearance of a relative who happens to be a rising country star herself.
Fusing Southern-fried noir atmospherics with the sequinned kitsch of a Music City backstage melodrama, “Heartland” often hits the same undemanding guilty-pleasure groove as “Country Strong” — or indeed the six-season run of TV’s “Nashville” in the 2010s. What it isn’t, at nearly any point, is an effective thriller. Feste’s thin screenplay is heavily reliant on Chastain’s brio to sustain a quest that only narrowly makes sense on a moment-to-moment basis, and never gathers much intrigue — since the villains are all glaringly identifiable as such from the get-go, while Misty’s rough-diamond integrity is never in doubt. The result is diverting straight-to-Netflix fare, sparkly and disposable as a rhinestone, though its star commits as though it were something more.
“There’s no such thing as good girls,” says Misty early on in proceedings. It’s not entirely true — the character hides a kind, true heart beneath a gruffly embittered exterior — but it’s a solid pointer for Chastain, always at her most interesting when playing characters who are either morally off-base (“Dreams,” “A Most Violent Year”) or at least a little prickly and defensive. And she comes out, quite literally, all guns blazing: In the film’s opening minutes, she feuds with a neighbor on the remote Georgia pecan farm where she’s settled, eventually taking a shotgun to the woman’s windows. It’s our first taste of the hot temper that cost her a mainstream music career years ago — they called her “the cunt of country,” she says with some relish — though she rarely wields it against someone who doesn’t deserve it.
It’s that hard-headed quality that her brother Donny (Paul Sparks) calls upon when he comes to her for help. His 20-something daughter Charlie (singer Carter Faith, in her film debut), herself a buzzy new talent on the Nashville country scene, has recently gone missing, and he suspects shady showbiz machinations at play — something Misty knows plenty about, even if she left that world behind long ago. And so she turns gumshoe, with an oversize felt Stetson instead of a fedora, and a lineup of men to question that range from Charlie’s too-slick-by-half manager Roy (Garrett Hedlund) to an obsessed incel stalker.
There are other, hidden reasons for Misty to take on a job that isn’t really in her skill set, though they’re not quite satisfyingly addressed, as Feste’s script toggles awkwardly between the procedural and the personal. Certain key relationships — notably that between Misty and Donny, brittle with shared secrets — are fleshed out in single scenes, never to be readdressed; elsewhere, the film dawdles on less pivotal connections, though there’s a lovely, wily supporting performance from Sugarland frontwoman Jennifer Nettles as a past friend-turned-rival, culminating in an onstage duet between her and Chastain that’s the highlight of the film’s original and on-the-money country song score. Where characters are sketchily drawn, casting is often more considered: Stalwarts like Hedlund, John Hawkes and Norbert Leo Butz all bring flickers of intelligence and eccentricity to fleeting or one-dimensional roles.
Still, this is Chastain’s show, and she’s clearly enjoying it, often daring to play things quite broad and blustery, which rather suits the occasional tackiness of the material; at other points, she convincingly locates a quiet seam of deep-set pain in the protagonist, a casualty of an industry that, it is suggested here, often takes young female talent for a ride. Misty seems vaguely inspired by the enduring mystique of Bobbie Gentry, the prodigious Nashville singer-songwriter who, after a few years at the top, retired from music and checked out of the public eye entirely. Yet the film’s somewhat half-baked mystery tends to distract us from more dramatically probing questions about Misty herself, a curious character in search of a more curious character study.

Mauricio Pochettino: Manchester United agree two-and-a-half-year deal with USA manager to replace Michael Carrick
Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United after the current international break; USA boss will replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday with the club in the Premier League relegation zone; Pochettino will sign deal until summer of 2029
Thursday 12 November 2026 23:39, UK
Manchester United and Mauricio Pochettino have agreed a deal for him to become the club's next head coach.
Pochettino is expected to sign a two-and-half-year contract at Old Trafford, replacing Michael Carrick, who was sacked earlier on Thursday.
Pochettino - who had a £7m release clause in his USA contract - will take charge of United after overseeing the USA's games against Haiti on Saturday and Wednesday.

The formal announcement of Pochettino's appointed is expected on Friday, with the Argentine set to be United's eighth permanent appointment since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
Pochettino's first game in charge will be the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool on November 22, live on Sky Sports.
Carrick departed less than six months after signing a two-year contract having overseen the club's worst start to a Premier League season, with United in the relegation zone after picking up one win in 10 matches.
In a statement on Thursday morning, shortly after Carrick left the training ground, United said they reached "the extremely difficult conclusion that a change is necessary in order to achieve our ambitions".
Carrick took training in Manchester on Wednesday as United reached a verbal agreement with Pochettino.
Meanwhile, club chiefs were at a Monaco summit with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe. That is where the decision to sack Carrick was ratified by Ratcliffe following the recommendation of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.
United's hierarchy, including Wilcox and Berrada, are understood to feel that the current squad is much better than results and performances have shown.
Carrick's exit follows United's 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on Sunday, when they fell 2-0 down inside four minutes and then 4-2 down early in the second half before mounting a last-gasp comeback to draw.
The rescue job followed a similar turnaround to beat Roma in the Champions League last Tuesday but was not enough to convince the United hierarchy to continue with the former midfielder in charge.
Jonny Evans and Jonathan Woodgate, who were part of the coaching set up under Carrick, have also left the club, along with Steve Holland, Travis Binnion and goalkeeping coach Craig Mawson.
The only coach who remains is assistant first-team goalkeeping coach Connor King, who joined the club two months ago.
Carrick was initially appointed as United boss in January 2026 on a contract until the end of the season following Ruben Amorim's sacking earlier in that campaign. He delivered a brilliant run of results, winning 12 of 17 matches to earn a third-place finish in the Premier League and a return to the Champions League.
Carrick was nominated for Premier League Manager of the Season and, on May 22, signed a new contract running to 2028. However, just three wins in 15 matches this term have cost him his job.
Former Tottenham, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss Pochettino has been considered for the United job on three previous occasions, but will now finally take the Old Trafford hot seat.
Neville: United need bigger solution than sacking Carrick
Sky Sports' Gary Neville to NBC:
"You can keep changing the manager and thinking that's going to be the answer. But this has been proven now over 12 years, that's not the answer.
"It's rinse and repeat. Ruben Amorim, Erik ten Hag, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Carrick, Jose Mourinho, Louis van Gaal, David Moyes, Ralf Rangnick - some of them are world-class managers who have had success. There are a lot of promising young managers there, ex-players who know the club as well.
"None of it has worked because if you've got a poor performance department, poor recruitment department, you've not got leadership that is strong right through the spine of the football club, you will fail."
Carrick's Man Utd reign in numbers
United won 12 out of 17 games last season under Carrick - a 70.1 per cent win rate, which saw him comfortably sit with the best record of permanent Old Trafford managers.
But he leaves with a record of 15 wins in 32 matches - a rate of just 46.9 per cent, which leaves him only ahead of Ruben Amorim, the man he replaced in the dugout last season, in the years since Ferguson's retirement.
Carrick has overseen three wins in 15 matches this campaign (20 per cent). They won eight out of 21 games before Amorim's sacking last year (38.1 per cent).
His drop-off brings echoes of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. The former United striker's win percentage fell from 73.7 per cent as interim manager (14 wins in 19 games) to 51.7 per cent having been appointed on a permanent basis (77 out of 149).
Carrick had three games as caretaker boss after Solskjaer's departure, wins over Villarreal and Arsenal and a draw with Chelsea. These matches are not counted towards his record as permanent manager.
Ferguson's shadow
Since the retirement in 2013 of Ferguson, who won 26 major trophies in 27 years at Old Trafford and had a 59.7 per cent win ratio, United have struggled to find a long-term figurehead.
Ferguson took charge of 1,500 games with United. In 731 games since he retired in 2013, Carrick was the club's seventh permanent manager in addition to interim boss Ralf Rangnick and caretakers Ryan Giggs, Carrick himself, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher.
Jose Mourinho has the best win percentage of those permanent managers, with 58.3 per cent, 84 out of 144 games.
Mourinho also won the most trophies of any manager since Ferguson, with a League Cup and Europa League double in 2016-17 having opened that season with the Community Shield.
Erik ten Hag won both domestic cups, Louis van Gaal lifted an FA Cup and David Moyes another Community Shield.

From Champions League finish to drop zone: How Carrick's reign unravelled

Michael Carrick has been sacked as Manchester United head coach, so how did his Old Trafford reign go so wrong, so quickly?
