President Donald Trump said he talked to Jensen Huang on Wednesday, a day before the Nvidia CEO resigned.
In an interview with Stephen A. Smith at the White House, Trump said Huang called him and talked about the impact the affair scandal has had on his family.
"I spoke to him yesterday. He's going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family," Trump said. "That's what he told me."
Huang resigned on Thursday. On Sunday, he admitted in a memo to staff that he had been "unfaithful" and the Nvidia board announced it was investigating whether he had been the target of a foreign intelligence operation.
The resignation also came after a New York Times report on Wednesday that said Huang had engaged in a second affair with an Nvidia executive that reported to him, Kimberly Powell. Following Huang's resignation, a Reuters report alleged a third affair, with another employee at Nvidia who was not named.
In the interview on Thursday, Trump praised Huang and his work at Nvidia. When Smith asked if Huang should've stepped down, Trump said it depended on whether a woman he had an affair with was actually a Chinese spy, as US officials suspected, according to the Times.
"If the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different," Trump said.
He also reiterated his belief that Tim Cook, the former CEO of Apple, should succeed Huang. Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO, was named interim CEO on Thursday as the board looks for a replacement.
Earlier in the week, on Monday, the president said he had talked to Huang to see how he was doing. He said the executive told him he did not know the person he had an affair with "was a spy."
"And I really believe him," Trump said.
The Times reported Trump also spoke to Huang on Tuesday this week and encouraged him to fight to remain as Nvidia's CEO.
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet’s atmosphere.
Except when we can’t.
On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we’ve been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that’s due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane.
Big changes
TOI-2535 is one of the many stars with exoplanet candidates identified by TESS, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite. It’s a K dwarf, meaning it’s somewhat smaller than the Sun. And TESS found signs of a Jupiter-sized planet orbiting it every eight days, an orbit close enough to make TOI-2535b a “hot Jupiter” exoplanet. At that point, there was nothing especially unusual about it.
But a closer look at the data showed two very strange things. First, the timing of when its transits occurred could shift by as much as six hours, a substantial variation for an orbit this brief. That’s typically a sign of gravitational interactions with another planet; depending on the details of that second planet’s orbit, it may slow the first one or accelerate it through a transit more quickly. Since the second planet doesn’t show up in TESS data, it appears to orbit in a slightly different plane, so it doesn’t pass between its host star and Earth.

Pakistan’s former Prime Minister Imran Khan was taken to hospital in Islamabad late on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) for medical treatment and returned to prison, sources said.
Khan, who is imprisoned in Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi, had an eye check-up at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), one of the officials said on Wednesday (November 11).
“He had some blood pressure issues ... and was given required treatment last night. He has been shifted back to his prison cell,” the person said.
The cricketer-turned-politician has faced multiple corruption charges since he lost power in a no-confidence vote in 2022, and has been in prison for more than three years. All of Khan’s convictions bar one have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending. He denies wrongdoing and says the charges are politically motivated, a claim the government denies.
Khan’s lawyers say the 74-year-old’s health has deteriorated in prison and that he has lost significant vision in his right eye.
It is the first known instance of Khan being taken to hospital for treatment and returned to jail since August, when his hospital visit was cut short.
A Pakistani court has also ordered jail authorities to allow Khan’s legal team to see him and his wife, his party said.
His party’s deputy chairman, Shah Mehmood Qureshi, was also taken to hospital in the eastern city of Lahore from a jail in the same city on Tuesday (November 10). He remains in hospital.

Snopes found not 20, but 25 bills related to the regulation of firearms had been prefiled for 2027 legislative session as of this writing. Of the state representatives and senators who'd introduced the bills, 11 were Democrats and three were Republicans. Of those bills, 20 were introduced in the House and five of them in the Senate.
Soon after Democrats swept the Texas House of Representatives in November's midterm election, a rumor spread that they had already filed approximately 20 bills related to gun control.
The claim circulated on social media, including on YouTube, Instagram and Facebook. Meanwhile, on X, posts like the one below enumerated the 20 supposed bills, alleging that "Texas Democrats are filing a FLOOD of proposed bills that would TAKE AWAY gun rights for Americans" (archived):
Snopes readers searched the website seeking to confirm the veracity of the claim.
The claim was true, though Snopes found not 20, but 25 bills related to the regulation of firearms had been prefiled for the 2027 legislative session as of this writing.
Of those bills, 20 were House bills and five were Senate bills.
Of the state representatives and senators who'd introduced the bills, 11 were Democrats and three were Republicans.
List of prefiled bills related to gun control in the Texas legislature
On Nov. 9, prefiling began at the Texas legislature — a period when the state's lawmakers can begin to file bills for consideration for the upcoming session. Sitting lawmakers reportedly filed "more than 1,000 bills" before midday that day.
(It's worth noting that while Democrats won the majority of the Texas House, Republicans kept theirs in the state Senate. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is a Democrat. She is set to replace Republican Greg Abbott.)
Among the bills Snopes identified, five would prohibit the transfer or sale of semiautomatic firearms to people younger than 21. Two of them would increase the criminal penalty for allowing children to access firearms.
The bills are as follows:
- HB 103 - Author: Rep. Mando Martinez (Democrat). This bill would make it possible to prosecute "the criminal offense of reckless discharge of a firearm" in larger swaths of the territory in Texas.
- HB 659 - Author: Rep. Joe Moody (Democrat). This bill would require "a licensed firearms dealer to report certain sales or transfers of multiple firearms or firearm magazines to law enforcement," creating a new criminal offense.
- SB 80 - Author: Sen. Judith Zaffirini (Democrat). This bill would ban "certain transfers, purchases, and possession of assault weapons," creating new criminal offenses.
- HB 613 - Author: Rep. Suleman Lalani (Democrat). This bill would require "a national instant criminal background check in connection with private firearm transfers" and create a new criminal offense.
- HB 712 - Author: Rep. Erin Gámez (Democrat). This bill would allow cities and counties "to regulate or prohibit the carrying of a firearm on the premises of certain libraries."
- SB 308 - Author: Sen. Roland Gutierrez, a Democrat (and others). This bill would ban the making and possession of 3D-printed "firearms and major components of firearms," but also "the distribution or publication" of the digital files that serve to print these firearms and their components. It would create new criminal offenses.
- HB 606 - Author: Lalani. This bill would ban "the transfer of firearms to or the purchase or possession of firearms by persons younger than 21 years of age." It would create a new criminal offense.
- HB 218 - Author: Rep. Ann Johnson (Democrat). This bill would allow members of a family or household and law enforcement officers to ask a court to curtail someone's ability to access firearms if they think the person poses an immediate danger due to mental illness. It would allow for the "creation, issuance, and enforcement" of "extreme risk protective orders."
- HB 618 - Author: Moody. This bill would ban the "transfer of firearm magazines to recipients who are prohibited from possessing the type of firearm for which the magazine is designed or made" and create a new criminal offense.
- HB 610 - Author: Lalani. This bill would ban "the transfer of firearms to certain recipients who are younger than 21 years of age."
- HB 660 -Author: Moody. This bill would require "certain persons prohibited by law from owning, possessing, or controlling a firearm" to give up the firearms they own, possess or control.
- HB 173 - Author: Moody. This bill would ban "the transfer of certain semiautomatic rifles" people younger than 21 and it would both create a criminal offense and increase a criminal penalty. It would also create some exceptions when a person younger than 21 may access such weapons.
- HB 857 - Author: Rep. Rafael Anchía (Democrat). Similarly to HB 173, this bill would ban "the transfer of certain semiautomatic rifles to certain recipients younger than 21 years of age," creating some exceptions.
- SB 327 - Author: Gutierrez (and others). Similarly to HB 173 and HB 857, the bill would ban "the transfer of certain semiautomatic rifles to certain recipients younger than 21 years of age."
- HB 806 - Author: Rep. Ron Reynolds (Democrat). Similarly to HB 173, HB 857 and SB 327, the bill would ban "the transfer of semiautomatic rifles to certain recipients" younger than 21 years old.
- HB 771 - Author: Pooja Sethi (Democrat). Similarly to HB 173, HB 857, SB 327 and HB 806, the bill would ban "the transfer of semiautomatic rifles to certain recipients" younger than 21 years old.
- HB 533 - Author: Rep. Carl Tepper (Republican ). This bill would ban "the carrying of concealed handguns by handgun license holders on the premises of certain polling places on the day of an election or while early voting is in progress."
- HB 658 - Author: Moody. This bill would make it possible to prosecute and punish "the offense of making a firearm accessible to a child" and it would increase a criminal penalty.
- HB 612 - Author: Lalani. This bill would ban "a sex offender from possessing a firearm."
- HB 576 - Author: Lalani. This bill would ban "sex offenders from purchasing firearms."
- SB 170 - Author: Sen. Brent Hagenbuch (Republican ). This bill would increase the criminal penalty for burglarizing a vehicle to steal a firearm.
- HB 773 - Author: Rep. A.J. Louderback (Republican). This bill would make it an aggravating factor to use or show a firearm during the commission of certain felony offenses, raising "the minimum term of imprisonment" and changing parole rules.
- SB 234 - Author: Sen. Carol Alvarado, a Democrat (and others).This would ban people convicted of "certain family violence misdemeanors" from owning a firearm.
- HB 609 - Author: Lalani. Similarly to HB 658, this bill would increase "the criminal penalty for the offense of making a firearm accessible to a child."
- HB 859 - Author: Anchía. This bill would increase "the criminal penalty" for "discharging a firearm in certain municipalities."

A claim is spreading online that a bald eagle attacked a $950 "government drone" in midair, sending it crashing into Lake Michigan.
Social media users shared the story on Facebook and Reddit, prompting Snopes readers to search the website to determine whether a bald eagle had, in fact, launched a successful attack against a foreign object in its airspace.
This story is true — although it happened years ago, not in 2026. It is also worth noting that while some posts online appear to show a bald eagle flying at a drone, there is no actual footage of the incident, according to the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy, or EGLE — the agency whose drone lost to the eagle.
Michigan state officials confirmed the eagle's assault in an Aug. 13, 2020, news release titled, "Shoreline-mapping EGLE drone sent to watery Lake Michigan grave by U.P. bald eagle." (U.P. is a reference to Michigan's Upper Peninsula.)
Here's how that release began:
An Upper Peninsula bald eagle launched an airborne attack on a drone operated by a Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) pilot last month, tearing off a propeller and sending the aircraft to the bottom of Lake Michigan.
The brazen eagle vs. EGLE onslaught took place near Escanaba in Michigan's Upper Peninsula on July 21 when EGLE environmental quality analyst and drone pilot Hunter King was mapping shoreline erosion for use in the agency's efforts to document and help communities cope with high water levels.
King had completed about seven minutes of the mapping flight — his fourth of the day in the area — when satellite reception got spotty. He pressed the "Go Home" recall button. The drone dutifully turned, reacquiring a strong satellite feed.
King was watching his video screen as the drone beelined for home, but suddenly it began twirling furiously. "It was like a really bad rollercoaster ride," said King. When he looked up, the drone was gone, and an eagle was flying away. A nearby couple, whose pastimes include watching the local eagles attack seagulls and other birds, later confirmed they saw the eagle strike something but were surprised to learn it was a drone. Both King and the couple said the eagle appeared uninjured as it flew from the scene of the crime.
The release also confirmed that the drone was "a $950 Phantom 4 Pro Advanced" and shared data indicating that the eagle tore off a propeller, as many of the claim posts said (emphasis ours):
Data from the flight records detailed the drone's final moments:
- The eagle strike occurred 7:39.7 into the flight roughly four-tenths of a mile from King and 162 feet above the water
- Its speed instantly dropped from 22 mph to 10. Within a half-second the flight record shows the beginning of downward spiral along with "excessive spinning" warnings
- In the next 3.5 seconds the drone sent 27 warning notifications including one indicating a propeller had been torn off
- Gaining momentum as it fell, its last communication came at 34 feet above the water, falling at 30 feet per second, or 20.4 mph.
Per the release, King and the unidentified couple searched for the drone, "but hours of scouring the shoreline were fruitless." An unmanned aircraft systems coordinator with the state agency, Arthur Ostaszewski, also attempted to find the drone using a kayak, snorkeling gear and "telemetric data from the flight that pinpointed exactly where the drone hit the lake." He, too, was unsuccessful, even after walking a grid pattern for two hours — "like I was playing Battleship and wanted to cover the entire board," he said.
A week later, however, a team of Michigan state employees — which the agency cheekily dubbed in a news release as the Willful Eagle Trauma Team Engaged in Retrieval, or WETTER — managed to uncover the drone in almost the exact same location after "the previously murky water had cleared due to shifting winds and currents." EGLE shared a few pictures of the recovery effort on X, then known as Twitter:
The agency noted that the drone was not recording at the time of the bald eagle's assault, meaning that there would not be any footage of the fight over airspace.
Michigan officials speculated that the attack could have been "a territorial squabble with the electronic foe, or just a hungry eagle."
"Or maybe it did not like its name being misspelled," EGLE said, poking fun at its agency acronym.
At the time, EGLE said it was considering steps to try to prevent a repeat attack, including adding a design to make the drones look less like seagulls. Snopes found no evidence of any bald eagle drone attacks since EGLE's incident in 2020, however, so this may have just been a one-time thing.
EGLE also said the Michigan Department of Natural Resources was unable to issue a citation or violation notice to the "rogue eagle."
"Unfortunately, there's nothing we can do," the agency's spokesman said. "Nature is a cruel and unforgiving mistress."

IIT Kharagpur becomes first IIT to offer MD programmes approved by national medical body
IIT Kharagpur become the first IIT to offer postgraduate medical courses recognised by NMC, introducing 12 MD seats across six specialisations.
Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kharagpur in West Bengal has become the first IIT in India to introduce postgraduate medical degree programmes recognised by the National Medical Commission (NMC), offering 12 MD seats across six specialisations for the 2026-27 academic session, the institute announced on Thursday.
“The Institute undertook the prescribed regulatory process with the NMC, including submission of applications, documentation of academic and clinical facilities, and fulfilment of the applicable requirements in March 2026. The process culminated in permission for the six MD programmes for the academic session 2026–27,” director of IIT Kharagpur Suman Chakraborty said.
The programmes will be offered at the institute’s Dr B C Roy Multi-Speciality Medical Research Centre, with admissions through the second round of NEET-PG 2026 counselling from November 10 to 23, according to the announcement. Fees of the PG medical course and stipends paid to students will be on the lines of AIIMS.
“The postgraduate medical programmes are supported by the in-house expanding clinical infrastructure of Dr. Shyama Prasad Mookerji Superspeciality Hospital - new Hospital of IIT Kharagpur, together with the South Eastern Railway Hospital, Kharagpur, under the established institutional partnership. This arrangement provides the clinical training ecosystem for the approved postgraduate programmes, in accordance with the applicable NMC requirements,” Chakraborty said.
The six specialisations are general medicine, radiology, physiology, pathology, community medicine and biochemistry, with two seats in each discipline. The programmes will be available for eligible candidates through the Medical Counselling Committee’s (MCC) online counselling process.
MCC is the government body responsible for conducting online counselling to allot medical and dental seats based on NEET scores.
The move marks the entry of an IIT into postgraduate medical education and is aimed at bringing clinical medicine closer to engineering, artificial intelligence (AI), biomedical sciences and translational research.
IIT Kharagpur said in a statement that the programmes would provide opportunities for medical students to engage with research across areas such as AI-assisted clinical decision-making, advanced medical imaging, computational pathology, biomedical devices, molecular diagnostics, precision medicine and population health.
The institute added that its existing strengths in microfluidics, bioengineering, healthcare diagnostics, AI, computational sciences and translational medical technologies would provide a foundation for the interdisciplinary approach.
Chakraborty said the institute’s objective was not limited to training specialist doctors but also included developing medical professionals capable of addressing healthcare challenges through research and technology.
“India’s first IIT is now taking a historic step towards shaping the future of medical education. Our vision is not simply to train specialist doctors, but to create an ecosystem where clinical excellence meets engineering ingenuity, artificial intelligence and translational research,” he said.
“We want our medical graduates to be not only outstanding clinicians, but also innovators capable of addressing some of humanity’s most pressing healthcare challenges,” Chakraborty added.
He said the first batch would be pioneers of a new academic journey, with the institute aiming to nurture doctors who can combine clinical understanding with scientific discovery and technological innovation.
Established in 1951, IIT Kharagpur was the first institute in the IIT system. Its entry into postgraduate medical education comes in its 75th year and is part of its broader ambition to expand the role of technological institutions in addressing healthcare challenges.
The institute also said that it has identified research-driven learning and international academic exposure as elements of the proposed academic environment.

Paul Barril, French ‘Supergendarme’ Turned Mercenary, Has Died
After years in elite police units, he drew scrutiny from human rights groups for selling arms and providing other services to unsavory governments. He was 80.
Paul Barril’s offer to African dictators was straightforward: Your opponents will be subjected to surveillance and manipulation. Newspapers will be “infiltrated.” Plots against the state will be “neutralized.”
Plenty of heads of state took up the services he offered, including Omar Bongo in Gabon and Denis Sassou-Nguesso in Congo. Other clients went to Paris to do their shopping at his Security Action Store, which offered the latest in bulletproof vests or night-vision goggles, as Mr. Barril recounted in one of his six autobiographies, “The Elysee’s Secret Wars” (1996).
Mr. Barril was often described in the news media as a former French “supergendarme” for his longtime work in elite units. After he left the gendarmerie, or national police, in 1984, he became a security adviser and mercenary provider across the African continent and was implicated by human rights groups in the Rwandan genocide of 1994.
His death, on Oct. 20 at 80 at his home in Antibes, France, was announced by the French interior ministry. He had Parkinson’s disease.
By the time he founded his mercenary-security company, Secrets, a French acronym for Security Equipment Planning and Realization Company, in 1984, Mr. Barril was a well-chronicled public figure.
In the gendarmerie, which in France is under the military, he joined a new military police intervention unit, the GIGN, in 1974. The French news media chronicled Mr. Barril’s reputation as an ultrafit top cop, a military-grade swimmer and diver, a black belt in karate, a parachutist, a hostage liberator and a policeman working inside and outside the law. With the GIGN, he participated in the 1979 operation against Islamist militants who had seized the Grand Mosque in Mecca, taking dozens hostage.

- The claim that a video shows two Muslim New York Police Department officers taking away a woman's dog for disturbing the peace, supposedly in the interests of enforcing the Islamic teachings known as Shariah, is still under investigation.
- We contacted the NYPD to ask questions and request an incident report to independently confirm several details, including to fully verify the woman's purported charge or charges. - The person who says he recorded the video told Snopes he knew of "no evidence" regarding the claim the officers were Muslim, or that Shariah or the Islamic faith played any role in the incident at all.
- The video made the social media rounds as a 3-minute clip with dramatic background music, showing NYPD officers questioning and detaining a woman walking her dog. At least one officer grabs hold of the dog's leash and also grabs the woman's arm. The clip's onscreen captions read: "Sharia is starting in NYC" and "Muslim police taking dog for disturbing the peace."
- A viewing of the original 16-minute video revealed that the officers didn't appear to actually take away the dog, and that they apparently charged her with disorderly conduct.
In early November, people shared a video allegedly showing two Muslim New York police officers taking away a woman's dog for disturbing the peace, supposedly as their way of enforcing Shariah (Islamic law).
Shariah serves to guide the moral and religious practices of Muslims, such as prayer, pilgrimages, fasting, charitable donations and personal virtue.
As a prime example of the rumor, on Nov. 8, an X user posted (archived) the 3-minute clip showing an incident that apparently began moments earlier. Two NYPD officers stand on a street corner at night, with one of the officers alleging that the woman, who identifies herself as a nurse who recently had surgery on her foot, was standing or dancing and recording a video "in the middle of the street" and wouldn't move to the sidewalk, blocking the officers' vehicle.
The officer grabs the woman's arm, briefly takes her dog's leash and tells her that if she doesn't identify herself, they will arrest her and take her "to prison," adding, "We'll take the dog, too." He then grabs her arm again.
The clip's soundtrack features dramatic music as the action takes place.
The onscreen caption reads, "Sharia is starting in NYC," and "Muslim police taking dog for disturbing the peace. Oh wait for that dog ban boy oh boy."
Reverse image searches found others sharing the same video and captions on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and X (archived), as well as clips with similar (archived) claims (archived).
The video appears authentic in that someone on the scene genuinely recorded it and did not create it with artificial intelligence.
The brief clip shared on social media omits 13 minutes of the original 16-minute video (archived), which shows that while one of the officers did briefly grab the dog's leash, it doesn't appear he actually took away the animal — nor did he or the other officer mention the dog as a problem. The longer, raw video not only lacks the dramatic music heard in the shorter clip but contains no mention of religion or Shariah at all.
TikTok user @nuyoricannomad, who said he recorded and first posted the raw video, told Snopes he knew of "no evidence" regarding the claim of the officers' religion playing a factor in the incident.
Pending more corroboration, Snopes hasn't added a fact-check rating to this article. We contacted the NYPD to ask questions and to request an incident report. We also filed a formal request to receive the police body camera footage. We will update this story if we receive further data.
People reposting the video with mentions of Shariah and a "dog ban" appeared to be playing on the exaggerated notion that Muslims hate dogs and view them as unclean. The stereotype apparently originates from an overgeneralization not from the Quran, but instead from the hadith, a narrative record of the sayings or customs of the Prophet Muhammad and his companions.
Video location and citation
In our interview with @nuyoricannomad — who wished to not be identified by name — he said he recorded the video around 3 a.m. Nov. 8. The incident occurred on the northwest corner of Second Avenue and East 39th Street in Manhattan's Murray Hill neighborhood.
According to @nuyoricannomad, both he and the woman, who he indicated is his friend, were walking north and using the East 39th Street crosswalk on the west side of Second Avenue. "We were walking slowly but she had recent surgery," he said, referencing her foot, which she briefly mentions in the clip (at 8:55).
At about the same time, the officers were traveling by car south on Second Avenue and attempting to make a right over the same crosswalk and onto East 39th Street, similar to the turning white SUV visible in this Google Street View image (archived).
Regarding charges for the woman, @nuyoricannomad said, "The citation was written for disorderly conduct." That charge, which Snopes is attempting to independently verify, would line up with a moment in the video in which one of the officers appears to make a phone call and mention disorderly conduct (at 3:30), possibly referencing New York state law's descriptor of obstructing vehicular or pedestrian traffic.
What the full video shows
The full video appears to begin moments after the incident started. One of the officers grabs the woman's arm and she tells him to stop touching her. He also takes her dog's leash for a brief period of time, tells her she will go to prison if she doesn't identify herself and says he'll take her dog, too. He doesn't clarify whether he's joking about taking the dog to prison or seriously warning he'll take her dog away if they take her into custody.
At least one person standing nearby tells the officers he's calling 911 to ask for a supervisor to come to the scene. One of the officers tells that person to stand back and says, "You can do whatever you want." (A user posting one popular Instagram video (archived) about the incident falsely claimed the officer said not "You" but "We," as in, "We can do whatever we want.")
The woman identifies herself as a nurse and challenges the officers' version of events. For example, one officer says, "You were in the middle of the street taking video." She responds, "I did not make a video." He then tells her she's being detained, saying, "You are not free to leave right now."
The woman says she had the right to walk across the crosswalk with a walk signal (at 6:25 and 8:10). We haven't yet been able to independently confirm the status of the traffic signal.
One of the officers alleges he, with the other officer in his passenger seat, was turning right and that the woman and others were in their way (ar 9:30). In that moment, he doesn't challenge the woman's claim she had the right of way with a walk signal.
Later in the video, an apparent police supervisor arrives and tells one of the officers to place @nuyoricannomad and another pedestrian under arrest if they interrupt the officers' investigation again (at 12:20).
The video ends with one of the officers appearing to hand a citation to the woman, who then appears to be free to leave with her dog and friends.
As to what started the incident, @nuyoricannomad told us that "at no point were we just standing on the crosswalk or 'dancing,'" referencing the officer's allegation that the woman had been dancing (at 8:55).
"The point of the video was to show how the cops mishandled the situation and escalated to a point that was not necessary," he said.

Black Turnout Rose in Georgia, Powered by Younger Voters
Black voters under 30 outpaced young white voters for the first time since 2012, contributing to a statewide sweep by Democrats.
The Black share of the electorate in Georgia rose to its highest level in more than a decade, with the turnout rate among young Black voters outpacing that of young white voters. Both trends contributed to a heavy leftward shift in the state this year.
Democrats had a historically good election night in Georgia. Senator Jon Ossoff won re-election by 18 percentage points, which was the largest margin of victory for a statewide Democrat in more than two decades. Down the ballot, the party romped to victory, flipping the state house and every statewide office. That included the governorship, with Keisha Lance Bottoms elected the first Black governor in Georgia’s history.
Black voter enthusiasm, particularly in the South, was closely watched in the midterm elections after a Supreme Court ruling in April that weakened the Voting Rights Act, setting off a wave of redistricting that diluted Black representation in several states.
Georgia is one of the first states to report its validated voter history for 2026, which is a record of exactly who voted in the election. It is also one of only a handful of states where voters can provide their race when they register to vote.
The result is a glimpse at Black voters’ role in elections that gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress, albeit from one state.
Turnout was crucial. Based on voter data taken directly from the state, Black voters made up at least 30 percent of Georgia’s electorate in 2026, the highest of any election since 2012, when President Barack Obama ran for re-election. The true share is likely to be slightly higher — around 7 percent of voters in Georgia’s voter file are listed as “other” or “unknown” for race. Times Voter Trends, which models the race of these voters, estimates the Black share of this year’s electorate at around 32 percent.
Because Black voters in Georgia are overwhelmingly Democratic — more than 95 percent of them voted for Mr. Ossoff this year, according to Times Voter Trends — even small increases in the Black share of the electorate can translate to sizable gains for the party.
Georgia’s young Black voters closed the turnout gap this year.
For the first time since 2012, turnout rates among Black voters under 30 were slightly higher than those of white voters under 30.
Much of the surge in Democratic support in Georgia was fueled by voters under 30, across all racial groups. Their swing toward Democrats was more than twice as large as Georgia voters’ as a whole. Like young voters in other states, this group shifted modestly toward Donald Trump in 2024 before lurching back to the left this time.
Turnout tends to decline in midterm elections, particularly among younger voters, but higher turnout among young white voters has been the recent norm in midterm and presidential years.
In 2022, 33 percent of registered white voters under 30 cast a ballot, compared with 22 percent of registered Black voters under 30 — a gap that was virtually erased in the 2026 election.
Evan Reynolds works in the Election Analytics department of The Times and is a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

VS Hospitals has introduced a new 2D digital mammography system to strengthen breast cancer screening and diagnosis.
The AMULET SOPHINITY system from Fujifilm uses a high-resolution detector with a pixel size of 50 microns, allowing detailed imaging of breast tissue, including tiny microcalcifications, which can sometimes be an early indicator of breast abnormalities.
Mammography uses low-dose X-rays to examine breast tissue and can help identify abnormalities that may not be detectable through physical examination. The new system has intelligent exposure control, which adjusts X-ray exposure according to breast composition while maintaining image quality. AI-based positioning support is designed to assist in accurate positioning and consistent image acquisition.
The equipment takes approximately five seconds for standard image acquisition and 12 seconds for high-resolution imaging. It also has features such as flexible positioning, intelligent breast compression and automatic decompression to help reduce discomfort during the examination.
Speaking at the launch, S. Subramanian, Chairman and Managing Director of V.S. Hospitals, said early detection was important in breast cancer care and that mammography played a key role in identifying breast abnormalities.
The hospital will offer free mammography screening to underprivileged people throughout November 2026. Those seeking to avail themselves of the screening can contact the hospital at 7448850500.

Pope tells Peru's bishops to accompany their flocks and respond to abuse victims with truth, justice
Pope Leo XIV is opening his first day in Peru by giving marching orders to the country’s Catholic bishops
LIMA, Peru -- After his emotional homecoming, Pope Leo XIV got down to work Thursday telling Peru's Catholic bishops to accompany their flocks as they face poverty and injustices, and respond to victims of clergy sexual abuse with truth, justice and amends.
Leo made it clear he knows the Peruvian church and people well in his opening events in Lima, identifying some of the biggest challenges facing them and calling the influential Catholic hierarchy especially to task to be models of unity and communion.
Peruvians turned out in droves to catch a glimpse of Leo, with crowds outside the church residence where he is staying and an even bigger gathering at the central Plaza Mayor where he had his first events Thursday. Leo thrilled them by looping around the plaza in his popemobile.
At every turn, Leo has been serenaded by a children’s choir belting out a catchy tune composed especially for his trip, accompanied by Andean flutes: “Papa León, hermano del camino, Papa León, sembrador de fraternidad." (“Pope Leo, brother on the journey, Pope Leo, sower of brotherhood.”)
“It’s a blessing not only for us Chiclayans but for all of Peru," said Ángel Esquives, a craftsman originally from Leo's former diocese in Chiclayo who now lives in Lima. He said he left his home at 3 a.m. to go to the historic center and stand in line to get as close as possible to the pope.
As he showed in the first two legs of his South American trip, Leo was in fine form despite having undergone lung cancer surgery last month. He bounded up a steep flight of stairs Thursday morning without any apparent problems and joked with the bishops that some “doubting Thomases” had predicted he wouldn’t be able to come.
“But God is great and his grace is bigger than all of us and I'm very happy to be here with you,” he said to applause.
Citing local authorities, the Vatican estimated that some 3 million people had lined Leo's motorcade route on Wednesday to welcome “Padre Robert” home. The Chicago-born pope, who also has Peruvian citizenship, responded with an emotional ode to all that Peru had given him.
The former Robert Prevost spent two decades as a missionary priest and bishop in Peru and credits the place with teaching him how to be a shepherd. He in many ways has modeled his vocation as a bishop on the 16th century St. Turibius de Mogrovejo, the first archbishop of Lima.
Mogrovejo is revered for having traveled long distances to be with his flock and for having defended the rights of Indigenous and enslaved peoples. He studied Quechua and Aymara and oversaw the printing of the Catechism of the Catholic Church in these Indigenous languages, because he believed the faith had to be transmitted in the language people could understand.
Leo urged bishops on Thursday to model their vocation on his example. Being a bishop, he said, means “entering people’s homes, accompanying the sick, meeting young people and reaching out to communities which, due to their geographical remoteness or social vulnerability, are rarely able to make their voices heard.”
While the clergy sexual abuse scandal hasn’t exploded publicly in Peru as it has in other Latin American countries, Leo identified it as a “reality that has caused us so much pain.”
“We must respond as Jesus would, with truth, justice, forgiveness, making amends and an ever more resolute commitment to fostering a culture of prevention and protection for the weakest in light of such crimes,” Leo said.
The online database BishopAccountability has identified 77 priests, brothers, seminarians and lay consecrated in Peru who have been publicly accused of sexually abusing minors. But based on trends in other countries, the organization said that number is a “small fraction” of the total, arguing victims simply haven't come forward yet in the overwhelmingly Catholic country where the church wields significant influence.
Leo, who was the Peruvian bishops' point-person to welcome victims while he was Chiclayo bishop, was expected to meet with survivors during his stay in Peru. A protest by a victims group was also planned later Thursday.
Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, the president of the Amazonian bishops conference, said Leo was acutely attuned to the needs of the Peruvian people and church, and would offer words of consolation and advice during his days crisscrossing the country, from his beloved Chiclayo in the north to the Andes and rainforest.
“Leo will listen to the anguish and hopes of the Indigenous peoples, especially the pain caused by the violence affecting girls, boys, adolescents, and young people,” said Barreto, who was close friends with both Prevost and his predecessor, Pope Francis, a Jesuit like Barreto.
He predicted Leo would pay special attention to a recent case in the province of Condorcanqui, in the northern Peruvian jungle, where teachers sexually abused Indigenous Awajún and Wampis girls.
“Pope Leo will reaffirm the church’s commitment to continue accompanying Indigenous peoples in defending life, their dignity as persons, their cultures, and in caring for the Amazon,” Barreto said.
The Rev. Peter Hughes, an 84-year-old Irish priest who has lived in Peru for more than 60 years, said Leo was comfortable in Peru not only because he had it as his home, but because he sees its poverty and political polarization as mirroring the global situation.
“That is what makes leaders like Pope Francis and Pope Leo speak the language of the Gospel in very human terms, putting a premium on justice and peace,” he said. “In the Christian sense of justice, the most important people are the poor, the marginalized, and those who have no voice."

Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
- Published
As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.
But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.
His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," one woman watching the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.
Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.
There's a sense of injustice that Australia can't escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja was telling the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".
Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Cameron Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.
Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.
But he was also frank - using strong words to reject Khawaja's claims and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."
As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioning Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.
"I don't know what the outcome will be."

Passing out parade of over 2,700 Agniveers at INS Chilka today
Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan will be the chief guest and reviewing officer of the passing out parade in Chilka
More than 2,700 Navy Agniveers will complete their 16-week ab-initio training and pass out of the INS Chilka training facility in Odisha today, officials said.
This will be the first batch of Agniveers to join service after the government rolled out a revised Agnipath framework offering those who miss out on retention two additional years in uniform and another chance at becoming regular soldiers. More than 600 regular Naviks of the Coast Guard will also complete their training alongside the Navy Agniveers.
Navy chief Admiral Krishna Swaminathan will be the chief guest and reviewing officer of the passing out parade in Chilka. The latest batches of Army and Indian Air Force Agniveers will pass out of their training establishments in December.
Changes to the Agnipath Framework
The new framework was cleared by the Cabinet and unveiled by Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani on November 4. The revamped scheme will apply exclusively to the 3,00,000 Agniveers currently in service. It is expected to undergo further changes for recruits inducted after December 31.
Also Read: CAPFs debated merit, ex-Agniveer postings before Union Cabinet’s Agnipath overhaul approval
The Agnipath reboot was announced by Subramani weeks before the three services were set to release 75% of Agniveers from their first batch after four years of service, retaining only the 25% selected on merit for another 15 years under the scheme’s earlier provisions.
All existing Agniveers will become permanent after this two-year extended service, subject to meeting specific eligibility criteria and individual consent. Around 18,300 Agniveers were set to be discharged between mid-November and December 31, forming three-fourths of the 24,400 recruits inducted into the Army, Air Force and Navy in the first round of recruitment.
Defence Minister on the Revamped Scheme
On Thursday, defence minister Rajnath Singh said the scheme will further strengthen the three services. He said the scheme was revamped following feedback from the armed forces, reiterating the government’s commitment to incorporating the services’ suggestions into policy decisions.
Marriage Rules and Eligibility
The armed forces are expected to allow Agniveers to marry after completing their four-year tenure, including the 25% selected on merit for permanent service and those granted a two-year extension and another opportunity to enrol as regular soldiers under the revised Agnipath scheme. The marriage restriction will remain in force only during the initial four-year service period. Only young men and women aged between 17-and-a-half and 21 are eligible for recruitment under the scheme.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

BOUGAINVILLE DISPATCH
A Sweaty, Muddy Jungle Trek to a Famed World War II Wreck
Seven Chinese tourists, a dozen villagers and a couple of journalists forded streams and bushwhacked to the downed plane of Isoroku Yamamoto, the Japanese admiral. Machetes proved handy.
Halfway through the morning, I’m being tossed around like a popcorn kernel in the back of a troop carrier playing an eclectic medley of Backstreet Boys and Papua New Guinean jams.
We’re traveling along what feels more like a collection of loose rocks, arranged to be roughly vehicle width, than a road. I’ve lost count of the number of river crossings, including one where the water lapped a few inches from the car’s windows. And this is during a dry spell.
Our caravan is headed for an unlikely tourist destination deep in the jungle on Bougainville Island, an autonomous region of Papua New Guinea in the Solomon Sea.
The piecemeal remnants of a Mitsubishi G4M1 — Betty, as the planes were code-named by the Allies in World War II — have remained for some 80 years at the crash site of Japanese Navy Adm. Isoroku Yamamoto. This is the spot where Admiral Yamamoto, mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack, archvillain to Americans in the war, a respected and memorialized figure to the Japanese, met his end in 1943.
Bougainville was occupied by the Japanese in early 1942, in the months after Pearl Harbor, as the Imperial Navy pushed into the South Pacific, with Admiral Yamamoto at the helm. In April 1943, Allied forces intercepted and deciphered Japanese communication on the admiral’s travels, and American P-38 Lightning fighters gunned down his plane over southern Bougainville, a feat the Americans triumphantly dubbed Operation Vengeance.

Jensen Huang and his leather-clad likeness had become synonymous with the technological giant he co-founded, Nvidia. They were so entwined that, this year, the company sold $178 sweaters with a pixel-art version of Mr. Huang on the front.
Now, in the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation on Thursday after back-to-back cheating scandals, including an extramarital affair with a woman the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy, the internet has taken ahold of his image to unleash a flood of memes.
In many cases, they are being made by A.I. enthusiasts who revered Mr. Huang.
Images of Mr. Huang have appeared in online parodies of music videos, Bollywood movies, American sitcoms and kiss-cams at Coldplay concerts — many generated using artificial intelligence, the technology that became widely available through the chips Nvidia produces.
The revelations about Mr. Huang, 63, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. boom, are part of a long list of infidelity scandals that became memes.
Last year, the married chief executive of a tech start-up was caught on a kiss-cam at a Coldplay concert embracing the married but separated head of his company’s human resources department.
Mr. Huang’s image was superimposed on that viral moment by Peter Dedene, a Belgian software engineer. He said in a phone interview on Thursday that he was up late this week on his phone, scrolling the headlines about Nvidia.

In Maine, a new approach to practicing medicine in the sky
Clipboard in hand, pilot Will Bradbury stands near a helicopter at LifeFlight of Maine's Bangor headquarters. He's running down emergency landing tips with his crew.
"If we need to get out quickly because of smoke or fire, just watch the terrain so that you're not walking uphill into the rotors," he reminds flight nurse Denise Saucier and paramedic Brian Merklin.
The team is getting ready to take off on a medical transport flight. Saucier folds herself into the compact helicopter. She's worked for the air ambulance service for seven years and still calls it a dream job.
Dream job or not, the life of a flight clinician is hard and, given the headwinds slamming rural healthcare, getting harder.
Since 2015, demand for medical flights in Maine has doubled. In 2025, LifeFlight crews flew 3,031 flights, more than one every three hours. This year, demand is up another 10%.
Nationwide, air medical services are filling the gaps left behind as rural hospitals close, convert to outpatient-only rural emergency hospitals, or stop offering unprofitable services like labor and delivery.
And, as Medicaid cuts estimated by the Congressional Budget Office at $911 billion over ten years take effect, it's going to get worse. Hundreds more rural hospitals or maternity departments are at immediate risk of closing. With every closure, medical care gets further away.
And, increasingly, ground ambulance stations, many of which are also struggling to keep their doors open, can't meet the need. That leaves flight clinicians like Saucier and Merklin seeing more patients every day.
"We're seeing this across the board. The need for air medical services is increasing year over year," says Nicholas George. He runs the ETHOS Database, a national tracking system for air medical programs.
When the rural health care system breaks, EMS — on the ground and, increasingly, in the air — is the backstop.
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Healthcare of last resort
Every week or two, Saucier finds herself on a flight to one of Maine's thousands of islands. Occasionally, crews even land in the state's vast forests and mountains, then take snowmobiles to reach patients.
But "scene calls" to roadside — or trailside — accidents are less than 10% of LifeFlight's transports. (They're a higher percentage in urban areas.)
Most are interfacility transports, like today's. They'll stabilize a patient at a small, local hospital and fly them to a larger, better resourced one.
Saucier glances out the window for hazards. The view still reminds her of the role the organization plays in Maine, one of the country's most rural states.
"You go so long of a distance without seeing any houses, any roads," Saucier says. "It really hits home how rural Maine is and how necessary EMS is in the state."
And the pressure is on air ambulances as ground services in Maine are increasingly strained. The system is so fragmented that patients can fall through the cracks. Last year, a woman in a small northern Maine town died while the county dispatch center called 10 ambulance services. None responded.
Air ambulance services, though, come with unique challenges, particularly since the COVID-19 pandemic. It's been difficult to retain staff with the medical expertise to treat everything from heart attacks to injuries to fragile newborns, and who can stick with the demanding job without burning out.
Almost a quarter of ground-based EMS workers leaves the field every year. While there's no comprehensive staffing data for air medical services, flight clinicians face a slew of unique stresses, including dangerous conditions; long shifts and unpredictable hours; ever-increasing training and certification requirements; and significant mental health burdens. And then there's the pay, which is low throughout emergency medical services.
For years, LifeFlight retained only 60% to 70% of its workers, says CEO Joe Kellner.
"This is a really hard job," Kellner says. "By their job description, they are seeing people on their worst day, over and over again."
Training elite clinicians
This year, for the first time in nine years, LifeFlight is nearly fully staffed. One of the nation's handful of independent nonprofit air medical companies, LifeFlight has taken an innovative approach to the problems that plague the industry, including a combination of better training, higher pay and in-house mental health support.
Mike Abernethy, an EMS expert and retired emergency medicine professor at the University of Wisconsin, considers the company one of a handful of model programs for the industry. LifeFlight of Maine is a nonprofit, unlike much of the industry, which is dominated by for-profit businesses with reputations for charging exorbitant prices.
"There's just absolutely no comparison in the aviation and medical quality of these programs" versus an average for-profit air medical business, Abernethy argues.
When Kellner, a paramedic himself, became CEO in 2023, he began addressing the recruitment and retention problems. What LifeFlight calls the "Critical Care Academy," a six- to eight-month orientation program, is intended to address both issues.
Emergency critical care advances quickly. So most clinicians need regular education, both to remain successful on the job and to get hired in the first place.
On another day at headquarters, four instructors sit in a claustrophobic control room. Through a window looking into what appears to be a hospital room, paramedics Daniel Horne and Brad Alleger are undergoing an annual skills assessment, a simulation of a real-life medical crisis.
Dr. Dave Saquet turns on a mic and coughs. "It's hard to breathe," he whispers urgently. "It hurts everywhere."
His voice seems to be coming from the patient — a breathing, bleeding mannequin lying on a hospital bed.
"What happened to you?" Horne asks.
"My house was on fire," Saquet chokes out.
A wall monitor displays the patient's vital signs — which Saquet is manipulating on his laptop.
Medics and nurses here do simulations often, both to pass the Critical Care Academy, and also to stay up to date on occasional but critical events, like emergency births, newborn resuscitation, and burns. Before the assessment ends, the paramedics will have tried and failed to intubate the patient. After that "failure," they performed an emergency procedure to enable breathing, switching from the mannequin to a pig trachea.
Because it's hard to find recruits qualified enough for the rigorous training, the company also started a mentorship program for people considering applying. Some even attend the academy, gaining skills even if they'll never work for LifeFlight.
Success comes slowly: Recently, LifeFlight hired one of last year's mentees.
Experiments
Kellner instituted an unusual change that he says even nurses endorse: LifeFlight raised paramedics' pay to match flight nurses' compensation. Industrywide, paramedics make less. That keeps costs down, which is why pay equity is rare. Kellner believes the change has helped with recruitment.
Another experiment: LifeFlight hired a full-time mental-health counselor.
EMS workers' rates of post-traumatic stress injury, anxiety and depression are more thanfive times higher than the average American's.
"That has led people to leave this profession," Kellner says.
That was true for paramedic Brian Merklin, who was working for a different service in Nevada during the pandemic.
"We got hit really hard," he says. "The crews were just flying nonstop. We did four-day shifts, so for 96 hours we were just going, going, going."
About a third of the staff quit, he says. "They were getting air medical service plus COVID, right in the teeth."
Eventually, Merklin too needed a break. He left the profession for a few years. Then, when he felt the urge to fly again, he found LifeFlight.
Today's trip
The helicopter, which took off from Bangor, lands on a community hospital's rooftop helipad. Merklin and Saucier hurry to the patient's side. Most LifeFlight patients are unconscious or too ill to consent to share their stories, so the details are private. The injuries are shocking. If this patient doesn't get to a trauma center quickly, they might die.
Merklin and Saucier are unfazed.
But it's this kind of incessant trauma exposure that makes mental health support for first responders so invaluable.
Merklin serves on a peer support team.
"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."
If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."
As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.
Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.
Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

Former Italy defender and World Cup winner Marco Materazzi said the death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel last week had left him thankful he was not seriously injured when Zinedine Zidane headbutted him in the 2006 final.
Tenerife’s De Miguel passed after colliding with Andorra keeper Jesus Owono during a second division match.

Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest
- Published
Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.
A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.
Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.
The demonstrations by the student wing, called Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024 following a huge uprising against her rule.
Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.
Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.
A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.
"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.
"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.
Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.
Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.
The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.
The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.
A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.
She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".
Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.
But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".
"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.
"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.
A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.
Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.
Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

Social media giant Meta has once again come under the radar of Indian authorities over alleged child sexual abuse material (CSAM) prevalent on Meta-owned platforms. Now, National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) member Priyank Kanoon has urged the women and child developement (WCD) ministry to look into the financial relationship between the social media giant and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). Citing advocacy group Legal Rights Observatory, Kanoongo reportedly said that UNICEF is trying to offer its help to Indian authorities in the ongoing government probe into the child sexual abuse material (CSAM), sold as ads, on Meta platforms. Speaking with news agency PTI, Kanoongo flagged that Meta has given ‘millions of dollars” to UNICEF and continues to fund the organisation. He argued that this financial relationship could create a conflict of interest, particularly because UNICEF is engaged in child-protection work while Meta faces allegations involving exploitative content on its platforms. In a letter written to WCD secretary Anil Malik, he called for a probe into the financial ties between Meta and UNICEF. Kanoongo also raised concerns that UNICEF could end up serving Meta’s interests rather than supporting child protection. He also urged the government to ensure that Meta is not allowed to use UNICEF as a “shield to evade accountability”. “Therefore, there is a concern that this organisation, which is supposed to work on the issue of child sexual exploitation material while receiving funding from Meta, might end up serving Meta's interests. The activist group has expressed apprehension that this organisation could potentially work in favour of Meta's interests,” Kanoongo reportedly said. The NHRC member said that he has already brought the matter to the attention of the WCD ministry, external affairs ministry, home affairs ministry and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre. He also urged Indian authorities to keep the alleged conflict of interest in mind while conducting investigations and taking enforcement action. The concern, he claimed, was that allegations of vested interests being served through financial funding should not turn out to be true. This comes a months after a BBC Eye documentary, aired in July, allegedly found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India. As per Kanoongo, the NHRC has already identified about 100 such instances. The aftermath saw the Centre pull up the social media giant and summon the company’s top leadership. The government also directed Meta to strengthen CSAM detection, increase human oversight of moderation and improve safeguards for content in Indian languages and local contexts. Earlier reports suggested that government was considering waving off Meta’s “safe harbour” protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. This could have potentially forced the company to face greater legal liability in cases of CSAM or other illegal content being posted on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Post this, the social media giant agreed to report instances of child sexual abuse to the local law enforcement agencies in September. Days later, Meta also said that it has introduced LLM-driven systems to identify “signposting” within ads to counter predators who advertise illicit material in ways that can evade automated detection. The social media juggernaut also claims to have deployed AI-driven sweeps to uncover missed CSAM material and integrated “red-teaming” AI agents to strengthen detection mechanisms.

How good is Hamilton and how long can he stay in F1? - Q&A
- Published
McLaren's Lando Norris converted pole position into a race win at a wet-dry-wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.
Max Verstappen came through the field to take second after starting at the back of the grid because of an engine penalty, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar was on the podium in third.
Mercedes sealed the constructors' championship for the first time since 2021 at Interlagos following a fourth-place finish for George Russell and fifth for new world champion Kimi Antonelli.
Here BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.
Lewis Hamilton has just completed his 400th F1 grand prix, with more than 100 of these races having him on pole position. There are drivers with a better pole percentage than this, so just how good is he and for how much longer can he stay at the top? - Clive
Lewis Hamilton is unquestionably one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history.
He's statistically the most successful - with the most race wins and pole positions.
He's tied with Michael Schumacher for the most championships with seven, and many would - and do - argue he should have eight, given the controversy of the mishandled final race of the 2021 season.
Greatness as an F1 driver is about more than raw statistics, but even so Hamilton has consistently proved to be at the very highest level, with a series of outstanding drives in races that will go down in history as some of the greatest ever.
Examples of those would be the 2008 British Grand Prix and the 2021 Brazilian Grand Prix, along with many others.
All of this should go without saying.
He's also won races in nearly all his seasons - the only exceptions being 2022, 2023 and 2025.
There is no question that, within the context of his remarkable career, Hamilton struggled relatively in the era of 'ground-effect' cars from 2022-25.
He was beaten by Mercedes team-mate George Russell in two of their three seasons together, and looked a shadow of his usual self against Charles Leclerc in 2025.
Those performances led some to question why a driver formerly famed and lauded for his adaptability did not seem as able to adapt to the driving style required of those cars.
And that, in turn, led to questions as to whether the fact he apparently could not was related to his age - he is now 41.
But with this year's cars, Hamilton is back in much more familiar territory, is performing extremely well again and is neck-and-neck with Leclerc.
Those questions about the four years from 2022-25 will remain just that, but there is no doubt Hamilton is sensitive to them. He has referenced them a number of times this year, including last weekend in Brazil, when the topic of his 400th race came up.
"I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," he said. "It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important and the focus. For me, that number is kind of irrelevant."
Longevity in sport depends on many factors, and each athlete is different.
On the face of it, however, there is no obvious reason why, on an age front, Hamilton cannot continue for a good few more years - Fernando Alonso is 45 and is still performing at an extremely high level, as he proved yet again in Brazil at the weekend.
Hamilton has said he wants to race at least until F1 returns to Africa, which will not be until 2030 at the earliest, when he, too, will be 45.
For that, he will need at least one new contract, as his current one with Ferrari is believed to end next year.
