This image was AI-generated — OpenAI detected its own watermark on the image. However, the devastating flooding in Gaza is real, and there are dozens of authentic images illustrating the extent of the damage.
As winter flooding hit Gaza — where roughly 65% of the population, about 1.4 million people, lives in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the United Nations — a striking image circulated online in early November purportedly showing the magnitude of the flooding's damage.
Apparently shot at night, the image showed blue and white tents flooded by murky water, several buildings standing in the background as light from windows and streetlights appeared to reflect across the surface of the water.
Posts of the image shared across social media collectively gained millions of views and reactions, with hundreds of commenters appearing to believe the image was authentic. Prominent accounts, including British Parliament member Jeremy Corbyn, posted the image before deleting it (archived).
Although intense rainfall in Gaza early November has caused flooding and put thousands of people in danger as Israel continues to blockade crucial supplies — including 150,000 tents waiting just outside, according to the U.N. — this image was a fake.
The image contained multiple signs of being generated with artificial intelligrnace, including an OpenAI watermark that OpenAI's verification software identified. It's unclear precisely where it originated.
(OpenAI)
OpenAI reconstructs its images in a systemic grid pattern (autoregressive approach). Upon zooming in more closely, the pixel pattern of the image showed signs of a star-like grid, which digital forensics expert Hany Farid has described as a tell-tale sign of AI-generation.
(X user @ahmed_nashwan1 and Heny Farid, Snopes illustration)
The image displays other signs of AI generation, including unnatural light interruption, a mottled sky texture, and harsh lines between blurred pixels and textured pixels.
(X user ahmed_nashwan1, Snopes illustration)
Despite the fact that this image was AI-generated, there are hundreds of publicly available images showing the extent of the flooding destruction in Gaza.

Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.
The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.
A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

A few hours of exposure to firecracker smoke can be enough to trigger coughing, wheezing or breathlessness, particularly in people living with asthma or other respiratory conditions. The effects, however, are not limited to those with an existing diagnosis. High concentrations of particulate matter and gases can irritate the airways in anyone.
The Air Quality Index (AQI) is a numerical measure that converts the levels of different air pollutants into a single figure to indicate how polluted the air is and the likely health effects. India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) calculates it using eight pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide.

How many SpaceX Starship rocket tests have failed?
The answer isn't so simple.
In late September 2026, SpaceX's Starship entered orbit for the first time, deploying 26 Starlink satellites in what was heralded as a major step for SpaceX's cosmic ambitions. However, the celebration was cut short when a failed engine forced the mission to end shortly after reaching orbit. The malfunction prevented the intended six-revolution trek through Earth's orbit, falling well short of its 10-hour goal.
This result is typical for Starship, as the company's "fail fast, learn fast" mindset recasts the program's failures — anywhere between four and 11 of 14 total launches, depending on how generous you are — as opportunities for growth. This has been true since its first test flight in April 2023, which exploded 65 miles short of its intended climb into Earth's atmosphere. As Musk tweeted after the fiery test, "Congrats @SpaceX team on an exciting test launch of Starship! Learned a lot for next test launch."
Given SpaceX's success to date, it is hard to argue with the company's logic. According to analytics firm BryceTech, SpaceX launched 85 percent of all spacecraft in 2025, including over half the world's orbital launches. To boot, Starlink's 9,800 active satellites currently account for over half of the world's total, according to satellite tracker Orbital Radar.
The largest and most powerful rocket ever assembled, Starship has a cargo capacity five times larger than SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket. This makes it essential for SpaceX's grander ambitions, including its million-satellite constellation, NASA's lunar missions and Musk's Mars colony dream. With another launch set for November 13, 2026, stakeholders will soon see whether the September launch represented progress or foreshadowed further additions to SpaceX's growing list of frustrations.
A checkered history
Gauging the success of the Starship project is difficult. Although some missions may fit within a binary success-failure matrix, most land somewhere in between. And while it has yet to deliver a fully-reusable rocket capable of missions to "Mars and beyond," progress was always going to be incremental. As such, its only fair to judge each mission against its own standards of progress.
Starship's start was turbulent. After its initial test combusted within minutes, its second flight saw the first-stage booster separate before the booster and vessel met fiery ends. Five months later, Starship's third test flight completed many of its objectives, reaching an altitude of 145 miles before disintegrating on its return. SpaceX then had two back-to-back successful launches, culminating in its launch tower successfully catching Starship's first-stage booster.
Unfortunately, another troubled period followed. Test six saw SpaceX call off its lauded mechanical arm before crashing the Super Heavy booster into the Gulf of Mexico. Two months later, Starship 7 exploded over the Bahamas just eight minutes after takeoff, sparking investigations by both the FAA and the Turks and Caicos government. The FAA launched another investigation after Starship's eighth test exploded in space, grounding planes across Florida. Starship 9 achieved minor improvements before spinning out of control, forcing SpaceX to cancel its planned deployment of 8 mock satellites.
Starship followed the disastrous run with a pair of its most successful tests. In August 2025, Starship released its first cargo of Starlink satellites. Two months later, SpaceX successfully launched and landed its 11th Starship rocket, fulfilling all major objectives.
Starship's twelfth test launched its upgraded Starship V3 rocket. While it accomplished several objectives, engine failures caused it to crash into the Gulf, triggering yet another FAA investigation. In July 2026, Starship 13 successfully deployed 20 of Starlink's new high-powered satellites before its first-stage booster failed to stick the landing. Considering its scattershot history, Starship 14's semi-successful run is par for the course.
Failing towards the stars?
Judging each mission against its stated objectives, most Starship launches have failed to meet expectations. SpaceX, however, would likely claim that its willingness to learn from mistakes puts its true failure rate closer to zero. The better question is whether the program is learning quickly enough to keep pace with its own meteoric ambitions.
If one takes Musk's proclamations as a measuring stick, Starship has underdelivered. In 2025, Musk predicted there was a 50 percent chance Starship would land on Mars in 2026. And with the once-every-26-months Mars launch window closing this November, you can guess which side of the coin SpaceX landed on. Of course, Musk is notorious for overpromising, so this is business as usual at Starbase.
Earlier this year, NASA announced that the program had fallen behind schedule by at least two years since the Agency selected SpaceX's rocket to carry its Artemis moon lander in 2021. With China aiming to reach the moon by decade's end, the pressure is mounting. NASA hopes to return to the moon in 2028; to do so, Starship must meet the Artemis III deadline in summer 2027.
Beyond being Musk's conduit to Mars, SpaceX's most ambitious projects depend on Starship to slash costs. SpaceX's proposed 1 million-satellite datacenter constellation Starmind, for example, is impossible without a high-capacity reusable rocket. The November 13 test should provide another data point to judge SpaceX's progress, especially given its ambitions. In a Q3 earnings call, Musk stated that SpaceX will attempt to catch both the rocket and its booster, making it the 
"first time that an orbital launch vehicle has been fully recovered." During the event, Musk said the mission was "more likely than not" to succeed. Starship's history may say otherwise.

Microsoft Struggles to Repair Worldwide Outage

In November, right around Veteran's Day, posts online claimed to show former U.S. President Bill Clinton personally helping a homeless veteran outside The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in 1997.
According to the tale, Clinton offered the man, Marcus Williams, his coat, before asking him questions about his service. He then supposedly ordered a Secret Service agent to get Williams food, and personally contacted the Department of Veterans Affairs to help Williams get back on his feet.
The posts began:
"On a freezing December night in 1997, President Bill Clinton was leaving a holiday concert at the Kennedy Center when he noticed a homeless veteran sitting near the entrance. The man wore a thin jacket and was shivering in the cold. In his hands, he held a piece of cardboard with a simple message written on it: "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." What happened next caught the attention of people in the presidential motorcade. Clinton stopped, took off his own coat, placed it around the veteran's shoulders, and sat beside him on the icy concrete.
The veteran, 42 year old Marcus Williams, later told reporters that the President never questioned how he had ended up on the street or lectured him about his choices. Instead, Clinton asked about his military service, the battles he had experienced, and whether anyone had ever properly thanked him for what he had done. According to Secret Service agent Larry Cockell, who later wrote about the encounter, Clinton stayed with Marcus for nearly 25 minutes despite the freezing temperatures. When Marcus admitted that he had not eaten in two days, Clinton sent an agent to a nearby restaurant to get him food. He refused to leave until Marcus had finished his meal.
The posts were accompanied by images supposedly showing the two meeting as well as Williams holding a cardboard sign reading "Marine. Desert Storm. Hungry." Snopes readers contacted us to ask whether the story and images were real or fake.
We first uploaded the images into Google Lens to perform a reverse image search. Next, we used search engines such as DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo with phrases such as "Bill Clinton Marcus Williams Homeless Veteran" to see whether any reputable news outlets had documented the events. If the scene had occurred and the images were real, we would find evidence in newspapers and media archives like Getty Images. That was not the case. We did not locate any examples of credible outlets publishing the images, nor reporting on the alleged meeting.
We found that neither the story nor the images were real, and that they were generated using artificial intelligence tools. Therefore, we've labeled the claim false.
We uploaded the images accompanying the story into several tools that screen visual media for signs of AI: Sightengine, Hive Moderation, and Google's integrated SynthID detector. The first two found a high likelihood that the images were AI-generated, and the SynthID detector found the invisible watermark indicating Google's AI tools generated the images. We also ran the story through the AI text detection tool Pangram, which also determined that all of the text was written using a large language model such as ChatGPT.
Let us note here: These types of AI detection tools are fallible. Snopes cautions people against using them for definitive answers on media's authenticity without supporting evidence.
Detecting that the image was fake without using those tools was more difficult, given it was grayscale and grainy, but not impossible. We noticed that the writing on the cardboard sign looked too perfect, the cardboard itself looked unusually bright and the supposedly parallel sidewalk cracks didn't form straight lines or meet at a single vanishing point.
Our searches also uncovered a January article written by the fact-checking organization Lead Stories debunking the exact same story, though featuring a real archival image of Clinton instead of an AI-generated one. That fact-check also noted some factual errors in the text, most prominently that one of Clinton's Secret Service agents wrote about the encounter in a memoir. (No such memoir existed.) Because the exact claim was also previously been fact-checked almost a year ago, we concluded that users posting the claim in October and November were doing so in an attempt to make money.
The fictional story is an example of glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." These types of low-quality posts often use standard or template language, making small tweaks in an attempt to game the social media algorithms. They rely on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories and hope to generate a profit from advertising revenue if the posts go viral.
Snopes previously explained the ongoing trend of politically motivated, AI-generated slop content similar to the claim debunked in this article.

Here is a quick look at Ola Electric’s Q2 FY27 numbers: Operating revenue tanked 39% YoY to ₹421 Cr Consolidated net loss narrowed 13% YoY to ₹362 Cr Total expenses declined 28% YoY to ₹639 Cr Operating EBITDA loss rose 7% YoY to ₹218 Cr, while gross margin tanked 100 bps YoY to 29.9% Supply Woes Bite: The EV maker’s Q2 performance was defined by supply chain constraints, with component and charger bottlenecks restricting vehicle output and triggering a sharp sales decline. Despite weaker dispatches and rising commodity prices, aggressive cost reductions helped narrow net losses. That said, the management now plans to focus on ramping up supply chain and expects the output to improve to 25,000 in December The Dealer-Led Pivot: The quarter also saw the EV maker halt orders from company-owned stores and pivoted towards the traditional dealer-led network. By transferring inventory and financing to external partners, Ola Electric aims to trim expenses and streamline working capital cycles. While the initial dealer payouts are expected to compress near-term margins, the company expects improvements in margins as retail velocity stabilises across the new outlets. The Cash Question: All said and done, Ola Electric continues to report negative free cash flow during the quarter. While the company said that the gap was largely due to capex at the Gigafactory, it claims to have bolstered its cash reserves through fundraises and pared down legacy borrowings. It also expects changes to India’s GST refund mechanism to shorten refund cycles and free up working capital. Rivers in the sky are raining down on the Pacific Northwest. What are they?
It's the wettest time of the year for one of the wettest parts of the country: the Pacific Northwest.
This week is no exception as heavy rain, high tides and a rising sea level hit the West Coast.
And more storms are on their way.
Two atmospheric rivers, bringing heavy rain, will pound parts of Oregon and Washington state back-to-back on Friday and Saturday. Two other atmospheric rivers already dropped multiple inches of rain on both states earlier this week.
"What's really problematic is when you get compounding impacts from multiple atmospheric rivers," said Josh Weiss, a meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Weather Prediction Center. Those impacts include flash flooding, urban flooding and even landslides, he said.
This year's atmospheric river season, which runs from October to March, is off to a fast start, said Weiss.
What do we mean by a river in the sky?
An atmospheric river is a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind. Loaded up with moisture, it dumps rain or snow. These rivers can be up to 2,000 miles long and 600 miles wide, said F. Martin Ralph, the director of the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography.
"It's literally a river in the sky," said Ralph, one of the leading researchers on atmospheric rivers. These rivers are a natural climate pattern. In fact, about 50 to 60% of rain in California comes from atmospheric rivers, Weiss said.
Residents in the Pacific Northwest are used to heavy downpours. But the atmospheric rivers are hitting as El Niño's warm ocean waters contribute to rising sea levels and fuel storm systems. And right now, these natural weather patterns are coinciding with annual high tides, known as King tides. That leaves coastal and inland waterways along the West Coast at risk for flooding.
Ralph said that according to 40 years of data from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, 90% or more of all flood damage in the Western U.S. is from atmospheric rivers.
This weekend, Jeff Michalski, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Seattle, said that Washington's coast could be hit by significant 20-foot swells.
Pineapple and rum
People may know atmospheric rivers from their nicknames, such as Pineapple Express or Rum Runner Express. These names describe where the atmospheric river originates. A Pineapple Express, which came across the Pacific Ocean from Hawaii in late October, caused devastating flooding and multiple deaths in the Southwest's Four Corners regions.
Atmospheric rivers aren't just a West Coast phenomenon. Some larger nor'easters on the East Coast can pack a "nasty" atmospheric river, UCSD's Ralph said.
The term atmospheric river is one of a few technical science terms that have gained traction on social media and in the news over the past few years, along with El Niño and Kelvin waves.
But is there a relationship between El Niño and atmospheric rivers? Do the warm ocean temperatures associated with El Niño and the heat those waters release make the rivers stronger? That was Ralph's theory back in 2015, but his research showed the opposite.
"[Atmospheric rivers] don't dance to the tune of El Niño," Ralph said
Climate scientists say there also isn't enough data to connect the weather pattern to human-caused global warming, although a warming world does mean more water vapor in the atmosphere.
"We've got to keep our eyes" for atmospheric rivers, Ralph said. "Whether it's an El Niño year or a La Niña year or a No Niño year."

On 11 November 2026, terrorists opened fire on a CRPF checkpoint near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district of Jammu and Kashmir, injuring three personnel. The attackers fled after the firing, and security forces launched a search operation to track them down (here, here, and here).
Amid the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel, a video is being shared on social media (here, here) with the claim that it shows defence expert Wing Commander (Wg Cdr) Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the attack was a false flag operation orchestrated to divert public attention from mounting political pressure on the Narendra Modi government, including Congress protests demanding the Chief Election Commissioner’s resignation and the Arunachal Pradesh controversy. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) stating that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) did not describe the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel as a false flag operation. In the original ANI video, he discussed the security situation in Kulgam, the presence of terrorist sleeper cells, and the need for better intelligence coordination and proactive security measures. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also confirmed on 12 November 2026 that the viral video was digitally altered and falsely attributed remarks to him. AI detection tools, Hive and Hiya, also indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords but found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating it.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 11 November 2026, featuring the same footage of Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd), wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background. However, in the original video, he does not describe the Kulgam attack as a false flag operation or link it to the political developments mentioned in the viral clip. Instead, he expresses concern over the incident, noting that Kulgam has witnessed several such attacks in the past. He emphasises the need for a more proactive security approach, better intelligence coordination, and improved intelligence gathering in areas where terrorists operate and maintain sleeper cells. He also highlights the need to investigate how these groups receive logistical support, including accommodation, ammunition, and water.
We then analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear that Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd) was describing the Kulgam attack as a false-flag operation.
The Indian Army’s fact-check wing also debunked the claim in an X post dated 12 November 2026, stating that the video was digitally manipulated and falsely attributed remarks to Wing Commander Praful Bakshi (Retd). It clarified that he did not make any such comments in the original video and had instead spoken about terrorist organisations and the need for offensive action and better coordination to prevent such attacks.
To sum up, this video of Wg Cdr Praful Bakshi (Retd) alleging that the Kulgam attack on CRPF personnel was a false flag operation is digitally manipulated.

Mexican Prosecutor Who Helped C.I.A. Secretly Operate in His State Flees to the U.S.
The prosecutor, who faces arrest in Mexico after allowing C.I.A. officers into Chihuahua state, is under the protection of the U.S. government, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
A Mexican former prosecutor facing arrest after allowing Central Intelligence Agency officers to operate in his state has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.
The former prosecutor, Guillermo Zuany Portillo, shepherded C.I.A. officers for more than six months beginning last year as they trained forces in his state, Chihuahua, joined those forces on counter-cartel missions and provided expertise during ground operations, a New York Times investigation revealed this week.
Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, had repeatedly said she did not want U.S. forces taking part in operations on the ground in Mexico, calling it a breach of sovereignty. Under the Trump administration, meanwhile, the C.I.A. sought to expand its activity in the country, and saw Mr. Zuany as a partner to help it do so quietly.
The C.I.A.’s cover in Chihuahua was blown when a car crash in April resulted in the deaths of two C.I.A. officers, leading to a national scandal and Mr. Zuany’s resignation. While an investigation determined the crash an accident, the Mexican authorities recently issued a warrant for Mr. Zuany’s arrest on charges related to his involvement with the agency.
Ms. Sheinbaum expressed fury at the C.I.A.’s presence during raids in Chihuahua and denied knowledge of the agency’s activities. On Wednesday, she said in a regular morning news conference that investigations into matter must continue.
“It’s worth finding out who this person is and how he worked with one of the U.S. agencies,” she said of Mr. Zuany.

Abdul El-Sayed will soon become the first epidemiologist in the Senate at a moment that would keep anyone with a public health background up at night. More than 5,000 Americans have been sickened by the measles this year and the United States is expected to lose its formal measles elimination status by the end of the month. Dengue fever is spreading in Florida, respiratory virus season is underway, and the United States just weathered a foodborne illness outbreak that sickened more than 20,000.
In a wide-ranging interview with STAT, the Michigan Democrat emphasized that he is hopeful the United States can fix its growing trust-in-science problem, but he expressed frustration — at Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., at drug and insurance companies, and at the field of public health — for leading America down this path.
“We’ve created the space for a few grifters to come in and in effect lie to the public,” El-Sayed said. “To create a level of distrust in science and in public health that has had disastrous consequences.”
Below, El-Sayed speaks about his plan to rebuild trust in science and public health, his intentions toward Kennedy, and how gatekeeping has kept scientific discoveries from the public. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
As the senator-elect from Michigan, how can you help restore trust in health and science? What can you do from Washington to improve these issues?
Well, No. 1, I think you can start taking on greed. Which is why I support “Medicare for All,” because it gets the greed of the insurance industry and the greed of the pharmaceutical industry and the greed of the hospital corporations out of the way so folks can benefit from the incredible things that science creates.
No. 2, I think you have to show the grifters for who they are and how they are, the ways that they use big words that they don’t understand to trick the public, the ways that there’s always a catch at the end where they’re making money off of their grift.
And No. 3, I want to reinvigorate a movement for public health that is willing to stand up to the power of big corporations. … I think we need to be willing to pick a righteous fight in service of the public health.
You’ve mentioned your eagerness to investigate RFK Jr. Are you concerned at all that grilling RFK could serve to further polarize the people that do believe in him?
Well, depending upon how you grill him.
What do you mean?
You can grill a steak and get it to perfect medium rare, or you can grill a steak and it’s well done and inedible, the way the president likes it.
The mistake would be to focus on areas that are polarizing. I wanna understand why he DOGE’d away or he allowed the DOGE’ing away of the CDC [Centers for Disease Control and Prevention] and the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] in ways that left us eating crap lettuce. I want to understand why he hasn’t led the effort to take on the pesticides that are in our food or the additives in our food, why he’s kowtowing to the same corporations he said he was going to stand up to. I want to understand that. Let’s start there.
Why Kennedy supporters should trust him
I’m curious if you have a message to the people that do support Kennedy on why they should trust someone like you on issues of public health.
Well, he told you he’s gonna stand up to the corporations. He hasn’t. I have.
There’s no candidate who’s taken more spending against them in a primary election in their own party than I have, not in history. So at least you know I’m gonna stand up.
I’ve spent my whole career trying to make people healthier, trying to address the greed in our health care system.
There’s all this talk of back and forth: Should RFK Jr. be investigated? Should he be removed? What’s your latest thinking on this?
I think we focus too much on him. I think the bigger question is how do we build the CDC and FDA and NIH [National Institutes of Health] that are worthy of the people that they serve, and that’s gonna always be my focus.
So any investigation that we’re doing is about trying to correct the problems and address the flaws and the faults rather than trying to achieve any sort of retribution.
The people are struggling. They are suffering. They can barely afford groceries, can barely afford gas, can barely see a doctor, are worried about the air they’re breathing, the water they’re drinking, the quality of groceries they’re even buying for an exorbitant price.
My job is to serve them. The personalities involved are secondary to me. My job is to go in and figure out what went wrong, how do we fix it, and how do we hold accountable the people who — if they knowingly broke something — how we do we hold them accountable for it. It’s that simple. It’s less about the personalities. I think we focus too much on that.
Working with RFK Jr.
There’s been this desire among folks within your party to find common ground with RFK on issues. Are there issues that you think you could work with RFK and his team on, or are we kind of past that?
If he actually wants to show up and start doing the things he said he was going to do on pollutants, on additives, sure. I’ll work with anyone. He could be wrong on 95 things, but if he’s right on five, I’ll work with him on those five and hold him accountable for the 95.
Obviously Democrats can’t fix all of these issues. Trust issues started before RFK and I’m sure they’ll go on past RFK. How do you think about how we should judge Democrats’ progress on these issues?
Are we achieving goals that keep people healthy, reduce their costs, empower them. … If we’re doing that, then we’re winning and we’re succeeding. If not, then we’re not. I want people to be able to be their healthiest and their wealthiest. That’s really the bottom line.
It seems like a foregone conclusion, the U.S. will lose its measles elimination status. Do you have thoughts on that?
It’s a travesty. We didn’t have to get here. In a lot of ways, obviously, I blame mis- and dis-information mongers like RFK Jr. for that, but I also blame our collective scientific and health care apparatus for creating the circumstances where somebody like him could step in, and he would have a willing audience willing to listen.
Where did we go wrong in making health care so untrustworthy that somebody with such limited cognitive ability and who is so obviously a grifter, where he could step in and change so many minds? That’s on us.
Science is ‘a beautiful, incredible gift’
The belief that the measles vaccine causes autism is going up over time, and it’s been debunked for 20 years. … How do we break through here?
It starts with basic science education. … Too often the way that scientists speak is about speaking to other scientists to make themselves sound smarter rather than speaking to the public, to help the public feel as smart as they really are. By making sure that everybody understands how and why these things work. Science for the public good … that ethos is something that we’ve forgotten. And I really, desperately want us to remember it.
Science is a gift. It’s a beautiful, incredible gift, and we missed the opportunity to communicate it in all of its elegance because too often it is this thing that is sort of held among the scientific community for consumption by the scientific community. And then we allow a lot of our best science to sit behind paywalls people can’t hop over. So there’s a resentment that happens in publicly funded science for the most part, and we’re keeping [it] out of the hands of people who need it most.
These are big structural questions that ought to animate the way we do science for the rest of the 21st century, and I’m hoping that I can use my role as a doctor and a scientist in the Senate to start driving that conversation among the folks in science.
You can focus on RFK Jr. all you want, but he identified a set of weaknesses that those of us who have committed our lives to science and the public’s health that we allowed to exist in the first place.
How hopeful are you that we can solve these trust issues?
I wouldn’t be doing this if I didn’t believe we could. Science always wins. I just hope that it wins quickly. But the beautiful thing about science is that in the end it always finds the right answer.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Jensen-Gate isn't just Nvidia's problem anymore. Data center operators across Southeast Asia might be getting caught in the fallout.
In case you missed it, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has had a rough week. On Sunday, The New York Times published an exposé that the executive had an affair with Singapore-based Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, believed to be passing sensitive Nvidia information to Beijing.
Alice Huang worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that is the largest Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia, per Bloomberg. US authorities have investigated the company on suspicion that it helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of US export restrictions.
Huang resigned from his role on Thursday.
Industry sources in data center financing and operations told Business Insider that Jensen-Gate could increase scrutiny on Southeast Asia's AI infrastructure companies.
Jensengate could lead to increased oversight
Chris Miller, the author of "Chip War" and a professor at Tufts University, said to Yahoo Finance on Monday that it was widely known that Megaspeed was "primarily building data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese customers, especially Alibaba in their case."
He added that Megaspeed isn't alone, and that there are many data centers in Malaysia, Thailand, and Singapore that buy advanced American chips and sell them to customers in China.
He expects these relationships to face more oversight from Washington after Huang's scandal.
SEA AI infrastructure operations may get slower and more expensive
More scrutiny means slower and more expensive processes.
Lior Prosor, the managing partner of Deep33, an NYC-headquartered venture fund that invests in AI infrastructure, told Business Insider that the Huang affair would intensify scrutiny of American tech deployments in Southeast Asia, especially which customers' hands they end up in.
"That could increase financing costs and create additional hurdles for some operators," Prosor said.
He said this could temporarily create a broader risk premium for Southeast Asian operators, even those with no connection to Megaspeed.
Chinmoy Baruah, the CEO of Dublin-based semiconductor company ChipX, said he expects approvals for AI infrastructure projects in the region to take longer, as investors and partners will ask more detailed questions on compliance. ChipX has committed to building wafer fabrication plants in Malaysia.
"That may slow some projects at the margin, particularly those with less transparent structures," Baruah told Business Insider.
Michael Heinrich, the CEO of Singapore-based decentralized AI compute company 0G, said he could see fundraising for AI infrastructure get more selective over the next year.
"The next round of capital will go to the operators who can prove where their chips are, who uses them, and who owns the business," Heinrich said.
Bitter medicine, but better long-term health
The Huang scandal won't have a lasting impact on demand for Southeast Asian AI infrastructure, but rather on the standards for it, said Baruah.
He said the region's fundamentals — growing digital economies, supportive governments, improving connectivity, and rising AI adoption — remain strong. This incident, however, will make rules clearer and increase diligence among operators, chip suppliers, and regulators.
"That is a positive outcome for Southeast Asia, because it strengthens the region's position as a reliable, long-term destination for global digital infrastructure investment, not a shortcut around the rules," Baruah said.
Prosor from Deep33 added that AI compute is in "extraordinarily short supply, and capital will flow to wherever companies can reliably build up compute.
"Southeast Asia remains an important part of that equation," he said.
Southeast Asia's data center boom
The Huang scandal comes as the data center industry in Southeast Asia is booming.
Ember Energy, a London-headquartered energy think tank, wrote in a 2025 report that ASEAN — a bloc of 11 member states in Southeast Asia — was emerging as a "global data center hot spot" due to lower construction costs and electricity levies.
Malaysia, for instance, had live data center operations totaling about 1.3 gigawatts in June, which was a tenfold increase from 2022, per a report by BloombergNEF, a think tank under Bloomberg. It has another 4.7 gigawatts planned or under construction, the report added.
Indonesia had about 450 megawatts of live data-center capacity as of June, with more than four times that amount currently under construction or committed, per the BloombergNEF report.
A rough week for Nvidia
Huang's resignation comes after a tumultuous few days for Nvidia.
Its stock took a hit after the US midterm elections on November 3, which flipped control of Congress to the Democrats, many of whom had made anti-data-center messaging a major part of their campaigns.
A few days after reports on Huang's affair, on Wednesday, the Times published another report that said Huang had had a second extramarital relationship, this time with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The Wall Street Journal wrote on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang.
Early Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned from the role, and CFO Colette Kress would take over as interim CEO.

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

Online pharmacy startup PlatinumRx is in talks to raise around $32 Mn (over ₹300 Cr) in a funding round led by Belgium-based investment giant Sofina Ventures, as per sources familiar with the discussion. The proposed transaction is expected to value the Bengaluru-based startup somewhere in the range of $150-200 Mn (₹1,400-1,878 Cr). The proposed investment comes around a year after the startup raised $6 Mn in its Series A round. Stellaris Venture Partners and India Quotient backed the startup in its Series A round. The startup had previously raised around $800K in a seed round in April 2024, also led by India Quotient. Inc42 has reached out to the aforementioned investors to understand whether they will participate in the round. The September 2025 round had helped the startup strengthen its supply chain, expand fulfilment capabilities and build its product and technology teams. It had also outlined plans to add five fulfilment centres and improve sourcing efficiencies to make affordable substitute medicines more accessible. The discussions are understood to be ongoing, and the final terms of the transaction, including the valuation and investor participation, could change. Questions sent to PlatinumRx and Sofina Ventures didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. If concluded, the funding round would mark a significant jump in PlatinumRx's valuation and provide it with the fresh capital required to strengthen its presence in India's online pharmacy market. Founded in 2023 by Ashutosh Pandey and Piyush Kumar, PlatinumRx operates an online pharmacy platform focused on helping consumers find affordable alternatives to prescribed medicines. The platform recommends substitute medicines with the same composition, allowing customers to access lower-cost options, particularly for recurring and chronic medication requirements. These medicines are sourced directly from pharmaceutical companies and offer alternatives with the same composition, addressing the price difference between branded medicines and their substitutes. It claims to have served over 10 Lakh customers till date. The proposed funding comes amid continued investor interest in specialised healthcare and pharmacy platforms. While quick commerce platforms are expanding into medicine delivery, online pharmacy startups are also attempting to build differentiated models around affordability, assortment and access. Broadly, the online pharmacy segment has continued to attract sizable investments. Quick medicine delivery startup Plazza raised $15 Mn in a Series A funding round in July 2026, co-led by Accel, Elevation Capital and Nexus Venture Partners, with participation from existing investors All In Capital and Better Capital. The Bengaluru-based startup operates a pharmacy-first quick commerce model focused on 15-30 minute medicine deliveries. On the other hand, last year, Truemeds had raised $85 Mn in funding to scale generic medicine delivery.

The British comedian Russell Brand is a major figure in health secretary Robert F. Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again movement. He regularly joined conference calls organized by the super PAC MAHA Action, on one occasion dialing in naked from a bath tub. He was a keynote speaker alongside Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz at the September 2026 MAHA Summit. He is also a convicted rapist who was just sentenced to 10 and a half years in jail.
During Brand’s trial, Tony Lyons, MAHA Action’s founder, was at the courthouse to support him. Lyons had argued that Brand was falsely accused, saying “he’s been vilified, persecuted, deplatformed, demonetized, censored, prosecuted.” On Tuesday, after the conviction came down, MAHA Action Inc.’s newsletter published a 3,700-word defense of Brand.
I’ve followed MAHA closely and I’m not at all surprised that the movement’s leadership is standing by Brand. There is a rot of toxic masculinity and violence at MAHA’s core.
Even before the prison sentence, MAHA happily palled around with Brand, despite the British police charging him in April 2025 and again in December 2025 with multiple counts of rape and sexual assault. The charges did not come out of nowhere: In 2023, three British outlets jointly published a special investigation into allegations against Brand.
National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya, who has said he wants the NIH to become “the research arm of MAHA,” shared billing with Brand at a November 2025 MAHA Summit. Earlier that year, Kennedy posted a photo of himself clutching a lizard, as Brand and a shirtless Oz put their arms around him, all smiles.
Perhaps most shocking of all, Oz chuckled at a joke about sexual consent that Brand made at the October 2026 MAHA Summit.
Oz told the audience that Brand was almost late because he was backstage “hugging the Secretary of Agriculture,” Brooke Rollins, to which Brand replied, “She initiated that contact, I should make clear, doctor!” I agree with Holly Baxter, senior reporter at The Independent, who said that of course the jocular exchange between Brand and Oz looks bad now, “but it should’ve looked bad then, when the court case was on the horizon, so let’s not expect much hand-wringing from Oz, MAHA-maven RFK Jr., and the other Trump health officials who embraced Brand over the past two years.”
The alliance between MAHA and Brand is not an aberration, it’s a pattern of befriending violent misogynists. MAHA made Mike Tyson, another convicted rapist who said in 1989 that he enjoyed hurting women, the face of its healthy eating campaign. Bhattacharya even posted a picture of himself with a Tyson face tattoo and the message “Be like Mike Tyson.” The New York Times reported that Donald Trump Jr., who championed the MAHA movement at Turning Point USA’s 2025 annual conference, “once called Andrew Tate a friend and publicly defended him against previous criminal allegations.” Tate is a leader of the manosphere who faces extradition to Britain on multiple charges including rape and sex trafficking.
You might think the shellacking that MAHA-allied candidates suffered in the midterm elections, despite major financial support from MAHA Action, would have led the MAHA bosses to rethink their allegiances. You’d be wrong.
On Nov. 6, for example, Kennedy celebrated Stephen Miller’s appointment as President Trump’s chief of staff, saying, “Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.” Miller is the man behind the inhumane family separation policy in Trump’s first term. He is also the architect of ICE’s brutal tactics during Trump 2.0. Kennedy has defended ICE tactics on Joe Rogan’s show and provided support for the horrific treatment of undocumented immigrants. Across the country, unaccompanied immigrant children as young as 3, who came to the U.S. to be reunited with their families, have faced sometimes tough interrogation by judges, nearly always having to represent themselves in court without a lawyer. Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services is legally required to care for them through its Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), and federal law requires these children be provided with legal counsel, fair hearings, and accommodation appropriate to a child’s age. But Kennedy, who has adopted harsh anti-immigrant rhetoric and who falsely argues that immigrants are disease vectors, refused to renew the contract to provide legal services for these children. And almost 90% of undocumented children are now being held in unlicensed ORR shelters in Texas, exempt from oversight and inspections.
Since the MAHA wipe-out in the midterms, there have been an endless slew of articles pondering how MAHA will change course. But MAHA’s rotten core of violence, including its love for Brand (who Lyons called “an incredible human being”), is one big reason why I’m deeply skeptical that “MAHA 2.0” will be any different. Beth Mole, senior health reporter at Ars Technica, notes that leaders of the grassroots wing of the MAHA movement remain “doggedly loyal” to Kennedy. They’re loyal to a man who has worked with Trump to roll out policies that I believe are inherently violent, who has espoused eugenicist views, and who shows zero signs of remorse.
There was violence in the MAGA/MAHA administration enacting policies that will throw 15 million people off health insurance, that cut off an estimated 2 million kids from food assistance, and that killed federal health research that could have improved the health of minoritized Americans. There is eugenics in the way that Kennedy blames the weak for their sickness, believes only “sick kids should die of measles,” and once said he wants to remove Black kids from their families and “reparent” them on government-run farms.
So when I think of MAHA’s future, there’s an old proverb that comes to mind: “The fish rots from the head down.” The head is, of course, Kennedy, MAHA’s supreme leader. Unless he radically changes his views and policy directions — which seems extremely unlikely — MAHA is destined to be that rotting fish in perpetuity.
Gavin Yamey is a professor of global health and public policy at Duke University in Durham.

Nations Championship: England, Ireland in points race, return of Eddie Jones to Twickenham, injury-hit France face Springboks
Second week of Nations Championship Tests in northern hemisphere sees England host Japan as Eddie Jones returns to Twickenham; Ireland welcome Fiji; injury-hit France vs Springboks in blockbuster; inaugural tournament concludes at Allianz Stadium from November 27-29
Thursday 12 November 2026 18:27, UK
The second weekend of Nations Championship Tests brings an England-Ireland points battle, Eddie Jones’ return to Twickenham and an injury-hit France facing the Springboks.
Points race for England and Ireland
Heading into the fifth weekend of six Nations Championship rounds - split between July in the southern hemisphere and November in Europe - England and Ireland have near-identical records.
Even with bonus points in play, Steve Borthwick's side and Andy Farrell's Ireland are set for a close finish, with their final standings potentially determining who reaches the title decider.
Both currently sit on 15 competition points, but England are 42 points better off in terms of points difference at the moment, owing to the fact they beat Fiji 73-8 in July, and added to that with a handsome 45-22 home success over Australia last week.
In July, Ireland edged a high-scoring win over Australia to claim a bonus point, followed it up with another bonus-point victory over Japan (despite winning by just 16 points), before losing to the All Blacks at Eden Park without securing a bonus point for either a narrow defeat or scoring four tries
On home soil, Ireland then dispatched of Argentina 42-12 last week, but failed to score a point in the final quarter of the Test, which they may yet pay for.
For England, they lost to South Africa at Ellis Park without banking any losing bonus points, then annihilated Fiji in Liverpool and held on to win in Argentina with a crucial bonus point.
Last week's morale-boosting win over Australia has now given England a great chance of at least finishing second and facing one of South Africa or New Zealand on finals weekend at Twickenham.
For Ireland to overtake England, they must outperform them across the final two rounds. That means beating South Africa in Dublin while hoping New Zealand defeat England at Twickenham, or securing more bonus points in defeat to the Springboks than England manage against the All Blacks.
With comfortable wins expected for England and Ireland against Japan and Fiji respectively this Saturday, the Irish are unlikely to make significant inroads into England's substantial points-difference advantage.
Instead, it is likely to come down to bonus points.
Jones stoking the flames on his return as Japan seek huge shock
Former England head coach Eddie Jones is plotting a historic upset, backing Japan to stun England at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.
The Brave Blossoms have lost all six previous Tests against England and are 40-1 outsiders to pull off a seismic Nations Championship shock.
But Jones, who coached England from 2016 to 2022, is preparing a few surprises for his former side.
"It's a big week for Japanese rugby," Jones said this week. "We realise England are a nation we've never been able to beat.
"Everyone knows the record and we want to do something a bit different this week and we've trained like that, so I'm really pleased with the team.
"We've had really good training to prepare us for the game we are expecting against England.
"We had two days of very settled and pretty training but Wednesday was quite dirty. We had to adapt to certain situations and in the end we did it really well.
"I was really pleased with the players, really pleased with their effort, really pleased with the way they adapted to the situations.
"I'm looking forward to going to Twickenham with this young Japanese team that's going to play the house down."
Jones remains England's most successful coach by win rate, with 72 per cent, having won two Six Nations titles, including the 2016 Grand Slam. He also guided England to the 2019 World Cup final, but his tenure ended acrimoniously, with his side booed by fans in 2022.
"If you look at the stats, they stand the test of time," Jones said. "So there's no reason why I shouldn't be pleased to go back to Twickenham."
The 66-year-old has been doing the media rounds this week, also saying his Japan side are aiming to "make the Twickenham sky fall in on" Steve Borthwick's "distracted" charges in Saturday's Test.
Injury-hit France welcome Springboks to Paris in blockbuster
Two of the world's top sides go head-to-head on Friday as France host South Africa.
The Springboks insist they have no special plans to contain Antoine Dupont at fly-half, instead trusting their defence to limit the space available to the French playmaker.
With Romain Ntamack injured and Matthieu Jalibert already ruled out, Dupont will wear the No 10 jersey, with Maxime Lucu at scrum-half.
Both are more accustomed to playing at nine but have featured at fly-half for their clubs, and South Africa expect the pair to interchange positions during the match.
"He's [Dupont] played at 10 before for his club [Toulouse], and we saw the game where he played there. He was very good," captain Siya Kolisi told reporters on Thursday.
"I mean, he can play almost anywhere on the field, so I don't think it is a surprise to see him there.
"Obviously, nobody wants injuries, but every team experiences them and you have to adjust. He's a good enough player to do it. He's shown that over the years."
Kolisi said the Springboks had no specific plan to stop Dupont at fly-half, insisting their defence would stick to its usual system regardless of the opposition or individuals they face.
"Our system doesn't change for any team we play against. We have a system that works and we've prepared for them," he added.
"We haven't done anything special for him individually just because he's playing at 10. We know Lucu has also played at 10 for Bordeaux, so it will be natural for them to swap positions.
"We know Antoine wants to be on the ball a lot and creates a lot, so for him to move to nine [during the game)] will also be natural."
Kolisi expects an intense atmosphere in Paris, the scene of the Springboks' epic 29-28 victory over France in the quarter-finals of the 2023 Rugby World Cup.
South Africa have won nine of their last 10 Tests against the French, the only blemish a 30-26 loss in Marseille in 2022.
They are unbeaten in their last five Tests in Paris, last losing in the French capital in 2005.

A video (here & here) of a man stabbing a girl is being shared on social media with the claim that a Hindu schoolgirl was stabbed in Dhaka, Bangladesh, by a local Jamaat youth leader for rejecting his advances. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video showing a Hindu schoolgirl getting stabbed by a Muslim Youth in Dhaka, Bangladesh.
Fact: The incident took place in Kushtia city, Bangladesh, on 09 November 2026. Both the victim and the attacker involved in this incident belong to the Muslim community. The victim is identified as Zakia Sultana, daughter of Zakaria and Sumi Akter. The attacker is identified as Imon, son of Abbas Uddin Ali. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to Bangladeshi news reports (here & here) covering the incident. According to these reports, the attack took place in Kushtia city on 9 November 2026, when Zakia (Jakia) Sultana, a Class X student, was stabbed by a youth named Imon outside her house.
Further searches led to more media reports (here, here & here) identifying the victim as Zakia Sultana, daughter of Zakaria Hossain and Sumi Akter. Zakia was reportedly returning home after an examination and waiting at her house’s gate when Imon approached and stabbed her repeatedly. She was subsequently taken to the hospital for treatment and is now out of danger.
According to Zakia’s mother, Imon had allegedly been harassing her daughter for a while at the coaching centre where they both studied. After Zakia’s family informed Imon’s guardians about the harassment, he reportedly stopped. The family suspects the attack was carried out in retaliation for their complaint. The police arrested Imon and identified him as the son of Abbas Uddin. We found no credible news reports linking Imon to Jamaat-e-Islami. The evidence clearly indicates that the victim is a Muslim, not a Hindu.
To sum it up, a video of a personal dispute and stabbing involving two individuals from the Muslim community in Kushtia is being falsely shared online with a communal angle.
