Christina Applegate asks if breast implants are behind symptoms after MS misdiagnosis
On her podcast, the actor questioned if her implants might be leaking and contributing to her health problems
Actor Christina Applegate, 54, says she is exploring whether her breast implants could be linked to her pain and fatigue after learning she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis (MS) — the diagnosis she received in 2021.
On the Nov. 10 episode of MeSsy, the podcast she co-hosts with actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler, Applegate, who first gained fame as a teen in the hit sitcom Married With Children, said someone had recently sent her a study describing breast implant-related symptoms as resembling MS.
"I swear, over the last five years or whatever, I thought, 'What if they're leaking and they're poisoning me?'" she said, noting she plans to discuss the possibility with her doctors.
- As Christina Applegate reveals MS misdiagnosis, doctor warns of wrong treatment risks
- The subject of Lyme disease is littered with misinformation. Celebrities are part of the problem, experts say
Applegate underwent a double mastectomy and breast reconstruction in 2008 after being diagnosed with an early form of breast cancer and testing positive for a BRCA1 gene mutation, which carries a higher risk of breast and other cancers. On her podcast, she said she was "way overdue" to have her implants replaced.
She has also described worsening pain and difficulty moving her right shoulder, saying it can take her at least 10 minutes to sit up and get out of bed. Those symptoms, she said, are overwhelming because "there's so many different things that could be going on."
Her search comes after doctors told her in October that she does not have MS. At the time, Applegate said the news left her back at "Square 1," her physical struggles have continued and she's undergoing testing for other possible explanations, including rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and Lyme disease.
While the cause of Applegate's symptoms remains unknown, breast implants have been associated with illness in some cases, though the condition is not well understood.
What is known about breast implant illness
Breast implant illness, or BII, is a term for symptoms reported by some people with implants, including fatigue, cognitive changes, joint pain and muscle pain. This photo shows a Biocell textured breast implant by Allergan. (Nicolas Amaya/CBC)
Breast implant illness, or BII, is a term for symptoms reported by some people with implants.
As of Dec. 31, 2025, Health Canada had received 663 reports of symptoms or diseases associated with breast implants — about one report for every 1,025 implants sold in Canada.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom, followed by mood changes, gastrointestinal symptoms and cognitive changes. These are reports, not confirmed cases: Health Canada says the available information cannot establish whether implants caused the symptoms, which may have other causes.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says BII is not a formal medical diagnosis and has no specific test. Reports of symptoms such as fatigue and joint problems cannot establish how often they occur or whether implants caused them.
Julie Elliott, a Canadian breast implant illness and implant-associated cancer advocate with the Breast Implant Safety Alliance who says she experienced health problems after breast augmentation, told CBC News that some symptoms reported by people with implants can overlap with MS symptoms.
- National breast implant registry much needed but long overdue, patients and doctors say
- Alberta women with breast implant illness urge doctors to warn others of risk
"Chronic fatigue, changes in memory, concentration problems, numbness, tingling, nerve pain, muscle weakness, hair loss and so on — I mean, these are similar to MS symptoms," Elliott said.
But she cautioned against concluding that Applegate's implants are responsible. "I'm not saying that Christina Applegate's breast implants are responsible for her symptoms," she said, adding that it would be "premature and irresponsible" to assume they explain them.
"Similar symptoms do not necessarily mean the same diagnosis," Elliott said. "Nothing should be overlooked or ruled out without being properly medically investigated."
Christina Applegate, left, arrives for the 29th Screen Actors Guild Awards in Century City, California, on Feb. 26, 2023. (Valerie Macon/AFP/Getty Images)
Dr. Stephen Nicolaidis, a Montreal plastic surgeon who says he's seen more than 1,500 patients for implant removal, also emphasized the need to investigate other possible causes.
He described BII as a "diagnosis of exclusion," where patients "have to be evaluated thoroughly, and then if they don't find something else as the cause, you should consider the possibility that the implants might be contributing to the problems."
Nicolaidis said symptoms he commonly hears about include fatigue, hair loss, skin rashes, breathing difficulties, joint and muscle pain, sleep problems and brain fog. Some can overlap with symptoms associated with autoimmune conditions.
Referencing Applegate's publicly described symptoms, he said, "Those symptoms that she had can very much be attributable to her breast implants." But the cause of BII is not established, and he said researchers do not yet have definitive answers about how implants might contribute to symptoms.
There is no specific test that can diagnose BII, Nicolaidis said. Imaging may show silicone outside an implant, but he said that finding is not required for someone to report symptoms. He also stressed that BII is different from implant-associated lymphoma, a cancer linked to certain textured implants.
Rupture, removal and next steps
A rupture or leak is a separate concern from BII. The FDA lists rupture and deflation among possible implant complications and advises patients to discuss new or unusual breast changes with a health-care provider.
Similarly, Health Canada advises people with implants to check regularly for unusual breast changes and discuss signs or symptoms with their doctor. Decisions about keeping, replacing or removing implants should be made with a clinician after considering individual symptoms, possible causes and surgical risks, the agency said.
It does not recommend preventive implant removal because surgery carries risks, and advises people experiencing symptoms to discuss them with a health-care provider.
- Struggling with pain for years, N.S. woman heads to Montreal for breast implant removal
- Video The costly, complex and dangerous world of removing medical devices | The Implant Files
Nicolaidis advised people with symptoms to seek a thorough medical evaluation. He said if other causes are not found, they can discuss whether implants might be contributing and weigh options with their clinicians.
He stopped placing breast implants in 2021 because he came to believe their risks outweighed their benefits in many cases, and now focuses largely on implant removal. He adds that removal is not a guaranteed cure. Nicolaidis said some patients he has treated with MS reported only slight improvement, and people with a diagnosed autoimmune disease may still need medical treatment after removal, known as explant surgery.
Elliott said she believes implant-related symptoms should be taken seriously, while acknowledging that their causes are not fully understood. She urged patients to seek balanced, evidence-based information and keep track of changes in their health.
"The fact that we do not have all the answers does not mean women's experiences should be dismissed," she said.

Zelenskyy says Starshield has been slowed again, endangering Ukraine's defense
It comes three weeks after Ukraine’s speeds were restored following the last throttling incident.
As media headlines focus on Jensen Huang's resignation and the midterms fallout, you could almost forget that Ukraine is still fighting for its life — with all of Europe nervously watching. According to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, his job just got harder again. The country's access to Starshield, the military version of Starlink, has been hit with "systematic speed restrictions" for several days. And it just so happens to be while Trump's envoys are in Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelenskyy posted on X that the speed limits are being imposed along the war's entire front line and in Russian-occupied territory. He said any terminal moving faster than 161 km/h (100 mph) loses its connection to the satellite network. Following briefings from his defense minister and top commander, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's military had investigated and ruled out random errors.
"Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side."
A troubling pattern and odd timing
Ukraine's interceptor drones rely on Starshield to chase down Russia's jet-powered Shahed drones, which can fly up to 500 km/h (310 mph). Trying to catch them at 100 mph won't cut it. Zelenskyy says some strikes have already gotten through because Ukraine's interceptors couldn't go fast enough.
The timing is... curious. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed in Moscow today for talks with Putin. They're expected to meet Zelenskyy later at a summit in Ireland.
This isn't the first time Ukraine's Starshield access has been throttled. On October 14, Ukraine's military found that its speeds were being limited to around the same threshold. It happened as President Trump was publicly complaining about Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, which he blamed for high fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterms. Analysts agree that Trump's war with Iran has been the biggest factor in sky-high oil and diesel prices.
It still isn't clear who made the call to throttle Starshield the first time. Reuters, citing US officials, reported that the order came from inside the White House. But days later, the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk personally ordered the slowdown, possibly after talking with Trump. Trump denied any role, for whatever that's worth.
Musk's responses were all over the place. First, he said Starshield is "owned and controlled by the US government," then later claimed Ukraine had violated Starlink's terms of service. That's a strange thing to say about something you just said you don't own or control. Regardless, speeds were restored on October 24, reportedly after Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the caps amid bipartisan pressure from lawmakers.
Three weeks later, we're back where we started, with (so far) no one claiming responsibility.

New Delhi: The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has ordered strict nationwide monitoring to ensure patients benefit from recent price reductions on 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs. In an office memorandum issued on 11 November, the pricing regulator directed all state drug controllers (SDCs), state food and drug administrations (FDAs), and price monitoring and resource units (PMRUs) to enforce compliance with the trade margin rationalisation (TMR) framework. Notified via gazette notification on 17 October, the revised prices took effect from 9 November. "SDCs shall submit an action taken report to NPPA by 16 November 2026,” the memorandum stated. Citing the latest revised price list submitted by pharmaceutical companies on 11 November—and uploaded on the NPPA website and Pharma Sahi Daam portal—the authority warned stakeholders against non-compliance. "All manufacturers, retailers, dealers, stockists, hospitals and medical institutions are to ensure compliance with the reduced/revised prices. Any violation of these directions will entail initiation of overcharging proceedings as per extant provisions of DPCO, 2013," the memorandum read. To prevent arbitrary billing at retail and hospital pharmacies, the directive mandates transparent price disclosures. "Every retailer/dealer/hospital/medical institution is required to prominently display the revised price lists/supplementary price lists at respective business premises and websites,” it stated, adding that "hospitals and medical institutions are required to monitor the MRPs of formulations as per the said order and ensure compliance." Furthermore, "in order to ensure that the benefits of revised MRPs are passed on to the patients, SDCs shall strictly monitor compliance of the said order by the manufacturers, dealers, hospitals and medical institutions who shall assist the SDCs for the same," it said. The enforcement push follows NPPA's 17 October intervention under the drugs (prices control) order, 2013, which capped trade margins at 30% of the MRP—translating to a maximum 42.86% markup on the price to stockist—to curb exorbitant markups of up to 700% in the non-scheduled oncology market. According to market analytics cited in NPPA proceedings, India’s domestic anti-cancer drug market is valued at roughly ₹12,500 crore annually, of which over ₹10,250 crore comprises non-scheduled formulations outside direct ceiling-price controls. Subsequent company filings showed retail price reductions exceeding 90% on several high-cost therapies. Notable cuts included thiotepa (Samtepa 100 mg vial) dropping by ₹72,921.53, or 91.1%, from ₹80,071.86 to ₹7,150.33, and breast cancer drug palbociclib (Palbopro 125 mg) falling 93.3% from ₹40,421.33 to ₹2,720. Widely prescribed therapies such as pertuzumab, olaparib, and abiraterone acetate also saw major downward revisions, with overall annual patient savings estimated at ₹2,500 crore to ₹3,541 crore. The regulatory crackdown also comes amid heightened Supreme Court scrutiny questioning why distributor margin caps should remain restricted to select cancer drugs rather than wider pharmaceutical segments. To curb supply disruptions or hidden overcharging, the memorandum noted that "any violation or complaints of overcharging, shortage or non-availability may be reported to NPPA through the Pharma Sahi Daam app/portal; helpline No. 1800-111-255; email ID- monitoring-nppa@gov.in." Priyanka Sharma is a journalist at Mint, where she covers the Union Ministry of Health and the pharmaceutical industry. Her work focuses on explaining government policies and how they impact healthcare and the medicine market in India. With 12 years of experience in journalism, she has built a reputation for providing clear and honest news on important health topics that affect the entire country.

Her educational background includes a journalism degree from the prestigious Indian Institute of Mass Communication (IIMC) and specialized training in public health from the Public Health Foundation of India. Before her current role at Mint, Priyanka worked with India Today, The Pioneer, and ANI. She also served as a lead consultant for the National Health Authority, which gave her firsthand knowledge of how the government manages large-scale health programmes.

Maryland's Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for U.S. Senate leadership post
Van Hollen says Democrats 'need new leadership'
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said Thursday that he will run for Senate majority leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge to Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen said in a statement that "the American people called for change" and that is why he is running.
"It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership," Van Hollen said. "This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."
Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win the race. The closed-door, secret-ballot election will be held in early December.
U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer has said he has the necessary support to win. (Mariam Zuhaib/The Associated Press)
The race will be the first contested election for Democratic leader in decades.
The question of whether to re-elect Schumer has already divided the caucus and many senators will not say publicly how they will vote. They have privately deliberated about what message to take from the election, and Schumer recruited many of the party's winning candidates and raised money for them.
'I'm going to win it': Schumer
Schumer has been talking to Democratic senators since the election about forming an agenda for 2027. In private caucus meetings this week, Schumer laid out a broad plan for their first 100 days in power.
"I'm going to win it," Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview last week.
In a statement after Van Hollen's announcement, Schumer said he welcomes any discussion about the future of the caucus.
"I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," Schumer said. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."
While Schumer is the favourite to win, Van Hollen's run exposes a rift in the party that has put Schumer on the defensive since he sided with Republicans on a spending vote in March 2025.
Even as Schumer has redeemed himself within his caucus since then — leading them through a government shutdown last year and orchestrating huge wins in the election — many in the Democratic base are agitating for generational change.
Van Hollen, 67, is not that much younger than Schumer, 75. But he has positioned himself as a new face in the party. He has also said he is considering a run for president.
El-Sayed backs Van Hollen
While most Democratic senators have either said they are supporting Schumer or are undecided, Van Hollen has at least one backer in next year's caucus: Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who won a competitive election in his state last week, posted on X Thursday night that their majority will need "bold leadership."
U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed is backing Van Hollen to be the Democrats' leader in the U.S. Senate. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)
"I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience," El-Sayed wrote. "We need both right now. Which is why I'm proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority."
Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin also called for new leadership at a news conference Tuesday, though neither endorsed a specific candidate.
Several senators have said they are backing Schumer, including incoming Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who beat Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week.
Maine Sen. Angus King, an Independent who caucuses with Democrats and votes in the election, issued a statement after Van Hollen's announcement: "Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?
"Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible," King wrote.

Meta Platforms said on Monday it would expand its AI age-estimation technology globally to move millions more teens on Instagram into Teen Account protections, even if they have given birth dates showing they are adults, as the company faces lawsuits alleging its platforms harm young users.
Teen Accounts, available on Instagram, Facebook and Messenger, include built-in protections that automatically limit who can contact teens, the content they see and their time on the apps.
Parents in the US will begin receiving Instagram notifications this month explaining how teens are placed in age-appropriate protections, Meta said.
In Australia, Meta has begun using Apple’s age-range signal as an additional method to help determine users’ ages.
Meta said it is continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook and will begin launching similar technology globally on Threads later this year.
Meta faces multiple lawsuits over allegations that its platforms harm teens.
In August, Meta struck settlements worth up to $18 billion with nearly every US state and territory to resolve lawsuits brought by attorneys general over the platforms’ harm to teens.
Under the settlements, Meta agreed to improve how it identifies teens and children under 13.
Meta settled with a teen plaintiff last month in a Los Angeles trial testing claims that Instagram and Facebook were designed to be addictive, causing mental health problems and an eating disorder.

(Bloomberg) -- A shooting left one person dead and four people injured Thursday in Washington DC’s Logan Circle neighborhood less than a mile from the White House.
The suspect in the case, a White male, also died, according to a Metropolitan Police Department spokesperson.
The chaotic incident led to a massive police response and closed streets, schools, and businesses across the nation’s capital. According to police, the suspect shot and killed a person inside a Vida Fitness gym, and targeted others nearby, including workers at a construction site.
He then retreated to a nearby apartment, where he barricaded himself inside and shot at law enforcement attempting to enter. 
Police established a communication channel but during negotiations, another gunshot was heard. When officers entered the apartment, they discovered the suspect - who they identified but so far have declined to name - with what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. He ultimately died from that injury. 
One victim was in serious condition while three others were being treated for what interim MPD Chief Jeffery Carroll described as non-life-threatening injuries. 
DC Mayor Muriel Bowser called the incident a “senseless act of gun violence.”
“MPD will continue to investigate this situation. But this lone gunman has been contained,” she said.
The block, a short walk from the city’s downtown core, is also home to apartment buildings and a Whole Foods grocery store. 
Bowser said the White House had been briefed on the incident. President Donald Trump has deployed hundreds of National Guard troops in the city in what he has described as an effort to combat violent crime across the capital.

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

A strong El Nino and human-induced climate change fueled the hot and dry weather over Indonesia this year that sparked the country’s worst wildfire season in a decade, according to new research.
El Nino was the driver of the severe lack of rainfall, while climate change was the cause of high temperatures, a report by World Weather Attribution shows. Human-induced warming made hot and dry conditions about three times more likely, as well as more intense, researchers said.
Indonesia’s worst fire season in years cloaked local towns and neighboring countries such as Singapore and Malaysia in toxic smog, prompting schools to close, straining diplomatic ties and crimping palm oil output. Poor rainfall from June through the end of October left the landscape bone-dry, making blazes often linked to slash-and-burn agricultural practices harder to contain.
“El Nino turned off the taps, but fossil fuel emissions turned up the heat,” said Friederike Otto, a professor of climate science at Imperial College London and a co-author of the study published Friday. “Without rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels and strengthened land-management protections, we will see more and much worse fire seasons like this in the future.”
Climate change amplified the hotter conditions from August to October, making the seasonal heat about 1.6 C hotter and more likely to occur, according to the study. Parts of Indonesia have also seen decades of deforestation and peatland draining, significantly increasing the fire risk, the authors wrote.
The ongoing El Nino is estimated to have reduced Indonesia’s seasonal rainfall by about 50% this year, and together with higher temperatures, the country experienced “record breaking fire weather,” the report said.
“Our analysis shows that climate change acts as a force multiplier during El Nino years,” said Theodore Keeping, an extreme weather and wildfire researcher at Imperial College London and lead author of the study. “When a strong El Nino hits, global warming makes the resulting fire weather significantly hotter, drier, and harder to contain.”

As former state health leaders, we know the challenges and opportunities facing the 21 new governors stepping into their roles on Jan. 1. Health is what lets people go to work, raise their kids, and enjoy the years they’ve earned. Health is also the largest line item in most state budgets and a primary driver of the affordability crisis for American families.
To succeed in harnessing the power of state government to improve health and well-being and tackle affordability, new governors need to do three things: hire operators, see the trouble that’s already here, and set a focused agenda.
Hire operators
A governor’s three most consequential health appointments are the state’s health and human services secretary, Medicaid director, and public health officer. The attributes that matter most in these leaders include, foremost, a track record in getting things done in and with government. Look for leaders who have managed large government teams, legislative processes, and stakeholder associations.
Expertise matters, especially in this moment. The Medicaid director should understand evolving federal financing rules, eligibility systems and operations, and the state’s Medicaid delivery system, which is often managed care. The public health officer should have run an outbreak response.
Relationship and communication skills are paramount in managing a large government agency through change. The governor’s health leaders need to have the trust of legislators of both parties, hospitals, health centers and other health care providers, local leaders, consumer groups, and community partners. This team will be the state’s public face and primary communicators in a crisis.
See the trouble that’s already here
Issues that are already hitting states hard will become even more challenging in the coming year. Governors-elect should be briefed on them now.
Medicaid eligibility requirements: In expansion states, work requirements and more frequent redeterminations of Medicaid eligibility are set to go live on Jan. 1, 2027. These new road rules require expansion adults ages 19 to 64 to document 80 hours a month of work, school, or service and to prove eligibility for Medicaid every six months. Experience shows that coverage losses will be high and come from paperwork, not because residents aren’t eligible for Medicaid anymore. These federal mandates will have major local impact. Governors should know:
- How well state systems verify eligibility data, especially new work exemptions, automatically from existing data.
- Who is most at risk of losing coverage over paperwork, and what the agency is we doing to reach them and prevent that outcome.
- Whether the state submitted a request to CMS to delay work requirements implementation.
Measles: The U.S. has already recorded more cases of measles in 2026 than in any year since 1991, nearly all among unvaccinated people. An international review this week will assess whether the country has lost its elimination status. On day one, governors should know kindergarten vaccination rates by county, confirm outbreak plans and surge staffing, and have a crisis communication plan at the ready for when an outbreak hits.
Medicaid program integrity: Medicaid program integrity is a concern for every state, and governors should expect CMS scrutiny to continue. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has required all 50 states to submit Medicaid provider revalidation plans and has withheld federal payments from at least one state. New executive health teams should assume a review is coming and give the state’s fraud and inspector general units the resources they need and make program integrity the state’s own priority.
Set a focused agenda
Aligning priorities across program and funding silos is a core job of the governor and their health team. With sustained leadership and clear focus, a state can unlock enormous untapped potential across Medicaid, public health, social services, insurance regulation, the state employee health plan, and rural health funds. This should include clarity of which levers states control and which require federal partnership (such as Medicaid or ACA waivers and financing changes). Governors should prioritize action in those areas that the state can drive.
Governors should elevate key priorities to name in the first State of the State, fund in the first governor’s budget, and show results within two years. Strong candidates for priorities are:
Coverage: Ten states still have not expanded Medicaid access. For these states, four of which have new governors coming in January, expansion should be a priority. It’s still the biggest lever for coverage, rural hospital sustainability, and funding. In any state, governors can create a public option to make premiums more affordable and give struggling small employers relief.
Affordability: The first affordability priority for new governors — indeed, for all governors — should be relief that families feel soon. Options to consider include capping out-of-pocket costs for high-use medications, making primary care available before the deductible kicks in, and reining in pharmacy costs through pharmacy benefit manager reform and drug price transparency.
States can also protect patients from surprise and excessive bills by limiting facility fees, strengthening hospital financial assistance standards, and adding medical debt protections.
Lasting affordability also requires bringing down the overall cost of care — something that is a shared responsibility across hospitals, insurers, and drug manufacturers. Governors can set cost growth targets and compel public reporting. They can use combined state purchasing power to drive value-based payment and cut administrative waste. They can also pay for care models that improve access and chronic disease management, such as value-based primary care and technology-enabled models aligned with Medicare’s ACCESS model.
Rural health: Every state received a Rural Health Transformation Program award, averaging about $200 million a year through 2030, and later funding depends on meeting the commitments in each state’s application. It’s critical to avoid the “peanut butter” approach — spreading the dollars over so many priorities that the money is thin for all. Set a few measurable goals, such as keeping obstetric and emergency services open, building regional referral networks, and building and maintaining primary care and behavioral health access. Plan for how to sustain the work after federal funding ends.
States should approach artificial intelligence thoughtfully as they invest rural health and other state funds. Used well, AI holds promise to improve access, health, and the work of state government. Used poorly, it can drive up costs and deny care.
To guide AI investment, governors should set clear, simple rules that protect consumers through disclosure, consent, and clinician review, aligned with other states. Use Medicaid managed care contracts and state purchasing to require disclosure of AI use and reporting of outcomes, steering vendors toward tools that improve access and affordability rather than AI automation billing wars. Start small with initiatives inside state government where AI can support your workforce including by piloting AI in chatbots, call centers, and eligibility processing, with human review of any decision that denies or ends coverage.
A divided government in Washington likely means few federal solutions are coming soon. States have always been laboratories of innovation, and that power has never been more critical to harness than at this moment.
Mandy Cohen, M.D., M.P.H., is former secretary of health and human services for North Carolina and former director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She is a national adviser at Manatt, a legal and consulting firm. Ellen Montz, Ph.D., is former chief deputy at the Virginia Department of Medical Assistance Services (Virginia Medicaid) and former deputy administrator and director at the Center for Consumer Information and Insurance Oversight at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. She is a managing director at Manatt.

PM Modi to visit Philippines for Asean-India Summit, East Asia Summit
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit the Philippines on November 16 for the Asean-India Summit and East Asia Summit, with trade, maritime security and regional stability on the agenda.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s engagements with leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) and other countries in the Philippines next week will be crucial for bolstering trade and building resilience amid rapid geopolitical changes, the external affairs ministry said on Thursday.
Modi will travel to Manila on November 16 to participate in the Asean-India Summit and the East Asia Summit the following day, on the margins of the Asean Summit being hosted by the Philippines. He is also expected to join the leaders of Australia, Japan and the US for a Quad Leaders’ Summit and hold several bilateral meetings.
Asean has emerged as a central pillar of India’s Act East policy and vision for the Indo-Pacific, and Rudrendra Tandon, secretary (East) in the external affairs ministry, told a media briefing that the 11-member bloc serves as a “locomotive for peace, stability and economic prosperity”. Annual trade between India and Asean member states is worth about $122 billion.
“India strongly believes that as an Indian Ocean country that abuts this very important Southeast Asian maritime zone, a strong strategic relationship with Asean member states, as a collective as well as individually, is good for both of us,” Tandon said.
“It will make us more resilient to handle the very rapid geopolitical changes that are taking place around us. It will also contribute to peace and stability in Asia as a whole.”
Tandon highlighted the importance of maritime cooperation with Asean member states, especially for coordinated patrolling and maritime domain awareness, in order to counter problems such as piracy and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing. India can also offer training and other assistance to bolster the maritime capabilities of Asean member states, he said.
At the same time, India has developed strong defence cooperation with several Asean member states, he said, pointing to the deal finalised with the Philippines for supplying BrahMos cruise missiles.
In the context of trade with the Southeast Asian bloc, Tandon said New Delhi wants the review of the Asean-India Trade in Goods Agreement (AITIGA) to be completed “as soon as possible”. India is also engaged in discussions with individual Asean member states for trade facilitation and trade agreements to open up new opportunities, he said.
Tandon acknowledged that the review of AITIGA is a “difficult” process as it involves developing consensus with all Asean member states. AITIGA entered into force in 2010 and the review began six years ago, largely because of India’s concerns about a trade imbalance due to imports of more than $80 billion from Asean member states.
Asked about India’s position on dealing with the situation in Myanmar, Tandon said: “We have always said that isolating Myanmar is not the right approach because if we do, someone else will fill that vacuum. There is no alternative to engagement.”
India strongly supports Asean initiatives to engage the Myanmar government, while taking into account the country’s complex history and society. “Patience and consistency in engagement is very important,” Tandon said.

When one thinks about the key supporters of MAHA, they likely don’t envision Black people, and rightfully so. A 2025 poll from KFF and The Washington Post found that only 30% of Black Americans support the MAHA movement, compared with 43% of white Americans.
But the data belie a stark reality: On an issue-to-issue basis, Black people are strikingly aligned with MAHA, at least in terms of their concerns around the movement’s tentpole issues. I’ve been studying why, or rather how, this came to be.
According to a May poll from Global Strategy Group, 47% of Black people, compared with 35% of white people, strongly agree with the statements “I am concerned about environmental toxins and pesticides” and “I am concerned about ultra-processed foods and artificial ingredients in our food” — key MAHA flashpoints.
The same poll found that 51% of Black people, a staunch Democratic voting bloc, either strongly or somewhat agreed with the statement “I am skeptical of vaccines,” compared to 58% of Republicans and 28% of Democrats. Moreover, the poll found that 26% of Black people strongly or somewhat support eliminating fluoride from public drinking water, a not-so-secret desire of health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. This figure nearly mirrors the 28% of Republicans who also want the additive nixed from our water supply, while
18% of Democrats felt the same.
This crossover makes some sense. MAHA is perhaps the sole part of the Trump administration’s sprawling attempt to remake American society that can be said to be, at least on the surface, apolitical. Its broad agenda amplifies everyday public health issues like food quality and safety while elevating thorny but universally relevant topics like Big Pharma’s role in the overmedicalization of Americans.
This explains why a number of people on the left who would seem to be politically opposed to MAHA sometimes begrudgingly, and sometimes warmly, endorse it. In recent months, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who appears to have 2028 ambitions, has glowingly discussed her conversations with MAHA activists and characterizes the MAHA cause as nonpartisan. Uber-progressive physician and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed actively campaigned on some of MAHA’s hallmark principles.
Many in clinical medicine have also come out in support of MAHA, or at least components of it. In The Atlantic, emergency physician Craig Spencer encouraged public health practitioners to swallow their pride in service of the lightning-in-a-bottle moment for reform that MAHA was serving up, aligning with a number of respected public health influencers who’ve encouraged the same kind of acquiescence.
To some, including me, this sudden embrace of MAHA and pandering to the movement’s voters looks like acute Stockholm syndrome. And that’s largely because its intentions are often assumed a priori to be politically neutral, and its origins are rarely questioned.
A January tweet from California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s press office noted that “MAHA started in California,” highlighting the likely 2028 Democratic presidential contender’s statewide ban on ultra-processed foods in 2025. In early October, Democrat Rep. Chellie Pingree (Maine), who made MAHA a centerpiece of her successful reelection campaign, tweeted that she’d “been fighting for a food system that puts people and farmers first long before the ‘MAHA movement.’”
But Black scholars and activists played the biggest role in bringing to light the systemic fissures in our health care and food systems that MAHA — and some left-leaning opportunists — now assume a gatekeeper role over.
Throughout the 1960s and 1970s, Black activists around the country began to lead coordinated efforts to address the harms caused by industrial pollution in the U.S. and tackle the industrialization of the food system.
In 1969, Fannie Lou Hamer, a Black organizer, pioneered land cooperatives in Mississippi to usher in food sovereignty, aiming to curb her Black contemporaries’ increasing reliance on large, sprawling food production systems. Hamer foresaw what would become a reality in the 21st century: a loss of community control over food production and the proliferation of ultra-processed, unhealthy foodstuffs, a talking point deeply embedded in Kennedy Jr.’s Eat Real Food initiative.
In 1978, Black residents in Warren County, N.C., began organizing to protest a landfill that was poised to store some 60,000 tons of cancer-causing PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls) in their rural, low-income community. Over the next several years, as legal motions to stop the state government-endorsed plan were quashed, hundreds of Black demonstrators would be arrested in nonviolent protests against the site. It wasn’t until two decades later that the protesters’ persistence would pay off: An $18 million site detoxification process was initiated in 2002 and completed in 2004.
It’s evident Kennedy, a trained environmental lawyer, learned a great deal from cases like these. When running as a presidential candidate in 2024, Kennedy made several direct appeals for addressing environmental injustice, the racially inequitable distribution of environmental harms in minority communities. For instance, during a visit to Loyola Marymount College while on the campaign trail, Kennedy discussed the legacy of polluting facilities and noted, “We’ll have a cleaner environment if rich people and white people have to bear the equal burdens for people who are poor among the minorities.”
This was a racial justice battle cry, virtually right out of “Dumping in Dixie,” a seminal environmental justice text authored by the godfather of the movement, Robert Bullard.
This past “woke” iteration of Kennedy is deeply at odds with the present version, considering the term “environmental justice” is now essentially forbidden in research grant applications submitted to the National Institutes of Health, and that the NIH has substantially curbed funding for studies focused on racial disparities.
Ultimately, MAHA’s template is a retread, warmed over and confusedly repackaged for the anti-science and contrarian crowd keen on bringing the culture wars as deep as possible into public health.
To this end, Kennedy’s subtle homages to Black activism have been undercut by his public commentary and policy, which in addition to distorting and cherry-picking aspects of evidence-based science, is imbued with MAGA’s distinctive brand of political grievance and racial myopia.
Even as Kennedy and his MAHA consorts have cribbed from the Black activist playbook, they’ve actively undermined and misrepresented Black identity and culture. Part of this has been accomplished by playing into the fears that many Black people harbor against doctors and the medical establishment, including by using disinformation to gin up concerns about vaccines in Black communities, a population already highly skeptical of immunizations. Going back to the Tuskegee experiments, where Black men’s treatment for their syphilis was withheld, Black populations have held significant distrust for clinicians and medical research.
In a Kennedy-produced documentary, “Medical Racism: The New Apartheid,” a piece of unabashed agitprop released in 2021, the current health secretary recruited Nation of Islam Minister Tony Muhammad to help peddle the fantastical claim that vaccine-makers are nefariously targeting Black kids as a means of widening racial disparities.
And this tactic isn’t new. Republicans and anti-abortion activists have long sought to curry the support of Black people by claiming abortion is a subversive tool being used by white liberals and medical elites to facilitate Black genocide.
On a podcast before the 2024 election, Kennedy argued that Black people have a stronger immune response to certain antigens than other races, thereby warranting a change in their vaccine scheduling, a scientifically debunked notion that he nevertheless doubled down on during his Senate confirmation hearing.
He has also been a vocal cheerleader for a controversial study to assess the effects of hepatitis B vaccine dose timing on a cohort of infants in the small West African country of Guinea-Bissau, where local officials recently raided the offices of an RFK-Jr.-allied research group supporting the study.
The most positive reflections on MAHA have largely centered around the trope of the genteel “MAHA mom,” a racially coded term painting white mothers as singularly focused, doting caregivers who just want their kids to be healthy. Contrast this with Kennedy’s thoughts on Black parents. In a 2024 podcast, he advocated “reparenting” Black kids with ADHD, a population he said was “just standard put on Adderall, SSRIs, benzos, which are known to induce violence.”
It’s no surprise that prominent Black politicians haven’t accepted the Faustian bargain that MAHA represents and rallied around MAHA as their white peers have. Kennedy’s vision of and prescription for Black America is antiquated and dangerous. The spoils MAHA may otherwise offer — if we’re willing to whitewash its ethos — are no consolation.
With the midterms serving up a colossal defeat for MAGA, it stands to reason that MAHA’s day of reckoning may not be too far off. Calls for RFK. Jr’s impeachment are already bubbling among Democratic party leaders, a group that no longer needs to actively curry favor with MAHA proponents.
Only time will tell if the movement and its baggage can thrive without a titanic political force like MAGA behind it. Public health will be better off if it doesn’t.
Jerel Ezell is an epidemiologist and assistant professor at the University of Chicago Medical Center.

Finland says it will restrict entry to the country for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine, potentially affecting a raft of winter sports.
The move follows a backlash in Finland to Russia being reinstated for the ice hockey world championships, but its effects could mostly be felt in other sports.
“As long as Russia’s war of aggression continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland. Their entry into the country would be a threat to Finland’s international relations. The same is true of other short-term work under visas that is not essential to Finland’s national interests,” Minister for Foreign Affairs Elina Valtonen said in a statement.
The Finnish foreign ministry said the measure would affect Russian athletes competing under neutral status as well as those competing for national teams.
Finland hosts a figure skating Grand Prix next week and a cross-country ski World Cup this month. Both sports allow Russians to compete as “neutral athletes.”
One major event likely to be affected is the figure skating world championships in Tampere, Finland, in March. Russian skaters are expected to be among the top medal contenders.
The change takes effect from Monday, so it is does not appear likely to affect this week’s NHL games in Helsinki between the Seattle Kraken and Carolina Hurricanes. Finland is among a group of European teams which have vowed not to play against Russia at upcoming hockey world championships.
In the longer term, Finland is also hosting the European track and field championships in 2030. Track’s governing body, World Athletics maintains a blanket ban on Russian participation, though that is facing a legal challenge.

England Women’s tour of West Indies has lost its much-awaited Test match, with the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) revising its April schedule to make room for a more extensive red-ball programme ahead of the Women’s Ashes.
The tour will now consist of three T20Is and three ODIs. The ECB said there was insufficient time to fit in the Test originally anticipated, because the trip takes place once the English domestic season is already under way.
The change allows England to play four red-ball matches in home conditions before the Ashes Test against Australia at Headingley, which starts on June 24. They include a three-day fixture against Australia A and three best v best matches on English soil. At least two of the intra-squad games will let selectors look at a wider pool of players in the format.
The programme begins in January with a 10-day red-ball training camp in Bengaluru, ahead of the inaugural ICC Women’s Champions Trophy.
The ECB said the current domestic structure offers few chances for players to experience multi-day cricket, so management looked for the best way to prepare the team for four days of cricket against Australia.
Dates and venues for the West Indies tour will be confirmed by Cricket West Indies in due course. It will follow the opening round of One-Day Cup matches, which will involve all England players. The ECB thanked Cricket West Indies for agreeing to its request and for its “understanding and collaborative approach”.
ECB Chief Executive Richard Gould said the Headingley Test would be “one of the highlights of the summer” and is worth four points in the multi-format series, making preparation vital.
“A 10-day warm-weather red-ball camp in India followed by four further matches in English conditions will provide Charlotte Edwards and her team with the appropriate game time to be ready for that challenge,” he said.
Gould added that best v best cricket in English conditions would help the ECB gauge its strength in depth and give more players competitive multi-day experience. “We appreciate the constructive conversations with Cricket West Indies,” he said, “that have enabled us to look forward to an exciting tour of the Caribbean before focusing our attentions back on our home summer.”

Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
- Published
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".
The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.
The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.

Six more women have accused Russell Brand of sexual misconduct in a new investigation by The Times and The Sunday Times, the newspapers whose earlier reporting on the comedian features in Netflix’s just-unveiled documentary “Russell Brand: Open Secret.”
The accounts were published days after Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault. The papers could not report them while his criminal case was ongoing, because of the risk of prejudicing the trial.
Brand did not respond to the new allegations. The papers said they reached out through his lawyers following his conviction, and that his lawyer reportedly mentioned the possibility of “injunctive relief” but sent no answer to the claims, even after being granted more time. Brand has denied wrongdoing in the past and has insisted that all his relationships were consensual.
According to The Times, the paper took “extensive steps” to corroborate what the women said, and none of them received payment.
The new allegations stretch from 2005 to 2015. The earliest comes from a woman, then in her mid-20s, whom Brand approached that year.
“Please I just need to have sex with you, I will pay you,” she said he told her.
After winning a BBC 6 Music competition in 2006, a woman then in her late 20s appeared as a guest on Brand’s show. The pair saw each other on and off over the following year, and she said that at one point he demanded she lick a toilet seat in his home. When she refused, “[He] seemed pissed off that I wouldn’t let him humiliate me,” she said.
A third woman was 19 in 2007 when she lined up with a friend to meet Brand. She said that when they later had sex, she told him it was painful and asked him to stop, but he did not, and that he insisted afterward that the night had been consensual.
Another woman said she and Brand had an on-again, off-again relationship in the late 2000s that began with a work meeting at his London home. She said that on one occasion she realized he had no condom on, asked him to stop and tried to pull away, but could not, and decided not to fight him. He later apologized to her, both in person and by text, she said.
In 2013, a fan in her late 20s met Brand after he played The Chapel in San Francisco. She said he handled her roughly and pushed his hand down her pants.
The most recent account dates to 2015. A woman employed at a London venue where Brand was a regular said one of his staff told her Brand wanted her and was waiting in the disabled toilets. She said the lights were off when she went in and that Brand, who claimed he needed toilet paper, grabbed her as she passed it to him.
The Metropolitan Police said that during and since the trial, it has heard from several people, some offering further information and some reporting potential crimes, and that detectives are assessing what they received. The force confirmed after the verdict that it is investigating rape allegations from two further women. Met chief Mark Rowley said he “wouldn’t be surprised” if more victims came forward.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called on the media industry to “look at itself” and “step forward” in protecting women and girls, following Brand’s conviction and separate allegations against comedian David Walliams that emerged from a joint Guardian and ITV News investigation. Walliams has rejected the claims.
Brand, 51, received a prison sentence of 10 and a half years on Monday. A Southwark Crown Court jury in London had found him guilty of three sexual assault counts and of raping a fan who was 21 at the time, while clearing him of a further two rape counts and an attempted indecent assault charge. The offenses took place between 2004 and 2009.
The first allegations against Brand surfaced in 2023 in a docuseries made by The Sunday Times with Channel 4’s “Dispatches.” Until then, he was known chiefly for his comedy and for film roles in “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.”

Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
- Published
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.
In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

USA coach Mauricio Pochettino is expected to replace Carrick, with the Argentine set to be in charge for the first time when United travel to Anfield to face rivals Liverpool on 22 November.
United will be hoping that Pochettino's arrival will persuade Fernandes to commit his future to the club.
Fernandes came close to joining Pochettino's Tottenham in 2019 but a move failed to materialise, with the midfielder signing for United six months later.
The former Sporting midfielder has scored six times in 13 matches for United this season.
'Fernandes wants to compete for biggest prizes' - analysis
In theory, the current contract stand-off between Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes is not a big deal.
It is usual for the first, second and sometimes quite a few more offers to be rejected as part of the rough and tumble of negotiations.
United do have the option to trigger an option to add an extra year. However, there is reason why both sides might be wary to commit beyond that at this stage.
On Fernandes' part, there is a clear desire to compete for the biggest prizes. He can see the best years of his career drifting away. Yet again United have failed to build on a season of promise and he will now be wanting to see what impact Mauricio Pochettino has when he eventually arrives from the United States.
Fernandes was coveted by the Saudi Pro League 18 months ago, although the feeling has been he would prefer to stay in Europe.
On United's side, they will have noted Fernandes' alarming drop-off from the levels he hit last season, when he broke the Premier League assists record and won all the major player of the year honours.
Liverpool committed a huge amount of money to Mohamed Salah's last contract and that turned out to be a heavy financial burden. United will not want to get saddled with a major contract over an extended period for an underperforming player.

England thrashed by Australia in first ODI
- Published
First one-day international, Perth
England 131 (33.4 overs): Atkinson 29*; Beardman 6-24
Australia 132-3 (23.3 overs): Marsh 50, Connolly 27
Australia won by seven wickets
England meekly offered Australia respite from the ongoing sandpaper scandal by being bowled out for 131 in a seven-wicket thrashing in the first one-day international in Perth.
Hours after Pat Cummins emphatically hit back at Usman Khawaja's comments, Harry Brook's England folded as 21-year-old fast bowler Mahli Beardman emerged with a stunning 6-24 on his ODI debut.
Beardman nicked off Brook in his second over for his first international wicket. Less than two hours later, bowling accurately and at good pace, he had the best figures by an Australian on ODI debut.
His second ODI wicket was the prized scalp of Joe Root for 17 and he also dismissed Tom Banton, whose 25 was one of only three scores over 20, Jordan Cox and Sam Curran in an opening spell of five overs that returned figures of 5-18.
Ben Duckett, Banton and Root, plus Beardman's later victims Liam Dawson and Jofra Archer, fell driving in Perth – dismissals familiar from England's wretched start to last winter's Ashes series on the same ground.
This was another Perth surface offering pace and bounce and England had no answer.
Talk of the sandpaper scandal still swirls around the game - the day began with David Warner accusing Cummins of throwing Khawaja "under the bus" on the Australian TV coverage - but England missed the chance to apply more misery to their oldest foe.
Captain Mitchell Marsh, who repeatedly dodged questions about ball tampering in his news conference on Thursday, thrashed a 29-ball fifty as Australia chased their target with a massive 26.3 overs to spare.
The second of three ODIs is on Sunday in Adelaide (03:30 GMT) with England, who suffered damaging defeats in the tri-series against Pakistan and Sri Lanka last month, desperately needing a response as they attempt to build towards next year's World Cup after four defeats in their past five matches.
Familiar feeling in Perth
England floundering in Perth? You'd be forgiven for thinking you were back in 2025. Next week marks a year since the last Ashes began.
On that occasion, and after minimal preparation, batters were guilty of driving on the up and gifting their wickets.
The openers here - Banton getting a thick edge to a drive with his feet planted and Duckett slicing left-armer Spencer Johnson to backward point - were eerily familiar. England have had lengthy build-up here. That is no excuse this time.
In fairness to Brook, he got a good ball from Beardman which was fiddled behind. Root's ball was of driving length, but he got a thick edge.
Cox then tentatively nicked off from the crease for two and Curran's issues against the short ball were laid bare when he top-edged a hook to fine leg off Beardman, who exceeded 90mph at times, for a seven-ball duck.
From 65-8, Will Jacks offered brief resistance with 25 and Gus Atkinson hit the innings' only six for 29 not out. England were still dismissed inside 34 overs - the 15th time they have been bowled out in 29 ODIs since Brendon McCullum took over as coach. Eleven of those instances have come when batting first.
"England are trying," former England captain Michael Vaughan said on Test Match Special.
"It's not what it was a year ago when the message was just 'we'll just go harder and, if we get bowled out, we'll go harder the next time'.
"I didn't see that today but what I saw were some basic errors on the pitch they're playing on and for this side to become a side that can win the World Cup in a year, they need to improve quickly."
Beardman shines bright
The win will not banish all talk of sandpaper in Australia but at least provided a distraction.
It is unlikely Beardman would be playing in this series had Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood – the three fast bowlers whose role in Cape Town has been pushed back into the spotlight by Khawaja's new book – not been rested.
Now front and centre after a young career hampered by back injuries, Beardman hinted at what future could await when those three iconic bowlers do retire.
Using the life the pitch offered, he threatened with full balls and short, and bowled an ideal line. Xavier Bartlett, 27, was also impressive with the new ball while Johnson added the wickets of Jamie Overton and Jacks after the scalp of Duckett.
Travis Head, who put England to the sword in the Perth chase a year ago, dragged on for a first-ball duck. Australia's chase was still a formality.
Like Head before him, Marsh flogged the bowling, looking far more comfortable than England on his home ground when clubbing four sixes over the leg side.
"Batting here with extra pace and bounce you need to invest a bit more in the early part of your innings," former Australia all-rounder Tom Moody said. "You don't have to leave every ball, but be a bit more mindful.
"England didn't make the assessment and make the adjustment to be productive. I'm not saying it's a 300 surface, but you would be disappointed with something between 230 or 250.
"There was a consistent theme in their whole innings where they were pushing at length balls which were bouncing and moving away."
After Marsh holed out for 50 and Cooper Connolly 27, Josh Inglis and Matthew Renshaw calmly steered Australia to their win.
They took their time but only twice before had they beaten England with as many balls to spare.
'We talked extensively about the conditions'
England coach Brendon McCullum, speaking to TNT Sports: "It all happened pretty quickly. I thought we weren't quick enough to adapt to the conditions, we talked extensively leading into the game about the surface here at Optus is a bit like batting on a trampoline, there's certain shots that are obviously very difficult to try and execute and we talked a lot about trying to put those away.
"And also looking at some of the history of the games here as well, the last four games have all been over in 30-odd overs. So we knew we were probably in for a bit of a low-scoring contest, but we expected to get a few more runs than 130.
"Overall, obviously disappointed, but there's some good lessons in it for us as well. If you look towards the World Cup and South Africa there's going to be some pitches there that may not have quite the same bounce as this but will definitely test us from a bounce point of you. And we'll have to find ways to be able to counter that and we'll have those conversations."

Mumbai: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has issued a circular outlining the UPI Vyapar Saksham Scheme to expand digital payments among small merchants. The November 11 circular sets out incentives for deploying physical QR codes and soundboxes and increasing UPI transactions.
Merchant Eligibility
The scheme covers merchants with annual turnover of up to Rs 40 lakh in the previous financial year. It prioritises tier-3 to tier-6 cities, the northeastern states, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh. Merchants in tier-1 and tier-2 cities must be covered by notified central schemes such as PM SVANidhi or PM Vishwakarma.
Deployment Incentives
Payment providers can earn Rs 300 for installing a physical QR code and Rs 750 for deploying a soundbox at a new merchant outlet. The merchant must record at least 25 eligible UPI transactions totalling at least Rs 5,000 per month in at least two months of a quarter.
Transaction Incentives
The scheme offers a 0.03 percent incentive on eligible transaction value for participating payment providers, with a 50 percent uplift in designated areas. Banks must record at least 5 percent quarterly growth in eligible transaction volumes. In targeted areas, an additional 0.20 percent applies to the quarter-on-quarter increase in eligible transaction value.
Funding and Timeline
Issuing and acquiring banks, payment service providers and UPI app operators will contribute 5 percent of their respective merchant discount rate (MDR) shares. The fund allocates 30 percent to merchant onboarding, 50 percent to transaction growth and 20 percent to incremental growth in targeted areas. Transfers between allocations are barred.
The scheme will run for three years from the date UPI MDR takes effect. The circular leaves the start date and rates unspecified. Only eligible payments of Rs 2,000 or less qualify. Artificially split payments are excluded.
NPCI targets annual deployment of 60 lakh to one crore QR codes and five lakh to 10 lakh soundboxes, alongside 30 percent to 50 percent transaction growth among existing small merchants. Incentives will be calculated quarterly and processed within 30 days of claim submission.

England crumble against Australia in Perth again as Mitchell Marsh's side win first ODI amid 'Sandpapergate' storm
England wilt to 131 all out as Australia take 1-0 lead in three-match ODI series on day Pat Cummins launches stunning response to Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' claims; seamer Mahli Beardman, 21, takes best figures by an Australia bowler on ODI debut, including Harry Brook and Joe Root
Friday 13 November 2026 08:49, UK
England capitulated in Perth for the second year running as an Australia side engulfed by the 'Sandpapergate' storm cruised to a seven-wicket victory in a series-opening ODI in which debutant Mahli Beardman recorded a six-wicket haul.
England's raft of rash strokes in last November's first Ashes Test at Optus Stadium led to them losing that game inside two days en route to a harrowing 4-1 series defeat.
Unlike the previous winter, the tourists played a proper warm-up game at another Perth venue in The WACA, beating a Western Australia side by 92 runs last Saturday as 21-year-old pacer Beardman went wicketless from 10 overs.
Fast forward six days and Beardman bagged the best figures by an Australian on ODI debut - his 6-24 from 7.4 overs topping Tony Dodemaide's 5-31 versus Sri Lanka in 1988 - with his five-for on his home ground coming in 28 balls as England slumped to 132 all out, a total Australia eclipsed in 23.3 overs.

Harry Brook (1), who became Beardman's first wicket when he poked behind in the 12th over, saw his side bundled out in just 33.4 overs with Joe Root (17), playing his 200th ODI, one of a number of players to perish on the drive, the sort of shot that had got England in all sorts of bother during their Test trouncing here a year ago.
Brook's men rallied somewhat from 65-8, passing their lowest-ever ODI score of 86 and reaching three figures thanks to Will Jacks (25) and Gus Atkinson, who top-scored with 29 not out from 32 balls from the No 10 spot and hit England's sole six.
But a target of 132 was never likely to trouble Australia, despite Atkinson bowling Travis Head - who had slammed a match-winning hundred in that Ashes clash in Perth in 2025 - for a golden duck in the second over and so it proved, as stand-in captain Mitchell Marsh tonked a 29-ball fifty before holing out with 65 runs needed.
Marsh's eight-boundary onslaught (four sixes, four fours) came a day after dead-batting all questions about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in Cape Town, which has been catapulted back onto the news agenda following the release of Usman Khawaja's book.
Beardman the star after Cummins hogs the headlines
Marsh is leading Australia in this three-match series in place of the rested Pat Cummins - but the latter was, along with Beardman, the undoubted story of Friday as he held an extraordinary, 68-minute press conference to address Khawaja's comments.
Cummins insisted Khawaja's claims that every member of the Baggy Greens dressing room back then was aware of the plot to alter the ball using sandpaper to be "100 per cent untrue" and "utter nonsense" before lauding "really exciting prospect" Beardman.
As fans and media digested Cummins' startling response to Khawaja's accusations, a couple of hours later they were hailing Beardman's record-breaking ODI bow, where he displayed accuracy, speed and skill and offered a glimpse into the future.
The seamer nicked off Brook, Root and Jordan Cox (2), bounced out Sam Curran (0), had Liam Dawson - once again preferred in the England XI to fellow spinner Adil Rashid - caught at backward point for a duck and ended the innings when last man Jofra Archer (11) was athletically pouched by a diving Jack Edwards in the gully.
An Australia attack missing Cummins and two other rested fast-bowling stalwarts in Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazelwood excelled with left-armer Spencer Johnson's 3-42 including Ben Duckett (9) caught square driving to backward point after England lost the toss and new-ball partner Xavier Bartlett (1-46) removing Tom Banton (25).
England took a few scalps in the chase in Head, Marsh and Cooper Connolly (27 off 30) but Australia eased to victory and will now look to wrap up a series win with a game to spare in Adelaide on Sunday ahead of next Wednesday's final game in Hobart.
Brook's team are not at full strength - they are shorn of the injured Jacob Bethell (knee), Jos Buttler (hamstring) and Josh Tongue (toe) - but neither are Australia, so this defeat, following swiftly on from their tri-series travails in Pakistan last month when they lost three of their four matches, leaves England with plenty to ponder.
