Democrats Hold Kansas Governorship, Retaining Power on the Plains
State Senator Cindy Holscher won the race. Though Kansas is reliably Republican in presidential elections, its voters often break for Democrats in midterms.
State Senator Cindy Holscher won election as governor of Kansas, keeping the seat in Democratic hands for a third straight term, The Associated Press said on Thursday.
She narrowly defeated Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee and the president of the Kansas Senate. Gov. Laura Kelly, the Democratic incumbent, was barred by term limits from seeking re-election.
Ms. Holscher’s victory added to a momentous election for Democrats in Kansas and across the country, and it maintained a rare lever of power for the party on the Great Plains.
Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, became the first Kansas Democrat to win a U.S. Senate race since the 1930s. In addition, Democrats flipped several legislative seats to break a Republican supermajority in the Kansas House of Representatives, which will make it much harder to override vetoes by Ms. Holscher.
Kansans also voted out Attorney General Kris W. Kobach, a Republican who helped elevate illegal voting as a political issue. Republicans prevailed in other statewide races and will still have majorities in both legislative chambers.
Though Kansans reliably vote for Republicans for president, they have shown an independent streak in midterm elections, swinging for decades between Republican and Democratic governors. High costs, dissatisfaction with President Trump’s policies and a tangle of challenges facing farmers made the Plains region more winnable for Democrats this year.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental hospital.
Fact: The video is clipped out of context. RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat was recounting an incident from the 1930s where a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS against an attempt to ban it. While making this argument, Ibrahim had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Bhagwat was quoting Ibrahim’s statement, not remarking himself. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a Facebook post (archived) by The Economic Times, dated 09 November 2026, featuring a longer version of the same video. Upon reviewing the video, we found that Mohan Bhagwat was not making the statement himself but was quoting a person named Ibrahim. Referring to an incident from the 1930s, Bhagwat said that when the Central Provinces Assembly first attempted to ban the RSS, there were no volunteers or supporters of the RSS’s ideology to defend it. In this context, he recounted that a person named Ibrahim defended the RSS by saying that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. Ibrahim further stated that he knew Dr Hedgewar, that he was not insane but a good man, and therefore, the RSS could not be communal.
We also found multiple media reports (here, here, and here) covering the statement made by Mohan Bhagwat on 09 November 2026, while inaugurating the newly constructed auditorium at the renovated headquarters of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Limited in Nagpur.
We also found a video of the event, which was livestreamed on 09 November 2026 on the Facebook account of Nagpur Nagarik Sahakari Bank Ltd. In the approximately 1-hour-and-36-minute-long video, we found the segment corresponding to the viral clip at around 1:16:00.
During this segment, Mohan Bhagwat said, “The RSS, which was formed 100 years ago, is being discussed everywhere. That’s why so many books are being published now. I held an intellectual class here in Nagpur, where I explained that when the first attempt to ban the RSS was made in the Central Provinces Assembly in the 1930s, none of the RSS volunteers came forward to defend the RSS or support its ideology.”
He further said, “There was a Mr Ibrahim who spoke in favour of the RSS. He said that the RSS should not be banned and that it was not communal. But how did he make this argument? He said that those who say India is a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. This is my opinion, and I know Dr Hedgewar. He is not insane; he is a good man, and therefore, the RSS cannot be communal. So, that was in the 1930s. Five or seven years had passed since the RSS was founded. Everyone knew about the RSS, but Dr Hedgewar knew“
We also found that Jagran reported that a book on the lives of former RSS pracharaks was released during the event. Bhagwat discussed the lives of former RSS pracharaks and recounted an incident from the 1930s in this context. This confirms that the viral clip presents Bhagwat’s statement without the necessary context. In the original video, Bhagwat was quoting a person named Ibrahim, who had said that those who call India a Hindu nation should be sent to a mental asylum. The remark was made by Ibrahim, not Bhagwat.
To sum up, this video shows Mohan Bhagwat quoting Ibrahim’s remark about sending those who call India a Hindu nation to a mental asylum.

SHANGHAI: Investors dumped shares in Chinese AI models and hardware suppliers to the US on Friday (Nov 13), worried the resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO could usher in an even deeper technological divide between the world's two biggest economies.
AI model stocks Z.AI and MiniMax Group fell sharply on worries of reduced access to advanced AI chips, while data centre suppliers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology, whose businesses are heavily reliant on US markets, slumped.
Local chip stocks gained as investors bet on tech self-reliance, leaving both the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index and the blue-chip CSI300 Index little changed by the lunch break.
"The market fears that after Huang's resignation, Nvidia will reduce sourcing from Chinese suppliers," said Wu Zhou, fund manager at Shenzhen Deyuan Investment.
"The US will also likely tighten restrictions on China's access to advanced chips, including the renting of offshore cloud computing power."
Wu said such a prospect bodes ill for AI firms that desperately need computing power, but benefits homegrown AI chipmakers.
Shanghai-listed AI chipmaker Cambricon Technology rose 1.2 per cent and was on course to jump 22 per cent this week in its best showing in six months.
Domestic chipmaker Hygon Information Technology was poised to gain 7 per cent this week.
TIGHTER RESTRICTIONS
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy, plunged the chipmaker into a crisis and sent shockwaves across the AI industry.
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after the scandal.
Meanwhile, Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China, worried that the development around Nvidia's Huang could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their remote use of advanced processors.
"The biggest risk to China's AI industry is that the scandal leads to a tightening of US export controls on advanced chips and chip-making equipment, possibly by the end of this year," Gavekal Dragonomics said in a report.
Huang was the most influential opponent of tight chip export controls to China, so his scandal, "combined with the arrival of a more AI-skeptical Congress, will make it ever harder for Chinese AI companies to gain access to the advanced compute they so desperately crave", the think tank said.
“If the US government tighten Chinese access to US chips, we expect all the companies with LLM business will be negatively impacted,” Chelsey Tam, senior equity analyst at Morningstar, said, referring to Chinese AI model firms.
The US government is also working on a measure on national security grounds to bar imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, potentially dealing a blow to Chinese suppliers Innolight and Eoptolink, which derive most of their revenue from the US.

From postcards to texts, the different ways a manager gets the sack - Pulis
- Published
When you hear about a manager parting company with a club, he has usually either been sacked or has resigned, but there are actually lots of different ways you can leave.
Over the years I spent working at every level of the game in England, from the bottom to the top, I have witnessed and been involved in many break-ups.
Some are smooth but others are far more fractious and don't happen face-to-face. I've witnessed managers being sacked over the phone or by text, or hearing they are losing their job by word of mouth.
One of the most soul-destroying times for a manager is when speculation is rife regarding not only your imminent sacking, but also about who is going to replace you.
During my career, I've known certain individuals who actually put their names forward for jobs before a manager is even sacked. Some go to the club involved through agents, some directly to the owners themselves.
Many managers are sounded out before eventually being appointed and another policy which has become popular with clubs is to drop names out to the press about possible replacements, to see the supporters' reactions to the names in the frame.
For the manager who is still in place, and whose stress levels are through the roof, it is devastating... but it is just another part of the job that you have to handle.
I've experienced that situation myself, in a scenario which went on for many months. Your confidence, not only in yourself but also in the club's hierarchy, takes another massive knock.
When it happened to me, I'd heard about the club's intentions from people in the media at quite an early stage and also worked out where the new manager would be coming from, but I had to bite my lip - myself and my staff were under contract, so we had to just carry on.
We kept pulling results out of the bag which delayed the inevitable, but eventually I knew my time was up.
Sacked on the drive up for pre-season
When they are getting treated this way, you can hardly blame managers for sometimes wanting to stick two fingers up to the people in charge.
One story comes to mind of a manager I know who was relieved of his duties by being placed on gardening leave while the club found a way to release him permanently.
During that time, and while he was still getting paid, the manager decided to go on holiday somewhere hot with his family. After watching his old team lose on TV in the sunshine, he sent a postcard to his chairman, which simply said 'wish you were here!'.
When he got home, he was sacked - but I bet he was still glad he did it!
Sadly, most managers don't get that kind of satisfaction - and often you don't even get a chance to say a proper goodbye to the players and staff you have worked closely with for many months or years.
My first spell at Stoke ended when I was driving up the motorway from my home in Bournemouth for the first day of pre-season in the summer of 2005.
I'd had a pretty good idea of what might happen since the end of the previous season but, over the next few weeks, the club's Icelandic owners did not say a word - until then.
I didn't have a problem with the decision, by the way. They were nice people and my view has always been 'if you don't want me, you don't want me'.
Anyway, I'd already been driving for four hours and, just as I got to the junction that would take me to the ground, my phone rang. It was the chairman, who told me he'd been meaning to call.
I was told I was no longer the manager, but also that I could not enter the stadium at any cost - I soon understood the urgency of the situation because it turned out the new manager had already arrived there. I had to just turn the car around, and head back home.
That kind of thing can happen to any manager, and you learn to be ready for it.
'Every manager needs to think about their cardboard box'
I always remember playing at Swansea in one of my early games in my first job with Bournemouth, and their manager Frank Burrows inviting me into his office afterwards.
Frank, who sadly passed away in 2021, was a wonderful man and also a superb old-school manager who was always happy to offer advice to younger coaches and share his experiences.
We were having a drink and I noticed he had this big empty cardboard box next to his desk. I asked him what it was for, and he said it was to hold all his belongings - from his files on players to his family photographs - that were in his office.
"All the important stuff I'd like to keep is on the top of my desk," Frank said. "And every time I lose my job, because that time always comes, I can just sweep it into the box and off I go again. That box has travelled around the football world with me."
That always stuck with me. Management is such a precarious occupation that every manager has to think about that box, even if they don't have it sitting next to their desk every day!
It was not long afterwards that I found out what it was like to be sacked for the first time.
I still had a year left on my contract with Bournemouth but the chairmanship of the club changed and, in the summer of 1994, I was out.
It was hard enough to go from doing almost everything at the club to doing nothing, not even going in for pre-season training - but, because it was my hometown club, I also had to come to terms with listening to stories of my children being teased about my exit at school.
I also had my mortgage and my family to look after and unfortunately Bournemouth were not very helpful with the money they owed me.
It's a lot to think about, when you have just been thrown out into the real world, especially when it's a world you have no experience in or any other qualifications to fall back on. I was lucky enough to get another chance in management, but not every young manager does.
Fortunately, I've not always left clubs on bad terms, either. I've already mentioned a few difficult separations, but I've had some happier endings too.
Finishing as friends
I've talked a lot in these columns about my affection for Peter Coates and his wonderful family. As well as owning Stoke City, they are a special group of people who have been unbelievably successful in their own ways, but they have never lost that human touch.
When the time came for me to part company with the club in 2013, they did so in a proper manner - Peter and John, his son and now chairman, were dead straight with me about wanting to go in a different direction, and made a difficult situation into a respectful parting of the ways.
I spent almost 10 years at Stoke over two spells but, while I was only at Middlesbrough for 18 months, it was a similar story with their owner and chairman Steve Gibson.
Steve has spent his entire life looking out for Boro but his commitment to his club goes far beyond being a lifetime supporter. He cares deeply for the people of that area and has devoted so much of his hard-earned cash towards making Boro a success.
I loved my time there because of the warmth of Steve and his family, and beyond. The area reminded me so much of south Wales, where the community was cherished and people, especially at the club, could not do enough for you.
After the last game of the 2018-19 season I was completely shot, and frustrated that we had not reached the Championship play-offs. My drive home that night was long and lonely but I felt worn out.
Once the dust had settled on that season, Steve and I met up in London. Our discussions were honest and open but my contract was up and we both agreed it was a good time for me to leave - I wanted it to end on good terms, and we certainly did that.
After dinner we had a fair few drinks and it ended up being a very, very late night. We arranged to have breakfast the following morning but I told him I have always been an early riser so, by 6am, I was up and on my way to the station to get back home.
My wife had just picked me up in Bournemouth at just after 8am when Steve rang to ask if I was down for breakfast yet - and he didn't believe me when I said no, I am back home.
I missed breakfast, but we remained good friends. Steve is a class act and I always hold Boro up as a club that deserves to be successful because of the attitude, commitment and honesty of everyone we came across.
My family still talk about how much they loved going there, and were genuinely disappointed when I left - something that doesn't apply to all my former clubs, obviously!
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.
Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.
Roots in fitness routine of vicar
The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.
“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.
When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.
“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.
The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.
The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.
For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.
‘A form of spiritual service’
The church sees the initiative as more than a fitness facility. “We want to groom a healthy generation. Many people suffer from lifestyle diseases, while youngsters often turn to private fitness centres. We felt that providing basic facilities here would benefit the community. Spirituality is also about nurturing a healthy mind and body. We consider this a form of spiritual service,” says assistant vicar Fr. Jees Akkara.
For Fr. Eluvathingal, there is another purpose. “Youngsters rarely come to church or participate in its activities these days. This is also an opportunity to bring more of them into the church community,” he says.

Journalist’s Arrest Adds to Fears Israeli Security Agency Is Being Politicized
Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, was detained without being charged with a crime, raising concerns that the domestic security service is overstepping its authority.
Abed Abu Shehadeh, a 38-year-old journalist and a Palestinian citizen of Israel, said he was putting on his pajamas on the evening of Nov. 3 when police officers and intelligence agents burst into his family’s third-floor apartment in Jaffa.
They strip-searched him, confiscated his phone, allowed him to dress and then whisked him away, he said in an interview at a restaurant in the city.
Five days later, after interrogations by Israel’s domestic security agency, the Shin Bet, Mr. Abu Shehadeh, who lives with his wife and two young children, was let go.
A former elected member of the Tel Aviv-Jaffa City Council, Mr. Abu Shehadeh has not been charged with a crime. The Israeli authorities have not publicly offered a reason for his arrest, though court records reviewed by The New York Times show that he was accused of being in contact with an unnamed “foreign agent.”
His highly publicized arrest — a week after Israel’s national elections — came as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies have claimed that foreign actors illegally funneled large amounts of money to bribe Arab citizens to vote for Arab political parties.
Critics say that Mr. Netanyahu and his allies are seeking to undermine the legitimacy of the record gains by Arab parties in the Parliament, or the Knesset, by contending without basis that Arab voters stole the election.

If a good night’s sleep has become your holy grail, who are the knights in shining armour you will employ to reach that chalice? Most people seem to be deploying melatonin and magnesium supplements, over the counter, but the question that remains is: are they effective, and if so, at what combinations or levels?
The consensus among most sleep specialists, is that both melatonin and magnesium (glycinate) can have an ameliorative impact – in the short term. Both these supplements, however, work differently – while melatonin is a key body clock signal, magnesium helps relax the body. When and how you take both supplements makes a great deal of difference to your hours of sleep and sleep quality as well.

In China’s Spy Operations, Romance Can Be a Long Game
Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman U.S. officials say is a Chinese spy has drawn attention to the role of intimate relationships in espionage.
At the height of the Cold War, a top official in China’s intelligence agency said that his country would never use seduction to entrap a person.
Such tactics might be for the C.I.A. or the K.G.B., the official named Kong Yuan, of the Central Investigation Department, told a group of agents in training in April 1960, but China was guided by principles. He looked at the few female comrades in the audience. “Rest assured, we will not be asking you to go run beauty traps.”
Despite that pledge, captured in a 2010 memoir by a former Chinese diplomat, China’s intelligence services have for decades used romantic entanglements to compromise or extract information from prominent people.
American officials say that China’s Ministry of State Security, which runs intelligence operations today, recruited a Chinese businesswoman to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and one of the most powerful figures in the artificial intelligence boom.
It was not clear what role the woman, Alice Huang, or Huang Le, might have had with the Chinese spy agency. Ms. Huang was a top executive of a Singapore company that operates data centers in Southeast Asia using Nvidia chips and that rents their computing power to Chinese firms.
Mr. Huang has acknowledged that he had an affair with Ms. Huang. President Trump has said that Mr. Huang told him that he was not aware that the woman was a spy. China has rejected the espionage allegations against Ms. Huang, calling them smears against the country. U.S. officials have not provided evidence for their claims. Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

Vallari Sheel wishes she could carry a camera or a pair of binoculars without being asked what her father does for a living. Once, looking at a tree in her south Delhi neighbourhood, about 50 metres away from her home, a man in a car screamed at her: “You have been clicking photos here for 10 days. What are you going to do with them?”
Sheel, an urban ecologist, spends hours observing trees of all types in all seasons. She often travels by car for her own safety, worries about the impact of her work on her family, and has clear guidance for her female interns when they are, inevitably, approached: don’t engage, don’t respond.
“It’s the men who ask such intrusive questions: Who are you? Where are you from? What does your father do?” she says.
Sheel was recounting these experiences atop Delhi’s oldest fort inside Sanjay Van, a sprawling city forest overlooking a 12th-century minaret. She was one of about 20 women who had gathered on a crisp Sunday morning in October to enjoy nature, safely. Many had never experienced a forest before.
Among the group were a scientist who had stopped birding since she moved to Delhi, a psychiatrist who can’t find a safe place to run, and an environmental planner who cycles everywhere. For many women, simple pleasures such as enjoying nature have become beset by gender crimes.
“The city feels designed to crush any form of freedom, any form of exploration,” says Neha Sinha, who organised the walk. Author of My Wild City: Finding Nature, Meaning, and Hope in India’s Capital, Sinha has been organising these walks for two years.
During her own walks around the city’s forts, forests and wetlands to observe the diminishing number of fireflies, flying foxes, howling jackals, leopards and hyenas, civets and owls, and groves of 350-year-old trees, she has faced the wrath of men. She has changed her route countless times to mislead stalkers, and been asked by men on the street how much she would charge for sex.
“As has everybody else,” she says. “Nearly every woman I know has called a cop saying ‘I have a stalker.’ In a culture that tells you not to go out … how do you make nature your own?”
Two weeks before the women gathered on the walking trails of Sanjay Van, dotted with ruellias, vajradantis and jaal trees, hundreds of people had joined a protest in Delhi over the gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park.
Their demand was to make public spaces safer for women. The government’s response was to ban entry to public parks after sunset.
For Alankrita Narayan, a wildlife conservation student who often needs to work alone at night, that rule was unhelpful. During an internship, she recalls, her organisation trained her for worst-case scenarios in the jungle: What if something happens to your partner? What if you encounter a man carrying a weapon? What if you encounter a forest officer asking for sexual favours?
“And I was like, where did the animal come in here? What if I’m caught alone and a leopard comes in front of me? And they were like, ‘Oh, don’t worry about the leopard. It’s a man you don’t want to run into,” she says. Sinha agrees: “Animals have rules.”
Paroma Mukherjee, a photographer, recalls the advice she once got from a well-known photographer: be inconspicuous, wear clothes that blend in, keep your equipment small. “But then, he was a man. So he could blend in,” she adds.
“Men can pee on the road and we can’t even carry a camera,” another woman says. “You know, we had to take a detour today to avoid a lonely stretch on our way here,” says another. “I carry a pepper spray,” another adds.
On group walks, the women pick up and drop off each other at their homes, wait outside the forest gate until everyone has arrived, and stick together in isolated areas. “I always tell women, ‘Don’t go alone’,” Sinha says.
“We started the walk at 7am today, which is late for birdwatching, but everybody could not leave home while it was still dark,” she says.
However, the group agree that many of these measures might not work for women from less privileged backgrounds, who then miss out.
“No woman in the city is fully free,” Sinha says.
Walking as a woman is an act of resistance, as is observing nature. “Because you’re actually slowing down when you do that,” she says. “It’s so different from the instant gratification culture that we have today. It is more of an immersion, rather than conquering. Both are very political acts.”
In the heart of New Delhi, where India’s senior officials and dignitaries live, there are thousands of fruit bats that swarm out of their roosts every evening to feast on mahua trees.
“And on very clear wintry nights, when everything is silent, I even hear jackals crying and laughing from my home. It’s almost like a parallel city,” Sinha says.
Over three hours, the women collect cuttings, peer and marvel at speckle-like flowers through a pocket microscope, discuss the colonial concepts of wild plants labelled as weeds, chat about the drongo, black kite and tailorbird they spotted, and the next walk.
“Can we do it at night?” someone asks. “What would the forest look like at night?”
Sinha describes a previous night walk experience when frogs had put up an orchestral noise, fireflies lit the bushes and jackals were laughing. “It was the most eerie, magical, bewitching atmosphere I have ever experienced,” she says.
Men, she points out, can simply go ahead and enjoy such experiences, but women have to create an ecosystem around them to be able to.
But, she promises her enthusiastic group, she will try to arrange a night walk.

The Apple Silicon iMac got its fourth refresh this month.
Every other Apple Silicon Mac has found a way to move forward over the last half-decade—we’ve gotten a more Pro design for the MacBook Pro, a mini-er design for the Mac mini, and a Mac Studio that has finally made Apple admit it doesn’t want to make the Mac Pro anymore.
But the Apple Silicon iMac has always been more interested in looking backward. It’s the thin, screen-on-a-stand iMac design by way of the original Bondi Blue G3 iMac. It’s a clean and pretty desktop computer, one I see all the time in small offices and on TV shows that depict small offices. We’re long past the days when it was Apple’s primary workstation computer.
So I wanted to write about this new iMac from the perspective of that entry-level iMac buyer, who chooses the iMac because it’s simple and then uses it until it breaks. What does a new iMac get you if you’re stepping up from the M1 model or comparing it against an older refurbished M4 model? Without any real external updates, what makes this iMac iteration interesting?
Same friendly face
If you haven’t used an Apple Silicon-era iMac before, here’s a brief primer.
The new iMac is much thinner than the older aluminum Intel models. Its front is mostly one big 24-inch screen, surrounded on all sides by a relatively thick white bezel (I still wish black were at least an option, but Apple apparently doesn’t agree).
White bezel aside, it’s by far Apple’s most colorful computer. The iMacs ship with color-matched fronts, backs, stands, keyboards, mice, trackpads, and cables. Apple has tweaked the color offerings and changed the tints of each specific color a few times over the years, but the M6 iMac uses the same six color tints (plus silver) that the M4 iMac did.
The basic $1,499 iMac is essentially a MacBook Air in terms of ports—it has two Thunderbolt ports on the back and a headphone jack on the left side. Choosing this model also locks you into a lesser version of the Apple M6 with 10 CPU cores and 10 GPU cores instead of 12 of each, a maximum of 24GB of RAM, a minimum of 256GB of storage, and a maximum of 1TB. Its default keyboard doesn’t have Touch ID support, and the only way to get it is to buy the version with the built-in number pad, an $80 upsell.
The M6 iMac still comes with either two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports. The four-port version can run two external displays; the one-port version is limited to one. Ethernet is available on the power brick for an extra $30.

The $1,699 version is the one to get if you still intend to use the iMac as a workstation. It includes the full-speed version of the M6 with all its CPU and GPU cores intact (though there are performance caveats here we’ll talk about later), plus options for 32GB of RAM and up to 2TB of storage. This version also includes four Thunderbolt ports on the back for connecting additional accessories. Both available keyboards on this version have Touch ID.
A 2.5 gigabit Ethernet port can be added to any iMac for $30. This port is located on the desktop’s power brick rather than the iMac itself, an elegant solution that keeps even a wired Internet connection hidden beneath your desk with the other cables. All iMacs also offer a VESA mount adapter option in place of the default stand at no extra charge.
I still really like the effect created by the color-matched keyboard, mouse/trackpad, and cables—even the white bezel complements the white keycaps and mouse. Just know you’re paying quite a lot for how the desktop looks. The $899 Mac mini is $800 cheaper than the iMac with the same chip, the same amount of RAM, and the same amount of storage. Sure, it would cost something to add a nice-looking 4K monitor, but not $800, even if you go for extra frills like a high refresh rate.
It’s fine that the iMac upcharges you for style and convenience. That’s the point of the computer. Just make sure that’s what you want to pay for.

Here are the basic specs for every entry-level iMac Apple has shipped, going all the way back to the last of the Intel models.
The iMac’s evolution has been slow and gradual during the Apple Silicon era. The computer has never gotten a base storage upgrade, and the base M4 and M6 models still only support a single external display (the upgraded models support two external displays, finally surpassing the old Intel model).
If you have any kind of Apple Silicon iMac and you’re happy with how it’s performing and you’re not hankering for more RAM or more displays, I don’t think the M6 model really adds anything worth upgrading for. It’s definitely faster, but even six years on, the Apple M1 remains perfectly serviceable for daily use, especially when it’s attached to 16GB of RAM.
And if you’re in the market for an iMac now, I think the M4 model still gets you the best bang for your buck if you can find one refurbished or on sale. That one still gets you a minimum of 16GB of RAM, Thunderbolt in all four ports for the four-port model, the 32GB RAM option, the nano-texture display option, and support for multiple external displays (again, in the four-port model).
The M6 iMac builds on that, and it comes with real performance benefits (more on that shortly). But the brightest dividing line in the Apple Silicon iMac model history is between the M3 and M4 model, not the M4 and M6 model. And that’s true despite the two-generation silicon upgrade.

A quick recap on the M6: a total of 12 CPU cores (two super cores, four performance cores, six efficiency cores), either 10 or 12 GPU cores, 16/24/32GB RAM options, and a doubled Neural Engine NPU with 32 cores instead of 16. For the iMac, the M6 also introduces some of the architectural tweaks introduced with the Apple M5, including the addition of neural accelerator hardware to the GPU cores. This boosts the speed of some kinds of local AI workloads compared to the M4, including MetalFX upscaling and frame generation in games.
The M6 in the Mac mini and the M6 in the 14-inch MacBook Pro both perform similarly within a roughly 28 W sustained power envelope. The version with 16GB of RAM will perform slightly worse in games and other workloads sensitive to memory bandwidth—the 16GB M6 offers 153 GB/s of memory bandwidth, and the 24GB and 32GB versions offer 170 GB/s. But that’s a pretty minor difference.
The iMac is slower than either of those two Macs, particularly in multi-core CPU benchmarks and graphics benchmarks, and the HandBrake video encoding test shows the likely culprit. The iMac’s M6 consumes an average of 18 W of power under sustained heavy load. It won’t throttle its speeds as aggressively as a MacBook Air because the iMac still includes an active cooling fan, but the reduced power envelope does mean that the Mac mini or MacBook Pro are 5 to 8 percent faster than the iMac in heavy multi-core CPU tasks and about 8 to 12 percent faster in graphics benchmarks.
One benefit of the smaller power envelope is that the iMac’s chip is even more power-efficient than the regular M6 and the iMac’s version of the M4, using much less power to do the same amount of work.
That still makes it a solid upgrade over the M4. The iMac’s M6 is 15 to 20 percent faster in our single-core CPU benchmarks, between 20 and 30 percent faster in multi-core CPU benchmarks, and between 20 and 40 percent faster in graphics benchmarks (the Blender GPU benchmarks do even better—they seem to like the neural accelerators in the M5 and M6 GPUs). Especially with 24GB or 32GB of RAM, it’s perfectly capable of being the heart of a multi-monitor workstation setup or a light photo/video editing rig.
What meets the eye
The M6 iMac changes almost nothing about who the iMac is for, its position in Apple’s lineup, or what it’s technically capable of. It’s a box-ticking upgrade, and the box being ticked is “keep the insides up to date.”
That means today’s iMac is best for the same kinds of computer users it was good for in 1998: people who don’t want a laptop, people who need a friendly and approachable kiosk or office computer, and people who just want something pretty that doesn’t require a lot of fussing with screens or cables.
That’s the main thing I miss about being an iMac user. I like how my current Mac Studio desktop works, and I need flexibility and complexity in my specific setup to get the Mac and a gaming PC connected to all the same stuff. But despite my best efforts, the cable situation has always been a barely managed mess.
If someone you know has a cable management problem and doesn’t need the complexity, congratulations, you’ve found someone the iMac is for. I just wish Apple would use these kinds of pretty, saturated colors in a laptop or desktop that meets my needs, you know?
The good
A pretty and capable desktop computer that minimizes the cable mess that most desktops make
Energy efficient and quiet, on the rare occasions when you can hear the fan spinning at all
Apple M6 is fast, and especially with 24GB or 32GB of RAM, will be more than capable of handling most tasks
Like the M4 version, it can support multiple external displays if you pay for the faster chip
The bad
Limited port selection

Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
- Published
Ukraine's president has welcomed a pledge from US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, to include delegates from the European Union in the next round of peace talks with Russia.
European leaders have expressed deepening security concerns this week, and Volodymyr Zelensky said bringing them into the talks would ensure the EU has a "voice" in negotiations.
Kushner and Witkoff met Zelensky in Dublin on Thursday evening as part of a busy day of shuttle diplomacy - they met Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier, who said that Russia's position on the war - and its demand for territory - has not changed.
The meetings follow talks in Abu Dhabi last week that failed to reach a breakthrough in ending the war.
But Thursday did see Russia and Ukraine agree to another prisoner exchange - the largest swap yet since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Kushner said it would return "thousands of people to their families", but further details like how many prisoners would be exchanged or a timeline, were not given.
- US envoys meet Zelensky in Dublin after talks with Putin in Moscow 
  - Published5 hours ago
- Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine 
  - Published11 hours ago
Zelensky has for several years been calling for European delegates to be included in the peace talks, and says it makes sense because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
On Thursday, Kushner said that the US has been "working very, very closely over the past several months with Europeans and I think that that's been very important."
He added that he had stressed to Putin how important it is to have European delegates "at the table".
"He's willing to give it a try," Kushner added.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US government's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Kallas also expressed doubts that there was Russian momentum towards a peace deal.

Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine remains under control of Russian forces, and cross-border incursions are increasingly common.
Tensions between the US and Ukraine were on display on Thursday before Witkoff and Kushner's meeting with Zelensky.

The technology owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company has played a vital role in government and military connectivity in Ukraine, and increasingly assists in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

New Delhi: Taxpayers who have availed of the safe harbour provisions for specified international transactions cannot seek further relief under the mutual agreement procedure (MAP), according to the Central Board of Direct Taxes' (CBDT) updated guidelines on cross-border tax disputes. In its 22-page guidance, the apex direct-tax policymaking body under the finance ministry has also clarified how disputes will be handled when the same tax issues are pursued through domestic appeals, advance rulings and settlement schemes. MAP is a dispute-resolution mechanism under India's double taxation avoidance agreements (DTAAs). It allows taxpayers to seek intervention by the competent authorities of two countries when a tax action results, or could result, in taxation inconsistent with the applicable treaty or double taxation. Such disputes commonly involve transfer pricing adjustments, determination of a permanent establishment and attribution of profits to overseas operations. The updated guidance is significant as India expands its network of free trade agreements (FTAs), having signed trade deals with the UK, Oman and New Zealand, besides agreements with the UAE, Australia and the European Free Trade Association. India has also concluded FTA negotiations with the European Union and is pursuing trade talks with several other partners, including Canada, Chile and Israel. As cross-border trade and investment expand, clarity on international tax disputes and mechanisms to avoid double taxation becomes increasingly important for businesses. On safe harbour, the guidance bars a taxpayer who has opted for the provisions from seeking MAP relief for the covered transactions. However, if a foreign tax authority’s decision disturbs the return filed in India under safe harbour, the foreign associated enterprise may seek MAP through its own competent authority, which will notify India. India will allow MAP, but will keep the safe harbour price and only ask the other country for relief, it noted. The CBDT has clarified that Indian authorities will not deviate from ITAT orders on issues decided on merits. If the tribunal rules in favour of the taxpayer, the MAP case will be closed. If it remands the matter for fresh adjudication, taxpayers can seek MAP after a fresh order is passed. According to the document, if a resident has already settled under Vivad se Vishwas (VsV) 2020 or 2024, India will not revisit that settlement in MAP. It may just ask the other country to provide relief, usually when the overseas associated enterprise seeks MAP. If a non-resident has settled under the VsV scheme on the same issue, MAP will not be available for that issue. Indian authorities will not grant MAP access to taxpayers who have already availed the scheme's benefits on the same issue. However, overseas associated enterprises can seek MAP, with Indian authorities agreeing to the settlement outcome and seeking corresponding relief from the treaty partner. Where an Indian taxpayer has applied under the scheme but is yet to pay the applicable taxes, MAP access will be granted. If the taxpayer subsequently avails the scheme's benefits, the settlement outcome will prevail. On advance rulings, the guidance allows MAP access to taxpayers who have obtained a ruling from the board for advance rulings (BAR). However, Indian authorities will not deviate from the BAR's decision on issues decided on merits and may instead seek corresponding relief from the treaty partner. The guidance also covers withholding-tax disputes. Non-residents can seek MAP access against tax deduction orders under Section 398 of the Income Tax Act, 2025. However, discussions between the two countries' competent authorities can begin only after an assessment order is passed in the non-resident's own case and the taxpayer considers it contrary to the applicable treaty. The CBDT has also asked taxpayers to keep competent authorities informed about material developments, including changes in documents submitted earlier and the status of parallel proceedings in India or overseas. Sharing relevant information with both authorities will help "ensure information symmetry" and avoid differences in their understanding of the facts. The updated guidance incorporates changes under the Income Tax Act, 2025 and Income Tax Rules, 2026, replacing the earlier guidance issued in August 2020 and updated in June 2022. Under most Indian tax treaties, taxpayers have three years from the first notification of the action resulting in treaty-inconsistent taxation to file a MAP application. Indian residents must use Form 55 under Rule 121 for tax years 2026-27 onwards, while Rule 44G of the repealed Income Tax Rules, 1962, will continue to apply to earlier assessment years. India will endeavour to resolve MAP cases within an average of 24 months, though the CBDT clarified that this is not a guarantee. After a resolution is communicated, taxpayers have one month from the end of that month to convey acceptance and submit evidence of withdrawal of pending domestic appeals. Assessing officers will have a corresponding one-month period to give effect to the resolution. The guidance also clarifies that where its provisions conflict with domestic laws, rules, circulars or applicable tax treaties, the relevant legal and treaty provisions will prevail. Tax experts said that the CBDT's consolidated MAP guidance for 2026 would provide greater certainty to multinational companies by clarifying the interaction between international tax dispute resolution and domestic tax proceedings. Nitin Narang, partner, transfer pricing at Nangia & Co LLP, said the guidance aligns treaty dispute resolution with the Income Tax Act, 2025 and Income Tax Rules, 2026, while clarifying the treatment of parallel litigation and safe harbour provisions. “The guidance strikes a balance between taxpayer facilitation and procedural discipline. While it provides greater clarity on the interaction between domestic tax appeals, Safe harbour rules and treaty-based dispute resolution, it also places greater responsibility on taxpayers to keep competent authorities informed about developments in parallel proceedings. This should make India's MAP framework more predictable and accessible for multinational businesses," Narang said. New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'
- Published
An Indian court has ordered an investigation into allegations that a public library in the southern state of Tamil Nadu bought hundreds of books suspected of being generated using AI.
The controversy began after Tamil novelist Perumal Murugan raised concerns about books containing false information and questionable authorship at a newly opened library in Coimbatore city.
The Madras High Court has ordered the state's anti-corruption agency to investigate the purchases and freeze bank accounts linked to a publisher accused of supplying the books.
The state government has blamed the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party-led administration for buying the books. The DMK denies allegations.
Tamil Nadu's School Education Minister A Rajmohan has described the allegations as potentially "India's first AI scam" and said the investigation would cover purchases at other public libraries across the state.
The case has raised wider questions about the growing use of AI in publishing, where tools can generate entire books quickly and cheaply, but also produce false information and invented references.
It has also highlighted the challenges facing libraries and publishers in checking the authenticity of books as AI-generated content becomes more widespread.
The controversy centres on the Periyar Arivulagam library, built at a cost of about 3bn rupees ($34m; £26m). Named after social reformer Periyar EV Ramasamy, it was inaugurated on 16 October by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay.
Murugan, whose novels Pyre and One Part Woman have received international recognition, raised concerns after visiting the library last month.
Writing in an online magazine, he alleged that nearly 1,800 books in its Tamil section had been supplied by a little-known publisher called Agal Vilakku Pathippagam.
He said many of the books carried unfamiliar authors' names, unusually high prices and questionable International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs).
One book cited in the controversy, Naladiyar Vaazhvin Vazhikatti (A Guide to Life through Naladiyar), was reportedly priced at 1,445 rupees for 300 pages.
It describes Naladiyar as a Tamil poet and philosopher, although Naladiyar is a classical Tamil work consisting of 400 four-line verses on morality and ethics.
Another book reportedly attributes the ancient Tamil poem Madurai Kanchi to an incorrect author. It remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the disputed books.
Questions have also been raised about a book found at another public library in Madurai which names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author.
The book, Democracy and People's Rights in the Contemporary World, names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author and was published by Phoenix Publishing House.
Drèze did not respond to BBC Tamil's request for comment but told The Hindu newspaper earlier this week that he had not written the book, raising concerns that his name may have been used without his permission.
BBC Tamil visited a Chennai address listed by Agal Vilakku and another publisher named in the controversy, Phoenix Publishing House, but found no signs identifying either business.
A woman at the address confirmed that Agal Vilakku operated there. Its proprietor, Mohan, declined to comment, saying the matter was before the courts.
The controversy has prompted writers, academics and publishers to question how the books were selected for public libraries.
More than 160 writers, researchers, artists and publishers have signed a joint statement calling for an independent inquiry, the release of procurement records and an audit of library collections across Tamil Nadu.
They have also called for the recovery of public money if the investigation finds that funds were misused.
The group questioned how the disputed books could have passed through a selection process involving expert committees, price negotiations and several levels of review.
The state government has ordered an internal audit of public library collections.
Rajmohan said 523 books had already been removed from the historic Connemara Public Library in Chennai city after preliminary checks raised concerns about their authenticity and quality.
Disputed books have also been removed from Periyar Arivulagam, while anti-corruption officials examine procurement records and inspect other libraries, he added.
The controversy also sparked a political row in Tamil Nadu. Rajmohan accused the previous DMK government of ordering the disputed books and said the state would seek to recover public money if the investigation found wrongdoing.
The DMK has rejected the allegations as politically motivated and has called for an investigation into the purchases.

Google really needs you to know it cares about smart glasses privacy
Public trust in smart glasses is very important for selling lots of smart glasses.
The world has changed in the ten years since Snap first launched its camera-equipped Spectacles. Not only has the smart glasses market grown, the number of people sharing videos online has also jumped significantly. Nowadays, thanks to the rise of platforms like TikTok and Reels, anyone can be an influencer. And the possibility of innocent passersby inadvertently being included in a viral clip is far higher than it was.
It is in this climate that Google launches its intelligent eyewear devices today. This year has already seen Meta catch heat for what people called its "pervert glasses" or "creep glasses." In addition to making people feel uncomfortable about being spied on or filmed without their consent, the controversy has also discouraged existing users of those glasses from continuing to wear them, not to mention possibly putting off potential buyers.
Google has been working on this launch for years, and it can be easy to see why it doesn't want its own camera-equipped glasses to suffer the same backlash or be painted by the same brush. Perhaps that's why it's taking pains to make its privacy policies around the intelligent eyewear platform clear today. It's published a blog post outlining the privacy protections it's bringing to the platform, and they don't just revolve around preventing tampering with the LED indicator lights. Google is taking a fairly comprehensive approach that goes beyond device-specific measures, and includes using its wide sphere of influence to prevent surreptitious videos spreading online. In fact, Juston Payne, the lead for XR at Google, told Engadget that there are quite a few ways privacy protection has been considered.
Privacy protection around the onboard camera, microphones and Gemini AI
Let's start with what's happening on the glasses. It's basically table stakes at this point, but they all have an LED light on them to indicate when someone is taking a picture or recording a video. The light, which sits on the left side of the frame while the camera is next to the right eye, has sensors to detect if it's covered or tampered with and will prevent the capture of pictures or video.
"Unfortunately, some of the glasses that have launched in the past launched without any kind of detection for those things, and that broke trust." Payne said. "And that's a problem," he added. He also said Google's methods are "pretty effective," though that's something that we'll have to test for ourselves to verify.
And just as there are bad actors who will continue to try to break security protections for any safe in the world or online, there will be people attempting to get around Google's anti-tampering measures here. Payne said "there will always be ways around what we build, and then we'll try to fix those holes," and that he expects there will be an ongoing back-and-forth. "But nonetheless, we're very happy with where we're starting on this one."
One of the main functions of Google's smart glasses is the ability for Gemini AI to use the camera to see what the wearer is looking at and provide more relevant information. During this process, the company says that the camera visuals won't be stored in your Gemini history. When there are faces in view, Google says "your glasses are also designed to automatically redact bystanders' faces before Gemini processes the visuals."
The camera stream also won't be used in AI training or ad targeting, and Google says any data that is sent off the glasses for processing, say in the cloud or on your phone, is encrypted for transit. It's also promising to bring the Private AI Compute processing platform to glasses, enabling these new devices to use the "hardware-secured sealed cloud environment" for greater processing.
While the camera may be the most obvious recording sensor on these devices, they also have four microphones onboard to allow you to speak to Gemini or get translations for people around you. Google uses beamforming to help focus on the individuals you're looking at when deciding whose speech to translate, and the company also said it "designed Gemini to focus on your voice by default, and not other voices around you, using directional microphones on the glasses."
Payne said that the microphones will filter out "all the world audio, as we call it, the bystander audio," It helps prevent accidental recording of people in your vicinity, but also improves Gemini's effectiveness by making sure it doesn't confuse someone else's heated argument as your query.
Of course, to make the glasses more useful, you'll have to grant it access to your apps and personal information. The intelligent eyewear can work with apps like Messages, Keep or YouTube Music, for instance, to send replies or create lists for you. Like on most phones, you'll have to grant permission to specific apps before they can access the camera on your glasses, and even after you do, you can still add or revoke access for every app.
Google also said you can view your past interactions with Gemini, delete individual chats or all of them. You'll also be able to decide if your conversations are used to train AI. And to make sure there's no confusion over whether you left the glasses on or off, and if the microphones or camera might still be tuning in, all the new eyewear have a power switch with a clear red indicator to tell you when they've been shut down.
Prevention beyond just the glasses and across the Google ecosystem
Most intriguing are the measures Google is implementing across its entire ecosystem. The company said it has protections in place "across Google apps and services to deter misuse of the glasses," and they're pretty far-reaching.
For one thing, Google Shopping and Google Ads will "ban the sale and advertising of stickers or accessories designed to hide recording lights."
The company is also working to cull the demand for videos of a harassing or creepy nature. Payne said that one of the problems Google has seen is a small number of people "who use glasses to take creepy videos."
YouTube will "prohibit content that depicts things like harassment and unwanted sexualization. Any video uploaded to YouTube — whether it's recorded on a phone, a camera, or glasses — has to follow these policies, and videos that don't are removed."
There are also considerations for apps that request permission to use the cameras on these devices. "There's multiple approval layers if an app wants to use the camera," Payne said. "And there's actually some use cases that we're just blanket cutting off."
To that end, Google said that the Play Store and API policies will "prohibit apps from using the camera for social live-streaming or real-time facial identification, and from changing the behavior of the outer indicator light." This live-streaming restriction also applies to YouTube.
Of course, since the eyewear will be compatible with iOS devices as well, it's possible that someone finds an app of that nature in the App Store and uses it. And though Google may ban the advertisement or sale of physical goods that can be used to hide the LED indicator, people could very easily procure one on Amazon or Temu. There's more that needs to be done against this problem, and Google alone cannot cover all bases.
Sure, there's the honor system approach that most modern recording devices already use. Things like requiring an 18+ Google account to activate an intelligent eyewear device and asking users to agree to not recording others without permission or in sensitive places are in place here as well.
But the responsibility of prevention of misuse doesn't just fall to the user or Google. There needs to be greater collaboration across the industry for these measures to be effective. Payne said that Google is sharing these statements now in an attempt to set an example and send a message. "We hope that it resonates with people, and we hope that as a byproduct of that, some others in this space say, 'You know what? We should probably tighten up some of our policies.'"
Payne believes that there is time to regain the public's trust. He said that while there is momentum building in the smart glasses space, it is still early days for the category. It allows the company a chance to "reset this conversation a bit, raise the bar on privacy."
If it's able to get the attention and cooperation of other players in the space, Google stands to benefit. "We think that that will then earn a lot of trust back in the category, then we can focus a lot on how cool and valuable these are."

Pentagon backs war memorial guard who reprimanded Hegseth's group
- Published
The Pentagon has given its backing to a US Army guard who reprimanded a group that included US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Arlington National Cemetery.
A video of the Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
The footage showed the army sentinel on duty stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored - and will always honor - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
On Thursday, he presented an award to the soldier who reprimanded his group.
Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026," the Pentagon said in a statement.
In a post on X showing the soldier, Hesgeth said: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."
The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.
Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.
During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.

Rory McIlroy made a strong start to his bid for a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title with a three-under-par opening round at the DP World Tour Championship.
The world number two, whose round included five birdies and two bogeys in windy conditions, is two shots behind early leader Joost Luiten.
Spain's Eugenio Chacarra, who leads McIlroy by 533.93 points in the Race to Dubai standings - with 2,000 available to this week's winner - opened with a level-par 72, while third-placed American Patrick Reed struggled during a 75.
"I think it was a pretty fair score," said six-time major winner McIlroy.
"I could probably stand here and argue that I could have been better, but I could probably stand here and argue that I could have been worse as well.
"I hit the ball well for the most part. It's tricky, the wind makes it tricky. The course set-up is a little more difficult than in previous years.
"The greens are not like Yas Links (in Abu Dhabi) last week. They're not absolutely perfect, so you've got to have your patience a little bit on them too. Overall, happy with the score."
Nine players - Chacarra, McIlroy, Reed, Casey Jarvis, Aaron Rai, Jon Rahm, Ryan Fox, Jayden Schaper and Daniel Hillier - can still clinch the Race to Dubai, but only Chacarra and McIlroy can guarantee the season-long accolade with victory at Jumeirah Golf Estates this week.
Northern Ireland's McIlroy, who is aiming to match Scotland's Colin Montgomerie's record of eight season-long crowns, birdied two of his opening four holes before giving a shot back at the fifth.
He birdied the seventh and 11th, and while he took six at the par-five 14th, he finished with a two-putt birdie four to end joint third.
"You can't win it on the first day, but you can certainly lose it," added McIlroy.
"I played nicely, so there was never any threat of me shooting a bad one.
"But it was possible today to go out there and shoot a couple over and feel like you were sort of out of the tournament.
"To get off to a solid start was very important."
Chacarra, who has won three times already this season, finished his front nine with three straight birdies to turn in two-under 34 but dropped shots at 13 and 15 to lie five back of Luiten.
Rahm, who catapulted himself into contention last week in Abu Dhabi, by winning his first tournament since leaving LIV Golf, mixed four birdies and three bogeys in an opening 71 to sit alongside New Zealand's Hillier.
Jarvis (+2), Schaper (+2), Fox (+2), Rai (+4) all have work to do, while England's Tommy Fleetwood also struggled in an opening 76.
Dutchman Luiten, the lowest-ranked player in the field, turned in five under but cancelled two birdies with two bogeys on the back nine to settle for a 67, one clear of Denmark's Jacob Skov Olesen.

(Bloomberg) -- New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said city officials would commence sweeps of 100 construction sites after eight people died in the collapse of a three-story Brooklyn apartment building. 
The building collapsed shortly after 4 p.m. Wednesday, trapping people inside the rubble, with emergency crews working through the night to rescue survivors.
As of Thursday afternoon, the collapse had killed eight people and injured 18, according to the mayor. Two of the dead were children and four of the injured were firefighters. One of those injured was in critical condition, and most of those hospitalized were stable.
The city issued a stop work order for the adjoining lot, an excavation site where a new building and cellar had been proposed, according to city building records, which cited unsafe construction operations.
Mamdani in a press briefing on Thursday said the city had identified five entities associated with the neighboring construction site, which were associated with 100 other sites across the city. The mayor said the city Department of Buildings would commence sweeps of those locations the same day.
“A tragedy of this magnitude demands a comprehensive and thorough investigation that includes both the construction site and the building which collapsed,” Mamdani said. The mayor said the probe “will extend to any and all sites that those who operated these sites are currently operating.”
Construction workers were digging on the neighboring lot when the building collapsed, Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said. Officials don’t yet know how many people were inside the building or how many remain unaccounted for. 
In March, the city ordered demolition at the site to stop, because “overhead protection was not installed or provided for adjacent properties.” The violation was later resolved and it’s unclear whether it played any role in the collapse.
“These were our friends and our neighbors, parents and children,” Mamdani said. “Let us continue to hold close those who have been plunged into unimaginable grief.”

In a fresh legal challenge ahead of Cult.fit's proposed public listing, the Madras High Court (HC) has issued a notice on a petition seeking cancellation of the CULT trademark registration held by one of the company's subsidiaries. The rectification petition was filed by Deepak Poduval, who cofounded the CULT fitness business in Bengaluru in 2015. He has approached the court seeking cancellation of the trademark registration held by Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd, a subsidiary of Cult.fit, alleging that the documents used to establish ownership of the brand were forged. The court issued notice in the matter (OP(TM) No. 51 of 2026) on October 12, 2026. During a hearing on November 5, it adjourned the proceedings to December 2, allowing Cultfit Healthcare to file its response. Separately, Poduval has approached the Commercial Court in Bengaluru, seeking to have the 2017 deeds that purportedly transferred the CULT brand declared void. He has alleged that the signatures on these documents were forged. The matter is scheduled for its next hearing on November 16. How The CULT Trademark Dispute Began The dispute over the CULT trademark dates back to 2015, when Poduval first applied for the 'CULT – The Workout Station' trademark in August that year. Cultfit Healthcare filed a separate trademark application in November 2016, claiming usage of the brand from May 1, 2015 — the same first-use date mentioned in Poduval's application. When the Trademark Registry raised objections citing Poduval's earlier application, Cultfit Healthcare did not produce the alleged assignment deeds. Instead, it claimed to be the prior user and owner of the trademark in its own right. Poduval has since challenged the validity of the 2017 assignment deeds that purportedly transferred the brand to Cultfit Healthcare. He alleges that his signatures on the documents were forged and has cited a privately commissioned forensic examination that, according to him, supports his allegations. Cult.fit, however, has denied the allegations, maintaining that Poduval signed the assignment deeds. In a statement, Poduval said the dispute concerns the ownership of a brand that has become central to a company preparing to go public. He added that investors deserve transparency about how Cult.fit acquired the trademark. Trademark Dispute Part Of Larger Cofounder Row The trademark challenge is part of a broader legal battle between CULT's cofounders, Deepak Poduval and Rishabh Telang, over the transfer of the fitness business's assets and intellectual property to the Mukesh Bansal-led startup. In August 2026, Poduval filed an FIR against Telang at Bengaluru's Bellandur Police Station, alleging forgery, cheating and criminal conspiracy in connection with the 2016 transfer of certain assets and intellectual property from Cult Fitness Pvt Ltd to Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd. Poduval alleged that Telang forged his signatures on multiple documents used to wind up Cult Fitness, including board resolutions, shareholder consent documents and statutory filings. He also claimed that 50% of his shareholding in the company was extinguished without any consideration. Telang denied the allegations, maintaining that Poduval was involved in the transactions and the subsequent winding up of Cult Fitness. He further claimed that Poduval had received consideration for the transfer. Cult.fit also maintained that the transaction was carried out under appropriate contractual arrangements and that the consideration was duly paid and acknowledged by Poduval. The company added that neither it nor its subsidiary was an accused in the FIR. Following the FIR, Telang moved the Karnataka High Court seeking to quash the case. The court sought responses from Poduval and the state but did not stay the investigation. The latest petition before the Madras HC takes the dispute beyond the alleged transfer of assets, directly challenging the legal ownership of the CULT trademark held by Cultfit Healthcare. What The Dispute Means For Cult.fit's IPO The trademark challenge also raises questions about how Cult.fit has disclosed the ownership of the CULT brand in its draft IPO prospectus. In a written response dated October 14 to a complaint filed by Poduval with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), Cult.fit acknowledged that its draft prospectus did not correctly describe the ownership of the CULT trademarks. The company clarified that the trademarks are registered in the name of Cultfit Healthcare Pvt Ltd and not Cult.fit Ltd. It also undertook to correct the disclosure in its final prospectus. With the subsidiary's trademark registration now under challenge before the Madras HC, the dispute could become a point of scrutiny for prospective investors. Poduval has also questioned the company's treatment of the CULT acquisition in its IPO disclosures. According to his complaint, Cult.fit has described the acquisition as 'not material'. While the draft prospectus does not name the acquisition, the company has made the deeds relating to Fitness First, another brand acquired by the group, available for investor inspection. However, the corresponding deeds for CULT have not been made available, Poduval alleged. The challenge is significant given the extent to which Cult.fit uses the CULT brand across its operations. According to its draft IPO prospectus, hundreds of fitness centres operate under the brand. It also extends to Cult Neo gyms and the company's Cultgear products business. If the trademark challenge succeeds, it could potentially affect the group's rights to use, license or transfer the brand, raising questions about the implications for its operations and brand ownership. Cult.fit has filed its draft IPO papers for a proposed public issue. The company plans to raise up to ₹950 Cr through a fresh issue of shares, while existing investors are looking to offload up to 17.86 Cr shares through an offer for sale (OFS). The total IPO size is expected to be around ₹4,000 Cr.

Pilot killed in Remembrance Day crash had lifelong passion for flying, friends say
Friends say Daniel Parent, 68, was an experienced pilot
Friends of Daniel Parent — the 68-year-old man killed in a plane crash during a Remembrance Day event in Saint-Georges-de-Beauce, Que., — are remembering him for being an excellent and experienced pilot.
“He was driven by an all-consuming passion for aviation,” Robert Bergeron, a fellow pilot and friend of Parent, told Radio-Canada.
“Daniel had been passionate about aviation for more than 40 years.”
He recalled a story from Parent's earlier days, when he landed a small two-seater Cessna 150 in his parents’ farm field near Saint-Honoré, Que.
“It caused quite a sensation,” Bergeron said.
It’s normal for young pilots to be a bit more daring and adventurous, Bergeron said, but Parent had grown into a mature man with nothing left to prove.
Robert Bergeron was presiding over Wednesday’s Remembrance Day ceremony in Saint-George on Wednesday for a local branch of the Royal Canadian Legion. (Radio-Canada)
Parent’s plane of choice eventually became the Mooney M20C, a high-performance aircraft designed for cross-country flying. According to the Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB), Parent had been flying a single-engine Mooney on Wednesday when he crashed.
Bergeron shared his admiration of Parent, who he said flew his Mooney plane across the continent, "as far away as Alaska, California and the Grand Canyon."
“He was an inspiration to me,” said Bergeron.
He said it was only after Parent had completed several of those journeys that he found the courage to follow in his footsteps.
“I always described him — and I told him this on several occasions — as my mentor.”
The Remembrance Day ceremony in Saint-Georges was one Parent had been part of for many years, according to Bergeron.
He was performing what's called a "Missing Man" formation, where one aircraft separates from the formation and gradually climbs into the sky to symbolize the departure of someone in the Armed Forces who has died in combat.
“The formation took off, and the formation came back without him," said Bergeron of what happened Wednesday. "It's an absolutely terrible tragedy.”
“It was an immense sadness for me to see him leave us this way."
'You only find out afterward,' recalls pilot
On Thursday, the TSB provided an update about what happened.
"During a formation flight of six aircraft performing for Remembrance Day commemorations, one of the aircraft, a single-engine Mooney, broke away from the formation as planned as part of their show and briefing," said TSB spokesperson Nic Defalco in a statement.
"When attempting to rejoin the formation, the aircraft passed beneath the other aircraft and continued on that trajectory, ultimately crashing into a wooded area."
The TSB continues to investigate the crash.
The pilots taking part in the ceremony were all part of the Club Aéronautique de Beauce, a local flight club. Hugues Drouin was among them.
He explains that due to the technical nature of the "Missing Man" formation, the pilots are highly concentrated on the aircraft that’s guiding them during the manoeuvre.
Hugues Drouin was a friend of Daniel Parent. (Radio-Canada)
So he didn’t immediately realize Parent’s plane had gone down.
“What happened,” he said, “was that everything was going well during the flight. And at one point the leader said, ‘Missing Man Go, Missing Man Go,’” in reference to the procedure.
“Then we heard Daniel say, ‘OK.’ And he left the formation.”
Drouin says Parent was supposed to return. But when the leader asked for confirmation of his position, there was no response.
“So we really couldn't know what had happened. Because it's not like driving a car, where you can look to the left or right. You only find out afterward.”
Drouin said he realized after the accident, while he was still in the air, that Parent's plane was no longer there.
It was after landing, and when getting out of his plane, that Drouin began to have a strong physical response. He said his legs wouldn’t hold him up.
“I imagine it's probably the same for someone who's been in a car accident or something like that,” he said. “In the moment, you don't really realize what's happening, and afterward you have significant physical and mental reactions.”
As Drouin continues to process the loss of his friend, he remembers Parent as being an excellent pilot.
“He was someone you could rely on,” said Drouin. “He was a very, very good person.”
