Nvidia announced this morning that Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO following reports of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with a direct report. The situation surrounding Huang has unfolded quickly, with The New York Times only reporting on Friday that Huang and the suspected spy were “close” before other dominoes started to fall, leading to a swift fall from grace for one of the biggest names in technology. (Hours after Huang’s resignation was announced, Reuters reported that he also had an “intimate relationship” with another Nvidia employee.)
‘It’s a mistake’: reactions from tech leaders on Jensen Huang’s resignation
Many prominent voices in technology and the president of the US have publicly supported the former Nvidia CEO despite his ouster.
Prominent voices in technology have come out in support of Huang, with some calling the resignation a “waste” and a sad day for “all humanity.” The narrative among those leaders on X, at least, is that Huang’s resignation was rushed — perhaps an overreaction to salacious news stories about his personal life. Some others have had a more neutral reaction, commenting more on Huang’s achievements at the company’s helm. You can see a collection of those responses below.
President Donald Trump
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”, Trump said on Truth Social.
Elon Musk, SpaceX and Tesla CEO
Elon Musk said in a reply to an X user that it would “be an honor” to hire Huang. He also replied to a post that said “You’d think we’d have learned from Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick that one does not just simply replace the founder…” by saying “True words.”
Tim Sweeney, Epic Games CEO
Sweeney said that today is “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction.”
Ahead of Huang’s resignation, Sweeney posted about how Huang “saved” a GDC 2015 presentation by dropping off a graphics card and said that “The dude truly is the visionary driver of the future of tech from the gaming GPU era to CUDA to AI supercomputers.”
Palmer Luckey, Anduril founder
“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said last night, before Huang’s resignation was announced.
Matt Mullenweg, Automattic co-founder and CEO
Mullenweg reposted an X post that followed his brief September ouster as CEO: “Founder advice: If you don’t have a coup attempt every few years, you’re not hiring strong enough leaders.” He said, “Just putting this back out there, for no reason whatsoever.”
David Heinemeier Hansson, 37signals CTO and creator of the Omarchy Linux distribution
“What a waste,” Hansson said this morning, replying to his own post from hours before: “NVIDIA would be wrong to fire Jensen. His marital indiscretions are between him, his wife, and a reprimand from the board. Have some proportionality.”
Clément Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face (which Nvidia recently acquired for almost $13 billion)
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened,” Delangue said. “It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!
Changpeng Zhao, former Binance CEO
“It’s a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign,” Zhao said.
Peter Steinberger, OpenClaw creator and OpenAI employee
“If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” Steinberger said. “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.” (“I agree,” replied Sweeney.)
Aravind Srinivas, Perplexity co-founder and CEO
Srinivas thanked Huang for “33 years of bold leadership” in a post this morning. “You built a small startup into America’s most valuable company, with relentless improvement. Your grit and perseverance should always be remembered. Your personal generosity with time and advice to founders like me has secured a bright future for America and AI.”
Jason Calacanis, All-In Podcast host
Calacanis reposted Trump’s post, tagging Tim Cook and telling him to “Keep the seat warm” for Huang while “the investigation is sorted out” and saying that “America needs you Mr. Cook.” Last night, he also said that Nvidia shareholders should “decide Jensen’s fate after the investigation is complete — not the press or online mobs.”
Lex Fridman, Lex Fridman Podcast host
In a post talking about how he has seen Huang show “kindness, humility, care to everyone around him,” Fridman said that “I’m in shock frankly at all of this, including the mass hysteria around it. I love America, and I think NVIDIA letting Jensen go is terrible for America. I stand with Jensen.”

The world is full of unanswered questions and strange ideas. Do parallel universes exist? What would it look like if a pandemic wiped out life as we know it? Is time travel possible?
How science informs author Emily St. John Mandel’s fiction
The author of Station Eleven talks science, fiction, and doppelgängers.
I host the science podcast Unexplainable, where we often speak to scientists about their attempts to puzzle through life’s greatest mysteries, but academic researchers aren’t the only people wrestling with these concepts.
On the latest episode of the show, I spoke with Emily St. John Mandel, the award-winning author of Station Eleven, about her new book, Exit Party, which grapples with the question of the multiverse. We talked about how she approaches science in her fiction, and how, even if we never get clear answers to some of these strange ideas, they can still help us think deeply about ourselves and our world.
Below is an excerpt from our conversation, edited for clarity and length. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts and Spotify, or watch us on Netflix.
Emily, you are often writing about really interesting scientific ideas. Why do you put these scientific concepts at the heart of the books that you write?
Because they’re so interesting. I don’t have an educational background in science. I didn’t study it in school. I did work in a cancer research lab for years, so I’ve definitely hung out with scientists. I was great with grant budgets. But I could not actually tell you the mechanisms by which microRNA 335 impacts breast cancer metastasis,
Neither can I.
But you know what? Science is interesting to me. I like reading about ideas in the fringes of science. But my understanding is that physicists are more or less evenly split on the question of whether we’re living in a multiverse.
Where do you start with exploring these concepts?
It’s really book by book. Sea of Tranquility was the first book I wrote that had more of a hard sci-fi component, because I do have a time-traveling detective in that book.
And what that came out of was it was the spring of 2020. The pandemic hit. I was promoting The Glass Hotel on Zoom, and I thought that for my own sanity, it might be nice to be immersed in the grand project of a book. That can be good for you sometimes when everything is chaos, like in the early days of a pandemic.
I’ve always loved time travel novels as a reader and a fan. The problem with the time travel narrative, though, is that it falls apart instantly.
What do you mean?
If you think about it for a second, it’s like, if I walk out of this podcast studio and I’m transported back to 1812, was I not always going to walk out of the studio and be transported back to 1812? And doesn’t reality break upon my arrival? That raises other questions like immortality — am I always going round and round in time? The causation gets really complicated and weird.
But I felt like, you know what? I’m going to write whatever I want. So I start writing about my time-traveling detective, and then I run into the time travel narrative problem, the loops and the paradoxes and all the rest of it.
And my solve for that, I thought, “What if I added a whole other layer of science fictional weirdness to try to make that work?” Enter the simulation hypothesis, which is the hypothesis that all of our reality is a simulation. And something I love about that is you can find really smart people convincingly arguing either side.
I thought it was a cool idea, and I realized that I could use that to make time travel work. And so that’s what got me into that little branch of science for Sea of Tranquility.
And then Exit Party, I had an idea about writing about doppelgängers. I’d been thinking about it for years — the idea of a counter life.
Counter life?
The life you did not live, where you moved to a different city or took a different job or married a different person — any of those inflection points. I wondered if doppelgängers could be thought of as a sort of embodiment of a counter life. It’s another you who has lived a different life in a different version of reality. That’s what got me to the multiverse idea. But then I was also thinking, “Okay, well, I’ve thought about the counter life of the individual. What is the counter life of the state?”
And that can be a really interesting thought experiment. There are some very obvious inflection points in our recent history, but every country has them. You know, the election that went a different way or the decision made to go to war or not. A policy that was enacted or not enacted and the fallout from that, and any of those inflection points create a somewhat different country. It was thinking about counter lives and doubling, and that’s what got me to this idea of the multiverse.
You’re talking about these ideas almost like, “It’s a fix to this problem that I created.”
It often is. Exit Party opens with a woman going to a party, two doppelgängers show up, and somebody else disappears. I realized pretty early on, wait a minute, at some point I am going to have to account for where the doppelgängers came from, so in that case, it was definitely a fix. But it was also thinking about the double life of a state — the state that you could live in if things had gone a different direction at some inflection point.
Something that interested me as a thought experiment in writing this book is: How might the tropes of science fiction map onto actual lives? Doppelgängers are very science fictional. But we all have counter lives, so imagine those as the embodiment of the counter life. Or later in the novel, there’s a conversation about time travel. And the character says something to the effect of, “I think if you live long enough, you become a time traveler. It’s like you’re a migrant from another timeline.”
“I want to focus on how people respond in these interesting scenarios I’m putting them in.”
There’s nothing more science fictional than a time traveler. That is the definition of a trope, basically. But that is how adulthood works, or how time works. You learn to navigate the world as an adult, and then you look up one day and realize that world is long gone.
If you’re lucky enough to get to live for a while, if you live into your 80s or potentially even older, that world that you learned is really gone.
You get to a certain point in your life, you look back, and you realize you’re not really looking back at a life singular. It’s really one life after another, isn’t it?
I wanted to express that. You were a different person 10 years ago and living a different life, and I wanted to follow a character, Ari in this case, from one life into another.
I don’t think it’s a spoiler to say, you drop us into a fairly dystopian world.
I mean, I collapse the United States in the first sentence…
I was almost expecting that we were going to enter into another world where we made different choices and everything worked out so wonderfully.
I mean, my wife wishes I would write a utopia.
No, it’s true. I do then present an equally dark vision. I think the key, though, and where I find hope personally in my life, but also in this book, is in transience — this idea that nothing lasts forever and everything ends.
There’s such obvious grief and loss attached to that idea, but I think there’s also a lot of hope. Because if I look at it through the lens of my personal life, the worst moments of my life did not last forever. You move through them, and there’s something else after that. Or if you look at it at a larger scale, the worst moments in your country’s life don’t last forever either.
In the second universe of the book, the authoritarian state, I was thinking in terms of modern-day surveillance states, but I was also thinking about East Germany and the Stasi system of citizen informants.
And you know, here’s where transience and hope intersect. A lot of what I know about them I learned in the DDR Museum in Berlin, because the Stasi are gone. We make museums about them. They’re both fairly dark visions, but in both sides of the book, we are moving through them toward something else.
You won’t always be in a terrible situation. You also won’t always be in a good situation. That’s where the loss comes in.
How did you go about trying to think through what the fractal parallel universes would look like?
I was thinking about that with the character Ari. She’s got this character defect. She’s pulled toward criminality. It’s this deep, fundamental proclivity that she has, and there’s a world where somebody like that just goes toward criminality and becomes a criminal, as she did in a previous part of her life.
But what if that same person were growing up in a much more repressive state where the consequences were much worse for breaking the rules? Maybe that interest in criminality pulls a person toward law enforcement, and it was interesting to think of that as almost two sides of the same coin.
When you’re borrowing these scientific concepts, do you feel trapped by the science of it all? Do you feel like you have to stay within certain boundaries?
I don’t, which may annoy some readers of sci-fi, but I think there’s a really interesting choice that you have to make if you’re writing speculative fiction, and that’s how accurate do you want to be, or how deep into the weeds do you want to go with your science fictional technology?
On one end of the spectrum, you’ve got an author like Cixin Liu, who wrote The Three-Body Problem. I really love his work. He gets so granular about those technologies. When I first started working on Sea of Tranquility, I thought, “I want to figure out how the time machine works.” I guess it was a bit of insecurity on my part. So I spent some time reading about current ideas and technologies that I imagine eventually evolving into time traveling. I was reading about the quantum blockchain, and then after I’d spent a bit of time in that rabbit hole, I realized I don’t actually care.
I had this realization: If I’m not describing how a car engine works in the 2020 section, why do I care about the mechanics of the time machine? It’s literally just transport.
And that was kind of liberating, realizing that I care more about the characters. I want to focus on how people respond in these interesting scenarios I’m putting them in. So honestly, the level of scientific detail I’m aiming for is “plausible within the context of a literary novel,” which is a low bar.
For this parallel universe stuff, did you look into some of the physics debates about this?
A little bit. Like the simulation hypothesis, you can find smart people on either side. I feel very unqualified to participate in the debates.
But as a novelist, I’m like, This is interesting. I can work with this.

Keralam’s Opposition Leader Pinarayi Vijayan has alleged a conspiracy by former Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar and Vice-Chancellor (V-C) of Sree Sankaracharya University of Sanskrit (SSUS) Ciza Thomas in connection with the controversy over the complaint that activists of the Students Federation of India (SFI) had carried out a mock funeral of the V-C.
Addressing the relay fast staged by the suspended SFI activists at the SSUS main campus in Kalady near here on Friday, Mr. Vijayan alleged that the V-C had not raised any compliant of a mock funeral initially. However, such a false complaint was lodged after a few days. Mr. Arlekar, “who has always implemented the wishes of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh”, played a key role in coming up with “a lie” that the protesting students held her mock funeral, he said.
Criticises CM, Minister
He also accused Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan and Higher Education Minister Roji M. John of not trying to address the indefinite fast organised by the suspended students. Though they often claim about their involvement in campus politics, they have taken a stance against the students, he alleged.
The SFI staged an ‘Occupy Sanskrit University’ protest on Friday as its State leadership reiterated the demand that the suspension of its 16 activists must be revoked unconditionally. P. S. Sanjeev, SFI State Secretary, said the students would not tender any apology as directed by the varsity Syndicate.
3 shifted to hospital
The police on Friday shifted three SFI activists, including the federation’s unit president Archana P. S, who had been on a relay fast over the last 12 days, to hospital citing their deterioriating health. They were shifted to the hospital on the advice of doctors who had examined their health condition. The SFI leadership said the relay fast would continue until its demands were met.
On Wednesday, the mothers of the protesting students and members of the All India Democratic Women’s Association expressed solidarity for the relay fast at a meeting held at the protest site. They urged the university authorities to withdraw the disciplinary action against the students without further delay and permit them to write their semester exams.

Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
- Published
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".
Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.
Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.
Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.
But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
Huang's position vulnerable unlike other tech bosses
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.
Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.
Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.

Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

How Pochettino came on Man Utd's radar - and what Carrick was told when
- Published
Michael Carrick must have known what was coming.
Not just because reports of his imminent dismissal were widespread - followed by information about who would be replacing him as Manchester United boss.
But because, effectively, he and his representatives were given heavy enough indications of what was to follow.
On Monday, according to well-placed sources, Carrick's agent was contacted by chief executive Omar Berrada to be told he and director of football Jason Wilcox would be heading to Monaco for a planned meeting with co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe that would include a discussion about the head coach's future.
A day later, it is believed Wilcox had a similar conversation with Carrick.
It is understood that on both occasions it was communicated that a recommendation regarding Carrick's future at the club would be made.
What is not clear is whether Carrick and his representatives knew that recommendation was to relieve him of his duties.
By that point, BBC Sport has been told United were aware of a $10m (£7m) release clause in Mauricio Pochettino's contract with the United States national team. One source even indicated it was representatives of the Argentine who told the Premier League side.
There is some regret behind the scenes at United that machinations leading to Carrick's departure on Thursday were played out so publicly.
But with football clubs the size of United, keeping such developments completely private is extremely difficult - and there is a feeling they were as transparent with Carrick as they could be.
Following heavy defeats by Como and Bournemouth, United placed huge importance on the following three games - against Chelsea, Roma and Aston Villa.
It is understood United's leadership team were clear with Carrick that results and performances needed to improve. A defeat, a victory and draw weren't enough to save him.
There is a feeling that during that three-game period, there was not enough progress, particularly in terms of team structure - underlined by the fact they conceded eight goals.
Carrick has conducted himself with great dignity during the turmoil of the past few days and he leaves the club - certainly in the eyes of supporters - with his standing as a United great intact.
When United first appointed Carrick - initially on an interim basis following the sacking of Ruben Amorim in January - he had a positive impact on the squad, and subsequently results.
United liked his positive messaging to the players and media. They felt Carrick brought calm to rocky waters and protected his players at every opportunity - a contrast from at least the closing stages of Amorim's tenure.
On the pitch, the United hierarchy felt Carrick's style of play allowed the forward players more freedom, and they won 12 of their last 17 matches of the season.
While United considered other managerial options in the summer, there was ultimately a sense Carrick had earned a shot at the job on a permanent basis.
The 45-year-old signed a two-year deal, though it is understood United contractually protected themselves in the event of an early termination.
Part of the thought process was to provide the players with some managerial stability given the increased turnover of head coaches in recent years.
Yet the season started poorly with defeat at newly promoted Hull City - and has only spiralled downward since.
United are second bottom of the Premier League having won just twice all season and are 17th in the Champions League table.
Since Monday, talks have been ongoing with Pochettino.
On Wednesday, Berrada contacted the US Soccer Federation to confirm the existence of the release clause and their intention to activate it.
It is understood the news did not come as a surprise to those across the Atlantic.
Pochettino had been clear with his employers about the discussions with United and - most pertinently - his intention to return to the Premier League.
While United want Pochettino in situ as soon as possible, they are respectful of the fact the USA have two fixtures against Haiti to play - the second of which is on 18 November.
If Pochettino takes charge of the second game, it is understood he will be in place at United's Carrington headquarters on 19 November - four days before they face Liverpool.

A.I. Weapons Need Data for Their Training. Ukraine Has a Lot to Offer.
The Ukrainian government has opened up a trove of five million battlefield videos to defense companies at home and abroad.
The forest, seen from a drone, appeared as a vast, monotonous landscape of black tree trunks, shadows and patches of snow.
To the human eye, it appeared deserted. But to an artificial intelligence system looking for people, it did not. The system put a red box around a tiny human form, probably a soldier lurking in the trees.
Behind this feat lay vast volumes of data. Just as ChatGPT and other A.I. chatbots must be exposed to how humans write, military A.I. systems must be exposed to how humans fight. In Ukraine, this happens through a huge trove of battlefield videos, audio and text data collected over nearly five years.
The war database is being used by about 30 Ukrainian defense companies to develop A.I. weapons. Ukraine is now opening this repository, which it calls Avenger Labs, to firms in allied countries, hoping to deepen security partnerships.
Ukraine is providing the data at no charge, but companies must give the Ukrainian military licenses to any software they develop. Under the first agreement to be reached, 12 British defense companies will gain access. Ukraine is in talks with other countries.
While there is no shortage of Western companies developing autonomous weapons, there is a shortage of the data needed to train them. Ukraine can offer more of it than any other potential partner.

An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.
Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.
The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.
Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.
The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”
The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.
At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.
Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.
Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

The Jensen Huang scandal continues to snowball.
The Nvidia founder had an "intimate relationship" with an unnamed second Nvidia employee, Reuters reported on Thursday. Nvidia declined to comment.
The latest revelation deepens an extramarital affair scandal that has rocked the chipmaking company for the past two weeks — and ultimately led to Huang resigning as CEO on Thursday.
The report of a second employee relationship raises more questions about how much Nvidia knew about Huang's behavior and how it's navigated the situation.
In late October, The New York Times first reported that Huang had a "close relationship" with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed. The Times reported that the US government believed she was a spy for the Chinese government. China has said the allegations that she is a spy are unsubstantiated.
On Sunday, Huang wrote a memo to staff, apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." He did not name anyone.
On Wednesday, The Times reported that Huang also had another affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare and the CEO's direct report.
Huang's resignation a day later capped a 33-year career at the chipmaker that he founded in 1993. The Nvidia founder grew the company from a maker of graphics chips for gamers into the most consequential supplier of AI hardware, becoming one of the world's wealthiest people in the process.

Popular weight loss drugs including Ozempic and Wegovy will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday, November 9, 2026.
The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labelling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn't understood, the FDA said.
FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Eli Lilly's Ozempic.
An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.
Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a health care professional immediately, the agency said.

News of Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security was first met with a muted response in Silicon Valley—including inside Nvidia itself. Huang’s resignation, after news of two other alleged romantic relationships with Nvidia staffers, has left both the company and the broader AI industry stunned.
As revelations about Huang’s initial affair came out earlier this week, rank-and-file Nvidia employees at first pursued business as usual, according to two current and three former employees at the chipmaker, speaking anonymously to protect relationships at the company. They trusted the board to investigate and act accordingly, but few workers thought Huang would actually leave.
Nvidia’s roughly 60,000 employees are loyal to the point that its global turnover rate is reportedly among the lowest in tech. Workers say they have heard it called having “green in your blood” or being “green-pilled” or on “team green,” referring to the company’s signature color. Huang was the company’s soul and the founder who stuck with it through challenges for 33 years. Employees appreciated that he kept layoffs rare and red tape sparing.
“In just three days we went from superhero cape to ‘Oops, I forgot my pants,’ and nobody’s quite sure how to swallow that,” one employee said. One former employee insisted in Huang’s defense that something “more sinister” must have been in play, and that affairs alone shouldn’t have led to his departure.
Huang’s peers in Silicon Valley echoed that sentiment, remaining vocal in their support of the embattled CEO even after his ouster. “One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership and contribution in building NVDA,” venture capitalist Antonio Gracias wrote on X earlier this week, using the company’s ticker symbol.
The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang has also had an extramarital affair with a vice president at Nvidia, and Reuters revealed on Thursday a second “intimate relationship” with an employee. Before those alleged affairs became public, multiple industry executives told WIRED that Huang is “irreplaceable” and that his biggest mistake, aside from his relationship with Alice Huang, was admitting the affair in writing to the whole company.
That appears to still be the prevailing sentiment. “A founder who has spent 30 years building such a unique company so capably has earned the presumption that he should keep leading it,” venture capitalist Sarah Guo wrote on X after Huang resigned, and a few hours before the Reuters report.
Authorities and Nvidia’s board have yet to formally accuse Huang of wrongdoing in his interactions with the businesswoman and suspected intelligence asset Alice Huang, and China has denied that she’s a spy. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that the FBI “is looking into it.” Nvidia’s board has stated that it doesn’t believe Huang compromised any secrets, but it has hired the law firm Wachtell Lipton to investigate.
Add to all that, some corners of Nvidia had already been whispering about the relationship with Alice Huang; one venture capitalist who declined to be named recalled a recent dinner where an Nvidia executive claimed there had been rumors about Jensen’s romantic relationship with a young Asian woman.
On Monday, the venture capitalist had estimated a “less than 10 percent” chance Huang would lose his job at the top of the world’s most valuable company. “The wind’s going to blow over on this,” they said. “People are going to hate him for three months, and forget this ever happened.”
Huang’s resignation left them in shock.
The big anxiety in Silicon Valley remains the possibility that instability at Nvidia will burst an AI bubble, but analysts aren’t so sure.
The chief executive of one AI company, who spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to affect business relationships, says Nvidia’s recent bankrolling of AI startups and even buying companies such as model-hosting provider Hugging Face has helped prop up the need for chips. A “new professional CEO won’t do any of that,” meaning “systemic risk for the AI trade and AI bubble increases substantially,” the entrepreneur says.
Between bubble talk and Huang rumors, Nvidia shares in recent days have sunk to their lowest point in more than a year. Nvidia reports its latest quarterly earnings next week.
Inside Nvidia, meetings, projects, and the company’s aggressive culture are rapidly pressing ahead with what’s left of Huang’s vision.

The Karnataka High Court (HC) has rejected a plea by Razorpay cofounders Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar seeking to quash a serious fraud investigation office (SFIO) complaint. The complaint pertains to alleged lapses in merchant onboarding and monitoring of transactions linked to a digital lending company accused of predatory recovery practices. In an order dated November 4, Justice M Nagaprasanna held that the allegations against the cofounders involved disputed questions of fact that could only be examined during trial. The court said there was no reason to interfere with the proceedings at this stage, given the matter was still at a nascent stage. The SFIO has named Razorpay’s whole-time director Mathur and managing director Kumar as accused in the complaint. The allegations concern deficiencies in merchant onboarding, lapses in know-your-customer (KYC) verification of Mad Elephant Network Technology Pvt Ltd (MENTPL), and inadequate due diligence and monitoring of its transactions. The SFIO is investigating a network of 33 companies allegedly created through dummy directors by Jilian Consultants India Pvt Ltd (JCIPL), a subsidiary of Fininty Pvt Ltd. One of the companies under investigation, Mad Elephant Network Technology Pvt Ltd (MENTPL), allegedly operated an illegal digital lending business through its arrangement with NBFC X10 Financial Services Ltd. MENTPL allegedly employed unethical, predatory and coercive loan recovery practices and generated wrongful gains of ₹56.63 Cr. Where Does Razorpay Fit Into This? The agency alleged that Razorpay acted as a payment intermediary for MENTPL. During the proceedings, the Additional Solicitor General of India, representing the SFIO, told the court that Razorpay had acted as a conduit for approximately ₹320 Cr worth of MENTPL's transactions. Hence, Razorpay cofounders were accused of failing to exercise due care, skill and diligence and independent judgement as directors, attracting provisions under Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013. Against this, Mathur and Kumar argued that the SFIO had exceeded its jurisdiction by prosecuting them when Razorpay was not among the 33 companies named in the Central government's 2022 investigation order. They also contended that payment aggregators did not have a statutory obligation to undertake full KYC verification, which they argued was the responsibility of banks. Mathur had told investigators in a statement recorded on August 16, 2023, that RBI guidelines were still evolving and the onus of conducting full KYC did not rest with the executives. The cofounders further argued that mere negligence in merchant onboarding could not constitute a criminal offence. They also challenged the proceedings on grounds of limitation, absence of mens rea and lack of any direct nexus with MENTPL. They contended that there was no basis for imposing criminal liability on Razorpay's directors when the company itself had not been made an accused. Rejecting the argument, the court referred to Section 212(14) of the Companies Act, which allows prosecution of not only the company under investigation and its officers but also any other person directly or indirectly connected with its affairs. It observed that whether the executives had discharged their fiduciary duties and exercised adequate due diligence, particularly in transactions involving approximately ₹320 Cr, were questions that required examination during trial. The court also said Razorpay's role could emerge as the proceedings progress, despite the company not currently being named as an accused in the complaint. The court also reiterated that it could not conduct a mini-trial while exercising its powers to quash criminal proceedings. Consequently, the High Court dismissed the writ petition, allowing the proceedings against Mathur and Kumar to continue. The court proceedings come as the fintech major prepares to go public. Razorpay has received the final nod from SEBI for its proposed ₹5,000-6,000 Cr IPO, which is expected to value the company at around $5 Bn. The company pre-filed for an IPO earlier this year and is said to be eyeing a listing between January and March 2027, with the IPO expected to comprise a fresh issue and an offer-for-sale (OFS). More details on the company’s float would become more apparent when the company files its updated draft red herring prospectus.

They Left Iran, but Now the Regime Is Seizing Their Assets to Silence Them
The Iranian authorities are pursuing diaspora dissidents and journalists, extending the government’s repressive apparatus far beyond its borders.
The retired couple in Iran first realized that something was wrong when their bank cards stopped working in early May. After inquiring with the authorities, they discovered that their assets had been frozen by order of the country’s intelligence ministry.
The couple learned, eventually, that they were being punished for the actions of their daughter Noushin Najafiragheb, who lived in Europe — specifically, for her social media posts opposing the Iranian government, according to another daughter, Mehrnoush Najafiragheb.
Across Iran, the government has used asset seizures as punishment for actions taken abroad. Homes and businesses have been seized, life savings raided, family heirlooms taken. When those targeted had little inside Iran themselves, the authorities went after their family members back home, interviews show.
As the Najafiragheb family pressed their case with the authorities, Mehrnoush said, they encountered dozens of other people facing the specter of losing their life’s savings as punishment for the actions of their relatives abroad.
“We realized we weren’t alone,” Ms. Najafiragheb recalled her mother telling her. She said her sister Noushin had declined to be interviewed to avoid further government pressure on her family.

Editor’s note, November 12, 3:35 pm ET: This story was originally posted on November 9 and is being republished today in light of Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO.
Why the Nvidia CEO’s resignation is so important
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Now his love life is a national security issue.
The movie version of Jensen Huang’s jaw-dropping affair basically writes itself.
Cast BD Wong as 63-year-old Huang, the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies and a close friend of President Donald Trump. Kelly Hu can play Alice Huang, Jensen’s paramour and — even better — a purported agent of the Chinese government.
The role of Trump himself, who reportedly knew about Huang’s undercover girlfriend but on Sunday said Huang “probably has an excuse for it,” can be played by Alec Baldwin. (Or a flightless duck — your pick.) However you cast it, this whole sordid affair has “serialized Netflix drama” written all over it.
But in all seriousness…the possibility that one of the world’s most powerful men was targeted by Chinese intelligence is a big deal on multiple scores. Nvidia has opened its own investigation into whether Huang was compromised, and congressional leaders have requested he brief them in a closed-door session.
Nvidia supplies much of the computing power behind the AI boom, giving it enormous influence over the broader economy. “If they sneeze, everybody else catches a cold,” the writer and economic commentator Kyla Scanlon told Vox’s Today, Explained podcast last year. That makes this whole episode a little more weighty than your standard billionaire’s affair.
Go a little deeper
Nvidia is the most valuable company on Earth — but in many households, it’s still not a household name.
Huang and two other electrical engineers founded the now-$4.5-trillion company in 1993 with the fairly niche and nerdy goal of making high-powered chips that could render the 3D graphics for a new generation of video games.
Then, in 2006, the company released software tools that let programmers use its chips for other demanding computing tasks, like mining cryptocurrency and training AI models. When companies like OpenAI began developing tools like ChatGPT, they immediately turned to Nvidia.
That made the company a cornerstone of America’s AI buildout and a major economic force. In 2024, Nvidia alone accounted for more than a fifth of the S&P 500’s total return. And the rush to build out AI infrastructure has accounted for much of America’s recent economic growth, according to St. Louis Fed researchers.
Nvidia’s influence extends to the White House, too, where Huang is a regular guest of Trump. The two became fast friends after having dinner together at Mar-a-Lago last year, and Huang has said Trump regularly calls him late at night to discuss topics like “protecting national security” and “creating more jobs.”
But Huang’s ambitions have run up against one major obstacle: US restrictions on selling Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China. US officials worry that their enormous computing power could help Beijing develop weapons, strengthen its military, expand surveillance, and otherwise rival US military and technological dominance.
That helps explain why China (allegedly) sicced a spy on Huang: They really want these chips. The New York Times reports that China’s top intelligence agency recruited Alice Huang both to learn more about America’s advanced chip industry and to potentially influence Nvidia’s push to lift export restrictions. Alice Huang, it should be noted, was a data center executive in her own right, and her company has been investigated for purportedly helping to smuggle Nvidia chips into China.
All these investigations will hopefully, eventually, reveal whether their affair compromised anything beyond Huang’s marriage. They may also test how dependent Nvidia is on his leadership.
With Huang out as CEO, uncertainty over the company’s future could unsettle investors and trigger wobbles in the wider market. That’s the problem with concentrating so much power in any one person or company: One person’s (very) personal business can somehow become everybody’s problem.
One link for later
➨ Get a hobby. But not just any hobby: something that’s intentionally imperfect, unproductive or unquantified. There’s a tendency in American culture to try to optimize or commodify our leisure, the writer Jenny Odell explains. But that undermines some of leisure’s biggest benefits — like cultivating a sense of joy, wonder, or learning.

Microsoft 365 services is facing a massive outage impacting users worldwide. The outage which began late November 12, has left millions around the world without access to Outlook email, Teams meeting tools and other staples of modern office life. Banks, several government departments and courts in multiple countries including the US, Japan and others are affected. As the outage escalated, some came up with conspiracy theories about what may have caused the outage. While some called it a cyberattack, others said that the Microsoft 365 outage was caused after an AI agent went rogue. The company has debunked these theories clarifying that there is “no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity”.
Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna shared a post on X (formerly known as Twitter) saying that the company “regrets” today’s outages and is working to address the issue.
Here’s what the Microsoft executive said
Sharing the post, Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft said:
“We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue. We will continue to share more information as soon as we have it, and for now I can confirm that there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity”.
Microsoft says changes applied to fix outage not working 'as expected'
In a post shared on November 13, Microsoft admitted that the initial changes applied to fix the current Microsoft 365 outage is “not taking as expected” and the software giant is “identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied”.
"We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected. Sports retail startup PlayBlue has onboarded cricketer KL Rahul as an investor and brand ambassador days ahead of launching its flagship store in Bengaluru. PlayBlue is set to open a 20,000 sq ft flagship store on 80 Feet Road in Bengaluru and launch its mobile app this Saturday (November 14). The flagship store will be spread across three retail floors, a café level and a rooftop terrace. Its product portfolio will span sports apparel, footwear, equipment, accessories, recovery products and sports nutrition, catering to both amateur and professional athletes. Beyond conventional retail, PlayBlue is positioning itself around specialised product discovery and in-store experiences. The store will offer gait analysis, treadmill-based footwear testing and cricket bat sensors to help customers assess products before making purchases. It will also provide services such as racquet stringing, cricket bat knocking and bicycle servicing. The rooftop space, called The Playground, will have a pickleball court, one-on-one futsal turf and a cricket net equipped with a bowling machine. The company also plans to host community classes, recovery sessions and sports club events at the venue. The startup aims to expand to over 100 stores across 25 Indian cities over the next five years. Founded in 2025 by former GMR Sports’ CEO Satyam Trivedi and former Cult.fit’s executive Jayam Vora, PlayBlue sells an assortment of athleisure, footwear, gear, fitness equipment, recovery products and nutrition through its retail stores and ecommerce platform. "We're building the store we wanted to walk into ourselves. Having KL Rahul on board as both an investor and our ambassador gives us a partner who knows what the right gear means to someone who plays," Vora said. The development comes months after PlayBlue secured $2.7 Mn (₹25.7 Cr) in a seed funding round in July, co-led by Centre Court Capital and MIXI Global, with participation from WEH Ventures. To note, KL Rahul has backed numerous brands in the Indian startup ecosystem, including Boldfit, Flam, XYXX and Metaman. With the Indian sports market projected to more than double to $130 Bn by FY30, investors’ interest remains lukewarm in backing startups in this space. For instance, fitness and sportswear brand Boldfit raised around ₹400 Cr (about $41.8 Mn) from Bharat Value Fund as part of its Series B funding round in October, for its nationwide retail expansion, product innovation, and manufacturing. Earlier in April, sportstech startup SportVot raised ₹32.7 Cr (about $3.8 Mn) in a fresh funding round led by IAN Alpha Fund, to expand its international presence and strengthen its AI-powered production and analytics capabilities.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has shelved the fast-track drug review initiative launched during the Trump administration by former Commissioner Marty Makary, Reuters reports. Launched in June 2025, the Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program aimed to slash drug review timelines to just one to two months for therapies addressing national priorities, such as urgent unmet health needs. But critics pointed to possible preferential treatment for companies meeting demands of President Trump, such as offering drugs at lower prices. No new drugs have gotten a voucher since Makary’s departure, and a key component of the program — an executive council of political appointees that oversaw drug reviews and had a central role in speeding approvals — has gone dormant.
The U.S. Senate health committee has scheduled a pivotal vote for next week on the nomination of Heidi Overton to serve as FDA commissioner, despite lingering doubts from Republicans on the panel, STAT writes. The vote is set for Nov. 18 and, if it passes, her nomination would then go to the full Senate, where Republicans are racing to confirm nominees before Democrats take power in January. But even as he scheduled the vote, committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) remained undecided on Overton, he wrote in a post on X. It would take just one Republican on the committee to sink her nomination, assuming all Democrats vote against her.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

The first batch of Android XR smartglasses made me rethink my stance on specs without displays
I still want models with built-in screens, but Google’s first run of intelligent eyewear has a lot to offer.
The first device powered by Android XR came out last year when Samsung released the Galaxy XR headset. But this fall, Google is taking its augmented reality platform in a different direction with the launch of intelligent eyewear from partners such as Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. This gives Google its own version of lightweight smartglasses to rival competitors like the third-gen Ray-Ban Meta line, and after testing them out, it made me reconsider my feelings about smart specs without built-in displays.
As this first generation of intelligent eyewear is a bit of a departure from previous Android XR devices, I think it's important to get some of the basics out of the way first. For this family of specs, Google is in charge of the OS while Samsung is handling much of the tech — including things like the cameras, mics, touch sensors and more. All of that then gets handed over to Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, who are in charge of the glasses design, lenses, general sales and customer support.
Right off the bat, this seems like a great division of responsibilities because it allows each company to do what they're best at. Google handles the software, Samsung takes care of the hardware and the real glasses makers ensure you have good-looking frames with the right prescriptions (you can even opt for transition/photochromic lenses). And right out of the gate, it feels like there's already a lot of interesting styles and color combos to choose from, regardless if you're a bit more fashion-forward or if you, like me, prefer a more traditional frame.
Another important thing to note is that while Gentle Monster's eyewear will be a touch more expensive than Warby Parker's models ($449 and $395, respectively), they will have the same general tech specs. Those include the same 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage, a 12MP camera (that also handles up to 3K video), stereo speakers, far-field mics and a built-in touch sensor. Battery life is also the same across the board with around nine hours of use on a single charge, while the case for the glasses stores enough juice for multiple full charges.
Furthermore, you won't be required to have a paid Gemini plan to use any of the features of the glasses; it's all free. These glasses will even work with both Android devices and iPhones with feature parity across both OSes. That said, there won't be any options with a built-in display, which means Google won't have a true rival to the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, at least not yet.
When it comes to features, it's no surprise that these glasses have a lot of overlap with the Ray-Ban Meta specs. There's a physical button near the right temple for capturing images: A short press takes a picture while a long press records videos. There's also a touch sensor built into the right arm for doing stuff like controlling volume, pausing audio or dismissing Gemini. And of course, the glasses are connected to your phone wirelessly (either Bluetooth or Wi-Fi depending on the situation) so you have access to streaming music, notifications, messages, supported apps and more. However, the real lynchpin of the entire platform is Google's AI, which can be easily summoned via voice controls or by performing a long press on the touch panel.
Now I'll admit that I don't interact with Gemini all that often when I'm using a phone or a laptop. When I already have access to a screen, a keyboard and all sorts of dedicated apps, so I find I can often perform tasks faster manually than asking an AI assistant to do them. But when wearing smartglasses, it's a whole different story. If you want to respond to a text, get turn-by-turn directions or start some tunes, you can do all that hands-free with simple voice commands while keeping your phone in your pocket. Granted, that is sort of table stakes for smartglasses these days, but being able to walk around with your head up while dodging traffic or other pedestrians can't be understated.
But it goes deeper, because thanks to Gemini's intelligence and persistent memory between conversations, the AI in your glasses has a much deeper understanding of how to help you. Instead of constantly having to say a wake word all the time, you can have more natural back and forth dialogue. This allows you to get updates on your events, make adjustments to questions and pick up on previous queries even when they happen throughout the course of your day (you can specify how long you want Gemini to remember conversations).
Where things get really interesting is the combination of computer vision and AI, which allowed me to do things like pick up a physical invite card and simply ask Gemini to add it to my calendar. No need to grab my phone, open up an app and add details like the time, date and location myself. I was also able to do things like simply look at a bunch of different ingredients and ask Gemini to make a smoothie from what was in front of me. It can even do rough estimates for how much of a certain food has been added, so if you're not worried about being super precise, you can leave your measuring cups in a drawer. And if you run out of certain foods, you can easily tell Gemini to add something to your grocery list.
Then there are other features like live translation, which feels kind of magical. The glasses are designed so that the mics are directed in a cone-shaped space in front of you, so that even in a room with other conversations going on, the glasses don't get confused. Not only does this let you switch speakers naturally just by looking at someone else, Gemini will even adjust the output of a translation to sound similar to the original speaker. This allows you to follow along in real-time almost as well as someone who speaks the language naturally.
That said, the thing that impressed me the most about these Android XR glasses is the platform itself. Compared to some rivals where a lot of features feel like a work in progress, Google's OS feels much more mature. This includes little touches like dedicated sounds when Gemini accesses your camera, when the glasses take a photo or video, when Gemini leverages external AI and more. Google has done a pretty good job of translating a lot of the most important features you use on your phone to a medium without a screen.
Then there's Google's approach to privacy, which looks to be a step up from the competition. In addition to each pair of glasses coming with an LED indicator that blocks you from taking pictures or videos when it's covered up or disabled, Google also isn't supporting features like livestreaming video directly from the specs. Furthermore, Google says images and info sent to Gemini will stay on your device and will not be used to train AI or for ad targeting. That might not sound like much, but considering Google owns YouTube and generates billions from advertising, the simple act of leaving money on the table in favor of privacy is a welcome departure from Meta's glasses. Those have always felt like they are meant to expand the reach of Facebook and Instagram.
The one caveat to all this is that you do have to buy into talking to and relying rather heavily on Gemini. I'm still not sure I'm 100 percent on board with that, but at least for me, these glasses make a better argument for always-on AI support than almost any other class of device I've used. So while I'm still waiting for companies to deliver streamlined specs with built-in displays, these audio-first options feel like much more than a stepping stone towards that. They're surprisingly full-featured, and I don't think it's a stretch to say that compared to rival assistants like Siri, Muse and others, Gemini is the smartest of the bunch. So even if you primarily want these for playing music, keeping tabs on your schedule and getting occasional help from AI, Google's first batch of Android XR-powered intelligent eyewear feels like it's already jumped to the front of the pack.
Pre-orders for the new family of Android XR intelligent eyewear from both Warby Parker and Gentle Monster begin today with official sales slated for December 10.

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) indicated that it was considering steps to capture peak levels of particulate matter (PM), a major pollutant, that exceed the existing monitoring range, after air quality data from several government monitoring stations in Delhi went missing for hours during the pollution spike following Deepavali on Sunday.
The Hindu reported on Monday (November 9, 2026) that the data gaps had led to an artificially lower official air quality index (AQI), making air quality appear better than it actually was, according to experts.
In a statement on Tuesday (November 10, 2026) , the CPCB said PM levels were measured only up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre (µg/m³) for AQI calculations, which explained the missing data on Deepavali night, when actual concentrations exceeded this limit.
“The PM analysers deployed at the time of introduction of the NAQI (National Air Quality Index) [in 2015] were calibrated for a measurement range of 0-1,000 µg/m³. Accordingly, consistent with this, the designed system of automated data validation treats hourly readings beyond the calibrated range as outside range, and such readings are not used in the computation,” the CPCB statement read.
“During extreme episodes, which are occasional, like Diwali firecracker bursting, this may appear as a data gap at the particular station concerned, and those hours do not contribute to the 24-hour average of the relevant pollutant for the concerned station,” the statement added.
Deliberations under way
The CPCB said internal deliberations and consultations on processing data “beyond system design range” were under way.
The CPCB also said spikes in ambient pollutant concentrations, such as those caused by firecrackers bursting, are episodic and short-lived. “The NAQI recognises that prolonged exposure, rather than a momentary reading, is a more relevant indicator of ill effects on human health,” the statement read.
Under the AQI calculation methodology adopted by the CPCB in 2015, the overall index is based on eight parameters and is calculated only if data are available for a minimum of three pollutants, out of which one should necessarily be either PM2.5 or PM10.
“The methodology was formed in 2015 and at that time it was decided that the accuracy was good only up to 1,000 µg/m³ and both PM2.5 and PM10 were capped at it for calculation of AQI. But the equipment got better with time and Delhi’s air quality analysers and instruments were also updated, but the methodology was never updated after that,” an official told The Hindu.
“But now there are discussions of raising this cap so that peak values above 1,000 µg/m³ could be measured,” the official added.
Of the 59 air quality monitoring stations in Delhi, 46 are operated by the Delhi government’s Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), which does not calculate the AQI. The DPCC had recorded PM2.5 and PM10 levels exceeding 1,000 µg/m³ on Deepavali night, though several readings were initially missing.
The CPCB uses data from these 46 stations, along with readings from other monitoring stations, to calculate the AQI.
Air quality improves
Meanwhile, Delhi’s air quality improved to the ‘poor’ category on Tuesday (November 10, 2026), with the 24-hour average AQI recorded at 299, just below the ‘very poor’ threshold of 300.
Experts attributed the improvement to increased wind speeds and said air quality was likely to improve further over the next few days.

Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.
Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.
"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.
"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.
Prabowo accepts Raka's resignation
Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.
Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.
Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.
"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."
Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.
"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.
Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.
Long-running allegations over candidacy lead to court disputes
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.
The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.
Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.
Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.
Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.
Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.
"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

How word of mouth is helping an Amish community's fight against measles
Measles spreads incredibly fast. For the last few months, so has Dale Weiser's phone number.
Weiser is the clinical services supervisor for the Chester County Health Department in south-central Pennsylvania. Since August, she's been driving out to Amish homes to vaccinate people against measles. She says it usually starts with a phone call.
"I was at a house, like, at 4:30 in the afternoon, and I had a phone call at 8 the next morning saying, 'hey, I heard you were down the street. Can you come do that at my house?'" she says of a typical request she gets from Amish families. So far, she's administered more than 400 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine in Amish homes.
The house calls are part of the state of Pennsylvania's strategy to wage war on measles by flipping the script on traditional public health messaging. Instead of advertising vaccinations loudly, health officials have launched a quiet word-of-mouth campaign designed to win the trust of the state's Amish community, which has been particularly hard hit by the country's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. The state has confirmed six measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases so far — though the true count is likely much higher, since many people who get sick don't seek medical care.
Lower vaccination rates
Surveys suggest only about a third of Amish families in the region vaccinate their children. That's left the Amish community especially vulnerable to measles, one of the most contagious diseases.
There's no religious edict against vaccination among the Amish. It's very much seen as a family and individual choice, says Weiser. Often, she says, these decisions are driven by practical and cultural factors.
"They don't have health insurance. They're not interacting with the mainstream medical society. And measles wasn't a problem for 30 years, so there was no real risk to not being vaccinated, at least for measles," Weiser says.
But as measles cases have piled up in Pennsylvania, Weiser says many Amish families have changed their minds about getting the MMR vaccine. And when they do, she hops in her car and brings the shots to them.
"When I arrive at their home, there's usually a small child that will run from the back of the house to the barn to tell the men that there's somebody strange in the driveway, or that the nurse is here," she says.
A patient, personalized approach to outreach
Some days, Weiser will vaccinate a single family in their kitchen. Other times, she'll find dozens of people gathered to get the shot. She's also fielded a lot of questions. Some, like what's in the vaccine and potential side effects, are things anyone would ask, she says.
"But I was caught off guard when I was asked if there were tracking chips in the vaccine, and I was like, whoa. Flashback to COVID. Where did you hear that?" she recalls.
