‘The Body’ Creator on the Dance Team’s Sexuality, What Happened to Grace and Whether God Is Real
SPOILER ALERT: This story contains spoilers for “The Body,” now streaming on Netflix.
If you’re looking for clear answers about whether or not God is real in the world of “The Body” — Netflix’s spooky new drama series about mass hysteria originating from a Catholic school dance team — you’re not going to find them.
“If we ever fully defined it, it would break the rule of the show,” says creator Quinn Shephard. “The show is meant to mimic faith, so there’s people who believe, there’s people who don’t and there’s people in the middle, like me, who are like, ‘I don’t know.’”
But regardless of whether it’s the big man upstairs or just some devious teenage girls pulling the strings, “The Body” has a lot to say about faith and its role in the lives of young and sometimes queer girls. Shephard is a proud lesbian who was raised in the church and has stepped away from it without fully rejecting it, and the show’s up-and-down relationship with God is a product of that.
At the beginning of “The Body,” a devout Catholic named Grace (Sofia Wylie) is the clear standout at dance team tryouts, much to the chagrin of some of the team’s more senior members, who roll their eyes at her rule-following innocence. Thus, she’s put through a bit of hazing: At a Halloween party at an abandoned convent, she’s pressured to take Ecstasy by Elise (Sara Boustany), the team’s co-captain and resident badass, as everyone jokingly perform a ritual meant to sacrifice her soul to the devil. But the devil doesn’t seem to know that they’re joking. Anya (Kristina Bogic), who is Elise’s co-captain and the most popular girl in school, notices that Grace has wandered off alone. Alongside Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), an awkward new girl who got rejected from the team in favor of Grace, she finds Grace on the ground, convulsing until she passes out. Anya and Lisbeth decide to take her to a hospital, but on the way, Grace appears to die. Because Anya supplied the Ecstasy, she’s terrified she’ll get in trouble. Lisbeth sees this as her way onto the dance team and into Anya’s good graces, and takes charge. They take Grace’s body back to her own house and tuck her into bed, then use Grace’s phone to text a friend that she got home safe, giving themselves plausible deniability. But at the end of the first episode, Grace takes a breath.
She doesn’t wake all the way up, though, and spends the rest of the season in a coma as the dance team is wracked with guilt about the Ecstasy, which they don’t confess about. Needing support from the only other person who knows what happened, Anya brings Lisbeth onto the dance team to take Grace’s place, which intensifies the conflict between Anya and Elise. The two best friends are clearly in love with each other, and had been fooling around sexually at the party, but Anya insists that she’s straight and loyal to her boyfriend, Steven (Orlando Norman). Frustrated by Anya’s new closeness to Lisbeth, and with latent suspicion about Anya’s role in what happened to Grace, Elise fakes a spiritual experience, shrieking in front of the whole school that she’s having a vision of Grace. But everyone on the team — except Anya and Lisbeth, of course — buys into it. One by one, they begin faking their own visions. Soon, the whole town starts to believe that Grace is all-powerful, chosen by God to perform healing miracles from her apparent deathbed. People gather on her family’s lawn to worship her.
Lisbeth is delighted, using her relationship with Anya to increase her social standing at school and to protect her brother, Leo (Jackson Kelly), who at one point drew suspicion because of his crush on (and lewd drawings of) Grace. But eventually, Elise pieces together the truth, forcing Anya to confess to Father Franklin (Nnamdi Asomugha), the school principal and pastor. At that exact moment, though, Grace finally wakes up. Weakly, she whispers, “I’m God.”
Shepherd spoke with Variety about Catholicism, lesbian camp and who-slash-what God is.
Anya and Elise’s relationship feels lived-in and very unique — there’s not a lot of media set in the early aughts that depicts queer teens. How did you approach their hot-and-cold friendship and romance? Were you pulling from anything in particular?
I definitely put so much of myself into those two characters, and also some of my close friends who let me use their stories. I do find the era really interesting, because it wasn’t like being gay was illegal, or like you’re guaranteed to get disowned, but it was definitely not good. And it felt like the biggest threat was to your femininity, and your social standing as normal or cool. I didn’t go to high school in 2004; I was in high school a little later than that. But pre-smartphones and pre-gay marriage being legalized, that was a very specific era. Being lesbian felt like a bit. I remember my friends and I doing so many bits where we’d “pretend” to be gay for each other. It’s not that it wasn’t being talked about; it’s that it wasn’t cool. I was like, “I can’t be gay.” This is going to sound so bad, but I think I thought I had to be butch. I didn’t want to, like, get a short haircut and start wearing rainbow knee socks.
For Anya, that’s her worst fear. She’s not ready. She’s quite high femme, and on the top of the social hierarchy, and she’s like, “Oh my God. Not only am I going to threaten that, but I have to give up on all these ideas of what my life is going to be? Are people going to act differently around me in the locker room? Am I going to lose my girlhood? Am I going to lose my status?” And we talked a lot in the room about how much Catholicism plays into Anya’s fears — it is a fear that she’s going to go to hell, but it’s not the main fear. Certainly, a piece of her shame comes from Catholicism, but I think it’s more interesting and more relatable to more people that she’s equally afraid, if not more afraid, that she’s just gonna lose her identity.
Because of that, even though she also has a lot of kindness to her, she does a lot of really fucked up things. I wanted to make a very unsanitized, messy first queer love story. I was seeing too many shows where the characters are gay and it’s totally fine and no one has a problem with it. Like, there’s the parent who’s a little homophobic, and then there’s one conversation where they’re like, “Actually, I love you, honey.” No. It’s messy as hell. And you do some crazy stuff that you look back on, like, “Why did I do that?” I really wanted to give that to Anya and Elise.
Tell me about queerness as it exists — if it exists — elsewhere on the dance team. With Lisbeth, for example, it’s never totally clear whether she has any latent attraction to Anya.
I like to joke that with the amount of queer women involved in making the show, the core ethos and tone is so inherently like lesbian camp and a lesbian sense of humor. That even applies to the fact that there’s a lot of really lovable men in the story. The men are kind of innocent, and that’s from a lot of the women working on the show being like, “With the men that I dated, it wasn’t their fault that I wasn’t into them. It was me and my journey, and God, what I put that guy through!” Everyone in the show is linked to that twisted sense of humor and trying to turn shame and trauma into comedy. But we’ve got stuff to play with in Season 2 in terms of queer characters.
I actually really like that people have debates about Lisbeth. Because to make her relationship with Anya about sexuality would almost be too simple. I think it’s way bigger than that. Lisbeth’s character isn’t driven by sexuality, almost at all. She’s more driven by survival. She’s a child of trauma, and she’s got some slightly asexual and sociopathic tendencies coming out, but I don’t think that’s necessarily who she is forever. It’s more that that’s where we meet her, because she’s in survival mode.
Like Anya, she does things that feel a bit evil, but she’s also really charming, and it’s clear how her past drove her to make these decisions. She always keeps calm because she has to, but what’s her internal monologue saying as she’s trying to control this secret she and Anya have about Grace? Is she secretly freaking out?
I love Lisbeth. I don’t think she’s inherently bad. I just think she’s opportunistic in the first season, and too smart for her own good. It’s almost frustrating to her how ahead of other people her brain is. She’s definitely a bit on the spectrum. She struggles with social cues, but she’s brilliant, and she can’t help but see opportunities and strategies. For me, the lovable part of her is that she can strategize a takeover. She can play three-dimensional chess. She is starting mass hysteria to protect her brother and gain access to the dance team.
But at the end of the day, she doesn’t know how to act like a normal high-school girl at a party. She can’t do it. She tries so hard, and she literally studies it like gospel, but she can’t get there, and I think that’s so human. Sometimes it feels like there’s a way to study something and get there, but you can’t because that’s not how life works. And she had such a profound relationship with religion when she was younger that she lost. It’s like she’s searching for something that profound again, and when she finds it, she’s literally not going to be stopped. She’s a dog with a bone. If she wants to be on that dance team, she’s getting on that dance team no matter what, even if she has to hide a body. She’s getting there.
Outside of the question of her sexuality, how does she feel about Anya? Is Anya just a pathway to popularity, or does she have any genuine love for her as a friend?
I think it’s both. It changes. There are scenes where she’s like, “I’m so enamored with this girl. I wish I could be just like her. I don’t know if I want to be with her, be like her, be around her or be inside her skin. I don’t know. I’m just obsessed.” And then there’s other times where she’s like, “This girl is on my nerves.” It’s very hard for Lisbeth when Anya is like, “Why are you not freaking out?” And she’s like, “I am, but this is how I freak out.” She doesn’t understand Anya, but there are moments, like when she sees that Anya’s working on her dance team jacket, and Anya’s letting her into her closet, that’s like the happiest day of Lisbeth’s life. She’s like, “I finally have a friend, and I’m so happy.” Does she have some ulterior motives? Yeah. But there’s also a really wholesome motive in there too. She wants a friend.
What went into the writing of Maddie (Shirley Chen)? For much of the season, she’s the only one being truthful about the fact that she isn’t seeing visions of Grace. When she does become a Grace worshiper at the end, has she genuinely convinced herself she sees her? Or is she lying too?
Maddie’s quite an earnest character. I don’t feel like she’s ever purposefully deceiving. She really struggles with the lies that the girls are telling. One of the writers, Lily Houghton, told a story about how she lost both her parents. They were very beloved, and so many people came up to her, like, “Your dad came to me in a dream. I saw your mom yesterday, and she came with messages.” And she got to the point where she was like, “I don’t want to hear people’s stories about my parents visiting them, because if they’re going to visit someone, why would they not visit me?” And it was such a personal, vivid story. We were all so moved. It’s so human to still feel like a kid, like, “I feel like it would be me,” and also the bigger picture of people claiming someone else’s loss. So we baked a lot of that into Maddie’s desire to see Grace, and I would say she ends the show believing. And that gets validated, because she’s the one who says that when everyone confesses, that’s when Grace is going to wake up, and then that happens. She’s going to be telling anyone who will listen that she got a prophecy. I think she’s like,”My best friend is God, and it’s cool.”
Can you answer whether the show believes in the supernatural? And does it believe in God?
The rule that we have internally is that the show’s perspective on the supernatural needs to mimic a relationship with faith. So you can choose how you want to view the events that are presented. For every supernatural theory, there needs to be a countertheory, and the audience needs to be empowered to decide which show they’re watching and which character they align with. When people are like, “What is happening for you?” I’m like, “I don’t know! I don’t know what happens after we die. I don’t know the meaning of life. I don’t know exactly what God is.” The people making the show still have questions, so the show still has questions, and that’s the rule.
So there’s a spiritual perspective, and a supernatural perspective, and it’s both/and instead of either/or. But would you say that, in the world of the show, there is absolutely something happening beyond human understanding? Or is there also a version of the show where every event has been orchestrated by the characters and is grounded in scientific reality?
To me, that’s the same as being like, “On Earth, is there a God? Or is there not?” It is impossible for me to answer. And have a similar attitude with the show. The show exists in the unknown space. With the ending, there are clear supernatural and grounded, scientific theories that can explain that, and that’s the crux of the question we go into the next season with.
It’s part of why I love and gravitate towards spiritual journalism — journalism that follows people’s unexplainable events. I like material without an agenda, that’s just like, “This has happened to this many people. We don’t know what it means.” People say that when you have a near-death experience, your brain fires your neurons and it gives you this crazy hallucination. And then there’s this camp of people who says you’re really seeing the afterlife. But, literally, we can’t know. Unless we die. So I don’t know! If we ever fully defined it, it would break the rule of the show. The show is meant to mimic faith, so there’s people who believe, there’s people who don’t and there’s people in the middle, like me, who are like, “I don’t know.”
Since you’re hopeful for a Season 2, what can you say about the ending and what you hope to cover in the future? Thematically, what’s going on in that moment where Grace wakes up and says that she’s God?
We always knew the ending going into the first season, and I think that moment is so fun because it provokes exactly the conversation that we’ve been having in the writers’ room. We hear Michael say that people can hear things in comas sometimes, so there’s a part of you that goes, “Maybe she’s been hearing everyone talking about these theories, and she knows.” We also have heard countless stories in life about people in comas, or people who have died and come back, who have these crazy visions. Did she experience the afterlife? Has she changed? Did something happen to her soul? Is it supernatural? And also, since she’s waking up from a coma, is she going to remember what she says? People say and do crazy things when they’re waking up from comas they have no memory of. The fact that people are excited to discuss their theory on what that ending means is exactly what I want. Without saying too much, it’s a perfect encapsulation of what we’d like to do with the next season.
This interview has been edited and condensed.

A study of nearly 100,000 Americans identified thousands of new variants in a set of genes that influence our responses to prescription drugs, thanks to the inclusion of participants from a more diverse set of ancestries than previous studies of these so-called pharmacogenes.
Using data from the National Institute of Health’s All of Us program, the researchers found that every participant carried at least one variant in the 16 pharmacogenes they studied, and that one in four participants had taken a medication that could be affected by these variants.
The new paper, published Wednesday in Science Translational Medicine, advances efforts to use genetic data to personalize drug treatments, and should make this area of research useful to a broader population.
“This really furthers the emerging evidence of how genetically guided clinical care adds benefit across a diverse population,” said Loren Saulsberry, a health policy researcher who has done work on equity and pharmacogenomics but was not involved in the new paper.
Pharmacogenes can change the way people metabolize drugs such that they need higher or lower doses, face worse or new side effects, or in some cases make drugs entirely ineffective. The variants included in the study affect the functioning of drugs including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, statins, chemotherapy, and the blood thinner Plavix, among others.
“If you have a prior experience with a medicine that did not work for you, or had a side effect, we can’t say it’s absolutely because of genetics, but we are appreciating more and more that people are different, and genetics is one reason that may suggest where there may be differences,” said Philip Empey, who directs the Center for Clinical Pharmaceutical Sciences at the University of Pittsburgh and was the senior author on the paper.
The paper points to the need to give more attention to the role genetics plays in the clinic, Empey added. But there are a number of barriers before these results can make their way into patient care. Many people don’t have their genomes sequenced, physicians may not be aware of how drugs they are prescribing are affected by genetic variants, and there are a constellation of variants that could impact drugs.
The All of Us Research Program has the goal of collecting genetic data from 1 million Americans from diverse backgrounds. That diversity helped identify variants not found in previous work using other genomic databases like the U.K. Biobank.
Part of the concern with new technologies is that they may not be as effective for marginalized populations, but having such a diverse dataset to start with will help limit disparities in outcomes as the findings are translated into clinical use, Saulsberry said.
The potential benefits of All of Us’s data going forward may be affected by funding woes. The program is supported by two sources: the 21st Century Cures Act, enacted in 2016, and yearly appropriations from Congress. That former avenue will dry up in the 2027 fiscal year. Congress is currently operating under a temporary budget, called a continuing resolution, but the program expects to receive $122 million in funding once a budget is finalized, an 80% drop from its peak in 2023.
Those cuts have meant that All of Us has had to be less ambitious in its recruiting of patients, said Joshua Denny, who was CEO of the program until the end of October and is now in a leadership position at the University of Chicago. “The engagement activities, the brick and mortar that we had enrolling at academic medical centers and FQHCs and mobile units. These kinds of things … were cut back dramatically,” he said. The program has also stopped offering participants the ability to see the results of their genetic testing because of funding concerns.
Another area where All of Us has had to temper its aims has been with recruiting children, which it began in 2023. At this point, it has around 5,000 children enrolled in the study but those data are not yet available to researchers, said Sara Van Driest, director of pediatrics for All of Us.
“In order to really enroll children at scale and build a dataset that’s going to fuel the future of precision health, we’re going to need stable funding in the years ahead,” she added. “I should say, increased and stable funding in the years ahead.”

Quick Answer
Windows 11 is testing eight upgrades in Insider builds to reduce daily friction. Key updates include flexible taskbar positioning, faster Windows Search with inline actions, a Battery Status widget, phone-to-PC integration, per-app privacy controls, smarter Windows Hello, anti-glare tools, and enhanced File Explorer previews.
I can’t count how many times I’ve had to drag the window to full size, squint at a bright screen, or open Settings just to turn on dark mode. Each one takes a few seconds, but you repeat them all day. Thankfully, Windows 11 is about to trim a lot of that. Microsoft seems to have noticed, and over the past few months, it has been stacking up small but genuinely useful changes for Windows 11. The best part is that all these features are coming with future updates.
With new optimized features, Windows now feels up to 20% more responsive, with the gains showing up in Start, File Explorer, Search, and more. With the latest Windows Insider release notes, you are in for a eight-feature treat you should know about. One heads-up before we start: not everything is available to everyone yet. Many of these are still being tested in the Windows Insider Experimental channel, so I’ll tell you where each one stands.
Table of Contents
Taskbar customization
For years, the Windows 11 taskbar has been stuck to the bottom of the screen. There was no way to change its position. That is finally changing. Microsoft’s Windows Insider blog confirms that, with the current insider update, users can now park the taskbar on the top, bottom, left, or right edge. Here’s what you can do:
- You can choose icon alignment for every position. On the sides, icons can be top-aligned or centered. On the top or bottom, they can be left-aligned or centered.
- Start, Search, and other flyouts follow the taskbar. Meaning, if you put the taskbar at the top, Start opens from the top.
- On a vertical taskbar, when you choose “Never combine” and turn on labels, every app window gets its own labeled button, so you can see all your windows at a glance.
Moving the taskbar to the side can give you vertical space, handy for developers who want to see more code. To tweak the taskbar, you need to navigate to Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors. You can also choose to make the taskbar smaller, optimal for small screens. Simply choose the “Show smaller taskbar” option to Always, and you get smaller icons and a shorter bar. No restart or sign-out needed.
Things may not work perfectly, though. Auto-hide and the tablet-optimized taskbar don’t work in the new positions, touch gestures are still in progress, and the search box shows up as a plain search icon for now. Aside from this, the Recommended section is getting renamed to Recent, and you can hide your name and profile picture. There are also separate toggles to show or hide Pinned, Recent, and All.
Smarter Windows Search
This one might be the biggest everyday upgrade. Microsoft has confirmed that a new search built on WinUI 3 is incoming and says it makes it faster and lighter on resources. Windows Search also understands you better. Typos and synonyms are matched more intelligently, so a sloppy query is more likely to give you the right result.
The main highlight is inline actions. So, instead of finding a setting and then opening Settings to change it, you can enable/disable a setting from search. This means you’ll be able to:
- Switch to dark mode, turn on night light, or turn on Bluetooth
- Dim your screen or mute your PC
- Minimize all your windows or arrange windows on screen
Phone actions are coming soon too, allowing you to quickly do things like sending a text through a Phone Link-connected device. Search is soon expected to get inline previews of files, richer file details, web answers (think weather or “how tall is the Eiffel Tower”) and filters. This new experience is also expected to arrive for the Start menu, but only next year. Other features are expected for broader availability later this year.
Battery status widget
This is not a big update, per se, but if you want to know what the battery level is on your wireless mouse? Your headphones? Your laptop? Or any other connected device, usually you’d have to hunt through different menus for each answer.
With the Windows 11 26340.9616 release, Microsoft introduced a Battery Status widget that shows the battery levels of your PC and your peripheral devices in one view. To get it, you need to open the Widgets board > Add widgets > Battery Status. It is rolling out to Insiders on newer builds. Widgets are also getting lighter. Microsoft says on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets now load only when you open them. This helps free up more than 200 MB for your apps.
Phone to PC continuity
Microsoft seems to be making sure that your phone and PC act like one setup. With the upcoming updates, Windows 11 could allow users to reply to messages, answer calls, and open phone apps without picking up their phone. Here are all the features, reportedly available in the insider build:
- Messages and notifications: You will be able to preview them from your Android phone or iPhone right in Start. When you want to reply, you can open a window focused on that chat.
- Quick Settings: Put your phone in silent mode or ring a misplaced phone right from your PC.
- Phone apps on your desktop: Supported Android phones can open phone apps in separate, resizable windows.
- Files: You will be able to browse your phone’s files in File Explorer.
- Photos: You can snap a picture on your phone, and your PC shows a notification that you can open with one click.
- Resume: Pick up supported activities where you left off when you switch devices.
One thing to note is that this requires a compatible Android phone or iPhone, and features vary by platform. The rollout date, similar to other features, isn’t confirmed, but it may arrive by next year.
Better privacy controls
Until now, regular desktop apps were controlled by a single device-wide switch for things like your camera, microphone, and location. That was not something one would want, especially when you want to have granular controls. According to the 28120.3302 release notes, Insiders can now allow or deny access for each desktop app individually. For that, you need to head to Settings > Privacy & security, then open Camera, Microphone, or Location.
The rollout is gentle on your existing setup. All the apps that were granted access will continue to keep it, and apps that were denied stay denied. Nothing will reset. Apps that haven’t asked yet will prompt you the first time they request access.
Smarter Windows Hello
According to Microsoft, with the latest insider builds, it has introduced faster Windows Hello sign-ins, made them easier, and more reliable, with improvements to both face and fingerprint recognition. There’s also a very practical new trick for face sign-in. If you’ve ever tried to unlock your laptop in a dim room, you know the struggle. You have to turn on the light so that your face is detected correctly.
The 26340.9750 release notes say Windows Hello facial recognition can temporarily brighten your screen to help you sign in when the lighting is poor. To use it, go to Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Facial recognition (Windows Hello) and turn on Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition. This one is currently in the Experimental channel.
Anti-glare mode
Although Microsoft doesn’t use the name “anti-glare mode,” that’s exactly what the newly added option does. Notably, it’s a contrast theme toggle inside Magnifier, as mentioned in the 28120.3302 release notes. While many people use Night light or color inversion to calm a bright screen, but the downside of using is that it flips everything, including photos, charts, and videos.
With the new toggle, it will recolor the interface only. This way, your images keep their real colors. The dark theme is the default, and you can pick a different contrast theme under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. You still get the “Color inversion” option, and it isn’t going anywhere if you prefer it.
Magnifier also learned some multi-monitor tricks:
- Zoom per display: With your monitors set to Extend, each screen can have its own zoom level. So, one screen where you are writing can sit at 300% while your reference screen stays at 150%.
- View locking: Press Ctrl + Windows + K while pointing at a screen to hold its view in place, then press Windows + Esc to release all locks.
If you just want a softer tint, Windows 11 is also testing a “Screen Tint,” which lets you pick a color overlay and adjust its strength.
File Explorer previews
You might already be using third-party software for file previews inside File Explorer, but wait. Microsoft is also cooking the same feature, and it may arrive very soon for Windows 11. A couple of preview-related changes are incoming:
- Thumbnails in the Recommended section on File Explorer’s Home page are sharper, so they’re crisper and easier to read without needing you to open them.
- You can now preview and install fonts from File Explorer and desktop right-click menus.
If you work with fonts, that second one saves a few steps. For everyone else, it’s a polish update, and it’s good to see File Explorer getting some attention.
Can everyone try these features?
Unfortunately, these features aren’t available for everyone, for now. Most of the features above live in Windows Insider builds. If you’re comfortable with a few bugs, you can join through Settings > Windows Update > Windows Insider Program. You will see most features in builds 26340.9616, 26340.9750 and 28120.3302 in the Experimental channels.
These builds can be unstable, and features in them might change, be removed, or never ship. Many are also rolled out gradually to a subset of Insiders first, so you may not see everything right away. For those who are using Windows 11 on their primary device, you should probably wait.

For a woman who has been a witness to some of the most significant political moments in modern Indian history, Sonia Gandhi likes to insist her life has been far from remarkable. “Oh, I don’t know that I would say it’s an extraordinary story,” she says, shifting uncomfortably.
It’s hard to reconcile this modest characterisation with the course her life has taken over the last 79 years. Born to a working-class family in a small town in northern Italy, today she sits at the heart of Indian political power, having weathered assassinations and personal tragedy to become one of the country’s most influential figures. She held Indira Gandhi’s bloodied body after the then-prime minster, her mother-in-law, was gunned down at their home in Delhi in 1984. She then became India’s first lady when her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, took his mother’s place as prime minister. And when Rajiv, too, was killed, she threw aside her distaste for politics to step up and lead his fragmenting party. In 2004, having taken Congress to electoral victory, she famously turned down the prime minister post. She can still boast of being the longest-serving president of Congress, both when India’s oldest political party was in power and later, when it became the flailing opposition. When Gandhi stepped down in 2017, her son Rahul was appointed her successor.
Gandhi’s entrance into Indian politics began in Cambridge in the 1960s when, at 18, while she was studying at a language school, she fell in love with a bright-eyed boy at a Greek restaurant. At the time, she had no idea that Rajiv was heir to India’s most consequential political dynasty. “It was a coup de foudre,” she says. “After that, nothing else really mattered. He was, first of all, a handsome man. But I think his eyes told of the way he was – of his inner self. He was loving, he was comforting, he was caring. Everything I could have possibly dreamed of.”
Only later would she learn that Rajiv’s grandfather was Jawaharlal Nehru, Indian freedom fighter and the country’s first prime minister, and his mother was Indira Gandhi, who in 1966 became India’s first female prime minister.
Does she still recognise herself in that innocent Italian girl who was swept off her feet and transplanted to an alien land and culture? “Not really,” she says quietly. “Too much has happened, too much has changed.”
We meet at the grand white Delhi bungalow she has lived in for 36 years – a relic of British colonial rule, where peacocks roam the grounds. It was in this house in 1991 that Gandhi heard her husband had been assassinated by Sri Lankan Tamil separatist terrorists. Over the years, as she took on the mantle of Congress leader, her home became the centre of party operations.
The ghosts of Congress leaders past loom large in her study. A painting of Nehru, photographs of Rajiv, a carved stone bust and portraits of Indira line the walls, while a painting of Mahatma Gandhi, the freedom fighter who shaped the ideology of Congress, also hangs prominently. Heavy gilded tomes fill the floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, and a long meeting table dominates the space, but the vibrant rugs, patterned blinds and scattered antiques suggest Gandhi’s own light touch.
In a dark blue sari and maroon blouse, her signature neat grey hair pushed back with a black headband, Gandhi looks every inch the composed Indian political matriarch as she sits on the sofa. The only hint of her heritage is softly accented English and recognisably Italian gesticulation.
She has, she confesses, been very nervous and tense about our meeting. Gandhi has not done an interview in a decade, and throughout her life in the public eye, has tried fiercely to maintain her privacy. She has only agreed to this rare meeting to discuss her forthcoming memoir, a strikingly personal account of her life, and has asked her daughter Priyanka, also a senior Congress leader, to sit in for moral support.
India’s media has often cast her as cold and aloof, yet today she seems warm, open and often a little unsure of herself. She’s anxious about how personal the book is, worried it will be eviscerated by the Indian media, but suggests that after years of “horrible and crazy things written about me”, it will be comforting for people to know “the truth”.
Gandhi has good reason to be nervous of the press. In today’s India, the mainstream media landscape has been crushed into submission by the hardline, rightwing Modi government and is largely devoted to promoting the prime minister’s agenda, while mercilessly attacking the Congress party, in particular the Gandhi family. She does not hold back on criticism of Narendra Modi – accusing him of being an “authoritarian force bent upon changing the very nature of our country” – and of his party, BJP, which she says has “systematically dismantled our democratic institutions”.
The Hindu nationalist vision of India that Modi has enacted over his 12 years in power is directly opposed to the pluralistic, secular India that was championed by successive Congress leaders and which remains enshrined in India’s constitution. It has led to well-documented oppression of the country’s minority groups, in particular its 200 million Muslims.
“More than disappointing, it’s very painful, having known a different India,” Gandhi says. “In parliament, we are not allowed to debate. In the past, there were discussions, there were meetings between the opposition and the government, there was consultation. Now the opposition counts for nothing.”
Since Modi came to power, she has had barely any interaction with him; he tends to avoid eye contact when they’re in a room together – a stark contrast to the past, when opposition leaders would often meet the government and “treat each other with cordiality”.
A “Congress-free India” is one of the openly declared goals of Modi’s BJP, resulting in highly personal attacks on Gandhi and her children, who have found themselves with numerous police cases filed against them. As we talk, Gandhi’s phone lights up with a call from her son Rahul – later, we learn a judge has just cleared him of defamation in one of these many cases, this time for criticising Modi’s home minister back in 2018. “They are very vindictive and vicious. There doesn’t seem to be a heart there,” Gandhi says.
So effective is the BJP’s crackdown on any form of dissent or criticism – what Gandhi describes as an “atmosphere of fear” – that her memoir almost didn’t see the light of day in India. Penguin Random House India were originally meant to release the book domestically, but after she sent them the manuscript she was met with a deafening silence. Gandhi says simply that Penguin were “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and that after she refused to make certain suggested edits, the publisher dropped the book, just a week before it was due to be announced. It will now be published by another imprint. In a statement, the publisher denied dropping the book, adding, “Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish Belonging because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances.”
Gandhi admits she was disappointed, though not altogether surprised, at what she sees as an attempt to censor her book. It is far from an isolated incident. In the days before we meet, Gandhi’s 26-year-old grandson, who is an artist and curator, is forced to take down dozens of his photographs depicting political protests that had been due to go on show in Delhi.
Gandhi had an early insight into the difficulties and loneliness of being a female leader in India’s deeply patriarchal society. When she arrived in India in 1968, she and Rajiv moved in with his mother, who at that time was two years into her first term as prime minister. Her husband, also a politician, had died years before.
They lived all together in another crumbling colonial Delhi bungalow, in relatively close and modest quarters. To outsiders, Indira was often seen as severe, an “iron lady”, and Gandhi admits that, to begin with, she was deeply intimidated by her formidable mother-in-law. Yet while Indira was imposing in public, she could be vulnerable in private, once confiding to Gandhi how terrified she was when she first bcame prime minister.
“In the newspapers she was portrayed as tough or harsh, but at home she was just like any other mother,” Gandhi says – although Indira’s notoriously explosive temper, frequently directed at political colleagues, would erupt through the house on occasion. Gandhi’s memoir recounts one incident where Indira lost her temper during a family dinner and threw her thali plate across the table.
Gandhi’s book documents the hostility Indira grappled with, both from political opponents and rightwing groups, but also from the old guard of her own party. “I saw her work day and night, constantly under pressure, constantly attacked,” Gandhi says. “It did affect her, like it would anyone. And of course, in that position, there is a loneliness. She had many interests and many friends, but it is a lonely kind of life.”
For several years, Gandhi says, her own life was “carefree”. She and Rajiv were madly in love, often embarrassing their children with public displays of affection that were highly unusual in Indian households at the time. “For this man, I was ready to do everything, to lose even my Italian identity,” she says. Rajiv was working as a commercial airline pilot, and as relations warmed with her mother-in-law, Gandhi set about redecorating the austere Delhi bungalow with some Italian flair, and learning how to cook Kashmiri food. After a traumatic miscarriage, she gave birth to two children, who were doted on by Indira. Even her pangs for fresh Italian ingredients, impossible to find in India in those days, eventually ebbed.
But in 1975 Indira would make the most controversial decision of her political life. Amid mounting political unrest, economic hardship and a concerted effort by the opposition to bring down the Congress government, Indira decided to impose a state of emergency on the country, in a bid to instil order. The repercussions were profound: the constitution was suspended, civil liberties and democratic freedoms abandoned, the media silenced and opponents detained en masse without trial. It lasted for almost two years, and is still seen as the darkest period of India’s democracy; it is regularly used to tarnish the Congress party today.
According to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision. Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her hotheaded younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, “They must be stopped.” Sanjay’s forceful influence over his mother was a great source of public controversy at the time. Gandhi recalls that it inflamed tensions within the family, too; Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen. “Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” Gandhi writes in her book.
Today, she says it was a mistake for Indira to call the emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same. “I always feel that Mrs Gandhi was a democrat at heart,” she says. “I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her.”
In the following years, Indira would lose one election and be returned to power in another. Rajiv would also be persuaded to enter politics after the premature death of Sanjay. But by 1984, darkness came to their door again.
Months of escalating violence had stricken the north Indian state of Punjab. As separatist militants prepared to declare an independent Sikh state, Indira authorised a military operation at one of the holiest sites in Sikhism, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where the group were hiding out. The operation caused cataclysmic damage, killing Sikh pilgrims as well as militants, and led to desecration of the temple by tanks and heavy weaponry. Gandhi says that when her mother-in-law was shown images of the devastation, tears rolled down her face.
For Sikhs in India, it was a profound and painful attack on their religion, and Indira was inundated with threats. “She told us what to do in case she died – so she knew,” Gandhi says. “She was making preparations for her death. She told Rahul he must be brave and not to cry.” That summer Indira took her grandchildren on a trip to her ancestral home of Kashmir; Gandhi believes this was to “say goodbye”. Indira also defied advice to remove her Sikh bodyguards – something that turned out to be a fateful decision.
Gandhi was at home on 31 October when she heard what sounded like fireworks going off. Sprinting over to Indira’s office next door, she was confronted by her mother-in-law’s bloodied body, riddled with bullets, lying on the ground. Indira’s own Sikh bodyguards had opened fire on her in retribution for the attack on the Golden Temple.
What came next remains seared on Gandhi’s memory. After Indira was put into a car, she held her bleeding body and tried to revive her mother-in-law as they raced to the hospital. “There was blood everywhere and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she says.
Even after so many years, the story is clearly painful to recount and she speaks hesitantly, her soft voice growing even quieter. “I remember the drive from the house to the hospital was excruciating. There wasn’t much traffic, but it felt so slow. I also knew that because she wasn’t speaking, it must be over.”
Gandhi admits there are still parts of that experience she can’t bring herself to discuss. “I never talk about it. Only if I’m asked, then I struggle to.” Indira would be declared dead at the hospital. Her body was still lying there, cold, when Rajiv broke the news that he had been asked to step in as prime minister. Gandhi had begged him to stay out of politics and describes that conversation as a “knife going into my heart”.
In the aftermath of Indira’s death, she was traumatised and depressed, living “like a ghost”. Rajiv, too, had no time to grieve. Newly announced as prime minister, he immediately had to deal with deadly anti-Sikh riots that erupted after Indira’s death. He would later be accused of not doing enough to stop the bloodbath. “Rajiv never really showed his pain,” Gandhi says. “I remember seeing him in his mother’s study, on one of the chairs where she sat, with tears. But in public he felt he had to hide it.”
Fear took over their lives. The house became a fortress, with uniformed commandos stationed in the children’s bedrooms. Rahul and Priyanka were pulled out of school and no longer allowed to roam freely. She would worry if Rajiv didn’t come back from an engagement on time. He, meanwhile, would always want her by his side. “Fear was a very real thing,” she says. “My thought was always: he will be killed next.” By 1991, her premonition had come true.
A silence settles over the room as Gandhi struggles to recall how she went on living after Rajiv’s death. A Sri Lankan separatist militant had set off a suicide bomb while he was on the election trail, killing him instantly. Throughout our conversation, she still refers to Rajiv as “Papa”, as he is known to their children.
Priyanka, who sits on the sofa with us, interjects gently. She tells me how her mother would sit in the dark all day, listening to Mozart’s Requiem, engulfed by grief. “You were angry at him,” she says, speaking to her mother. “When you used to cry, you used to shout: how has he left me, why did he leave?”
Gandhi sits quietly for a moment. “After my mother-in-law was killed, we thought that, as we were always together, if something happens to one, it will happen to the other one,” she says. They had even written notes on how they wanted their funerals.
Yet when Gandhi’s sister pleaded for her to return to Italy, the thought was unfathomable. “India was my home, my children’s home,” she says. Gandhi last went back to Italy four years ago, when her mother died.
She found out later that, prior to the attack, Indian intelligence had intercepted death threats against Rajiv by the Sri Lankan separatist Tamil Tigers, angered over India’s intervention in the country’s civil war. However, these had been ignored by the newly elected government, who instead took away his top-level security. She still believes the truth of a wider conspiracy behind his death has yet to come out. The most recent commission to investigate it was shut down by the Modi government. “I don’t think we will get the truth now,” she says with a sigh.
Crucially, just as the foundation of her world was shattered, a wind of change was blowing across north India. A claim that a mosque in the city of Ayodhya was built on the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple had been gaining traction among hardline, rightwing Hindu nationalist organisations and political groups. In December 1992, supporters of the movement – including BJP figures – violently tore down the mosque.
Gandhi recalls crying as she witnessed the demolition on television. She says she knew then that they faced “a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build”. She accepts that failures of her own party in part contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics. “I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude,” she says. In 2024, Modi delivered on the BJP’s longstanding promise and inaugurated a vast Hindu temple in the place where the mosque had once stood.
Throughout her memoir, Gandhi is open about her distrust of politics, describing it as “menacing”, driven by “ambition, greed and hypocrisy”. But with Congress facing an existential threat and looking likely to fracture, Gandhi succumbed to mounting pressure and agreed to become its president in 1998. It was a decision, she says, driven by a sense of duty to her lost husband. Not only did she have to fight against her own ingrained shyness, she also had to take on political opponents in Hindi, her third language.
She insists she never had political ambition. Despite helping the party to win the most votes in the 2004 election, she shocked everyone by refusing to become prime minister. “It was clear in my mind I would never do it,” she says. “It was just not me.” Nonetheless, until she stepped back from the day-to-day of Congress leadership a few years ago, she had little time for herself. She would carry books to political events, history and autobiographies, to read on the way home. Music, both Indian classical and European operas, also became her solace. Having previously studied art restoration, “once in a while, I would slip away to an art exhibition”.
Today she stays out of the messy day-to-day of politics, though is still kept in the loop by her daughter and attends the occasional meeting. She finds joy in her small vegetable patch, but more than anything in spending time with her children and two grandchildren. Theirs has always been a dog-loving family (Priyanka once had seven golden retrievers) and Gandhi is devoted to her two jack russells, Noorie and Lapo, who were gifts from her son.
Nonetheless, the fortress of security that surrounds her home is a stark reminder of the restrictions still imposed on her freedom. Armed police man the barricades on the road outside, and my car is thoroughly inspected by security before I am allowed to drive through a towering metal gate and into her driveway.
While she was once credited with reviving the fortunes of Congress, over the past decade the Gandhi family have overseen its calamitous decline. Their previous government, in power till 2014, was marred by allegations of rampant corruption. (“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” is Gandhi’s defence.) After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Modi, and Congress remains in power in only a few states. Meanwhile, the BJP’s Hindutva has become the country’s dominant political ideology. As the family has maintained its control, Congress has been unable to shake off allegations that it is nepotistic and run by political elites.
Why can’t Congress free itself from the Gandhi family’s leadership, I ask? She is dismissive, perhaps a nerve touched. “You would have to ask the party,” she says. Gandhi also skates over the question of nepotism, simply saying, “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have.” But after so many losses, can a Gandhi-led Congress still be a credible alternative to the BJP? While she is adamant they can, many in the country remain unconvinced.
It is true that we are meeting at an interesting moment, for both Modi and the bruised opposition. As gen Z youth erupted on to the streets in protest against the government over the summer – satirically calling themselves the “Cockroaches” after an online joke transformed into a serious political movement – the long-crushed space for dissent has opened up.
In recent weeks, young Indians have once again been taking to the streets against the government, despite being met with draconian state force. The question of whether they can shake the BJP’s grip on power remains to be seen; so far, the Cockroach movement has kept its distance from the opposition alliance. But “what encourages me is young people are coming out and demonstrating,” Gandhi says. “With determination, they’re calling out the government on things that are not right. I feel like this is a real shift.”
Congress, too, has become more energised than it has been for many years. Images of Rahul and Priyanka being manhandled by police as they tried to protest against the government have gone viral in recent weeks. After once pleading with her children to stay out of politics, Gandhi now says, “It’s good that they’re there. Now more than ever before.” The Gandhi family, it seems, are not done just yet.

The day may have been wet, but Chennaiites still went all out to bring in light and sparkles on Deepavali day, which fell on Sunday (November 8, 2026). While awareness about safety has increased, ophthalmologists in the city have once again called for caution and reiterated protective measures, as they have received dozens of cases of cracker-related injuries.
The Regional Institute of Ophthalmology and Government Ophthalmic Hospital received around 50 cases, with about 10 cases having to be admitted, a senior official said.
Also Read: Firecracker-related eye injuries more serious than they appear, claims eye doctors
Over the Deepavali weekend, the emergency clinic at Sankara Nethralaya saw 45 cases of firecracker injuries at its main campus. Two underwent wound repair surgery, while two others were scheduled for surgery on Monday, November 9, according to T.S. Surendran, its chairman..
At Dr. Agarwals Eye Hospital, nearly 20 patients came in with cracker-related injuries, said S. Soundari, regional head, clinical services. One of these, she explained, was a very serious case that had been taken up for surgery. Another patient lit a firecracker, but it did not blast. He went near it to take a look, and it blasted in his face, injuring both eyes. The remaining injuries were mostly small, and would be treated medically, she said. Four cases involved children; the rest were adults, mostly in their 30s and 40s.
At Rajan Eye Care, about 15 patients have been seen over the past three days or so, said Mohan Rajan, chairman and medical director of the hospital. One patient had to undergo a surgery, while minor injuries were treated as outpatients.
Doctors have reiterated caution. Dr. Soundari called for wearing protective eye gear while bursting firecrackers, supervising children properly, and importantly, not trying to touch the eye or take objects out by oneself. “Come to a doctor immediately if there is an eye injury,” she stressed. Dr. Rajan noted that bystanders often got hurt and should be careful to maintain an adequate distance..

Google DeepMind employees in the UK have asked the government to intervene in a push to unionize the artificial intelligence lab.
On Thursday, the Communication Workers Union and Unite the Union—put forward by Google DeepMind staff as joint representatives—filed an application to the Central Arbitration Committee, a government body that resolves disputes between employers and unions.
The application, which was seen by WIRED, asks the CAC to confirm the unions have enough support from workers to trigger a unionization ballot. The company would be required by law to respect the results. If successful, roughly 1,000 staff working in product-focused roles at Google DeepMind would qualify for union membership.
The escalation follows a series of meetings between employees, the unions, and company representatives over voluntary unionization, which left staff with the impression their demands weren’t being taken seriously.
“They’ve been ignored. They feel like their problems have been minimized,” John Chadfield, national officer for technology at the CWU, tells WIRED. “Management has refused to come to the table. They sent it to the HR and labor relations people, who dealt with it as an administrative box-ticking exercise.”
Google DeepMind did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
The push to unionize began in February 2025, when Google’s parent company Alphabet removed a pledge from its ethics guidelines stating that it wouldn’t use AI for purposes like weapons development.
“When I joined, we really made a big deal about the principles—the red lines. We were really looking to benefit humanity and make the world a better place,” a Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of backlash, tells WIRED. “A lot of this is about reestablishing that ethical and moral framework that we started with.”
The employees pushing for unionization object in particular to agreements between the company and the US and Israeli militaries. If they succeed in unionizing, they intend to demand that Google backs out of those contracts.
“We feel extremely concerned about the direction that this technology is going in,” says a second Google DeepMind employee, who asked to remain anonymous for the same reason as the first employee.
The company has previously defended its deals with government organizations.
“We are proud to be part of a broad consortium of leading AI labs and technology and cloud companies providing AI services and infrastructure in support of national security,” Jenn Crider, a Google spokeswoman, told The New York Times in April. “We remain committed to the private and public sector consensus that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without appropriate human oversight.”
In an email delivered to all UK staff on Thursday, seen by WIRED, the Google DeepMind employees involved in the unionization push appealed to their colleagues to participate in the ballot, which they expect to take place in the coming months. “We want a union, we want collective bargaining, and we want a say in how AI is developed and deployed,” they wrote.
The group also hopes it can establish a playbook that employees at other major AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic can follow in the UK.
“It’s pretty rare that there’s been an industry that exercises such dominance and power over the economy, where there’s so little opportunity for employees or regulators to have any checks and balances,” the second Google DeepMind employee says. “We want to show what can happen when employees collectively organize and articulate a shared vision for the way their technology should be used.”

What we know about the global Microsoft outage
- Published
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products.
Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
What happened?
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
How many people have been affected?
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.
The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.
The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
Government agencies and services, including the Singaporean government and Australia's spy agency, have also said they have been affected.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.
Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
What has Microsoft said?
Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.
The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.
In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.
On Friday morning, Microsoft said it was seeing "early signs of stabilisation", but service capacity has "not yet returned to normal levels".
In an earlier statement, the tech giant had said that its attempted fixes were "not taking as expected".
What have experts said?
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
- Published
Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.
The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.
Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.
Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.
"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.
Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.
Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.
Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

Nvidia’s CEO and cofounder Jensen Huang is officially out, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress is in. The chipmaker’s board of directors announced Thursday that Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, has been named interim CEO following Huang’s resignation amid a scandal over his extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman believed by US officials to be an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security.
Harvey Jones, the newly appointed chair of Nvidia’s board, said in a statement that Kress “has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position.” He added that Kress will be supported by an “experienced leadership team” and that the board has “full confidence” in her.
Kress was among the most obvious candidates to fill the void after Huang’s departure, according to multiple tech executives and industry analysts who follow Nvidia closely, given her long tenure at the company, credibility on Wall Street and across the tech industry, and, perhaps most importantly, her deep familiarity with Nvidia’s business and finances.
“She’s extremely strong-willed, professional, and whip smart. She doesn’t tolerate nonsense. She can be friendly and gracious, too,” says a former Nvidia executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “She obviously has a keen sense for how Jensen thinks.”
“Colette is the logical choice,” says Patrick Moorhead, founder and chief analyst at Moor Insights & Strategies, who has tracked the chip industry for decades. “She has credibility with investors because she answers hard questions directly.”
Moorhead says Kress has operated as much more than a “numbers” CFO. “In my conversations with her, she goes deep on the product roadmap, from rack-scale systems to networking and software,” he says.

Nvidia’s board said on Sunday it was launching an independent investigation into Huang’s activities following a report by The New York Times that he had an affair with a woman named Alice Huang, who US officials suspected of being a Chinese spy. WIRED reported on Monday that Huang quietly hired a crisis communications firm sometime last year to handle matters related to his personal life. By October of that year, the firm was being looped in on all press inquiries involving Huang at Nvidia, around the same time The New York Times reported that US authorities were investigating whether a company linked to Alice Huang had helped Chinese firms evade US chip export controls.
While Huang has long been the public face of Nvidia, Kress has been responsible for managing the chipmaker’s relationship with Wall Street. On earnings calls, she often details Nvidia’s financial performance, customer demand, supply constraints, and other key metrics.
“One of the things we don’t focus on is the stock price. We focus on our investors and how we would like to innovate,” Kress told the Israeli business newspaper Globes in 2023.
Before joining Nvidia, Kress spent more than two decades in finance roles at Microsoft, Cisco, and Texas Instruments. Huang personally recruited her in 2013, when Nvidia was still best known for its gaming graphics cards, according to Globes. Huang laid out his vision for the company’s future on a whiteboard, explaining how Nvidia could become a major supplier of computing infrastructure for artificial intelligence.
Other potential successors to Huang included Ian Buck, a more than 20-year Nvidia veteran who created the company’s software platform CUDA and now oversees its high-performance computing business, and Jeff Fisher, who joined Nvidia in 1994 as the head of software sales and later became senior vice president of its GeForce unit, where he led Nvidia’s strategy for bringing GPUs to market.
However, Nvidia’s unusual corporate structure has long meant that dozens of executives report directly to Huang. The company lacks a traditional chief operating officer. Even executive vice presidents aren’t necessarily given direct control over budgets, sources have told WIRED. As a result, few people within the organization have the same level of understanding of the company’s financials as Kress.
The former Nvidia executive who spoke to WIRED on the condition of anonymity said that while Kress is incredibly sharp and “can step into the [CEO] role immediately without needing any guidance,” Kress doesn’t have the same engineering and technical expertise that Huang brought to his role as a founding CEO. She has also shied away from being “at the center of public attention,” this person said.
Given the intense scrutiny surrounding Huang lately, this leadership style might be a welcome temporary change for Nvidia.

Greetings from Senegal, where breakdancers are competing in the Youth Olympics
Hip-hop music blasted over a portable speaker while half-a-dozen teenagers practiced their best breakdancing moves in Senagal's capital Dakar. They glided on their shins and jumped into the air, clutched their heels and struck midair poses.
Senegal's breakdancers were honing their craft ahead of the country's historic hosting of the Youth Olympic Games this month. It's the first time an Olympic event is being held on African soil.
I took the photo above last month as 15-year-old Suzanne Toure struck a breakdancing pose. She is the only girl on the Senegal National Sport Dance and Break Team. Three years ago, her little brother introduced her to breakdancing.
Dancers on the Senegalese team mix traditional moves into their routines from national styles such as mbalax and Yela, swirling their arms and legs in a windmill-like motion. "You can sense some American and European influence in our routines, yes, but there are also African dances.
