Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”

The Hindu on Tuesday carried a standalone image of thick smog enveloping Rashtrapati Bhavan on Monday morning with the caption ‘Pollution unlimited’. On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”

In the aftermath of Diwali, doctors in Delhi began reporting an alarming number of juvenile patients, including newborns, arriving with breathing difficulties, even as hospitals are witnessing a significant rise in respiratory illnesses. According to reports, 397 patients with Diwali-related injuries were treated at four major hospitals in Delhi. The cases included burns, firecracker injuries and eye trauma.
AIIMS reported 42 burn injury cases by 11 am on November 9. Of these, 37 were caused by firecrackers. Eleven patients sustained major injuries, while 31 had minor injuries. Eight were admitted, including one in critical condition. Moreover, 18 of the 42 patients were under 18, including six below the age of 10. An eight-year-old child at AIIMS was in critical condition after sustaining burns over 45 per cent of their body surface area. Safdarjung Hospital recorded 135 burn injury cases. Of these, 129 were attributed to firecrackers and six to traditional diyas. Seven patients sustained major burns requiring hospital admission. The hospital also treated 35 children with firecracker-related injuries in its outpatient department.
Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital treated 41 patients with burn injuries from 9 am on Saturday. 18 of these injuries were reportedly caused by firecrackers, with two patients requiring admission. Eight patients were hospitalised overall, while approximately 10–12 of those treated were children. Guru Tegh Bahadur Hospital reported 172 patients with firecracker burns and other Diwali-related injuries within 24 hours. Among them were 25 children and 56 women. Thirty-four patients also suffered eye injuries.
The toll was not limited to burn injuries. The Dr Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences at AIIMS received nearly 110 patients with eye injuries on Sunday and during the early hours of Monday, most of them with firecracker-related ocular injuries. 18 patients suffered corneal perforations or lacerations and underwent surgical intervention.
In Pali, Rajasthan, sparks from firecrackers being burst on a road reportedly reached a firecracker shop near Swarn Mandir in Falna town, gutting three shops and killing two people. One person sustained burn injuries and three others were initially reported missing.

Dutch coalition near collapse as 1 party is upset over tax deal with opposition
Prime Minister Rob Jetten's Dutch coalition appears close to collapse
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- The ruling Dutch three-party minority coalition led by Prime Minister Rob Jetten appeared close to collapse Thursday, less than nine months into its four-year term, as a deal to support a tax plan for next year angered one of the coalition parties.
Jetten’s centrist D66 party and the center-right Christian Democrats reached the deal Wednesday with two center-left opposition parties to get the tax package — a crucial part of the annual government budget — through the Dutch parliament.
But fellow coalition member the right-wing People’s Party for Freedom and Democracy, or VVD, slammed it as a bad deal for the Netherlands and a breach of the coalition agreement the three parties hammered out in weeks of negotiations.
Jetten skipped a European Union leaders' summit in Ireland to attend a debate in parliament about the tax measures.
The parties that agreed the deal say it raises tax on the wealthy and cuts taxes for people with low incomes. PRO called that aspect of the deal a “millionaire's tax.”
After a meeting Wednesday night, VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius, who is also the Dutch defense minister, said her party was ambushed “by the fact that our coalition partners struck a deal with an opposition party.”
She called it “a poor proposal. Furthermore, it runs counter to the coalition agreement.”
She said that if the other coalition partners voted for the deal after the parliamentary debate Thursday, “we will at least need a fundamental reset.”
Ruben Brekelmans, the leader of the VVD's bloc in the lower house, said that a "very fundamental discussion has to take place within the coalition regarding the way forward."
“I am not pushing for any specific outcome, nor am I ruling out any options in advance,” he said, adding that it could lead to interim coalition-building talks or even D66 and the Christian Democrats continuing in a minority coalition with PRO.
Christian Democrat leader Henri Bontenbal told national broadcaster NOS before the debate started that he wanted the coalition to survive and serve its full four-year term. “Preferably eight years,” he added.

If the government were to fall, it would likely pave the way for fresh elections next year, the fifth general election in less than a decade in the politically splintered Netherlands.
The crisis echoes a similar impasse in neighboring Belgium, where Prime Minister Bart De Wever tendered his resignation to the king following a protracted crisis over the country’s budget. King Philippe last Friday rejected the resignation and asked De Wever's coalition to resume negotiations.
Jetten’s government was a risky political experiment from day one, holding only 66 of the lower house of parliament’s 150 seats. Jetten was sworn in in February as the Netherlands’ youngest and first openly gay prime minister.
He narrowly won an election in late October last year, securing the same number of seats as anti-Islam lawmaker Geert Wilders’ Party for Freedom, but with slightly more votes. The result was decided by a count of postal ballots.
Jetten said when he took office that he wanted to usher in a new era of consensus politics in parliament after years of bickering between parties. But that has largely failed to materialize, with his coalition unable even to avoid internal divisions over its plans and opposition parties making tough demands in return for supporting legislation.
That culminated in the deal Jetten’s D66 party and the Christian Democrats struck with the center left parties PRO and Volt, enraging the VVD.

As the Glee-boot takes shape, one of the New Directions is considering an encore performance as his beloved character.
Chris Colfer, who earned a Golden Globe for his performance as Kurt Hummel on the Fox series, teased that he’s had a “nice conversation” about a potential return, with more talks to take place soon, after Disney+ and Hulu gave the reboot a series order last month.
“Honestly, at this point, I’m just curious. I don’t have much information about it,” he said on Daily Beast’s Obsessed podcast, noting that he’s been busy traveling to promote his new movie The Restoration at Grayson Manor. “So, I haven’t had a chance to talk to anybody about it, but I recently had a nice conversation with someone, and I’m gonna have more conversations soon.”
Colfer continued, “But from what I’ve heard, it sounded very funny, and it sounded like a good idea. So, we’ll see.”
Watch on Deadline
The actor joked that he’s “secretly campaigning for Mr. Schue [Matthew Morrison] and Sue Sylvester [Jane Lynch] to do ‘WAP’. That might be what gets me back to it.”
Following co-star Cory Monteith’s death in 2013, Colfer recalled it was “really hard going back to the show.” And after Naya River’s death in 2020, he imagines it will “be really difficult” to return for a reboot, but he doesn’t see that as a reason not to do it.
“But I guess you have to think, are you going to let the loss of two people you love very much prevent you from being around a dozen other people you love as well?” he explained. “So, there’s a lot to think about with it.”
As for where Kurt is in the reboot, Colfer noted, “I would love to see him in a place of power. I would love to see him like a Miranda Priestley type, running his own fashion blog or magazine. I could also see him on tour with Chappell Roan, styling her. So, I think there’s a lot of fun venues they could explore.”
With the 2015 series finale “Dreams Come True” revealing Kurt and Blaine (Darren Criss) as dads, Colfer imagines they have “very different parenting techniques,” adding, “I think Blaine would be a very gentle parent, and Kurt would not. I think Kurt would punish his children with scathing looks.”
Following Glee‘s original six-season run from 2009 to 2015, series co-creator Ryan Murphy ended years of speculation about a reboot when he revealed in September that he finished writing a script for the project.
A month later, the reboot got a series order from Disney+ and Hulu, with Lea Michele, Heather Morris and Chord Overstreet in talks to reprise their roles.

Musk says it would be ‘an honor’ to hire scandal-struck Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
World’s richest man expresses support for under-fire executive, who could be forced out of the chipmaker he founded after its share value dipped 9 percent

Elon Musk has said it “would be an honor” to hire Jensen Huang, at risk of being fired as Nvidia’s CEO after reports he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy tanked the chipmaker’s share price.
The world’s richest man replied to a post on his social media platform X from a financial blog called Zerohedge appealing to him to take on Huang, 63, if he is ultimately let go by the company he founded in 1993, whose products are powering the current global AI boom.
“That would be an honor,” the SpaceX and Tesla boss wrote in response.
Musk and Huang have reportedly known each other for at least a decade, with Nvidia supplying chips for the former’s Tesla Model S and X vehicles and its hardware powering that company’s self-driving technology, as well as xAI. The two men have also collaborated on space-based data centers.
The forner paid tribute to the Nvidia boss on X just last month, saying that they were “old friends are the best friends,” adding: “Jensen rocks.”
Huang previously discussed his trillionaire friend (he is a humble billionaire by comparison) during an appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience last December, crediting him as being the “first customer” for his DGX-1 deep-learning supercomputer in 2016 when “nobody in the world wanted it,” giving his business a huge boost.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board of directors was meeting late Wednesday to decide Huang’s fate following the reports about his personal life. The company’s shares fell approximately 9 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday, knocking approximately $350 billion from its value.
The executive sent a memo to Nvidia employees Sunday admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife and saying he was “deeply sorry” for the hurt he had caused without going into details.
U.S. intelligence warned former Megaspeed director Alice Huang — who is no relation but with whom the tech boss has been pictured on a number of occasions — was a suspected spy for China.
China has denied the claims that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was recruited by its Ministry of State Security for corporate espionage purposes, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
The infidelity was first reported by The New York Times, which has since alleged that the executive had another relationship with Kimberly Powell, his company’s vice president of healthcare, who is also married.
Nvidia’s board responded to the initial affair by launching an internal investigation into the revelations led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz.
Huang’s potential exit would create a leadership vacuum at the $4 trillion chipmaker, which has found itself at the heart of the big tech arms race between the U.S. and China.
The fallout from the scandal has also reached Washington, where it has been reported that Trump was “warned” about Huang’s compromised position by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in May as the executive joined their visit to Beijing, despite his saying earlier this week he had been blindsided by the news.
Republican leaders of three House committees called for Huang to deliver closed-door testimony on his interactions with the alleged intelligence asset while North Dakota GOP Sen. Kevin Cramer has openly called for him to resign “as a matter of his own conscience.”
Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have also written to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to demand that all company records relating to Nvidia’s dealings with China be preserved.

Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat on Friday (November 13, 2026) said compassion and sensitivity are the foundations of humanity and society, stressing that people should serve others without expecting anything in return.
“Service is not a profession but a responsibility towards society. We do not work merely to earn our livelihood but to ensure that the world continues to function well,” Mr. Bhagwat said in an address after presenting the ‘Vidarbha Gaurav’ award to Dr. Sanjay Paithankar.
Emphasising the importance of sensitivity, Mr. Bhagwat said helping someone in distress, irrespective of whether one has a personal relationship with them, is a natural expression of humanity.
“Whether we have any relationship with a person or not, if someone somewhere is suffering, we should do whatever we can to alleviate that suffering. And while doing so, we should not feel that we are doing something extraordinary. This is a sign of humanity,” he said.
The RSS chief said awards were not given to people to motivate them to begin serving society, as those honoured had not worked with the expectation of receiving recognition.
“An award is given to honour their work and to encourage them to take it forward. The word ‘puraskar’ itself means to take something forward,” he said.
He explained that the word also meant a reward and encouragement, adding that recognising people engaged in social service was a way of appreciating their contribution and inspiring others.
Mr. Bhagwat said compassion was an expression of human sensitivity and that society survived on this sensitivity rather than merely on economic prosperity.
“Society survives on compassion and sensitivity. If this sensitivity remains alive, society will survive. If it disappears, humanity itself will be lost,” he said.
He said people often faced difficult circumstances, and their struggles could sometimes suppress their sensitivity. However, preserving compassion despite hardships was what made a person truly human.
“Whether a person is struggling with poverty or living in prosperity is not the question. What matters is what values they have preserved while living,” he said.
Mr. Bhagwat said the Indian understanding of work was different from the idea of a profession pursued merely for earning money. People should follow their respective occupations and fulfil family responsibilities while also contributing to society.
“Earning one’s livelihood is only a by-product of the work we do. The real purpose is to serve society,” he said.
He said the concept of ‘dharma’ was tied to humanity and brotherhood, and its essential characteristics were truth, compassion, purity and self-discipline.
“Humanity itself is dharma. Brotherhood is dharma,” he said.
The chief said people should live with the awareness that the divine exists within themselves and others, which would naturally create a sense of belonging and compassion.
He narrated an anecdote about a disciple who returned without eating a fruit after being asked by his teacher to consume it at a place where nobody could see him. The disciple said he could not find such a place because he believed God was present everywhere, including within himself.
Bhagwat said this awareness created a bond with others and encouraged people to serve without expecting any benefit.

Keeping up with UP| In the Lord’s name: A religious row with a political twist
Dhirendra Krishna Shastri’s remarks contrasting Lord Ram and Lord Krishna have triggered a row, exposing tensions among religious leaders and political parties.
In the 1990s, when the Ram temple movement was at its peak, people took serious offence to derogatory public utterances about Hindus having several gods and goddesses for the simple reason that worshipping multiple gods and goddesses was never a contentious issue. Regardless of many Hindus having a specific “aradhya dev” (beloved or tutelary deity), they revered all gods—Ram, Krishna, Shiva and Maa—who were often called by different names in different regions.
It was, therefore, shocking when the head priest of the Bageshwar Dham, Dhirendra Krishna Shastri, drew a divisive contrast between Lord Ram and Lord Krishna during a religious discourse in Madhya Pradesh recently. Shastri not only framed Ram as “hamare (our) Ram” and Krishna as “tumhare (your) Krishna” but also appeared to ridicule Krishna’s iconic three-fold posture, called “tribhangi”.
“Hamare Ram stands straight, looks straight and his name is also spelt straight while your Krishna is bent in three places,” Shastri said.
The derogatory tone and tenor appeared aimed at eulogising Lord Ram over Lord Krishna. Shastri had also asked Krishna devotees to raise their hands, conceding they would be hurt by his observation. He later apologised for his comment, but by then, his comments had created a furore. Many Krishna devotees, including the Yaduvanshis, were outraged. Samajwadi Party national president Akhilesh Yadav immediately demanded a ban on Shastri’s religious discourses in the state. Many others, including Union minister Chirag Paswan, also condemned the statement. “He has always been against dividing society in the name of religion and caste, but here, he is creating a rift in the name of our “bhagwan” (God),” Paswan said.
Some backed Shastri but Bharatiya Janata Party leaders maintained their distance from the controversy. This was perhaps because some in the party leadership had earlier lauded Shastri’s efforts to promote Hindu unity. Shastri is no stranger to controversies but his dismissive remark must have triggered unease within the BJP, whose politics revolves around “Sanatan and development.”
The issue also has a demographic dimension.
Krishna devotees form a powerful community in Gujarat, the land of Dwarka, and West Bengal, where the legacy of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu runs deep. These devotees have a strong connection with Vrindavan and Mathura. ISKCON followers are also spread around the globe.
The controversy has come at a time when the movement in Krishna Janmasthan in Mathura is gaining momentum, with the tacit support of Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath. The religious dispute over the temple and an adjoining mosque is in court, but it has become a poll issue.
The situation escalated when former Uttar Pradesh minister Raghuraj Pratap Singh alias Raja Bhaiya decided to proceed with Shastri’s three-day Ram Katha, from November 17 to 19, in his stronghold of Kunda in Pratapgarh, despite the growing row. Large-scale preparations with the support of the state government are underway.
Singh heads a party, the Jansatta Dal (Loktantrik), with two lawmakers. A Rajput leader with money and muscle power, Singh was put behind bars under POTA (Prevention of Terrorism Act) by then chief minister Mayawati over two decades ago. He has navigated various political parties and has maintained cordial relations with the CM.
Though he also enjoyed good ties with former CM Mulayam Singh Yadav, who withdrew the POTA charges against him within 24 hours of assuming power in 2003, Singh’s relationship with Mulayam’s son, Akhilesh Yadav, has not been cordial.
Singh has operated in the region with money and muscle power. He is a political influencer who helped form the Kalyan Singh government by mobilising MLAs from other parties and, in return, received a cabinet berth. But Kalyan Singh had once branded him “Kunda ka goonda (the thug of Kunda)”.
The recent war of words between Akhilesh Yadav and Singh, and their supporters has inflamed Rajput-Yadav tensions, with provocative statements flowing thick and fast. The Rajputs are seen leaning towards the BJP and the Yadavs towards the SP. Who will the row help politically?
Poll time
In an era of religious renaissance, where crowds increasingly flock to spiritual congregations, politicians are also seeking the services of social-media-savvy gurus. Politicians want crowds, and people seeking succour from the burden of their daily lives are drawn to these self-styled religious figures.
“When the desire for attention, recognition and self-importance overtakes genuine wisdom, silence and discernment, even the most revered figures begin to speak recklessly, contradict themselves and expose the hollowness beneath their public persona.This is particularly evident among some self-proclaimed Hindu spiritual leaders, who seem to mistake visibility for wisdom and popularity for spiritual authority. The constant need to remain in the spotlight often leads them to make sweeping statements, indulge in unnecessary commentary and eventually descend into absurdity,” said Sandeep Singh, author of two books on Temple Economics, a Decade for Mandir
The question arises: Are such figures promoting ‘Sanatan Dharma’ or spreading misinformation and superstition?
Political parties once relied on local muscle power or mafia dons to mobilise voters. But they later decided to take over the operation themselves even as the Election Commission struggled with reforms to check the criminalisation of politics. Could the self-styled emissaries of God – equipped with money and muscle power, private armies and blind followers – follow the same trajectory? Instead of mobilising crowds for others, they could claim power for themselves.

It was, says Ido Rakovsky, like reporting on "science fiction", rather than sport.
Israel, whose senior team have qualified for the World Cup just once, had beaten global powerhouses Brazil in the quarter-finals of the under-20 version of the tournament.
At the final whistle, the commentator covering the match for Israeli television vowed "you will tell of this night to your children, and they will tell it to your grandchildren".
Plenty heard him.
Five days later, the team's semi-final against Uruguay was the most-watched thing of the evening on Israeli television, drawing a 23% viewing share.
Politicians clamoured to congratulate the team.
It was June 2023.
"That summer, everybody was watching under-20 football, everybody knew the players," says Rakovsky, who was covering the team for Israeli media outlet Haaretz.
"Everybody in Israel fell in love with these kids."
It wasn't just their deeds on the pitch that felt otherworldly, though.
After scoring a stoppage-time winner against Uzbekistan in the last 16, Anan Khalaili had given an interview to Israeli television.
In it Khalaili, an Israeli Arab, thanked the viewers back home for staying up late to watch his team win in Argentina.
To do so, he used the words 'Am Yisrael' - a Hebrew phrase that means 'People of Israel' and is bound up in Jewish religion, community, culture and history.
"That an Arab player used that figure of speech said something about the identity of that team," says Rakovsky.
"That team made real the claim that football can really bring people together - that Muslim players are part of the national team of the Jewish state, representing Israel and creating something better, both for the present and future."
But a little over four months after Khalaili's interview and the win over Brazil, Hamas attacked Israel.
The armed Palestinian group killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza. The United Nations believes the retaliation has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians., external
As the war goes on, can the potential of a golden generation of Israel's footballers, in sport and society, be realised?
Beaten 1-0 by eventual champions Uruguay, Israel finished third at that Under-20 World Cup in 2023.
Their run was no fluke.
The same set of players, with a few additions and omissions, had already impressed at continental level.
They were runners-up at 2022's Under-19 Euros, beaten by England in extra-time in the final, and would go on to make the semi-finals of 2023's Under-20 Euros.
Israel has produced outstanding players in the past. Eyal Berkovic and Yossi Benayoun were technical, gifted attackers with long Premier League careers.
But a depth of talent, emerging together, sets the current cohort apart.
Khalaili has been one of the most sought-after young prospects in Europe this summer.
After his £21.5m move to Inter Milan fell through, Crystal Palace saw off competition from Nottingham Forest to pick him up for a similar fee from Belgian side Union Saint-Gilloise.
Playmaker Oscar Gloukh, 22, wears Ajax's number 10 shirt after his form earned a move from Red Bull Salzburg.
Left-back Roy Revivo signed for Spanish club Elche on transfer deadline day this month from Maccabi Tel Aviv, while Twente defender Stav Lemkin, also 23, is also highly rated.
Dor Turgeman, Ilay Feingold and Idan Toklomati are impressing in Major League Soccer in the United States.
All have now won full caps, but were moulded into a collective, cohesive unit - something that has often been beyond the senior side - by Israel's age-grade coach Ofir Haim.
"It isn't an issue at all here," Haim said, external of the different backgrounds in his squad during the 2023 Under-20 World Cup.
"We don't have any problem with religion. Not at all. We have players here who put on tefillin [Jewish ceremonial wear, containing verses from the Torah] - and Anan [Khalaili], Hamza [Shibli] and Ahmed [Salman] perform the Muslim prayers.
"We don't even talk about this. We unite everybody, and I wish the country were as united as this team."
Football has long been the part of Israeli society where communities mix together who may not otherwise meet.
"The majority of the Jewish people who arrived in the mandate period [a spell between 1923 and 1948 where the region was run by Britain] emigrated from Europe," says Dr Omer Einav, a historian and author of Defending the Goal, a book on Israel's football history.
"They were Europeans and when you think about cinema, music, theatre, dance, they had nothing in common with Middle Eastern culture. Nothing, except football. That was the only common language, the only thing they both love in the same way."
Encouraged by the British administrators who ran the region, teams from different communities, and some made up of elements of each, would play against each other.
When the modern state of Israel was formed in 1948, much of the Arab population that remained inside its borders continued to identify as or with Palestinians. Most still do.
They are also an intrinsic part of Israeli football.
While they make up 20% of Israel's population, they represent about 35% of those involved in the sport at elite level nationally.
The first Arab player to represent Israel's national team was Rifaat Turk in 1976. In 2018, Bibars Natcho became the first Muslim to captain the team.
Neither was without controversy.
Turk was roundly abused. Natcho's decision not to sing Israel's national anthem, the lyrics of which relate to the Jewish search for a homeland, was condemned by some., external
For a short time in the summer of 2023, it seemed as if Haim's under-20 side might offer a watershed moment of unity and co-existence.
But football, like everything in Israel, changed on 7 October.
Matan Segal directed Kick It Out Israel, an anti-discrimination initiative with similar aims but no link to the English organisation of the same name, for almost four years before stepping down a few months ago.
Racism has long been present in Israeli club football. Beitar Jerusalem's fans are among the most notorious.
In 2013, ultras burned down their own club's offices in protest at the signing of two Chechen Muslims.
The most extreme Beitar fans have long taunted Israeli Arabs with chants of "may your village burn", while declaring themselves "forever pure".
However during his time at Kick It Out Israel, Segal saw racism against Arab players become more virulent and widespread.
Covid, during which fans radicalised online during lockdown, was one cause.
The election of Israel's far-right government at the end of 2022, legitimising views towards Palestinians that were previously seen as extreme, was a second.
The war was undoubtedly another.
"Before 7 October, people generally respected the Arab players," Segal said.
"Even though they had difficulties with them not singing the Israeli anthem, they respected them and they could talk about it.
"After 7 October though, we saw an increase in racist remarks.
"It was happening at small clubs where we hadn't seen it before. There were terrible songs - 'Let's kill all Arabs', 'There are no schools in Gaza because there are no children left'."
Football, inevitably, has become a focal point for emotion generated by the conflict.
Clubs which are usually bitter rivals came together to remember those killed by Hamas. Scarves were part of the commemoration at the site of the Nova music festival, where hundreds were killed.
Hapoel Jerusalem's club badge now features a silhouette of Hersh Goldberg-Polin, who was abducted and killed in captivity and whose parents have campaigned for peace through their grief.
Meanwhile, Israeli Defence Force (IDF) soldiers have posed with club flags and banners while on operation in Gaza, dedicating their actions to the clubs and ultras back home., external
In such a heightened atmosphere, young footballers – closely connected to the conflict through Israel's programme of national service and a barrage of online commentary and images – are under constant scrutiny and pressure.
Gloukh's lifelong friend Afik Tery was killed by a Hamas explosive while serving in the IDF.
After his death, Gloukh posted a poignant set of pictures, external of the pair arm-in-arm over time - as young boys at birthday parties, as young men at a wedding - with the final slide showing Tery's funeral.
Among the online replies were the taunts of pro-Palestinians.
For Israel players with Palestinian heritage, the stakes are especially and dangerously high.
Dia Saba plays in a similar playmaking role to Gloukh. The 33-year-old has scored three goals in 13 appearances for Israel.
He is unlikely ever to add to that tally.
Saba was one of Maccabi Haifa's most high-profile stars when, at the start of the conflict, his wife Narmin posted a message to Instagram.
"There are children in Gaza, too," she wrote.
Saba apologised for the outrage caused, but could not save his career in Israel. He left Maccabi Haifa in 2025 and now plays for Turkish side Amedspor.
"My dream was to play for Maccabi Haifa, the club that I support, the team that I grew up with," Saba said at the time.
"I wanted to continue. But sometimes there are reasons that are stronger than us that don't allow it."
Saba and others are used to having their loyalty questioned. From all sides.
Many in the Arab world would like more Palestinian prospects within Israel to follow the example of Ataa Jaber.
Jaber captained Israel's Under-21 side but switched nationalities, external to represent Palestine in June 2023, saying he could no longer separate sport and politics after seeing police evict Palestinian families from their homes in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem.
Switching away from a high level of international football damaged his prospects of a move to Europe. At home, there were calls for his Israeli citizenship to be revoked. But, for Jaber, it was preferable to representing a country whose actions he deplored.
Those footballers who voice an opinion on the conflict choose their words carefully.
Beram Kayal, the former Brighton, Celtic and Israel player, knows the dilemmas and reality well.
"To be Arabic in Israel, it's sometimes hard," he says. "Sometimes it is tough.
"Opportunities-wise, sometimes we are not on the same level."
However, he believes in a pluralistic future for Israel and football as a tool to achieve it.
His friendship with Tomer Hemed - whom he first met as a young teenager at Maccabi Haifa's academy and later played alongside at Brighton and Charlton, as well as international level - sums up his approach.
"When I played with Tomer, he prayed like this," he says, touching his hand to his back of his head to indicate a kippah, the small skullcap worn as a sign of Jewish faith.
"And I was praying for Allah," he adds, raising his arms above his shoulders in worship.
"He was my team-mate and he is my brother.
"In football, on the pitch, you never look at colour, culture or religion. You just want the best people around you to win the game."
The 38-year-old is now employed by Israel's Football Association to work with young talents from Palestinian areas.
In doing so he works alongside former Israel goalkeeper Boni Ginzburg, who played across Glasgow at Rangers and is now the IFA's technical director.
After Arabic was relegated behind Hebrew as Israel's official language by a controversial 2018 law promoted by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the IFA put on Hebrew language lessons for Arabic-speaking coaches to ensure they could still obtain their qualifications.
"Not in our building," says Kayal when asked about the precedence given to Hebrew.
"I'm in this place [the IFA] to bring the culture of the Arabic people to the table.
"I say to the Arabic players when they come into the national team: Speak in your language, don't be afraid, don't be shy to speak, don't just afraid to show yourself.
"Israel is a young country. We need to learn from our DNA, to see the different between the Jewish, the Circassians, the Arabic, the Muslim, the Christian, the Druze – all the colours – put that together and learn what we could do better."
Israel's aim is to go better than their national team has managed in more than 50 years.
Ran Ben-Shimon was appointed as the senior side's head coach in 2024. He was given the goal of converting youthful promise into qualification for Euro 2028, which will be staged in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.
Success would place more stress on Israel's players and, potentially, squad unity.
Large-scale protests are planned for Republic of Ireland's forthcoming Nations League matches with Israel. Dublin will host seven games at the tournament.
Villa Park in Birmingham, from which Maccabi Tel Aviv fans were banned from attending a Europa League match in November, will stage four matches.
Hampden Park, two miles across Glasgow from where Celtic fans have held vociferous pro-Palestine protests, has six.
Wherever Israel play, players will be confronted with criticism of their country's treatment of Palestinians, both at home and in Gaza, that is rarely voiced at home.
"Israelis are very sensitive to anyone showing any kind of sympathy for what happened on 7 October," says Dr Sophia Solomon, part of Ben-Gurion University's Center for Sports Diplomacy.
"It is like denying the Holocaust, that is the proportion of it. A war is a special situation, it wasn't like this before, but to express your agony became more encouraged as we saw the European arena become more anti-Israeli.
"One reaction ignited another and there is more obligation to identify yourself with the victims of 7 October."
She believes that it will take time for Israeli society, footballers included, to understand the past three years and speak openly about the conflict.
"Until the ongoing war ends, no-one can say what he thinks," she said. "Even after the Middle East returns to its 'normal' craziness, maybe it will take a decade to pass before people can start talking about their experiences and expectations.
"Time has to pass until you can touch certain areas, and at the moment you can see a lot of avoidance about talking about it, even mentioning it."
The time for this stellar generation to fulfil their potential may come before that.
It may not. Translating youth-level promise to senior-level product is never simple.
But, whatever the future holds, for a few months, in the summer of 2023, Haim and his team gave Israel something special.
"We saw Anan Khalaili and Hamza Shibli scoring against Brazil and that was our hope, that was the future. That was our future," says Einav.
"I'm not so optimistic, but people thought maybe it's really a magical thing that can help Israeli society in general.
"There was something there, something new, something where people said 'OK, if we co-operate, if we work together, we can also succeed in sport.'
"That's what we all care about, right? We want to be good at sports. We are sick of watching the World Cup from our living room.
"I think football is in some isolated, sterilised dimension - some kind of bubble - inside Israeli society. It is not hermetic. A lot of dirt comes in - racism, violence - but I do believe that football can reflect good things that can happen. The equality of chances, the tolerance and solidarity of all people living here.
"It can't heal anything but it can help us see one another in a more human way.
"So, yeah there was definitely a moment, but it was before our world changed and collapsed."
Only time will tell what remains of that moment and whether it can be revived.

The Child Development Centre (CDC), Thiruvananthapuram, has received an Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR)-approved grant of ₹35 lakh for a three-year research project titled “Development and Validation of a Tool for Assessing Grief among Parents of Children with Autism Spectrum Disorders.”
The project, led by CDC director Deepa Bhaskaran, aims to develop and validate a culturally relevant tool to assess grief among parents of children with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD).
“The study will use focus group discussions and in-depth interviews involving parents of children with ASD, bereaved parents, professionals working with children with ASD, and members of the general population to understand the dimensions and cultural expressions of grief in the Indian context,” Dr. Bhaskaran said.
According to her, parents commonly experience shock, denial, fear, guilt, anger, sadness, and helplessness following their child’s diagnosis. The grief, described as chronic sorrow or non-finite grief, can recur at different stages of the child’s development, particularly when expected developmental milestones are not attained.
“The findings will help facilitate the identification of grief-related concerns among parents and support the development of appropriate grief counselling protocols and support group interventions, ultimately contributing to improved psychosocial well-being among families of children with ASD,” she said.
Inadequate social support compounds parental distress, she noted.
“There is a need for healthcare professionals to recognise and assess parents’ emotional well-being alongside the rehabilitation needs of children with autism. Early diagnosis, psychological support, and training for professionals to identify grief and help families develop coping strategies are vital,” she added.

- Twitch streamer and left-leaning political commentator Hasan Piker has filed a defamation lawsuit against conservative commentator Scott Jennings, seeking $72.5 million.
- The lawsuit pertains to a heavily edited video that Jennings reposted in August, to which he added his own commentary falsely presenting the clip as Piker saying he had a "plan of returning our country to lynchings," as well as that Piker "is out there calling for Black people to be lynched." The text of Jennings' post also falsely claimed, not as a direct quote, that Piker indicated "the USA should resume lynchings against black people."
- As Snopes previously reported, a full review of Piker's unedited remarks about lynchings confirmed he was sarcastically mimicking other people's opinions. The video's fragmented excerpts from three different streams presented Piker's words without full context, and in some cases out of order. As such, it was misleading.
- Piker's complaint, filed Oct. 27 in a U.S. district court in Washington, D.C., cites Snopes' reporting. The complaint accurately says Jennings had not responded to our email, in which we asked whether he researched the original clips from Piker's past streams and if he wished to provide further comment.

Editor's note: On Nov. 10, Scott Jennings' attorney Benjamin Chew filed a motion to dismiss Hasan Piker's defamation lawsuit against Jennings. Jennings' staff emailed Snopes a statement from Chew reading, "Mr. Jennings' filing today puts great trust in the U.S. Constitution, the truth, and the right of Americans to speak … even if Mr Piker doesn't like what they have to say."
On Oct. 27, Bloomberg Law reported that Twitch streamer and left-leaning political commentator Hasan Piker — who campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Party's U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan — had sued conservative commentator Scott Jennings, seeking $72.5 million for alleged defamation.
The lawsuit concerns a heavily edited 41-second video that Jennings shared in his own commentary video (archived) on Aug. 11. The edited clip shows Piker appearing to make several offensive statements targeting Black people, such as, "I don't give a f*** what Black people care about," and mentions going "back to a better time when lynchings were happening." Others (archived) shared the video, as well.
In Jennings' commentary, he falsely claimed the video shows Piker saying he had a "plan of returning our country to lynchings," as well as that Piker "is out there calling for Black people to be lynched." The text of Jennings' post also falsely claimed, though not as a direct quote, that Piker said "the USA should resume lynchings against black people."
The edited clip consists of genuine sentence fragments stitched together from three of Piker's streams out of context and out of order, twisting their original import. In one of the original streams, Piker's remarks on lynchings were sarcastic reactions to a user's chat comment and opinions expressed by someone else in a separate video.
A review of Piker's full, unedited remarks found he was speaking of a desire to prioritize winning elections over concentrating on matters that he believed resulted in past electoral losses.
Piker's complaint, filed Oct. 27 in a U.S. district court in Washington, D.C., alleges two counts of defamation and one count of false light, claiming Jennings "knew the portrayal was false or acted with reckless disregard for its falsity," as well as that, as a result, "Piker has suffered injury to his reputation, public humiliation, emotional distress, mental anguish, and damage to his professional interests."
Piker is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages, $45 million in punitive damages, attorneys' fees and other relief.
The complaint cites Snopes' reporting from August, specifically on pages 5, 29 and 30, including accurately stating that Jennings had not responded to our email in which we asked whether he researched the original clips from Piker's past streams and if he wished to provide further comment.
Piker spoke about the lawsuit during his stream on Oct. 27, saying Jennings "certainly messed up" and that the case was about "truth in the media." He added of Republican commentators, "I don't think you should be able to get away with lying like this, and if I don't put a stop to it they're going to continue maliciously defaming others as they have done so this entire time."
Daniel Watkins, one of several attorneys representing Piker, emailed Snopes the following statement:
Scott Jennings accused Hasan Piker of calling for Black Americans to be lynched. That is an extraordinary accusation. And it was a lie. Jennings took a manipulated video, put words in Hasan's mouth that he never spoke, and then held those words up as proof of something Hasan never said or believed. There is something especially disgraceful about exploiting this country's history of racial terror to destroy another man's reputation. Scott Jennings has every right to disagree with Hasan Piker. He has no right to invent what Hasan said. We brought this case because the truth matters, reputation matters, and there comes a point when lying must have consequences.
Snopes once again emailed Jennings and Piker for comment about the lawsuit and will update this article if we receive further information.

At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.
The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.

The Supreme Court on Friday (November 6, 2026) termed vehicular emissions a major contributor to air pollution in Delhi-NCR and said immediate, medium- and long-term measures were needed to curb the rising air quality index.
Hearing a suo motu case examining the regulatory framework governing air pollution, a Bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana also expressed concern over “bumper-to-bumper” traffic in Delhi-NCR.
“We keep talking and sometimes make statements and suggestions, but the point is that AQI is already touching 400,” the CJI said.
The Bench highlighted the large number of vehicles plying on roads connecting Delhi with neighbouring areas, including Ghaziabad, Greater Noida, Gurugram and Faridabad.
“Look at the roads in Delhi and the roads connecting Delhi with the NCR. Take a look at any road and the kind of vehicles moving on it. That is the major problem,” the CJI said.
The Bench said the poor people are the real sufferers, as they are on the roads, and moreover, the festival time is the only period when they earn a livelihood.
On stubble burning, the Bench stressed the need to educate farmers about using machines instead of resorting to farm fires.
On the plea seeking closure of schools or running them in hybrid mode for students of all age groups if the air quality index (AQI) rises above a certain mark, the bench said it will go by experts’ opinion.
Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre and other authorities, referred to the regulatory framework covering five major sectors: industrial emissions, vehicular pollution, construction and demolition dust, road dust and stubble burning.
She told the Bench that several measures had been introduced, including restrictions on the entry of certain vehicles, geo-tagging of pollution under control (PUC) certificates and action against visibly polluting vehicles through complaints received on applications and social media.
Ms. Bhati told the Bench that stubble burning accounted for 14% of Delhi’s pollution on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The Bench said it will pass some orders and take up the plea on November 16 after the court reopens following the Diwali vacation.
A thick layer of smog hung over the national capital on Friday (November 6, 2026) as the air quality deteriorated sharply and edged closer to the ‘severe’ category, with the overall AQI settling at 391.
Of the 59 monitoring stations across the city, 30 recorded ‘severe’ air quality at 9 a.m., while the remaining were in the ‘very poor’ category.
Rohini recorded the worst AQI at 475, followed by IIT Delhi at 472, official data showed.
